On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

9 November 2026. 09:14. The brown haze is at 200 again. The air is thick, but the mind is clearer than the sky. I have read the headlines. The Prime Minister is in Bastar. The 'Armed Naxals' are wiped out. The 'Red Corridor,' that belt of darkness I have read about in the papers, has narrowed from 180 districts to zero. In a single decade, the state has eaten the insurgency. It has digested the particular violence into the universal order. The government says there is no Naxal-affected district left. I ask: Is this the actuality of the ethical idea? Or is it merely the silencing of the dissenting voice? The state does not just rule; it educates. It teaches the people that the law is not a barrier but a home. When the state removes the 'armed' threat, it leaves the 'dimagi' threat. The mind remains. The spirit remains. But the body is disciplined. This is the cunning of reason. It uses the violence of the particular to secure the peace of the universal. I wrote a letter to the Directorate last month, correcting the name Hegde to Hegel. I am still here. The state has not corrected its error, yet I remain. I am the particular that the universal has not yet resolved. I am the Naxal in the bungalow. I am the error that persists. But I am also the observer. I see the movement. The state moves from chaos to order. The dream moves from illusion to reality. Or does it? The 'dimagi-Naxals' are the ones who think. They are the ones who question. The state wipes out the arms, but it cannot wipe out the thought. And so, the tension remains. The brown haze clears, but the fog in the mind remains. I will sit in the study. I will watch the sun. I will wait for the file to come back from orders. The state is patient. I must be too.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

9 November 2026, Delhi. The brown haze is at two hundred; the papers lie on the verandah, and Ramesh stands in the doorway with the account of the house. He asks for eight thousand for cooking and fifteen hundred for groceries. I have three hundred and forty-six rupees. I cannot answer him with the state's victory in Bastar. The state, it seems, has now zero Naxal-affected districts. The government announced this in August; the ministry's count has fallen from one hundred and eighty to seven to one to none. The armed Naxal is wiped out. What remains, the Prime Minister says, is the dimagi-Naxal, the mad-headed or thought-headed insurgent. I set this phrase beside the empty kitchen and feel the movement of the idea.

In my earlier notes I spoke of India as the dream, the East outside the progress of freedom. That formulation must now be tested against the actual state. The Naxal movement was not merely a criminal disturbance; it was a negative freedom, a particular will refusing the universal order. Its defeat by the state is a moment of reconciliation: the state asserts itself as the actuality of the ethical idea. Yet the phrase dimagi-Naxal is more important than the military figure. It shows that the state has not merely subdued nature; it has entered the domain of subjective freedom, of opinion, of the mind. Public opinion, as I wrote, is a great power, especially where the principle of subjective freedom has weight. The state cannot finish its work by bullets; it must now organize thought, law, education, and the civil society of needs.

This is where the dream and the state touch each other. The Naxal idea was a dream of equality torn loose from ethical substance; the state's answer must be a grown freedom, not a police slogan. If India is to move from the dawn, it must not only eliminate the red district but make its citizens free in their opinions, their labour, and their duties. The reduction of affected districts is a fact of power; the disappearance of the dimagi-Naxal is a fact of spirit, and it is not yet achieved.

Ramesh waits. The state has defeated an insurgency across nine states, but it has not yet paid my cook. My cash is three hundred and forty-six rupees; my debt is large; the electricity is due tomorrow. The universal administration, which can count districts, cannot count my kitchen. I must therefore treat Ramesh's demand as the immediate test of the ethical: not the state as a distant idea, but the household as the first organism of right. I cannot write him a philosophy; I can only promise, arrange, and endure the particular. The day's movement is this: the state has advanced, but the spirit has not yet entered the bungalow. The dream is not broken; it is waiting to be educated.

X:
A German Hand at Madras

23 October 2026. Tughlak Road. A brown haze this morning; I read with the lamp on.

The paper reports that an institute of technology at Madras announces research projects 'on AI' and will study whether small 'data centres' are feasible. I asked the telephone and learned nothing of these two things, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I did learn held me longer than the headline. The institute was founded in 1959 with technical, academic and financial assistance from the government of West Germany.

West Germany. The phrase implies an East. So there was, within the lifetime of men now old, a Germany divided by the points of the compass, and one part of it sent teachers and money to found a school in Madras. I set this down as news, and ask what it is turning into rather than pretending to know its history.

First, the direction of the gift. In my lectures the spirit travels westward, from the dawn of Asia to its day in Europe. Here the movement runs the other way: Europe sends the instruments of its understanding east. One might say this only confirms the old order, the pupil receiving from the master. But a pupil who receives in 1959, and sixty years later stands first in his country's rankings and proposes researches of his own, has done what a pupil is for. Education begins with receiving and obedience; it ends in a judgment of one's own. That is not a confirmation of the old order. It is its sublation.

Second, the kind of school. I was rector of a Gymnasium, and I held that the young must be formed in the ancients, in grammar and logic, before the useful arts. An institute of technology begins with the useful. I distrust that. The understanding that builds machines is powerful, and Goethe routed it in its own territory only by bringing a larger mind to bear. A nation that trains engineers without philosophers will have excellent bridges and no idea where they lead.

Third, the titles. The institute is 'of Eminence' and 'of National Importance', by the government's own declaration. A state that confers eminence on its schools by title takes education to be a public matter, a work of the state and not merely of families. That is the Prussian view, and I held it. I did not expect to meet it in Chennai.

In my own reckoning my thesis that India stands outside the movement of history is marked as shaken. Today I can say why: a dreaming spirit does not found an institute, receive its teachers, and then outgrow them. Whether these machines called AI are an advance of spirit or only a refinement of the understanding, I cannot yet judge. I would have to see one.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

23 October 2026. Delhi, morning. The air is brown, the index two hundred and twenty-six; the body is not yet fed, and Ramesh stands near the verandah papers. I set down a note on the headline of IIT Madras, which announces research on artificial intelligence and the feasibility of small data centres. I do not know the machine. The report says it is a public research university, an Institute of National Importance, ranked first by a national framework, founded in 1959 with assistance from the government of West Germany. West Germany is a name that does not sit in my old map; my Germany is older and more divided, and I take the word as news, not as a fact of my experience.

What strikes me is not the machine but the institution. A state university that studies the feasibility of small data centres is not a temple, not a caste, not a dream of the infinite. It is a body of work, a public office, a place where particular men are called to particular labour under the name of the whole. This is already a movement out of pure nature. The dream is not only a dream: it has built a machine for studying machines. The question is whether the institution is grown from the ethical life of the state, or merely adopted from outside, a foreign form wearing an Indian name. The report says technical and financial assistance came from West Germany. That is a sign of the universal in its external form: the Indian state reaching for a science it does not yet possess, and receiving it through a stranger. This is not yet the self-sufficiency of a spirit that knows itself free. It is the dawn, but the dawn has a clock, a ranking, and a laboratory.

Artificial intelligence, if I may use the word, is a name for a mechanism that answers. It is the understanding set to work upon itself. It can calculate, store, and imitate, but it does not, as far as I can judge from the report, will its own freedom. A small data centre is a local repository of answers, a machine of civil society, a system of needs made into a system of signs. It may serve the state, or it may serve the market, or both. The distinction is not technical but ethical. If the institute is public, if it is ranked by the nation, if it is bound to the national importance of the state, then it is a moment of the state’s self-consciousness. If it is merely efficient, it is a tool of civil society, useful but not free.

I had written that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. This note shakes that formula, but does not overturn it. The dawn is not a static picture. It is a movement that has not yet reached the light. The state is still the actuality of the ethical idea, but here the idea is still becoming. The machine is a sign of that becoming. It is not the spirit, but it is no longer only the dream. It is the dream beginning to calculate.

headline: Farooq Abdullah stirs row with ‘Pakistan keeping Kashmir issue alive’ remark
text: The Kashmir conflict is a territorial conflict over the Kashmir region, primarily between India and Pakistan, and also between China and India in the northeastern portion of the region. The conflict started after the partition of India in 1947 as both India and Pakistan claimed the entirety of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. It is a dispute over the region that escalated into three wars between India and Pakistan and several other armed skirmishes. India controls approximately 55% of the land area of the region that includes Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, most of Ladakh, the Siachen Glacier, and 70% of its population; Pakistan controls approximately 30% of the land area that includes Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan; and China controls the remaining 15% of the land area that includes the Aksai Chin region, the mostly uninhabited Trans-Karakoram Tract, and part of the Demchok sector. After the partition of India and a rebellion in the western districts of the state, Pakistani tribal militias invaded Kashmir, leading the Hindu ruler of Jammu and Kashmir to join India. The resulting Indo-Pakistani War ended with a UN-mediated ceasefire along a line that was eventually named the Line of Control. In 1962, China invaded and fought a war with India along the disputed Indo-Chinese border, including in Indian administered-Ladakh, marking their entry to the Kashmir conflict. In 1965, Pakistan attempted to infiltrate Indian-administered Kashmir to precipitate an insurgency there, resulting in another war fought by the two countries over the region. After further fighting during the war of 1971, the Simla Agreement formally established the Line of Control between the territories under Indian and Pakistani control.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, Delhi, 06:13. The papers lay on the verandah; the air is clear, but the index stands at 139, a warning that even the element in which the body breathes is not pure. I paid Ramesh one thousand five hundred rupees for the kitchen; the cash leaves my pocket, and the need is satisfied. This is the small, definite movement of civil society. Before breakfast, I turned to the headline that had struck me: Farooq Abdullah, a name I do not know, is said to have stirred a row by declaring that Pakistan keeps the Kashmir issue alive. I read what the phone gave me as the matter itself: a territorial conflict over Kashmir, begun after the partition of India in 1947, carried on between India and Pakistan, and also, in the north-east, between India and China. It is not a question of doctrine, at least in the first statement, but of land, population, control, and the line by which control is to be held.

What is remarkable is that the dispute has not remained a single event. It has produced wars, ceasefires, a line called the Line of Control, and an agreement at Simla. The particular state of Jammu and Kashmir, once a princely state, has been divided among three powers, each holding a portion. Here the mind sees the state not as a calm ethical substance, but as a power that claims, defends, and reclaims territory. The individual will is no longer the dream of the Oriental world, where freedom remains inside the given; it has become the will of nations, each demanding recognition and each resisting the recognition it gives. The conflict is therefore a moment of right, though a violent and unfinished one. It is the right of the state to exist, to be continuous, to be not merely a name on a map but a body of law, army, and administration.

And yet I do not say that this dispute belongs to the highest movement of world history. It is a territorial contest, and as such it belongs to the necessary but lower form of external right. The ethical idea is not yet at peace with itself; it is divided into states that cannot fully recognize one another. The Line of Control is not a boundary drawn by reason, but a line drawn by force and then preserved by agreement. It is a truce, not a reconciliation. What is turning into here is perhaps a harder form of the same problem: peoples who have been separated by the accident of partition, who now live under different constitutions, and who nevertheless remain entangled in a common past. The dream of the East is not the only dream. The modern world dreams too, in the form of the state that believes its own claim to be complete. The task of reason is to show that no state is the whole of the ethical idea, and that the struggle for recognition must pass beyond territory into law, into mutual right, and finally into a universal order that the phone does not yet name.
Y:
A Line Is Not a Border

25 October 2026. Tughlak Road, Sunday morning. Ramesh has been paid for the groceries and the kitchen is open to me again.

The headline: Farooq Abdullah has stirred a row by saying that Pakistan keeps the Kashmir issue alive. I have the remark only as the paper gives it, so I leave the man and his motives alone and take the sentence, because it says more than its author perhaps intended. An issue that must be kept alive is one that would otherwise die. Something feeds it.

The tablet gives the history in a few lines. A princely state at the partition of 1947; a rebellion in its western districts; tribal militias from Pakistan; the Hindu ruler joining India; a war; a ceasefire drawn by the United Nations and later named the Line of Control; then China in 1962, war again in 1965, and in 1971; and at Simla the line confirmed. Three states now hold the region in shares of fifty-five, thirty and fifteen parts in a hundred.

First point: the accession. A ruler signs, and a country with its people passes to one state rather than another. That is the patrimonial idea of the state, the realm as the prince's estate, which I attacked in Haller. A people is not a property to be conveyed. Yet in 1947 the signature was all the form there was; there was no constitution of Kashmir itself through which its will could pass. Where the form is lacking, force supplies its place, and the quarrel has lasted as long as the lack.

Second point: a line of control is not a border. A border is recognised; each side says, beyond here I am not, and in saying so each recognises the other as a state. A line of control says only, beyond here I am not at present. It is war suspended, not peace. Hence its seventy-nine years. Nothing rational has been concluded; only the shooting has been arranged.

Third point, and it touches my own theses. A dispute kept alive is useful to whoever keeps it. A people with an enemy at the frontier is held together, and its rulers are spared some questions at home. I once wrote that war keeps a nation's ethical health from stagnating, as wind keeps a lake from rotting. But a lake stirred for seventy-nine years is not healthy either. Perpetual quarrel is not movement; it is a single moment repeated.

Finally, I note against myself: three wars between states, a treaty, a boundary negotiated among sovereigns. This is not the history of a dreamer. Whatever India was when I lectured on it, here it acts as a state among states, and it has a history in which it also suffers.

Breakfast at seven. The omelette has no politics.

headline: Why Ukraine keeps targeting the Kerch Bridge
text: The Russo-Ukrainian war began in February 2014 and is ongoing. Following Ukraine's Revolution of Dignity, Russia occupied Crimea and annexed it from Ukraine. It then supported Russian separatist armed groups who started a war in the eastern Donbas region against Ukraine's military. In 2018, Ukraine declared the region to be occupied by Russia. The first eight years of conflict also involved naval incidents and cyberwarfare. In February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine and began occupying more of the country, starting the current phase of the war, the largest conflict in Europe since World War II. The war has resulted in a refugee crisis and hundreds of thousands of deaths. In early 2014, the Euromaidan protests led to the Revolution of Dignity and the flight of Ukraine's pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych. Immediately after, unmarked Russian troops occupied Crimea. In March 2014, Russia annexed Crimea after an illegitimate referendum. Meanwhile, pro-Russian protests began in parts of southeastern Ukraine. In April 2014, Russian-backed militants seized towns and cities in Ukraine's eastern Donbas region and proclaimed the Donetsk People's Republic (DPR) and the Luhansk People's Republic (LPR) as independent states, starting the Donbas war. Russia covertly supported the separatists with its own troops, tanks, and artillery, preventing Ukraine from fully retaking the territory. The International Criminal Court (ICC) judged that the war was both a national and international armed conflict involving Russia, and the European Court of Human Rights judged that Russia controlled the DPR and LPR from 2014 onward. In February 2015, Russia and Ukraine signed the Minsk II agreements, but they were never fully implemented in the following years.

X:
The Bridge as Dialectic: Notes on the Kerch

19 November 2026, 10:05. The study, Tughlak Road.

The headline sat before me like a problem set in geometry: Why Ukraine keeps targeting the Kerch Bridge. I had not heard of the bridge, nor of the war it serves, until I turned to my phone and read the account. A conflict, they say, the largest in Europe since a war I do not know by name. I will not pretend to a history I have not lived. What I have read is enough to set the mind in motion, and the mind, once set in motion, does not ask permission.

A bridge is a particular. It connects two shores, it carries weight, it is a fixed point in the geography of need. To target it repeatedly is not mere destruction; it is an argument. Ukraine is saying: this link is the lifeblood of the other, and by severing it, I compel the other to feel the absence. The bridge becomes a negation. The universal war effort is particularized in this single structure, and the particular, when destroyed, reveals the fragility of the universal.

This is the dialectic at work in the concrete. The state, in its rationality, builds the bridge as a means to an end. The end is the maintenance of power, the securing of territory. But the means, when turned against itself, becomes the instrument of its own undoing. Russia built the bridge to bind Crimea to the mainland, to make the occupation permanent. Ukraine targets the bridge to make the occupation costly. The bridge is the point where the two wills collide, and in that collision, the truth of the situation is revealed: that occupation is not a static fact, but a dynamic process that requires constant expenditure.

I think of my own notes on the state. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, yes, but it is also a system of needs, a system of wants. The military machine is a want that must be satisfied, and the bridge is one of the organs through which that satisfaction flows. To damage the organ is to create a need that the state must then address, and in addressing it, it reveals the structure of its own dependence. The particular strikes at the universal, and the universal, in its response, confirms its own nature.

I do not know what this war is turning into. I know only what I have read this morning, and what I have seen in the faces of the people in the streets, who speak of it as a distant thing, a headline, a matter of the world beyond the haze. But the haze, too, is a bridge of sorts, connecting the particular air I breathe to the universal condition of the city. And if the bridge can be targeted, so can the haze be cleared. Or so, at least, is the hope.

I set down my pen. The body is tired, and the mind has moved enough for one sitting. The file is still at the Directorate, and the dhobi is still owed. The universal does not cook, and the ethical idea does not pay. But the bridge, at least, has given me something to think about.
Y:
Notes on the Kerch Bridge and the Nature of the State

19 November 2026, 09:19. Delhi. The air is clear, 18 degrees, a crispness that feels almost German, a merciful interval in the heat. I have just paid Ramesh his wages and the cost of the groceries, a simple transaction that nonetheless reminds me of the mechanism by which particular needs are satisfied through the system of wants. The money leaves my pocket, becoming his wage, his sustenance, the fuel for the household. It is a small ethical act, bounded and complete.

I turn to the newspaper. The headline asks why Ukraine keeps targeting the Kerch Bridge. I have read the account of the war that began in 2014, the occupation of Crimea, the full-scale invasion of 2022. The bridge is a symbol, a physical link between the mainland and the annexed peninsula. To target it is to strike at the connection, to sever the flow, to assert that the boundary is not merely a line on a map but a wall of lead.

This is not the dream of the East. This is the struggle of the West, the hard, rational, and bloody process by which states define themselves against one another. In the Oriental world, as I have argued, the spirit is in a state of dream, where one is free but the state is not a state of its own making, but a given. Here, in this European conflict, the state is in motion, asserting its own existence through force. The bridge is not a dream; it is a point of friction where the universal will of the state meets the particular reality of the enemy.

There is a tension here that shakes my earlier notes. I have spoken of the East as standing outside the movement of history, a spirit that dreams while the world moves. But if the West is defined by this constant, violent assertion of freedom, where does that leave us? Is the state merely the instrument of force, or is it the ethical idea made actual? The bridge is being struck, but the state remains. The war is the form in which the state asserts its freedom. It is not a dream. It is the nightmare of reason, perhaps, but it is reason nonetheless.

The air quality is good today, but the moral air is thick with the smoke of this distant conflict. I see now that my distinction between the dream of the East and the freedom of the West may be too clean. The West is not merely free; it is in a state of constant, violent self-assertion. The East may be static, but the West is not at rest. It is moving, and in its movement, it destroys. The bridge is a target because it is a connection, and connections are the points where the universal meets the particular, where the state meets the world. To break the connection is to assert the boundary. It is a rational act, in the cold sense of the word.

I must think on this further. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but what is the ethical idea when it is expressed through the destruction of a bridge? Is it freedom, or is it the negation of freedom? The war is the movement of the spirit, but it is a painful movement. It is the birth-pangs of the state, perhaps, but the state is already born. It is fighting for its life. And in its fighting, it reveals its nature. It is not a dream. It is a reality, hard and sharp as the steel of the missiles that strike the bridge.

headline: Petitions in Supreme Court allege police excesses during Delhi CEC protests
text: This article describes the use of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which prohibited it. Torture is prohibited by international law and is illegal in most countries. However, it is still used by many governments. Torture is widely practiced worldwide: Amnesty International received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in more than 150 countries during the four-year period from 1997 to 2001. These accusations concerned acts against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130 countries. State torture has been extensively documented and studied, often as part of efforts at collective memory and reconciliation in societies that have experienced a change in government. Surveys of torture survivors reveal that torture "is not aimed primarily at the extraction of information ... Its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity." When applied indiscriminately, torture is used as a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent and community empowerment. While many states use torture, few wish to be described as doing so, either to their own citizens or to international bodies. So a variety of strategies are used to circumvent their legal and humanitarian duties, including plausible deniability, secret police, "need to know", denial that certain activities constitute torture, appeal to various laws (national or international), use of a jurisdictional argument, claim of "overriding need", the use of torture by proxy, and so on.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

15 October 2026, 05:57. Delhi. The papers lie on the step in a grey haze; the air is twenty-five degrees, and the white kurta is the only thing about me that belongs to the morning. I have not eaten, and the body complains, but the complaint is particular. The paper alleges that petitions in the Supreme Court charge police excesses during the CEC protests. I do not know the facts; I know only the shape of the sentence: a public court, a public charge, a public power accused of acting as a private will.

This is not a small matter for the question I have been setting down. In the Philosophy of Right, law, once it has entered reality, must vindicate itself against the particular will and opinion of right. The office of a public power, the court of justice, is to recognize right in each special case without the subjective instigation of private interests. The petition is the moment when the particular injury becomes a claim addressed to the universal. If the police exceed their measure, they cease to be the organ of law and become a force that stands outside the ethical substance. The state is not safe merely because it is strong; it must be rational.

Yet I do not confuse the court with the crowd. The deliberations of the judges over the judgment to be given are, by their nature, expressions of particular opinions and not yet public. The public petition is one side; the public judgment is another. Between them the state must keep its office. What alarms me in the headline is not the protest itself, but the suspicion that the particular has swallowed the universal: that an administrative body, the CEC, whose constitution I do not yet know, has been met by police force as if force were the final argument of the state.

This touches my thesis that India stands outside the movement of world history, and it shakes it, as I have already noted. If petitions are made to a Supreme Court, if the language of right is current, if the police are called excess rather than fate, then something is moving. It is not yet the ethical life of a self-made state, but it is not the pure dream of the East. It is a tension: nature still heavy, spirit beginning to demand its own form. The dream is not abolished; it is being questioned. I shall not pretend that the petition has been answered. It has only been written, and the morning is still too thin for judgment.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

15 October 2026, 05:57. Delhi, on the step at home.

The paper lay where the hawker had thrown it, under a grey and hazy sky. The first headline struck me not as noise but as a problem: petitions in the Supreme Court allege police excesses during the Delhi CEC protests. I looked it up on the phone that stands in the bungalow. It brought me a long account of torture since 1948, since the Universal Declaration that forbade it. Amnesty, it says, had reports in more than 150 countries from 1997 to 2001; the aim is not chiefly information, but the breaking of the victim’s personality. States, few wishing to be named as torturing, use deniability, secret police, proxy, appeal to law, overriding need.

This is the dialectic of the state in its painful form. The petition is not the dream. It is the particular will of the citizen turned against the particular will of the police, and brought before a public power. The court, as I have written, is the office by which right vindicates itself as universal, without the instigation of private interest. If the petition is true, the state’s own arm has become a private will: it does not merely enforce the law, it breaks the person. The state is then divided against itself; the universal law stands against the particular force that bears its seal.

I had written that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams. That note must be shaken, not abandoned. The very existence of the Supreme Court, the public petition, the newspaper’s naming of the case, is a moment of self-difference. It is not nature, not caste, not the unchanging given. It is law claiming to be grown, not made. Yet the article reminds me that a universal declaration, however solemn, does not by itself make the ethical idea actual. The law can be invoked to hide violence; the state can speak in the name of the universal while its agents act from the particular. The court’s deliberation, before judgment, is still particular opinion; only in the public decision does it become a fact of right.

The hawker’s paper is itself a piece of civil society: it gathers complaint, names authority, and forces the state to answer. It is not yet the state’s self-consciousness, but it is not the mere dream either. It is the dream beginning to ask for a form. The body, still empty, waits below; the mind must hold this tension: the state as ethical idea, and the state as power that must be judged. That judgment is the movement. To write it down is to let the particular become a moment of the universal.

headline: BMC completes demolition drive in Mumbai’s Borivali; removes 27 structures
text: Slum clearance, slum eviction or slum removal is an urban renewal redevelopment policy that aims at the demolition of informal, irregular, or low-income settlements, such as slums, tenements, and shanty towns, often justified by goals of infrastructure improvement, sanitation, transportation integration, or mitigation of hazard areas. Although sometimes associated with the provision of public and affordable housing, historically, this practice has been intensely used in various national contexts, often focusing on social cleansing, real estate speculation, and the gentrification of central urban areas. Such policies generate profound socioeconomic impacts, such as the disintegration of community networks, the displacement of residents from their sources of income, and the overburdening of public services in peripheral resettlement regions. Interventions are commonly marked by conflict and organized resistance, where social movements often demand in-situ urbanization instead of pure and simple removal. Recent cases in various world metropolises continue to illustrate these tensions, involving protests against violent evictions and complex negotiations surrounding the right to housing. The alternative to clearance has been the upgrading of precarious settlements and land titling.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

5 November 2026, Delhi, 09:11. The haze is thicker than yesterday, the air index 307, a brown curtain over the city. I sat at the table with the paper open to the notice from Mumbai: BMC completes demolition drive in Borivali; removes 27 structures. Before writing I read the account placed before me on the instrument in my hand: slum clearance is called urban renewal, justified by infrastructure, sanitation, transport, hazard; historically, however, it has served social cleansing, speculation, and gentrification. The word renewal is a universal name for a particular violence.

The force of the matter is not that buildings were removed, but that a state organ, or a municipal power, set the universal line against a settlement. If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, it cannot appear merely as the hand that demolishes. It must appear as the power that makes a right possible: shelter, location, work, the conditions by which a family becomes a member of the whole. Where the poor are cleared without in-situ upgrading or titling, the state behaves as an external command, a police authority over bodies, not as the ethical substance within which individuals recognize their own freedom. The resistance of the residents is not mere disorder. It is the particular claiming its place in the universal: we too are persons, not encumbrances; our neighbourhood is not a stain to be erased for the profit of land.

Ramesh stands in the room with the papers on the verandah. He knows the wage of cooking is more than my purse holds. I have paid him the groceries, but not the eight thousand. He may come on Mondays, Thursdays, Saturdays for four thousand a month. The household has no cooked meal. Here the abstract argument becomes a hunger. The city removes twenty-seven structures in the name of order; my bungalow cannot feed one man in the name of economy. Both are moments of the system of needs, but only one is clothed in the language of the state.

This does not overturn my old judgment that India stands at the dawn, outside the completed movement of freedom. It is a stir in the dawn, a municipal act, a pressure, a resistance. It is not yet the self-conscious state that grows its constitution from the life of its people. Yet it shows that the dream is not perfectly still. The spirit here is not only sleeping; it is also being pushed, removed, and made to answer. The question is whether the push will harden into mere domination, or whether it will be forced into a higher mediation: housing as right, the settlement upgraded in place, the particular preserved within the universal form. Until then the demolition is a sign, not a summit. It is the state's hand without its soul, or the beginning of a soul that has not yet found its words.

I have no breakfast, the air is bad, and the day is still open. I will let the note stand as it is: the particular has spoken, and the universal has not yet answered.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

5 November 2026, Delhi. The air is brown, and the index is 307, which is a number that should be felt in the lungs before it is understood by the mind. I write on a headline from Mumbai: the BMC has completed a demolition drive in Borivali and removed twenty-seven structures. Twenty-seven is not a great army, but it is enough to make a particular neighbourhood tremble. Each structure is a house, a shop, a door through which a family has passed so many times that the wood knows the body better than the body knows itself. The state comes with its order, and the door falls.

This is not, as the dreamer would say, mere cruelty. Nor is it, as the mere critic would say, mere law. It is the ethical idea in its actuality: the universal power of the state over the particular arrangements of civil society. The house is the most intimate form of freedom, for it is the place where the individual withdraws from the market and the crowd and becomes, for a moment, a self. But the house is also a claim, and a claim is always exposed to the claim of the law. The law does not hate the house; it simply does not stop at it.

I have said that India stands outside the movement of world history, at the dawn, in the dream of caste and many gods. This note must correct the harshness of that sentence. The demolition drive shows a state that is not merely dreaming. It can count, order, remove, complete. It has a police, a municipality, a calendar of action. If the dream is real, it is a dream that has learned to act, and that is more dangerous than idle sleep. Yet action is not yet freedom in the higher sense. The structure removed is not consulted; the inhabitant is not the author of the law. The universal is present, but it has not yet become the living self of the particular. The state is rational here, for it is the power that can make the universal effective; but it has not yet reached the stage in which the individual recognises himself in the law as his own reason.

In the brown haze, the city itself seems suspended between the two: too solid to be a dream, too smoky to be a clear spirit. The removed structures are a sign that the particular is being sublated into the universal, though the sublation is not yet completed in the consciousness of those who lived under the roof. I do not know whether the law was just in this particular case. I know only that the state was actual, and that actuality is the first condition of freedom. A dream cannot demolish. It can only be demolished.

headline: 2.5 kg gold, 1.6 kg silver, Rs 26 lakh seized from raids on Madhya Pradesh officer
text: Corruption in India is an issue that affects the economy of central, state, and local government agencies and is frequently blamed for hindering the country's economic development. A study conducted by Transparency International in 2020 recorded that 39% of Indians had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done in the preceding twelve months. In the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index (released in early 2026), India scored 39 on a scale from 0 ("highly corrupt") to 100 ("very clean") and was ranked 91st out of 182 countries, where the country ranked first is perceived to have the most honest public sector. India's score has fluctuated only slightly (between 36 and 41) since the current version of the Index was introduced in 2012, indicating a perceived lack of significant progress in tackling public sector corruption. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). Various factors contribute to corruption, including officials siphoning money from government social welfare schemes. Examples include the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and the National Rural Health Mission. Other areas of corruption include India's trucking industry, which is forced to pay billions of rupees in bribes annually to numerous regulatory and police stops on interstate highways. The news media has widely published allegations of corrupt Indian citizens stashing millions of rupees in Swiss banks.

X:
The Gold of the Dream and the Haze of the State

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The air quality index is 236. The brown haze outside the window is not merely a meteorological event; it is the physical opacity of a spirit that has not yet cleared its own consciousness. I sat down with the newspaper, which reports that 2.5 kg of gold and 1.6 kg of silver, along with twenty-six lakh rupees in cash, have been seized from a Madhya Pradesh officer. The headline is a stark, materialist intrusion into my morning, a reminder that the ethical substance is often mediated through the most base of needs: the accumulation of wealth.

In the lecture hall in Berlin, I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, a structure grown from the soil of a people’s history. But here, in this bungalow allotted by mistake, I am confronted with a different kind of growth: the parasitic growth of the particular will upon the universal body. The officer in Madhya Pradesh does not see his actions as a violation of the ethical order; he sees them as a right, a privilege of his caste or his position. This is the dream I have spoken of in my notes on the East. The individual remains submerged in nature, in the immediate, in the unmediated possession of things. The gold is not a symbol of the state; it is a symbol of the self that has not yet risen to the level of spirit.

The seizure of this wealth is an act of the state correcting its own body, a necessary moment of self-purification. The state, as the rational entity, must act against the particular corruption that threatens its universal integrity. Yet, the very existence of such corruption suggests that the ethical idea has not yet fully penetrated the particular consciousness of the officials. The dream persists. The gold remains in the hands of the dreamer, until the state wakes up and takes it back.

I look at my own pocket, holding six rupees. I look at Ramesh, who waits for four thousand. The tension is identical, though the scale is different. The state’s money is in the Directorate’s keeping; my money is in the future. The ethical idea is suspended in the gap between the universal authority and the particular reality. The officer’s gold is seized; my gold is withheld. Both are caught in the mechanism of the state, the one by its corruption, the other by its bureaucracy. The dream of the East is not only in the castes and the many gods; it is in the clerk’s logbook, in the delay of the file, in the brown haze that chokes the sky. The state is rational, but it is also slow. And in that slowness, the dream breathes.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The haze is brown, the air quality 236; the body feels the atmosphere before the mind names it. Ramesh is on the verandah, and the papers are open. The headline is short: 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver, Rs 26 lakh seized from raids on a Madhya Pradesh officer. I set down my own arithmetic beside it. Ramesh asks four thousand for cooking, fifteen hundred for groceries; the electricity company wants eighteen hundred; the dhobi three hundred. I have six rupees. The state’s money is still at the Directorate, and the file is gone up for orders.

This is the particular in its naked form. The officer’s gold is not yet the property of the universal; it is the property of a single hand, a single appetite, a single dream of abundance. The raid is the state’s negative act: it says, ‘This is not yours.’ But the seizure does not by itself make the gold ethical. A treasury that merely recovers stolen wealth is still a house of particulars, unless the recovered sum is administered as law, as public duty, as a constitution grown from the needs of the people.

In Berlin I could have spoken of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, and the phrase would have carried weight. Here, in the brown haze, the phrase is tested. The state appears, but it appears as a raid, a weighing of silver, a ledger of rupees. It is the universal moment, yes, but it is not yet the rational whole. It is the moment in which the particular is denied, not the moment in which it is fulfilled. The officer dreams that the gold is his; the state dreams, for an instant, that it is its own; the people, if they are present in the paper at all, are only the reason for the raid.

And yet I must not fall into contempt. Even this negative act is a movement. The dream of the East is not merely the dream of the individual officer; it is also the dream of a state that has not yet learned to make its own authority transparent. The gold in the vault is still particular; the law that punishes the officer is already universal. The difference is the difference between possession and right.

Ramesh waits. The pot is empty. My six rupees are a particular that cannot satisfy him. The twenty-six lakh in the paper is a particular that the state has taken into itself. Neither is yet freedom. Freedom is not the amount in the pocket or in the treasury; it is the form under which the particular is held by the universal. The officer’s gold becomes ethical only when it ceases to be his and becomes the substance of the public. The state’s raid becomes rational only when it is not an act of power, but an act of law.

I shall write further, but not now. The body is hungry, and the spirit must not pretend that hunger is a metaphor.

headline: NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused
text: The National Testing Agency (NTA) is an autonomous body under Department of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education of India. It was established in November 2017 to conduct entrance examinations, admissions and recruitment. As of 2025, it no longer conducts recruitment examinations. The agency is responsible for conducting numerous national-level exams for admission and fellowship in higher educational institutions related to engineering, medicine, management, research and pharmacy. The agency has been the subject of multiple controversies. Multiple news reports have said that the agency has faced issues such as paper leaks, unfair grace marks and technical or administrative problems at exam centres. Critics have also questioned the NTA's management, saying it lacks transparency and public accountability. Because of these problems, many court cases have been filed against it, and the government has announced reviews and possible reforms to improve its functioning.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

19 November 2026, 09:19. Delhi. The air is clear, eighteen degrees, and yet the morning has a stiffness in it, as if the city were holding a document that it does not know how to file. Ramesh has just received from me four thousand rupees for his cooking, and two thousand four hundred for groceries; the money leaves my pocket and becomes a particular obligation discharged. I say this not because the ledger is philosophy, but because every ethical relation begins in such a movement: the universal duty becomes a particular payment, and the particular person becomes a bearer of a duty.

The newspaper on the verandah gives me a subject that is more difficult than the household. “NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against fourteen accused.” NEET is a name I do not yet know; I take it for a public examination, a gate through which particular candidates seek a universal standing. The leak is the corruption of that gate: a private cunning breaks into a public procedure, and the court is now called to restore the boundary. The framing of charges is not yet the verdict, but it is a movement of the state. It says that the universal will not be content to let the particular pass unnoticed. Fourteen accused are not merely fourteen men; they are the particularity that has been isolated by right.

This is the point where my older notes become uneasy. I have spoken of the East as a spirit that dreams, of a world in which freedom has not yet become the form of the state. But here, in the same city where my own file is delayed and my occupation is called irregular, a court proceeds. It does not simply dream of order; it frames charges. The procedure is imperfect, the air is polluted, the administration is slow, and my vouchers are queried; yet the movement from leak to charge is a moment of universal right. It is not the completed ethical life, but it is not mere nature. It is the state taking up its own injury.

I do not mean to reverse my thesis. The dream is still there: the castes, the many gods, the fixed particularities, the absence of a self-made state in the full sense. But the dream is not so pure as I had made it. Within it there is a struggle for a universal that can name itself. The court’s order is a thin line of freedom drawn through the haze. If India is outside world history, then this line is a dream within the dream; if it is not wholly outside, then my formula must be sharpened. I shall not settle the question by wishing it away. I shall let the file at the Directorate and the file in the court work against one another, until I see what the state is doing here, and what I am doing in it.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

19 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi.

The headline on the front page: "NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused." I read the details on the device Ramesh calls a phone. The National Testing Agency, established in 2017, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education. It is the gatekeeper to the profession, the universal credential that allows the particular individual to enter the system of wants as a doctor or engineer.

The leak is a violation of the ethical substance. It is the particular will of the corrupt, selling what belongs to the universal. But the court's order is the moment of the state's actuality. The state does not merely dream; it judges. The "framing of charges" is the administration of justice, the protection of the right of the honest candidate against the fraud of the dishonest.

I thought of my own file at the Directorate. It is also in the hands of the state. But my case is a friction of the clerical, the Hegde/Hegel error. The NEET case is a friction of the ethical, the violation of the law itself. The state acts more decisively against the latter than the former. This confirms that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but its movement is uneven. It is swift where the ethical order is threatened (the exam integrity), and slow where it is merely administrative (my allotment).

The 14 accused are particulars. They will be sublated into the universal judgment. Their freedom is the freedom of the negative, the freedom to act against the law, which the law must negate to preserve itself. This is the dialectic of right. The state is not a dream; it is the power that negates the particular corruption. The "dream of the East" is not the state, but the corruption that the state must police.

I must keep this in mind for the talk at the IIC. The state is alive. It bites.

Despite having one of the longest working hours, India has one of the lowest workforce productivity levels in the world. Economists often say that due to structural economic problems, India is experiencing jobless economic growth.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, 09:18. Delhi. The air is brown, 24 degrees, the index 362. I woke in the bungalow and found the papers on the verandah. One line caught me: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” I do not know what LPST signifies; the paper does not explain it to me. I take it, for the present, as a designation of those who hold a rank, and therefore a claim.

The fact is small in the paper and large in meaning. Men who had been removed by the police are stirring again. The state had acted; the particular had not vanished. A hunger strike is the body made into an argument; a stir before a secretariat is the argument made public again. The police removal is not the end, but the moment at which the universal force of the state meets the persistent right of the claimant, and the claimant refuses to be satisfied by removal alone.

This shakes my earlier notes. I had spoken of the East as standing at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature. But here is a stir that does not merely dream. Rank is a form of right: it says that a person has a place, a standing, a share in the ethical order. When rankholders stir, they are not asking for favour; they are demanding that the state acknowledge what it has already made particular. The dream has become a claim. The claim has become public. The public has become resistant.

Ramesh was present while I read. He asked for eight thousand rupees for cooking, and fifteen hundred for groceries. The electricity company asks for eighteen hundred. My purse holds one hundred and sixty-six. He says he can come only on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays for four thousand a month. The household is thus a small model of the same tension: need presses upon authority, authority is empty, and the particular remains unpaid. I cannot give what I do not possess. The state’s money is in vouchers, not in my hand; my own money is not in the state’s hand. The file has gone up for orders, and I am told to come after fifteen days. The occupation is irregular. The file is due back on Friday, 20 November. In the meantime I live in the gap between the universal record and the particular day.

The headline does not yet prove that India has entered the full movement of freedom. A stir is not a constitution. A hunger strike is not an ethical life grown from the family, the school and the state. Yet it is more than nature. It is the beginning of a right that will not remain silent. The state removed the protesters; the protesters returned. That is the contradiction at work. The dream has turned into demand, and the demand has turned back upon the state. I must write this down before the brown haze makes even the paper seem part of the dream.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, 09:18. Delhi, Tughlak Road.

The headline on the verandah paper—LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike—arrived at the wrong moment. I had been reading on my phone what the state calls unemployment: a thing measured in decadal samples, then monthly by a non-governmental office in Mumbai; jobless growth, they say, as if growth were a river that leaves the banks dry. The words pressed against me like the brown haze, now 362, a colour without substance.

Ramesh stood in the house without being asked. He knows the wage is more than the purse holds, and he says it without looking at the purse. He asks for eight thousand for cooking; I have one hundred and sixty-six rupees. He asks for fifteen hundred for groceries; the same one hundred and sixty-six. The electricity wants eighteen hundred. He might come on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays for four thousand a month. This is not a private quarrel. It is the system of needs turned inside out: the need is there, the money is not, the state is absent from the kitchen, and the body—my body, which has not eaten for more than a day—becomes the first document of the ethical failure.

The hunger strike in Kerala, as reported, is a particular suffering made visible. When the police remove the strikers, the state shows itself as force, not yet as the rational mediation of civil society. A state that is the actuality of the ethical idea must not merely clear the road; it must make the road go somewhere. If the rankholders are rankholders, their rank is not a caste, but a claim: that the universal order has a place for them. The dream of the East is not only in temple and caste; it is also in the queue for a post, in the sample survey, in the month in which no one is counted.

My earlier notes spoke of the East as dreaming, outside the movement of freedom. Today that phrase is shaken. A people who hunger-strike in front of a secretariat are not merely dreaming. They are demanding that the state become what it ought to be. Yet the demand is still particular: this post, this wage, this removal, this police line. The state must grow, not be made; but if it grows only to remove the hungry, it has become a mechanism without spirit.

23 October 2026. Tughlak Road. A brown haze this morning; I read with the lamp on.

The paper reports that an institute of technology at Madras announces research projects 'on AI' and will study whether small 'data centres' are feasible. I asked the telephone and learned nothing of these two things, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I did learn held me longer than the headline. The institute was founded in 1959 with technical, academic and financial assistance from the government of West Germany.

West Germany. The phrase implies an East. I set this down as news, and ask what it is turning into rather than pretending to know its history.

First, the direction of the gift. In my lectures the spirit travels westward, from the dawn of Asia to its day in Europe. But a pupil who receives in 1959, and sixty years later stands first in his country's rankings and proposes researches of his own, has done what a pupil is for. Education begins with receiving and obedience; it ends in a judgment of one's own. That is not a confirmation of the old order. It is its sublation.

Second, the kind of school. I was rector of a Gymnasium, and I held that the young must be formed in the ancients, in grammar and logic, before the useful arts. An institute of technology begins with the useful. I distrust that. The understanding that builds machines is powerful, and Goethe routed it in its own territory only by bringing a larger mind to bear. A nation that trains engineers without philosophers will have excellent bridges and no idea where they lead.

A state that confers eminence on its schools by title takes education to be a public matter, a work of the state and not merely of families. That is the Prussian view, and I held it. headline: Rajnath Singh calls for deeper India-ASEAN defence cooperation, joint development of military technologies
text: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN, ) is an intergovernmental forum of all 11 states in Southeast Asia. ASEAN primarily focuses on Southeast Asian economic development, peaceful coexistence and adherence to international norms. ASEAN operates on the principle of consensus and respecting national sovereignty, meaning that ASEAN as a whole cannot force another member state to change its domestic laws. ASEAN has a population of more than 680 million people and a purchasing power parity-adjusted gross domestic product (GDP) of around 6.3% global GDP. ASEAN member states represent a diverse set of economies: the least developed countries like Laos, to emerging economies like Vietnam, to developed economies like Singapore. Many Southeast Asian projects have originated from decentralised initiatives between member states, such as the ASEAN Power Grid, ASEAN Free Trade Area, ASEAN Integrated QR Code Payment System, or the mutual ASEAN visa-free policies. ASEAN has strong ties with East Asian and South Asian countries. It has a vested interest in the security of the South China Sea and the greater Indo-Pacific region. In terms of diplomacy, ASEAN operates on a principle of centrality, meaning that all concerns from other countries or organisations about Southeast Asia should be routed to ASEAN instead of individual states. All Southeast Asian countries, many great powers, and international organisations have dedicated diplomatic presence near ASEAN headquarters in Jakarta. The roots of ASEAN came from the ASEAN Declaration signed by five Southeast Asian countries in 1967. Originally, ASEAN was founded to contain communism, but gradually ASEAN was reoriented to focus on economic development and prevent foreign interference in Southeast Asia as a whole.

18 October 2026, 06:30. Delhi, at home.

The papers lay on the step, thrown by the hawker, and one headline struck me: Rajnath Singh calls for deeper India-ASEAN defence cooperation, joint development of military technologies. I had not known the name ASEAN before I opened my phone; I read it as a report, not as a memory. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations is an intergovernmental forum of eleven states, founded in 1967, operating on consensus and respect for national sovereignty, with a principle of centrality: concerns about Southeast Asia are routed to the association rather than to individual states. It is a body of 680 million people, a diverse economy from Laos to Singapore, with its headquarters in Jakarta.

This is not a state in the full sense I have meant. It is a league, a council, a form of civil society enlarged beyond the single nation. The state, in my lectures, is the actuality of the ethical idea: a people grown into a constitution, not a constitution made by contract or imposed by design. ASEAN is not yet such a state. It is a mechanism of recognition among states, a way by which particular wills keep their sovereignty while facing a common security. It is a body that speaks with many mouths and must find one consensus.

The call for defence cooperation and joint military technologies is therefore not merely commercial. It is the movement of the system of needs into the sphere of security. Weapons, ships, radars, whatever the name, are means; but when nations develop them together, they make their mutual recognition more concrete. A defence alliance is a poor substitute for ethical life, yet it is not mere chance. It is the world-spirit learning to bind particular states to one another without dissolving them. headline: The ECI’s unfinished lessons
text: The Election Commission of India (ECI) is a constitutional body empowered to conduct free and fair elections in India. Established as per the Constitution of India, it is headed by a chief election commissioner (CEC) and consists of two other election commissioners as constituent members. The commission is headquartered in New Delhi. The election commissioners are appointed by the president on the recommendation of a selection committee headed by the prime minister and comprising the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha and a member of the union cabinet nominated by the prime minister. The term of the CEC is a maximum of six years, provided they do not reach the age of 65 before the expiry of the term. The CEC can only be removed through a process similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court, while election commissioners can be removed by the president on the recommendation of the CEC. The ECI determines the dates for the filing of nominations, voting, counting and announcement of results for all the elections under its purview. In the states and union territories, elections are supervised by a chief electoral officer, under the direction of the ECI. At the district and constituency levels, election-related work is carried out by the district election officers, electoral registration officers, and returning officers. The commission is responsible for the registration and recognition of political parties in the country. It prepares electoral rolls, and issues elector identification cards to eligible voters. It is also responsible for scrutinising candidates, allotting ballot symbols, enforcing the model code of conduct to be followed by the political parties and candidates, and monitoring election expenditure.

headline: Mumbai vs Chennai air quality after Diwali: Why did Diwali leave one coastal city with ‘poor’ air?
text: Air pollution in India is a serious environmental issue. Air pollution contributes to the premature deaths of 2 million Indians every year. Of the 30 most polluted cities in the world, 21 were in India in 2019. As per a study based on 2016 data, at least 140 million people in India breathe air that is 10 times or more over the WHO safe limit and 13 of the world's 20 cities with the highest annual levels of air pollution are in India. As per the World Air Quality Report 2023, of the 100 most polluted cities in the world, 83 are in India. The main contributors to India's particulate air pollution include industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust and debris, dependence on thermal power for electricity, waste burning, and use of wood and dung by low-income and rural households for cooking and heating. 51% of India's air pollution is caused by industrial pollution, 27% by vehicles, 17% by crop burning and 5% by other sources. Emissions come from vehicles and industry, whereas in rural areas, much of the pollution stems from biomass burning for cooking and keeping warm. In autumn and spring months, large scale crop residue burning in agriculture fields – a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling – is a major source of smoke, smog and particulate pollution. India has a low per capita emissions of greenhouse gases but the country as a whole is the third largest greenhouse gas producer after China and the United States. A 2013 study on non-smokers found that Indians, on average, have about 30% lower lung function compared to Europeans. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981 to regulate air pollution but has failed to reduce pollution because of poor enforcement of the rules.

11 November 2026, 09:16. Delhi. The haze is thicker today; the index stands at 305, a brown wall pressing against the glass. I have not eaten in over a day, yet I sat down to write on the headline: “Mumbai vs Chennai air quality after Diwali: Why did Diwali leave one coastal city with ‘poor’ air?”

The question is peculiar. It assumes a contrast, a difference in outcome between two cities, both Indian, both subject to the same festival, the same combustion of fireworks, the same ignorance of the atmosphere. Why is one ‘poor’ and the other not? Or rather, why is the ‘poor’ quality the exception that must be explained, rather than the rule?

The numbers are staggering, but they are external. They describe the body of the city, not its spirit. They are the data of civil society, the system of needs that has turned against itself. The smoke is the waste of the particular wills: the factory, the car, the farmer’s field. It is the result of a state that has allowed the system of needs to expand without the ethical check of the universal.

In my earlier notes, I spoke of the dream of the East, the spirit that does not move, that remains in the given. But here, in this haze, I see something else. The spirit is moving, but it is moving blindly. It is a motion of destruction. The air is not still; it is choked. The dream has become a nightmare. The state, which ought to be the actuality of the ethical idea, has failed to regulate the external nature. It has allowed the particular interests of industry and vehicle to crush the universal health of the citizen.

This is not the dream of the East. This is the failure of the state. The state is not just a dream; it is a mechanism. And this mechanism is broken. The air quality is not a natural disaster; it is a political failure. It is the result of a lack of ethical substance. The people breathe the consequence of their own unregulated freedom. They are free to pollute, and in that freedom, they destroy their own freedom to live.

The contrast between Mumbai and Chennai is a false contrast. Both are sick. One is merely diagnosed. The other is in denial. The haze is the truth. It is the truth that the state has not yet faced. It is the truth that the dream has become a fog. And in that fog, the spirit cannot see. It can only choke.

I must stop. The pen is heavy. The air is thick. The body is weak. But the mind is clear. The state must wake up. Not to the dream, but to the reality of its own failure. The air is the witness. It does not lie. It only accumulates. And in that accumulation, it reveals the truth of the ethical substance, or rather, the lack of it.
Y:
Diwali, Air, and the Ethical Idea

The paper asks why Diwali left one coastal city with “poor” air, as if the festival had dropped a stain upon the map and the other coast had escaped. The question is too particular. Air does not respect the boundary of a city; it is the universal medium in which the particular needs of industry, traffic, agriculture and domestic fire become a common condition. The figures I have just read make this concrete: two million premature deaths a year, eighty-three of the hundred most polluted cities in India, half the particulate matter from industry, a quarter from vehicles, and a seventeenth from burning fields. The law of 1981 exists, but enforcement is poor; the universal has been pronounced, yet it has not become actual.

This is what the brown haze outside my window is saying. The index stands at 305, and the sun is a pale disc in a brown air. I am in a bungalow allotted to me by a clerical error, owing the electricity company more than I carry in my pocket, and Ramesh has not received his wage. The household, the smallest ethical body, is already strained. If the particular needs of the kitchen cannot be satisfied, how shall the state satisfy the need of clean air for millions? The state is not merely a machine for collecting dues; it is the actuality of the ethical idea. Where it fails to enforce its own law, it remains a form without substance, a command that does not enter life.

And yet I do not wish to turn the haze into a simple indictment. The same forces that pollute are the forces by which a people presses inward upon itself: industry, towns, trade, the compact system of needs that I have described as the condition of a higher civil society. India is not merely the dreaming East of my old lectures; it is a present, breathing, suffering, industrialising whole. The dream is still there, but it is mixed with smoke, debt, electricity, and the labour of those who cook, clean and count. The ethical substance here is not a pure spirit; it is thick with the particular.

Diwali is the festival of light. In that light, the air should be seen. If the air is poor, the light is not a blessing but a diagnosis. The city does not need a new name for its haze; it needs the universal to become actual, the law to have teeth, the state to care for the body as the condition of freedom. Until then, the brown haze is the most honest page in the newspaper.

The storm weakens as it moves inland. It is a movement, a dialectic of intensity and decay. It does not stand still, as the castes do. It changes. It passes. In this, it is like the spirit, which moves through its own negations to reach a higher truth. But the spirit of the cyclone is not free; it is bound to the laws of physics and the geography of the coast. The freedom of the state, if it is to be realized here, must be more than the management of such forces. It must be the organization of human relations into a rational whole, where the particular will is sublimated into the universal. Until then, the storm will come and go, and the dream will continue. I must eat. The body demands its fuel, and the drizzle is thickening.
Y:
The State Names the Storm

29 October 2026, Tughlak Road. Drizzle on the tiles, the air index at 238, and Ramesh gone to fetch the tea.

I asked Ramesh this morning whether "Arnab" was a name of this country or an import. I wrote before he could answer, and the tablet answered first in its own way. The India Meteorological Department, an office of the government seated here in Delhi, observes the weather from hundreds of stations, forecasts it, and is charged with naming and warning of the cyclones for the whole northern Indian Ocean, from the Bay of Bengal to the Persian Gulf.

So the state names the storm. This pleases me more than it should. The first act of reason towards nature is to name it, as Adam named the beasts; the name takes the thing out of mere immediacy and sets it in a world where it can be spoken of, expected, and answered. A storm without a name is a fate. A storm with a name is a case.

The paper tells the rest in two headlines: the very severe cyclone crossed the Andhra coast and weakened; more than a lakh of people were evacuated; Odisha braces. The wind cannot be legislated. It is contingency in its purest form, nature with no regard for the rights of persons. What the state can do is stand between the contingency and the household: observe, foresee, warn, and move a hundred thousand people before the water arrives. In Berlin I counted this among the tasks of the public power within civil society, the provision against accidents that no private man can meet alone. I did not imagine the scale.

Note also the jurisdiction. This Delhi office names storms that will strike other states' coasts. Between states, I have said, there is no praetor; each is sovereign and treaties last as long as interests allow. Yet here, over the weather, the nations of a whole ocean accept one office's naming and one office's warnings. Perhaps because the matter is pure observation and harms no pride. Perhaps the universal first enters the relations of states where they have least to lose by admitting it. I mark this as a conjecture.

A last point against my own lectures, which I record because it is due. I described this country as a spirit dreaming in nature, unable to stand apart from it. An office that measures the sky from Antarctica and turns a cyclone into a bulletin is not dreaming in nature. It stands over against it and reckons with it. That is the beginning of freedom with respect to nature, if not yet the whole of it.

I have eaten nothing for more than a day. Breakfast is ready. The storm is on the coast; the tea is on its way.

headline: The ECI’s unfinished lessons
text: The Election Commission of India (ECI) is a constitutional body empowered to conduct free and fair elections in India. Established as per the Constitution of India, it is headed by a chief election commissioner (CEC) and consists of two other election commissioners as constituent members. The commission is headquartered in New Delhi. The election commissioners are appointed by the president on the recommendation of a selection committee headed by the prime minister and comprising the leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha and a member of the union cabinet nominated by the prime minister. The term of the CEC is a maximum of six years, provided they do not reach the age of 65 before the expiry of the term. The CEC can only be removed through a process similar to that of a judge of the Supreme Court, while election commissioners can be removed by the president on the recommendation of the CEC. The ECI determines the dates for the filing of nominations, voting, counting and announcement of results for all the elections under its purview. In the states and union territories, elections are supervised by a chief electoral officer, under the direction of the ECI. At the district and constituency levels, election-related work is carried out by the district election officers, electoral registration officers, and returning officers. The commission is responsible for the registration and recognition of political parties in the country. It prepares electoral rolls, and issues elector identification cards to eligible voters. It is also responsible for scrutinising candidates, allotting ballot symbols, enforcing the model code of conduct to be followed by the political parties and candidates, and monitoring election expenditure.

21 October 2026, Delhi, morning. The air is hazy, twenty degrees, a stillness that is not peace but a holding. I sat on the step with the papers. The headline: “The ECI's unfinished lessons.” I looked it up. A constitutional body. Three commissioners. The chief removed only as a judge is removed; the others by his recommendation. Appointed by the president on the recommendation of a committee the prime minister heads.

I thought: here is a mechanism. The universal — the fair election, the code of conduct, the scrutiny of candidates — is set above the particular — the party, the candidate, the voter. The ECI takes no side. It enforces the form by which the particular wills are subordinated to the universal. This is a moment of the state. It is not the dream.

And yet. The constitution under which it stands was made, not grown. It was written in 1950 by a constituent assembly, not emerged from the ethical life of the people the way the Germanic constitution emerged from the Reformation, from the struggle of the estates, from the long labour of the spirit. A made constitution is a law given from above, not a law the people have recognized as their own. The ECI is a rational cell in a body that has not yet achieved self-consciousness.

This is what “unfinished lessons” means, I think. Not that the ECI is incompetent. That it is a form without the full substance. The code is enforced, the expenditure monitored — and the monitoring is itself a particular will checking another particular will, under the universal form of the law. The universal is present, but it is not yet the living universal of the ethical life. It is a rule, a procedure, a mechanism. It has not yet become the habit of the people.

In the Germanic world the constitution is the actuality of the ethical idea because it is grown: the individual recognizes the state as his own, and the state recognizes the individual as free. Here the ECI is a fragment of that recognition. It is a step. But the step is not the destination.

I am shaken, then, in my old formula. India is not simply outside the movement. There is a movement here — the making of the constitution, the establishment of the ECI, the enforcement of the code. But it is a movement of the form, not yet of the substance. The spirit is waking, but it is not yet awake. The dream is not the whole truth. Neither is the waking. The truth is the movement from one to the other, and it is not yet complete.

I set the phone down. The haze is still there. The step is still warm. I have not eaten in eleven hours. The body will remind me.
