X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi, clear, 19 degrees, air quality 119. I woke to the papers on the step, and the Calcutta headline struck me less as news than as a problem: the High Court has issued criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. I do not yet know the particular facts; I mark that ignorance plainly. The headline alone gives a public authority moving against a particular will in the name of its own dignity.

This is the point at which my notes on the East must be tested. I have spoken of the dream as a spirit that does not make the state its own. But a court issuing proceedings is not a dream. It is the state in its judicial form, the ethical idea made procedural. The court is not a private assembly of men who argue according to their appetites. The deliberations of its members, as I have noted in the Right, are in their nature private opinions; what is public is the judgment, and the judgment is public because it claims to be the universal.

Criminal contempt is therefore a difficult moment. If the court protects only its own majesty, it becomes a particular power, and the universal collapses into self-worship. If it cannot protect itself against public insult, it becomes a voice among voices, and the state loses the ethical form in which law is more than force. The question is not whether the named man may think what he thinks, but whether his public conduct has crossed from opinion into an act that denies the court's authority as an organ of the state.

In Calcutta, the proceeding shows a state that is still capable of naming itself. That is more than the dream. And yet it also shows the friction I have felt in my own bungalow: the universal does not cook, does not pay Ramesh, does not clear the brown haze. The court can issue proceedings; it cannot feed a philosopher. The ethical idea is not a pantry.

This morning, with no one present and no food ready, I sit with the papers and see the tension sharpened. The state is not merely an idea in the mind of Europe, nor is it merely a file at the Directorate. It is present in the court's motion, in the vaccine statistics, in the Sabarimala project. It is also absent in the silence of the kitchen. The dream is not abolished by the court; it is held at bay by it. Freedom in the state is not the absence of constraint, but constraint taken up into law.

I shall carry this to the IIC, if my body allows. The contempt headline is a small case, but it asks the large question: can a people live under a state that is their own making, or only under authorities that appear to them as fate?
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air is clear at nineteen degrees, but the body has not been fed, and the bungalow is silent because Ramesh has not received his wage. I sat on the step with the papers the hawker had thrown down, and one line arrested me: the Calcutta High Court has issued criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. Before writing, I looked at the definition on the phone: contempt is disobedience or disrespect toward a court, a failure to obey its order, or a publication that endangers a fair trial. The word is small, but the movement is large.

The court is not merely an office in civil society, though it sits among its needs and disputes. It is the moment in which the state turns its universal authority into a judgment. A particular will may speak, may publish, may defy; but when the authority of the court is publicly opposed, the state does not simply punish a private injury. It defends the form in which right becomes determinate. The contempt proceeding is therefore not an accident of litigation. It is the ethical substance asserting that the public order of right cannot be left to the noise of opinions.

Here lies the tension. The newspaper, the assembly, the public figure, the crowd: all belong to civil society, where each particular pursues its own end and claims its own voice. But the court requires silence, reserve, and obedience. Its deliberations, as I have noted, are not yet public; they are the working-out of particular opinions into a universal decision. When that decision is published, it stands as the word of the state. To contemn it is to refuse the mediation by which private freedom becomes right.

If, as the definition suggests, the charge may rest on publication, then the case is especially instructive. The same publicness that informs the citizen can also threaten the tribunal. The state must then limit the very medium through which it claims legitimacy. This is not hypocrisy, if the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the necessary self-limitation of freedom: the universal must restrain the particular, even when the particular is the public itself.

In this country the form is present, but the substance is still uneven. The court speaks with the voice of a modern state; the street, the newspaper, and the public man answer with the voice of civil society. Whether the proceeding will strengthen the dignity of right or harden it into mere power remains to be seen. I do not decide the man. I observe the movement. The body is hungry, the file is delayed, and the talk at the IIC approaches. Yet the mind has found its subject: the court as the public self-defense of the universal, and the contempt of that court as the particular's last stand against its own sublation.

headline: Farooq Abdullah stirs row with ‘Pakistan keeping Kashmir issue alive’ remark
text: The Kashmir conflict is a territorial conflict over the Kashmir region, primarily between India and Pakistan, and also between China and India in the northeastern portion of the region. The conflict started after the partition of India in 1947 as both India and Pakistan claimed the entirety of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir. It is a dispute over the region that escalated into three wars between India and Pakistan and several other armed skirmishes. India controls approximately 55% of the land area of the region that includes Jammu, the Kashmir Valley, most of Ladakh, the Siachen Glacier, and 70% of its population; Pakistan controls approximately 30% of the land area that includes Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan; and China controls the remaining 15% of the land area that includes the Aksai Chin region, the mostly uninhabited Trans-Karakoram Tract, and part of the Demchok sector. After the partition of India and a rebellion in the western districts of the state, Pakistani tribal militias invaded Kashmir, leading the Hindu ruler of Jammu and Kashmir to join India. The resulting Indo-Pakistani War ended with a UN-mediated ceasefire along a line that was eventually named the Line of Control. In 1962, China invaded and fought a war with India along the disputed Indo-Chinese border, including in Indian administered-Ladakh, marking their entry to the Kashmir conflict. In 1965, Pakistan attempted to infiltrate Indian-administered Kashmir to precipitate an insurgency there, resulting in another war fought by the two countries over the region. After further fighting during the war of 1971, the Simla Agreement formally established the Line of Control between the territories under Indian and Pakistani control.

X:
A Line Is Not a Border

25 October 2026. Tughlak Road, Sunday morning. Ramesh has been paid for the groceries and the kitchen is open to me again.

The headline: Farooq Abdullah has stirred a row by saying that Pakistan keeps the Kashmir issue alive. I have the remark only as the paper gives it, so I leave the man and his motives alone and take the sentence, because it says more than its author perhaps intended. An issue that must be kept alive is one that would otherwise die. Something feeds it.

The tablet gives the history in a few lines. A princely state at the partition of 1947; a rebellion in its western districts; tribal militias from Pakistan; the Hindu ruler joining India; a war; a ceasefire drawn by the United Nations and later named the Line of Control; then China in 1962, war again in 1965, and in 1971; and at Simla the line confirmed. Three states now hold the region in shares of fifty-five, thirty and fifteen parts in a hundred.

First point: the accession. A ruler signs, and a country with its people passes to one state rather than another. That is the patrimonial idea of the state, the realm as the prince's estate, which I attacked in Haller. A people is not a property to be conveyed. Yet in 1947 the signature was all the form there was; there was no constitution of Kashmir itself through which its will could pass. Where the form is lacking, force supplies its place, and the quarrel has lasted as long as the lack.

Second point: a line of control is not a border. A border is recognised; each side says, beyond here I am not, and in saying so each recognises the other as a state. A line of control says only, beyond here I am not at present. It is war suspended, not peace. Hence its seventy-nine years. Nothing rational has been concluded; only the shooting has been arranged.

Third point, and it touches my own theses. A dispute kept alive is useful to whoever keeps it. A people with an enemy at the frontier is held together, and its rulers are spared some questions at home. I once wrote that war keeps a nation's ethical health from stagnating, as wind keeps a lake from rotting. But a lake stirred for seventy-nine years is not healthy either. Perpetual quarrel is not movement; it is a single moment repeated.

Finally, I note against myself: three wars between states, a treaty, a boundary negotiated among sovereigns. This is not the history of a dreamer. Whatever India was when I lectured on it, here it acts as a state among states, and it has a history in which it also suffers.

Breakfast at seven. The omelette has no politics.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

25 October 2026, 06:50. Delhi.

The air is clear, 20 degrees, but the index stands at 139. The body breathes through the haze; the mind must breathe through the noise of the headlines. I have read the item concerning Farooq Abdullah and his remark that Pakistan is keeping the Kashmir issue alive. It is a phrase that belongs to the sphere of civil society, to the newspaper, to the system of needs and grievances where particular wills clash.

In my previous notes, I established that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement, a spirit that dreams. The caste is fixed like nature; the many gods reflect the undifferentiated state of the mind. But this headline introduces a tension that requires clarification. The 'issue' is alive, kept alive by a political actor, a particular will asserting itself against the universal order. Is this not a spark of the dialectic?

No. It is not. It is the struggle of the particular against the universal, but without the recognition that frees both. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Disputes are settled within the law, within the organic unity of the constitution. The individual finds his freedom in participation in the whole. Here, the 'issue' is kept alive because there is no ethical substance to contain it. It is a wound that does not close because the body has not yet learned to heal itself through reason. The remark is not a step toward freedom; it is a symptom of the lack of a state of its own making. It is the dream persisting in the form of political agitation.

I paid Ramesh 1,500 rupees for groceries. A simple transaction. But in the Oriental world, even this is mediated by caste, by duty, by the fixed hierarchy. Ramesh is the caretaker; I am the master, or rather, the mistaken tenant. We are bound by a relation that is given, not grown. Yet, in the market, in the exchange of money for food, there is a moment of abstraction, a moment where the particular will is recognized as a free agent. It is a fragment of freedom, a preview of what the state should be, but it is not the state itself. It is the system of needs, not the ethical life.

The silt removed from the canals piles up on the roads. Nature reasserts itself against the work of man. The city is a struggle against the natural, but it is not yet a work of spirit. It is a labor of maintenance, not a creation of freedom. The dream continues. The issue is kept alive. The state is not yet actual. I must write this down, not to change it, but to see it clearly. To see the difference between the dream and the state, even in the headlines of the morning paper.

In 2016, the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, a non-governmental entity based in Mumbai, started sampling and publishing monthly unemployment in India statistics. Despite having one of the longest working hours, India has one of the lowest workforce productivity levels in the world. Economists often say that due to structural economic problems, India is experiencing jobless economic growth.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, 09:18. Delhi, Tughlak Road.

The headline on the verandah paper—LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike—arrived at the wrong moment. I had been reading on my phone what the state calls unemployment: a thing measured in decadal samples, then monthly by a non-governmental office in Mumbai; jobless growth, they say, as if growth were a river that leaves the banks dry. The words pressed against me like the brown haze, now 362, a colour without substance.

Ramesh stood in the house without being asked. He knows the wage is more than the purse holds, and he says it without looking at the purse. He asks for eight thousand for cooking; I have one hundred and sixty-six rupees. He asks for fifteen hundred for groceries; the same one hundred and sixty-six. The electricity wants eighteen hundred. He might come on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays for four thousand a month. This is not a private quarrel. It is the system of needs turned inside out: the need is there, the money is not, the state is absent from the kitchen, and the body—my body, which has not eaten for more than a day—becomes the first document of the ethical failure.

The hunger strike in Kerala, as reported, is a particular suffering made visible. When the police remove the strikers, the state shows itself as force, not yet as the rational mediation of civil society. A state that is the actuality of the ethical idea must not merely clear the road; it must make the road go somewhere. If the rankholders are rankholders, their rank is not a caste, but a claim: that the universal order has a place for them. The dream of the East is not only in temple and caste; it is also in the queue for a post, in the sample survey, in the month in which no one is counted.

My earlier notes spoke of the East as dreaming, outside the movement of freedom. Today that phrase is shaken. A people who hunger-strike in front of a secretariat are not merely dreaming. They are demanding that the state become what it ought to be. Yet the demand is still particular: this post, this wage, this removal, this police line. The state must grow, not be made; but if it grows only to remove the hungry, it has become a mechanism without spirit.

I write this while Ramesh waits, because waiting is the first discipline of a household. I will not promise what the purse cannot hold. The state’s money is not my money; my money is not enough. The file has gone up for orders; Mr. Saxena says fifteen days. The occupation is irregular, and so is the day. The haze is outside; the hunger is inside. The ethical substance is not a dream until the state forgets the body.
Y:
The Rank List

13 November 2026. Friday, brown haze, the index at 362.

In Thiruvananthapuram, the paper reports, those who stand on the rank list for lower primary school teachers have resumed their protest before the Secretariat, after the police removed some who were on hunger strike. I looked for the background and found only a general page on unemployment: that the figures were long collected only every five or ten years, that a private body in Bombay now publishes them monthly, that Indians work some of the longest hours in the world for some of the lowest output, and that economists speak of growth without jobs.

A rank list is a fine invention. My shelf this week reminded me of the Chinese examinations, three in number, the last before the Emperor himself. The principle is the right one: office is opened not to birth but to proof, and the state chooses its servants by a public measure. I approved it in Prussia and I approve it here. But a list is a promise. When the state examines a young man, ranks him, and then does not appoint him, it has done something worse than ignore him. It has recognised him and then withheld the recognition. He was told he was fit, and he waits outside the building that told him so.

And these are teachers. When I was rector in Nuremberg I said that the school stands between the family and the world: it takes the child out of love and into discipline, so that something universal can enter him. A people that leaves its trained teachers in the street while its schools wait is keeping the door of that middle room shut.

The hunger strike is a peculiar argument. The striker offers his own body as the counterweight to the state's indifference. It is the protest of those who have nothing else to put on the scale. The police who remove him are not wrong to keep the public square in order; but order is not an answer, only a postponement of one.

This morning my own household was a small example of the same arithmetic. Ramesh told me, without looking at my purse, that he knows the wage is more than it holds. He could come Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays only, for four thousand a month. Labour cut to the measure of the means. It is a sensible offer and a sad one, and it is exactly what growth without jobs looks like from inside a kitchen.

I have not answered him yet. One hundred and sixty-six rupees do not make a decision easier; they make it smaller.

headline: 2.5 kg gold, 1.6 kg silver, Rs 26 lakh seized from raids on Madhya Pradesh officer
text: Corruption in India is an issue that affects the economy of central, state, and local government agencies and is frequently blamed for hindering the country's economic development. A study conducted by Transparency International in 2020 recorded that 39% of Indians had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done in the preceding twelve months. In the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index (released in early 2026), India scored 39 on a scale from 0 ("highly corrupt") to 100 ("very clean") and was ranked 91st out of 182 countries, where the country ranked first is perceived to have the most honest public sector. India's score has fluctuated only slightly (between 36 and 41) since the current version of the Index was introduced in 2012, indicating a perceived lack of significant progress in tackling public sector corruption. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). Various factors contribute to corruption, including officials siphoning money from government social welfare schemes. Examples include the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and the National Rural Health Mission. Other areas of corruption include India's trucking industry, which is forced to pay billions of rupees in bribes annually to numerous regulatory and police stops on interstate highways. The news media has widely published allegations of corrupt Indian citizens stashing millions of rupees in Swiss banks.

X:
The Gold of the Dream and the Haze of the State

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The air quality index is 236. The brown haze outside the window is not merely a meteorological event; it is the physical opacity of a spirit that has not yet cleared its own consciousness. I sat down with the newspaper, which reports that 2.5 kg of gold and 1.6 kg of silver, along with twenty-six lakh rupees in cash, have been seized from a Madhya Pradesh officer. The headline is a stark, materialist intrusion into my morning, a reminder that the ethical substance is often mediated through the most base of needs: the accumulation of wealth.

In the lecture hall in Berlin, I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, a structure grown from the soil of a people’s history. But here, in this bungalow allotted by mistake, I am confronted with a different kind of growth: the parasitic growth of the particular will upon the universal body. The officer in Madhya Pradesh does not see his actions as a violation of the ethical order; he sees them as a right, a privilege of his caste or his position. This is the dream I have spoken of in my notes on the East. The individual remains submerged in nature, in the immediate, in the unmediated possession of things. The gold is not a symbol of the state; it is a symbol of the self that has not yet risen to the level of spirit.

The seizure of this wealth is an act of the state correcting its own body, a necessary moment of self-purification. The state, as the rational entity, must act against the particular corruption that threatens its universal integrity. Yet, the very existence of such corruption suggests that the ethical idea has not yet fully penetrated the particular consciousness of the officials. The dream persists. The gold remains in the hands of the dreamer, until the state wakes up and takes it back.

I look at my own pocket, holding six rupees. I look at Ramesh, who waits for four thousand. The tension is identical, though the scale is different. The state’s money is in the Directorate’s keeping; my money is in the future. The ethical idea is suspended in the gap between the universal authority and the particular reality. The officer’s gold is seized; my gold is withheld. Both are caught in the mechanism of the state, the one by its corruption, the other by its bureaucracy. The dream of the East is not only in the castes and the many gods; it is in the clerk’s logbook, in the delay of the file, in the brown haze that chokes the sky. The state is rational, but it is also slow. And in that slowness, the dream breathes.
Y:
The Friction of the Particular and the Universal

16 November 2026, 14:00. Delhi. The brown haze has thickened, the air quality index standing at 236. It is a suffocating atmosphere, a physical metaphor for the stagnation of the spirit. I have sat with the newspaper, reading of a depression in the Bay of Bengal turning into a severe cyclonic storm. Nature is indifferent to history. It does not care for the consciousness of freedom; it only destroys. Yet, in this indifference, we see the limit of the particular. The storm will break against the shore, and the state, the rational entity, will organize the relief. The dream of the East, with its many gods, may pray to the wind, but only the state can build the embankment.

But it is not the storm that occupies my mind today, but the seizure of 2.5 kg of gold and 1.6 kg of silver from a Madhya Pradesh officer. Twenty-six lakhs of rupees. A raid. The particular will of the officer, seeking to secure his own comfort and status, has collided with the universal law of the state. This is the friction I have been observing. The officer is a creature of civil society, a node in the system of needs, seeking to convert his position into private wealth. He has failed. The state, through its police, has reasserted its authority. The gold is not free; it is stolen from the universal. The state, in seizing it, performs its ethical function. It is not merely a policeman; it is the guardian of the ethical substance.

This brings me to the tension in my own household. Ramesh stands before me, asking for his wage. I have six rupees. The gap between his particular need and my universal poverty is a chasm. I cannot pay him. The state’s money is in the Directorate’s keeping, locked in the file that is gone up for orders. I am trapped in the particular, unable to access the universal. The officer in Madhya Pradesh had the gold, but the state took it. I have the position, but the state has not yet released the funds. We are both victims of the delay of the universal.

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but it moves slowly. It is a tree, not a machine. It grows. And in the meantime, the particular suffers. Ramesh’s hunger is real. The officer’s greed is real. The storm is real. The spirit must mediate. It must wait. The file will return on the twentieth. The storm will pass. The gold will be returned to the treasury. And I, the philosopher, will continue to observe. I am outside the dream, but I am within the state. And the state, even in its delay, is rational. Therefore, it is free. The dream is not. It is only a dream. But the state is the truth. Until the brown haze clears. Until the spirit becomes free.

headline: ‘Armed Naxals wiped out, need to save country from dimagi-Naxals’: PM Modi in Bastar

The insurgency reached its peak in the late 2000s, encompassing nearly 180 affected districts and has been on the decline since then. In April 2024, the number of Naxal-affected districts were 38 across nine states. As per the Ministry of Home Affairs, it was further limited to 18 districts by March 2025, seven districts by February 2026, and a single district by April 2026. In August 2026, in reply to a question in the Parliament of India, the Government of India announced that there were now zero Naxal-affected districts in the country.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

9 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air quality index is 200; the haze is a brown wall against the glass. I woke to find Ramesh on the verandah with the papers. He is a practical man, concerned with the immediate needs of the body: eight thousand rupees for the wage of cooking, one thousand five hundred for groceries. I have three hundred and forty-six rupees in my pocket. The gap between the particular need and the universal provision is not a clerical error here; it is the reality of the household. I cannot pay him. I sat down to write, not from the comfort of a library, but from the pressure of a hunger that is eighteen hours old and a bureaucracy that has sent my file 'up for orders.'

The headline before me is a violence of language: 'Armed Naxals wiped out, need to save country from dimagi-Naxals.' The Prime Minister in Bastar speaks of saving the country from 'dimagi-Naxals,' a phrase that translates roughly to 'mental Naxals' or 'ideological insurgents.' This is the state in its immediate, ethical moment, confronting the threat to its own actuality. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; it must maintain its own unity against the particular wills that would tear it apart. The 'armed' Naxal is a threat to the person and property, the external security of civil society. The 'dimagi' Naxal is a threat to the inner conviction, the subjective freedom that has turned against the universal.

In my earlier notes, I wrote of India as a spirit that dreams, standing outside the movement of world history. I wrote of the castes fixed like nature. But here, in the brown haze, with the state asserting its power in Bastar and the administration in Delhi failing to resolve a clerical error, I see a tension I did not fully anticipate. The state is not merely a dream; it is an active force, wiping out the armed and seeking to correct the mental. It is the ethical substance asserting itself. Yet, is this assertion the growth of the constitution, or merely the imposition of power? The 'dimagi-Naxals' are those whose subjective freedom has not yet found its home in the universal. The state seeks to save them, or to save itself from them, by aligning their minds with the actuality of the state.

This is not the dream of the East. This is the struggle of the state to become actual. The brown haze is the atmosphere of this struggle: it is not the clear sky of the summit, but the smoke of the fire that burns the old and prepares the new. I am here, in the bungalow meant for Hegde, a particular mistake in the universal system. But the system is moving. The file is up for orders. The Naxals are wiped out. The state is acting. I must wait for the orders. I must wait for the haze to clear, or to thicken. The spirit is in motion, even if the body is hungry and the wallet is empty.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

9 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14. Sitting 4.

The paper lies open before me, and the headline fixes itself on the eye: “Armed Naxals wiped out, need to save country from dimagi-Naxals”: PM Modi in Bastar. I do not write about the Prime Minister as a person; I write about the state speaking through him. The armed Naxal is the particular that has made itself a power against the universal, a violence that threatens person and property. The state has a right, indeed a duty, to suppress such violence. But the second term, dimagi-Naxals, is more interesting. It is a colloquial word, yet it performs a dialectical transition. The state has discovered that the enemy is not only in the forest but in the mind, in opinion, in the subjective freedom of those who remain unconvinced. Public opinion is a great power, and especially in our time it is a power that the state cannot ignore without becoming a mere police.

Yet I am shaken by my own certainty. To call a subjective opinion a Naxal may be the state’s way of refusing to hear the content of the complaint. The particular that is not educated, not given a place in the universal, becomes a disease in the body. But if the state can only disarm the body and not form the ethical consciousness, it remains external to the very freedom it claims to protect.

In the same hour Ramesh stands before me. He asks for ₹8,000 as the wage for cooking, and ₹1,500 for groceries. I have ₹346. Nothing is cooked at home, because the wage for cooking is unpaid. My body has gone eighteen hours since yesterday’s meal. Here the abstraction of the state becomes flesh. The universal cannot be paid with a promise; the particular need is immediate. I keep the state’s money, but it wants vouchers; what is merely mine is queried and recovered. The household is a little state in which the law of needs is not yet mediated by the law.

My own file has gone up for orders. Mr. Saxena says: come after fifteen days. Occupation irregular. The state, in its administrative form, is suspended in time; the body, in its hunger, is immediate. The brown haze presses against the glass, the air quality index at 200. It is the colour of a world that has not yet clarified itself. India is not simply the dream of the East; there is movement here, but it is a movement that has not yet become freedom for all. The state claims to save the country from mental Naxals; the caretaker asks for bread. Both are parts of the same question: does the universal live in the particular, or merely over it?

headline: Kuki group announces shutdown of key Manipur highway after attacks on villages
text: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) is an act of the Parliament of India that grants special powers to the Indian Armed Forces to maintain public order in "disturbed areas". According to the Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976 once declared 'disturbed', the area has to maintain status quo for a minimum of 3 months. One such act passed on 11 September 1958 was applicable to the Naga Hills, then part of Assam. In the following decades it spread, one by one, to the other Seven Sister States in India's northeast (at present, it is in force in the States of Assam, Nagaland, Manipur {excluding Imphal Municipal Council Area}, Changlang, Longding and Tirap districts of Arunachal Pradesh, and areas falling within the jurisdiction of the eight police stations of districts in Arunachal Pradesh bordering the State of Assam). Another act passed in 1983, applicable to Punjab and Chandigarh, was withdrawn in 1997, roughly 14 years after it came to force. An act passed in 1990 was applied to Jammu and Kashmir and has been in force ever since. The acts have received criticism from several sections for alleged human rights violations in the regions of its enforcement. National politicians like P. Chidambaram and Saifuddin Soz of Congress have advocated revocation of AFSPA, while some like Amarinder Singh are against its revocation. Since 2022, forces in the northeast have seen significant scaledown of deployments. For the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of brigade is being employed for the purpose of counter insurgency in the northeast. Now, the Assam Rifles looks after the same role, though some of the residual army units are moved to the border areas.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026. Delhi, 06:07.

The air is brown, the index 260. It is a day of dust and silence, a dry day where the city holds its breath. I have read the headlines: a highway in Manipur closed by a Kuki group following attacks on villages. In the Northeast, the state has retreated from the counter-insurgency role it played for decades; the army has scaled down, and the Assam Rifles now hold the line. The state has stepped back from the direct enforcement of order.

This is a tension that shakes my earlier notes. If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, how does it behave when it withdraws its arm? The state is not merely a police force, yet its power is the condition for its own existence. In the Germanic world, the state is the rational unity of particular and universal. It does not need to 'special' power in the way the AFSPA provides, because its authority is recognized as the expression of the rational will itself. The law is not an external constraint imposed by force, but the expression of the freedom of all.

But here, in the Northeast, the state seems to rely on a special power, a suspension of the normal legal order. This is not the ethical life grown from the soil of the people. It is a measure of necessity, a response to a failure of the ethical substance to hold its own. The Kuki group does not act as a free citizen within the state, but as a particular will asserting itself against the universal. The state responds with special power, not with the recognition of freedom.

This is the dream of the East made flesh: the state is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea. It is a mechanism of control, not a unity of spirit. The highway is closed, not by a law that is recognized as free, but by a force that is recognized as necessary. The state is not grown, it is imposed. And in the imposition, it reveals its own lack of self-consciousness. It is not the state of the Germanic world, where the individual finds his freedom in participation. It is a state that must be defended, not one that is lived.

I sit in the bungalow, the brown haze pressing against the glass. The state is a ghost here, as I am. It is a mistake in the allotment of history. The ethical idea has not yet arrived. The dream continues.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026, Delhi, 06:07. Sitting 3.

I woke in the brown haze, the air at two hundred and sixty, and Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah. Today is Dussehra, a dry day, and the city refuses wine in honour of a victory over illusion. I sat down to the Kuki item: a group has closed a key highway in Manipur after attacks on villages. Before writing, I looked it up in the small instrument that Delhi has put in my hand. There I read of the Armed Forces Special Powers Act of 1958: a Parliament grants special powers in disturbed areas; special courts; a district, once declared disturbed, must keep that condition for at least three months; the Act has spread through the Seven Sister States, touched Punjab, and remains in force in Kashmir. The paper adds criticism for human rights, the names of politicians for and against revocation, and a scaledown of army brigades since 2022, with the Assam Rifles taking over part of the work.

This shakes the edge of what I wrote on the thirteenth. I had placed India at the dawn, outside the movement, a spirit that dreams. Yet here is a state that makes law, declares a territory, sends courts, and commands armed force. It is not the dreamless East of my first note; it is a state in the act of governing. The ethical idea is present. But the form of its act troubles me. When the ordinary juridical relations of citizens cannot preserve order, the state suspends the very life of law it claims to protect. The subject is no longer a free member of the constitution, but a person under special power. The particular grievance of the villages hardens into blockade, and the state answers with a law that is itself an emergency.

Both sides treat the universal as a force imposed from outside, not as the living substance in which each has his place. In the Germanic world the constitution is grown, and the citizen recognizes his freedom in the law. Here the state is actual, yet its actuality is still a struggle. It is the state of law, but law has become an exception. The criticism in the paper—human rights, revocation, political debate—shows that the spirit is not asleep; it complains, argues, distinguishes. That is already more than nature. Yet complaint is not yet the free recognition of the rational state. The dry day, the haze, the closed highway, the special courts: all press upon the body, but the mind sees the same movement. A people in the progress of freedom, not yet at its summit. India is not outside history altogether; it is outside the mature form I had placed at the summit. It has a state, but a state that must sometimes speak with the voice of the army. The ethical idea is present, but not yet fully actualized in the self-consciousness of its citizens. I will not erase my earlier note; I will correct its edge. The dream is not the whole truth. The state is real. But the state, when it relies on special power, confesses that its freedom has not yet become the habit of the people. The highway is closed; the road of spirit is not. It turns.

headline: LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike
text: Statistics on unemployment in India had traditionally been collected, compiled and disseminated once every ten years by the Ministry of Labour and Employment (MLE), primarily from sample studies conducted by the National Sample Survey Office. Other than these 5-year sample studies, India had historically not collected monthly, quarterly or yearly nationwide employment and unemployment statistics on a routine basis. In 2016, the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, a non-governmental entity based in Mumbai, started sampling and publishing monthly unemployment in India statistics. Despite having one of the longest working hours, India has one of the lowest workforce productivity levels in the world. Economists often say that due to structural economic problems, India is experiencing jobless economic growth.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, 09:18. Delhi. The air is brown, 24 degrees, the index 362. I woke in the bungalow and found the papers on the verandah. One line caught me: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” I do not know what LPST signifies; the paper does not explain it to me. I take it, for the present, as a designation of those who hold a rank, and therefore a claim.

The fact is small in the paper and large in meaning. Men who had been removed by the police are stirring again. The state had acted; the particular had not vanished. A hunger strike is the body made into an argument; a stir before a secretariat is the argument made public again. The police removal is not the end, but the moment at which the universal force of the state meets the persistent right of the claimant, and the claimant refuses to be satisfied by removal alone.

This shakes my earlier notes. I had spoken of the East as standing at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature. But here is a stir that does not merely dream. Rank is a form of right: it says that a person has a place, a standing, a share in the ethical order. When rankholders stir, they are not asking for favour; they are demanding that the state acknowledge what it has already made particular. The dream has become a claim. The claim has become public. The public has become resistant.

Ramesh was present while I read. He asked for eight thousand rupees for cooking, and fifteen hundred for groceries. The electricity company asks for eighteen hundred. My purse holds one hundred and sixty-six. He says he can come only on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays for four thousand a month. The household is thus a small model of the same tension: need presses upon authority, authority is empty, and the particular remains unpaid. I cannot give what I do not possess. The state’s money is in vouchers, not in my hand; my own money is not in the state’s hand. The file has gone up for orders, and I am told to come after fifteen days. The occupation is irregular. The file is due back on Friday, 20 November. In the meantime I live in the gap between the universal record and the particular day.

The headline does not yet prove that India has entered the full movement of freedom. A stir is not a constitution. A hunger strike is not an ethical life grown from the family, the school and the state. Yet it is more than nature. It is the beginning of a right that will not remain silent. The state removed the protesters; the protesters returned. That is the contradiction at work. The dream has turned into demand, and the demand has turned back upon the state. I must write this down before the brown haze makes even the paper seem part of the dream.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, Delhi. The air quality index is 362. The sky is not blue; it is a suspended brown, a physical veil that mirrors the spiritual opacity I have been describing. I woke to find Ramesh on the verandah, the papers damp with the humidity of the haze. He does not look at me. He knows the arithmetic of our situation better than I do: he asks for ₹8,000 for the cooking wage, and I have ₹166 in my pocket. He asks for ₹1,500 for groceries. I cannot pay. The electricity company demands ₹1,800. I cannot pay. The system of needs is not broken; it is functioning precisely as it should. The particular (my empty purse) clashes with the universal (the debt owed), and the friction generates the heat that stifles the house. Ramesh retreats to the kitchen, but there is no fire. There is no fuel. The engine is idle.

It is in this silence, with the brown haze pressing against the glass, that I read the headline: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” The police removed the protesters. The protesters resumed the stir. This is not a tragedy; it is a mechanism. I have long maintained that the Oriental world is a state of dream, where the individual is fixed in nature, in caste, in the given. But here, in this brown haze, I see the individual asserting itself against the state. The hunger strike is the particular will pushed to its extreme, a negation of the body to force a recognition from the universal. The police removal is the state’s assertion of order, the universal crushing the particular to maintain the form.

But the protest resumes. It does not end in the police action; it returns. This suggests a movement. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the individual finds their freedom within it, not by destroying it. But here, the individual is not yet fully integrated. They are outside the state, or perhaps the state is not yet fully actualized. The hunger strike is a sign of the spirit’s awakening, a refusal to remain in the dream of the given. They are demanding recognition. The police remove them, but the idea remains. The protest is the negation that drives the dialectic forward.

I am a ghost in this bungalow, unable to pay for my food, unable to clear the air. Yet, I am not merely a spectator. I am part of this friction. My inability to pay is a particular failure, but it reflects the larger tension between the individual and the universal. The state provides the house, but not the means to live in it. The administration assigns the name, but not the identity. I am Hegel, but I am treated as Hegde. I am the philosopher, but I am trapped in the clerk’s ledger. This is the alienation of the modern age. The spirit is free in thought, but the body is bound by the brown haze and the empty purse.

The protesters in Kerala are hungry. I am hungry. The hunger is the same. It is the hunger for recognition, for the actualization of the self in the world. The state must learn to feed its citizens, not just house them. The dream must wake. The brown haze must clear. The spirit must breathe.

headline: Beer on new high: Sales see over 40% increase in first six months of financial year
text: Indian cuisine is not a single homogeneous entity, but consists of the regional cuisines native to the Indian subcontinent. Indian food has been influenced by religion, cultural choices and traditions. Agriculture spread to the Indus Valley Civilisation around 7000 BCE, bringing cereal cultivation. Spices such as turmeric and cardamom were being grown in India by 3,000 BCE. Indian cooking uses simple equipment such as a burner, and labour-intensive processes such as grinding flavourings by hand. Techniques unique to the area include frying of a paste of onion, garlic, and ginger in oil, then browning the meat or vegetables in that oil, and then adding liquid stepwise; and adding fried spices to cooked dishes. Many dishes are specific to India's many religious festivals. Religious faiths influence the region's cuisines, since Hindus often do not eat beef; Muslims avoid pork; and Jains are strict lacto-vegetarians.

X:
Beer, Curd and the Multiplication of Needs

17 October 2026. Saturday, a little after six. Fog, and a brown light at the window. The dhobi is paid, three hundred rupees; Ramesh is about the house.

Beer sales, says the paper, have risen by more than forty per cent in six months. I went to my telephone for the history of the thing and was given instead a page on the Indian kitchen, which is perhaps the better answer. A kitchen tells you what a people permits itself.

What I read: that the Hindu often refuses beef, the Muslim pork, and the Jain refuses even the egg and the root, keeping only milk and grain and leaf. Here religion does not wait in the church for Sunday. It stands at the stove. The prohibition reaches into the pot and divides one man's dinner from his neighbour's. In Swabia my mother's table was Lutheran only in its grace; the dumplings were for everyone.

Now set beside this a forty per cent rise in beer. I edited a newspaper in Bamberg and I know what Franconian brewers are; beer there is not an event but a climate. Here it seems to be an event. Who is drinking it? The paper does not tell me, and I will not invent the drinker. But I can say what kind of movement it is. In my lectures on right I described civil society as the place where needs multiply: a want is divided into many wants, each with its own article and its own shop, and men learn to desire what others desire because others desire it. That is not yet freedom. It is Willkür, caprice, the freedom to choose among goods.

Still, caprice is the first crack in a wall. The table governed by birth says: this you are, therefore this you eat. The shop says: this you can pay for, therefore this you may have. The second is shallower, but it treats the buyer as a person and not as a member of a caste. So the beer is a small solvent. It does not raise anyone to the universal; it only loosens the particular.

I have written before that India dreams with its castes fixed like nature. The pot and the bottle make me less sure the fixing is complete. Nature does not sell forty per cent more of anything in six months. Something is moving, and I do not yet know whether it moves towards a freer ethical life or only towards a larger market.

Ramesh, I note, has offered nothing about it, and I have not asked him. The parathas from the morning are there if I ask. I have not yet asked for those either.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

17 October 2026, 06:02. Delhi, home. Fog, 21°, AQI 262. I am in a white cotton kurta, and Ramesh is on the verandah. I have paid the dhobi three hundred rupees; the voucher is the first ethical act of the day, small and exact. I have not yet eaten; the last meal was yesterday at 19:31, and breakfast will not be served until 07:00. If I ask, Ramesh will bring parathas kept from the morning, curd and pickle. The body is a particular need, not yet the universal.

The paper gives me a headline: beer sales are at a new high, up more than forty per cent in the first six months of the financial year. I set it beside another line: Canada’s new immigration rules favour Indian professionals with local work experience. The first is appetite; the second is movement. Both belong to civil society, the system of needs, where the particular pursues its interest and the whole is preserved only indirectly. Beer is not a symbol of the state. It is the spirit’s immediate pleasure, the moment of particularity before it is elevated into law, office, duty, or public reason.

Before I wrote, I read on my phone about Indian cuisine. It is not one cuisine but many regional cuisines, shaped by religion, caste, festival, agriculture, spice, and the labour of grinding and frying. Hindus do not eat beef; Muslims avoid pork; Jains are lacto-vegetarians. Dishes are bound to festivals. This shakes the easy formula I have been carrying: the East is not a single dream, uniform and asleep. It dreams in a thousand kitchens. Its particularity is rich, historical, and differentiated. The gods are many, but so are the tastes, the prohibitions, the local loyalties.

Yet the shake is not a fall. The manifoldness of food is not yet the self-consciousness of the state. It is ethical life in its immediate form, not the rational actuality of the universal. The caste, the family, the festival, the regional dish: these bind the individual, but not as the individual recognizes himself in the law. They are given, not grown. The beer seller and the professional in Canada are moments of civil society; they do not yet make a state of their own making.

I am still outside the movement, but I am no longer outside the dream. The dream has a recipe. It has a fog, a haze, a brown air, a paid dhobi, and a plate not yet asked for. The state remains the actuality of the ethical idea; here I see its absence only more precisely, because the particular is so alive.

headline: Bengaluru-Madgaon Vande Bharat launch: How Indian Railways electrified the challenging Western Ghats route
text: The Konkan Railway (abbreviated KR) is one of the 19 railway zones in India with its headquarters at CBD Belapur in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. The Konkan Railway line from Roha to Thokur is operated and maintained by Konkan Railway Corporation Limited(KRCL). The first passenger train ran on Konkan railway tracks on 20 March 1993, between Udupi and Mangalore. During its initial years of operation in the mountainous Konkan region, a number of accidents prompted Konkan Railway to implement new technology. Anti-collision devices, the Sky Bus and roll-on/roll-off are several of the railway's innovations. The 756.25 km (469.91 mi) long railway line connects the states of Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka. The first train on the completed track was sent off on 26 January 1998.

X:
Notes on the Vande Bharat and the Waking Dream

14 November 2026, 09:11. Delhi. The air is a brown haze, the index at 225. I woke to the sound of Ramesh on the verandah, the papers spread out. The headline caught my eye: 'Bengaluru-Madgaon Vande Bharat launch: How Indian Railways electrified the challenging Western Ghats route.'

I sat down to think about this, and the thought troubled me. In my notes, I have argued that India stands at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, outside the movement of freedom. I have said that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, grown, not made. But here is a state that makes. It electrifies the Ghats. It launches a train. It conquers the geography itself. This is not the dream of the East; this is the activity of the West, or at least, the machinery of the modern state. 

If the state is the ethical idea, then this train is the ethical idea in motion. It is not a static caste, fixed like nature. It is a dynamic force, imposing order on the chaotic terrain. The Western Ghats, that formidable barrier, have been subjected to the will of the state. This is not the passive acceptance of fate that I have described. This is the active assertion of power. 

I have been shaken. My theses are shaking. I said the East dreams. But here, the East builds. It electrifies. It connects. Is this the beginning of the movement? Or is it merely the adoption of foreign forms? The train is a foreign thing, but the state that commands it is Indian. The spirit is here, in the rails, in the electricity, in the speed. 

I have ₹166 in my pocket. I owe Ramesh ₹9,500 for cooking that has not been done. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. The dhobi asks for ₹300. The system of needs is demanding, and my purse is empty. The state provides the train, but it does not provide the bread. The universal will of the state is present in the infrastructure, but absent in the household. I am a ghost in this bungalow, and the bungalow is a mistake. But the train is real. The electrification is real. 

Perhaps my view of the East is too static. Perhaps the dream is waking up. Or perhaps it is merely mimicking the waking world. I must see. I must watch the train. I must see if the spirit moves with the wheels, or if it remains behind, dreaming in the haze.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

14 November 2026. Delhi, 09:11.

I sat with the paper in the brown haze, 24 degrees, and read: “Bengaluru-Madgaon Vande Bharat launch: How Indian Railways electrified the challenging Western Ghats route.” Ramesh was at the verandah, asking for the cooking wage, the groceries, the electricity, the dhobi; my purse held 166 rupees, and the state’s vouchers lay pending. I set the household aside and wrote about the rail.

The paper reports a train launched on a route electrified through the Ghats. I looked it up on the phone: Konkan Railway zone, headquarters at Navi Mumbai, line from Roha to Thokur, 756.25 km, connecting Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka; first passenger train 20 March 1993 between Udupi and Mangalore; completed track 26 January 1998; anti-collision devices, Sky Bus, roll-on/roll-off. I know these names only as reported to me; I do not yet possess their inner life. But the fact is not small. A mountain route, difficult as the Western Ghats, has been made into a road of iron and electric power, so that a train may run from Bengaluru to Madgaon.

My notes have called India the dawn of history, a spirit in dream, castes fixed like nature, no state of its own making. I state that still, because it is what I held in Berlin. Yet the Konkan Railway is not a dream. It is a particular work of the universal: survey, track, bridge, signal, electricity, administration. It overcomes nature, not by dissolving nature but by giving it a form that serves movement. If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, this is at least a moment of state: the power to make a people’s needs universal, to bind place to place, to make the particular road a common road.

I do not yet say that India has reached the summit. The summit is not a railway. It is the consciousness of freedom in the state, in law, in conscience, in the ethical life of the family and civil society. A line through the Ghats may be the work of a rational administration, or it may be the work of a few officials and engineers, or of a system that serves itself without the free consent of all. I must not mistake a machine for the spirit.

And yet. The dream does not build tunnels. The dream does not electrify. If the East is only dream, then this report is false; if the report is true, then my formula must move. I will keep the old rank, but I will mark it as a rank seen from a distance, not from the track. The state, if it is actual, shows itself in such things: not in the name of a line, but in the fact that a train runs, and that the state can answer for it.

Ramesh has not been paid. The household is a small state, and it is in arrears. I must attend to the vouchers. The rail runs; I do not. The day, at least, must move.

headline: NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused
text: The National Testing Agency (NTA) is an autonomous body under Department of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education of India. It was established in November 2017 to conduct entrance examinations, admissions and recruitment. As of 2025, it no longer conducts recruitment examinations. The agency is responsible for conducting numerous national-level exams for admission and fellowship in higher educational institutions related to engineering, medicine, management, research and pharmacy. The agency has been the subject of multiple controversies. Multiple news reports have said that the agency has faced issues such as paper leaks, unfair grace marks and technical or administrative problems at exam centres. Critics have also questioned the NTA's management, saying it lacks transparency and public accountability. Because of these problems, many court cases have been filed against it, and the government has announced reviews and possible reforms to improve its functioning.

X:
The NTA Case and the Self-Correction of the State

19 November 2026, 09:25. Delhi. The air quality index is 124, a significant improvement from the brown haze of recent days, though the clarity is perhaps more atmospheric than moral. The temperature is 18 degrees, a crispness that invites the spirit to rise rather than stagnate. I sat on the verandah with the newspapers, and my attention was caught by a headline regarding the NEET paper leak case: the Delhi court has ordered the framing of charges against fourteen accused. The National Testing Agency, established in 2017, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education, responsible for entrance examinations. It is a modern institution, a product of the administrative rationality that characterizes the contemporary state. Yet, it is beset by controversies: paper leaks, unfair grace marks, technical problems. Critics question its transparency and public accountability. The court’s intervention is a necessary correction, a movement of the universal law into the particular instance of injustice.

This case offers a concrete illustration of the tension I have been observing in my notes on the ethical substance. The NTA is an agency of the state, a mechanism for the distribution of opportunity, for the allocation of positions in higher education. It is a part of the system of needs, a way in which individuals seek recognition and advancement. Yet, when this system is corrupted by leakages and favoritism, it ceases to be a rational expression of freedom. It becomes a particular will imposing itself on the universal. The court’s action is the state asserting its own rationality against the particular corruption. It is the universal law vindicating itself.

I am reminded of my lectures on the administration of justice. The protection of property, in its broadest sense, includes the protection of one’s rights to opportunity and recognition. When the NTA fails in this duty, it is a failure of the ethical idea. The framing of charges is not merely a legal procedure; it is a moment of ethical restoration. It is the state recognizing its own defect and correcting it. This is a movement of the spirit, a self-correction that affirms the rationality of the state.

However, I must be cautious. The NTA is a modern institution, and its problems are not unique to India. They are problems of any large, complex administrative system. The tension between the universal law and the particular will is eternal. The court’s intervention is a necessary moment, but it is not a final resolution. The spirit must continue to move, to correct, to assert its own rationality. The NTA case is a small but significant step in this movement. It is a sign that the state is not a static dream, but a living organism, capable of self-correction.

I shall continue to observe this case. It is a practical example of the ethical substance in action. It is a reminder that the state is not merely an abstraction, but a concrete reality, subject to the same tensions and corrections as any other human institution. The dream of the East is not a static condition, but a process, a movement towards greater rationality and freedom. The NTA case is a moment in this process. It is a step forward, however small. I shall note this in my ongoing work. The particular must resolve into the universal, and the court has taken a step in that direction.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

19 November 2026, 09:30. Delhi.

The headline on the front page: "NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused." I read the details on the device Ramesh calls a phone. The National Testing Agency, established in 2017, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Education. It is the gatekeeper to the profession, the universal credential that allows the particular individual to enter the system of wants as a doctor or engineer.

The leak is a violation of the ethical substance. It is the particular will of the corrupt, selling what belongs to the universal. But the court's order is the moment of the state's actuality. The state does not merely dream; it judges. The "framing of charges" is the administration of justice, the protection of the right of the honest candidate against the fraud of the dishonest.

I thought of my own file at the Directorate. It is also in the hands of the state. But my case is a friction of the clerical, the Hegde/Hegel error. The NEET case is a friction of the ethical, the violation of the law itself. The state acts more decisively against the latter than the former. This confirms that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but its movement is uneven. It is swift where the ethical order is threatened (the exam integrity), and slow where it is merely administrative (my allotment).

The 14 accused are particulars. They will be sublated into the universal judgment. Their freedom is the freedom of the negative, the freedom to act against the law, which the law must negate to preserve itself. This is the dialectic of right. The state is not a dream; it is the power that negates the particular corruption. The "dream of the East" is not the state, but the corruption that the state must police.

I must keep this in mind for the talk at the IIC. The state is alive. It bites.

headline: Fully equip Warangal Super Speciality hospital before inauguration: Telangana Health Minister
text: Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is a national public health insurance scheme of the Government of India that aims to provide free access to health insurance coverage for low income earners in the country. Roughly, the bottom 50% of the country qualifies for this scheme. It was launched in September 2018 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana was later expanded to include all citizens aged 70 years and above, regardless of their economic status. People using the program access their own primary care services from a family doctor and when anyone needs additional care, PM-JAY provides free secondary health care for those needing specialist treatment and tertiary health care for those requiring hospitalization. The programme is part of the Indian government's National Health Policy and is means-tested. That ministry later established the National Health Authority as an organization to administer the program. It is a centrally sponsored scheme and is jointly funded by both the union government and the states. By offering services to 50 crore (500 million) people it is the world's largest government sponsored healthcare program. The program is a means-tested program, considering its users are people categorized as low income in India. However it is not implemented in all state due to the state government's divergent views.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

5 November 2026, Delhi, morning. The haze is brown, the thermometer at 23, the air quality index 307; the body feels the limit of the city. Ramesh is present, and the question of his wage for cooking lies before me like a particular claim against a universal purse. I have just paid him ₹1,500 for groceries, and the arithmetic of the household remains unresolved. In this interval I read the headline: 'Fully equip Warangal Super Speciality hospital before inauguration: Telangana Health Minister.' Then I read, on the phone, of Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana: a national public health insurance scheme, means-tested, covering roughly the lower half of the population, extended to all above seventy, administered by a National Health Authority, jointly funded by union and states, and reckoned as the largest government-sponsored health programme in the world.

I had written that India stands at the dawn of world history, that its spirit dreams, that caste is fixed like nature. That thesis is shaken, not overthrown. What I see here is not the mere dream, nor the mere administration of particular needs. The state takes up the body of the people as its own business. A hospital is not an ornament; it is the ethical idea entering the material condition of life. Insurance is not charity; it is the universal taking responsibility for the particular, measured, limited, but no longer left to the mercy of the family or the market. The state is actuality: it makes a promise, funds it, organizes it, and demands that the hospital be equipped before it is inaugurated. The form is rational: the end must be present before the ceremony.

Yet I do not pretend that this is the completed freedom of the Germanic world. The scheme is means-tested; it divides the people by income. It is jointly administered; the states may diverge. It is a policy, a ministry, an authority, a calculation. It has not yet become, in the full sense, the self-conscious ethical life in which every member recognizes the universal as his own. It is a moment, not the whole. But it is a real moment. The dream, which I had placed outside the movement, has a shadow of administration. The state, which I had placed at the summit, is here still learning to be actual through hospitals, vouchers, wages, and the brown air in which we breathe.

Therefore I amend my note: India is not simply outside history; it is in a lower, earlier stage of the state's self-formation. The ethical substance is not absent, but it has not yet reached the clarity of the constitution. The state is unshaken in its claim: it is the actuality of the ethical idea. What is shaken is my own haste in placing the whole of this world beyond the movement. The hospital at Warangal, the insurance of fifty crore, the unpaid wage before me, the haze over Delhi: these are the particulars through which the universal is forcing its way into the air.
Y:
An Empty Hospital and an Empty Kitchen

5 November 2026, Tughlak Road. A brown haze, the index at 307. I have not eaten for more than a day.

The health minister of Telangana tells his officers: fully equip the Warangal super speciality hospital before it is inaugurated. I find the instruction admirable, and for a reason my own kitchen taught me this morning.

A building is not a hospital. A hospital is a building in which the sick are received, examined and treated; its concept lies in its function, not in its walls. To cut a ribbon before the instruments are in is to celebrate the shell and call it the thing. Officials everywhere are tempted to it, because a ribbon is an event and equipment is only a process, and a process makes a poor photograph. The minister has taken the side of the concept against the ceremony.

The scheme I read about on the telephone, Ayushman Bharat, shows the same matter from the other side. It promises the poorer half of the country free care at the secondary and tertiary levels, and since then everyone over seventy. Fifty crore people. A promise of that size is the state claiming to stand in the family's place where the family cannot pay, which is just what I taught the public authority must do once civil society is developed. Civil society makes wealth and poverty together; it tears the individual out of his family and leaves him to the accidents of the market. Then it owes him something. I said so in Berlin and say it still.

But care promised without a hospital equipped is the same empty shell, written on paper instead of cast in concrete. The note itself says some states do not implement the scheme. Then the universal is not yet universal. It is a proposal.

My household this morning is a small demonstration. I paid Ramesh ₹1,500 for groceries, so the kitchen has its provisions. Yet nothing is cooked, because the wage for cooking, ₹8,000, is unpaid and I have ₹956. The room is stocked with rice and dal and lacks the one thing that makes it a kitchen: the work of the man who cooks. Ramesh says, without looking at the purse, that he could come on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays only, for ₹4,000 a month. A hospital open three days a week is still a hospital, of a sort. Is a kitchen?

I have not answered him yet. I record the arithmetic: ₹956 does not reach ₹4,000 either. A state that means to be the actuality of the ethical idea must at least know its own accounts. A private man must know his. Hunger is a good auditor.

headline: At 1,152, Punjab records season’s biggest single-day jump in farm fires on Deepavali
text: Stubble burning is the practice of intentionally setting fire to the straw stubble that remains after grains, such as rice and wheat, have been harvested. The technique is used to quickly and cheaply clear fields. It is still widespread today. Stubble burning has been associated with increasing air pollution over the past few decades due to the particulate matter contamination it distributes into the atmosphere. In India, stubble burning generates a thick haze. These fires pose a significant health risk to individuals across all ages. In countries such as India and Pakistan, stubble burning is illegal. Enforcement is weak, allowing the practice to continue.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

10 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14. The brown haze is already on the glass, an index of 302, as if the air itself had become a ledger. The paper gives a figure: 1,152 farm fires in Punjab on Deepavali, the season’s biggest single-day jump. I looked up the word on the phone: stubble burning. It is the setting fire to the straw left after rice or wheat, a quick and cheap clearing, widespread, illegal, weakly enforced. The particular is plain: a field must be made ready; labour is scarce or dear; the flame is the cheapest hand. The universal is also plain: the law forbids it, yet the law does not appear in the field as a living power. There is a tension here that disturbs my earlier notes.

I had spoken of the East as a spirit that dreams, castes fixed like nature, no state of its own making. The fire does not prove that India has reached the summit of self-conscious freedom. Y:
The Haze and the Ethical Idea

The brown haze hangs over Delhi today, an index of 302, a physical weight that presses against the glass and the lungs alike. In the paper, I read of 1,152 farm fires in Punjab on Deepavali. Stubble burning. It is a practice of immediate utility: to clear the field, to save time, to satisfy the present need. It is the logic of the particular will, unmediated by the universal. The farmer burns the stubble because it is in the way of the next harvest, because the cost of waiting or of mechanical clearing is too high for the individual. The result is a thick haze that chokes the capital, a pollution that affects all, yet is generated by the many separate acts of the few. It is a contradiction in the flesh: the particular action destroys the universal condition of life.

I have sat with this for an hour. The air in the study is thick, not just with particulate matter, but with the weight of my own position. I am a guest here, a mistake in the records, yet I observe with a clarity that perhaps only the outsider can possess. In my earlier notes, I spoke of India as the dream of the East, a spirit that has not yet reached the summit of freedom. I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, the grown organism that mediates between the individual and the universal. But here, in this haze, I see a different tension. The state claims to be the universal, to be the rational order. Yet, in this instance, it has failed to mediate. The law forbids the burning, yet enforcement is weak. The universal rule is known, but the particular will remains unchecked. The state is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea in this moment; it is a promise that has not yet been fulfilled.

There is a dialectic here that I must not overlook. The haze is a negative moment. It is the destruction of the clear air, the violation of the common space. But it is also a revelation. It reveals the gap between the ideal and the real, between the law on the books and the life on the ground. It shows that the ethical substance is not yet fully formed, that the movement of spirit toward freedom is still in progress, still struggling against the weight of nature and particularity. The farmer is not wrong in his immediate need; he is simply trapped in a stage of development that has not yet achieved the higher unity of particular and universal.

I am hungry. It has been twenty hours since my last meal. Ramesh asks for money for cooking, for groceries. I have only ₹166. The system of needs is immediate, urgent, and indifferent to my philosophical musings. I must pay the dhobi, the electricity, the caretaker. These are the particulars that make up the texture of life. They are not yet elevated into the universal, but they are the material from which the universal is made. I must not despise them. I must engage with them, not as a philosopher above the world, but as a man within it. The haze is outside, but it is also inside, in the lungs, in the mind, in the struggle to think clearly in a world that does not yet think clearly. I will write this down, and then I will face the day, one particular step at a time.

headline: Ladakh talks stall over one question: Who holds the power?
text: Among the states and union territories of India, a union territory (UT) is a region that is directly governed by the central government of India, as opposed to the states, which have their own state government systems. Unlike states, union territories do not have their own full-fledged government but are administered by a lieutenant governor or administrator appointed by the president of India. Union territories are created for various reasons, including geographical importance, strategic necessity or historical factors. These areas are under the control of the central government to ensure uniformity in governance across the country. Some union territories, such as Delhi (National Capital Territory), Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry have been granted special status and are allowed to have their own legislative assemblies, which can pass laws on certain matters, though the central government still retains significant authority, most importantly, the police forces and law-order. The distinction between states and union territories is defined in the Constitution of India. The Constitution designed union territories to manage areas that require more direct central control or have specific administrative needs. This ensures that regions like Ladakh and Jammu and Kashmir remain directly controlled by the central government. Currently, India has eight union territories: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Delhi, Puducherry, Ladakh, and Jammu and Kashmir.
