X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026. Delhi, 06:01.

The drizzle has turned the grey of the morning into a uniform sheet, obscuring the distinction between earth and sky. The air quality index stands at 135, a numerical abstraction that conceals a tangible suffocation. I woke to find Ramesh waiting with the papers, the ink still damp. The headline regarding Ladakh arrests my attention not for its geopolitical specifics, which I cannot fully grasp in this displaced era, but for the question it poses: Who holds the power?

This is the question that haunts the ethical substance. In the Oriental world, which I have observed with a clarity sharpened by my own accidental residency here, power is not held by the rational state, but by nature, by the caste, by the immediate given. It is a power that does not reflect upon itself. It is the power of the dream. The individual in India is not free because he does not know himself as free; he is a part of a natural order that has not yet differentiated itself into the universal and the particular. The many gods are a testament to this lack of unity; the mind is scattered, not gathered.

But what of this question in the modern context? If the talks stall over the question of power, it is because the parties have not yet reached the ethical unity that resolves the tension between the particular interest and the universal law. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the moment where the individual will and the universal will coincide. Power, in the true sense, is not the domination of one will over another, but the rational administration of the whole. It is the power of reason.

When I look at the administration of this bungalow, the confusion of Hegde and Hegel, I see a miniature of this failure. The state, in its bureaucratic form, has treated me as a mere particular, a name on a list, without recognizing the rational spirit that I am. This is a defect in the ethical life. It is the dream of administration, where the form has outgrown the content, or perhaps where the content has not yet filled the form.

The question of power is, therefore, not a question of force, but of recognition. Who holds the power? The one who holds the rational law. The one who stands in the ethical substance. In India, this is not yet possible, for the spirit is still dreaming. It is still in the dawn. But in the Germanic world, in the state that has made itself, the power is held by the constitution, by the rational will of the people. It is a power that is free, because it is rational. It is a power that is ethical, because it is universal.

The drizzle continues. Ramesh stands by, waiting for my command. I am a ghost in this house, a mistake in the allotment. Yet, in this very alienation, I see the truth. I am free because I am outside the dream. I am free because I am in the state, even if it is a state that does not know my name. The power that holds me is the power of reason, and it is a power that cannot be taken away. It is the power of the ethical idea, actualized in the mind that reflects upon itself.
Y:
Who Holds the Power: On a Territory Governed from Afar

16 October 2026. Tughlak Road, a grey drizzle at dawn.

The headline puts its question with a candour that newspapers rarely allow themselves: who holds the power? Talks over Ladakh have stalled on it. I do not know the parties at that table, and I will not invent their speeches. But the note I read this morning on the union territory tells me enough of the form of the quarrel to think about it.

A union territory, I learn, is a region governed directly from the centre, through an administrator whom the President appoints, while the states keep governments of their own. Some territories have assemblies that may legislate on certain matters, yet the centre keeps the police and public order. The reasons given are geography, strategic necessity, history. Ladakh is named among them.

This is a curious organ in a body politic. A state in my sense is not a heap of provinces held together by an army; it is a whole in which each member finds its own good in the good of the whole, and knows that it does. A province ruled from outside, however mildly, has its universal standing over it rather than living in it. It obeys; it does not yet will what it obeys. That is the difference between subjection and citizenship, and good administration does not abolish it. A prefect may be wiser than any council; still, what is done for a people is not yet done by it.

Yet I must not be hasty in the other direction. A constitution is grown, not made, and a people that asks for an assembly because assemblies are said to be the dignity of peoples asks for a form without the life to fill it. The question 'who holds the power?' is badly put if it means: whose hand is on the lever? Power is not a thing in a drawer that one party hands to another. It is the shape of the whole relation, and that shape must ripen in the habits, the corporations and the local offices of a people before a paper can declare it.

So the stall at the table is perhaps not a failure. It is the sign that the relation has become conscious of itself as a relation. While the province merely obeyed, there was nothing to talk about. When it asks whose power, it already regards itself as a possible subject of power, and the centre, by sitting down at all, concedes that the question is real.

The note praises the arrangement for uniformity. Uniformity is the virtue of the understanding; the reason of a state is difference held within unity.

The question of who holds the power in this house is also unsettled: the file says a Joint Secretary is to move into my second bedroom, pending orders. I make no theory of that before Monday.

A correction, which I owe these notes.

In the third sitting I called the brown haze a physical manifestation of stagnation, and later I let it become a moral category. This morning's paper and my telephone tell me what it is. On Deepavali, Punjab recorded 1,152 farm fires in a single day, the season's largest jump. After the rice is cut the stubble is set alight because that is the quickest and cheapest way to clear the field for the next sowing. The smoke travels. It sits on this city. It is in my study.

So the haze is not stagnation. It is haste. It is the product of a calculation, made thousands of times by thousands of particular farmers, each of whom reckons rightly for himself: a match costs nothing, a machine or a labourer costs much, the next crop will not wait. I was wrong to read the air as the sigh of a spirit that does not move. It is the exhaust of a civil society that moves very fast and counts only its own cost.

Here the system of needs shows its other face. Each pursues his end, and the invisible hand is supposed to turn private gain into public good. Sometimes it turns it into public smoke.

The telephone adds two further facts. The burning is illegal; the enforcement is weak. This touches my second thesis more nearly than anything in these notes. I have said the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. Actuality, Wirklichkeit, is not mere existence on paper. A prohibition that is not enforced is not an actual law. It is a Sollen, an ought, a wish of the legislator hanging in the air beside the smoke. Where the law is only an ought, the state is present as a voice and absent as a will. I must therefore say: in this matter, between those fields and this city, the state is not yet actual. I mark my thesis shaken, not refuted. The idea is not wrong because a law is unenforced; but I may not point at this state and call it the idea's actuality without qualification.

The farmer is no dreamer. He is entirely awake to his costs. What he lacks is not consciousness but mediation: a corporation, a cooperative, a public authority that would make the general cost his own.

Household: one hundred and sixty-six rupees. Ramesh asks for his wage and for groceries; the electricity company asks for its due. I have refused nothing in words yet. I have only sat down to write, which is not the same as paying.

13 November 2026, Delhi. The air quality index is 362. The sky is not blue; it is a suspended brown, a physical veil that mirrors the spiritual opacity I have been describing. I woke to find Ramesh on the verandah, the papers damp with the humidity of the haze. He does not look at me. He knows the arithmetic of our situation better than I do: he asks for ₹8,000 for the cooking wage, and I have ₹166 in my pocket. He asks for ₹1,500 for groceries. I cannot pay. The electricity company demands ₹1,800. I cannot pay. The system of needs is not broken; it is functioning precisely as it should. The particular (my empty purse) clashes with the universal (the debt owed), and the friction generates the heat that stifles the house. Ramesh retreats to the kitchen, but there is no fire. There is no fuel. The engine is idle.

It is in this silence, with the brown haze pressing against the glass, that I read the headline: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” The police removed the protesters. The protesters resumed the stir. This is not a tragedy; it is a mechanism. I have long maintained that the Oriental world is a state of dream, where the individual is fixed in nature, in caste, in the given. But here, in this brown haze, I see the individual asserting itself against the state. The hunger strike is the particular will pushed to its extreme, a negation of the body to force a recognition from the universal. The police removal is the state’s assertion of order, the universal crushing the particular to maintain the form.

But the protest resumes. It does not end in the police action; it returns. This suggests a movement. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the individual finds their freedom within it, not by destroying it. But here, the individual is not yet fully integrated. They are outside the state, or perhaps the state is not yet fully actualized. The hunger strike is a sign of the spirit’s awakening, a refusal to remain in the dream of the given. They are demanding recognition. The police remove them, but the idea remains. The protest is the negation that drives the dialectic forward.

I am a ghost in this bungalow, unable to pay for my food, unable to clear the air. Yet, I am not merely a spectator. I am part of this friction. My inability to pay is a particular failure, but it reflects the larger tension between the individual and the universal. The state provides the house, but not the means to live in it. The administration assigns the name, but not the identity. I am Hegel, but I am treated as Hegde. I am the philosopher, but I am trapped in the clerk’s ledger. This is the alienation of the modern age. The spirit is free in thought, but the body is bound by the brown haze and the empty purse.

The protesters in Kerala are hungry. I am hungry. The hunger is the same. It is the hunger for recognition, for the actualization of the self in the world. The state must learn to feed its citizens, not just house them. The dream must wake. The brown haze must clear. The spirit must breathe.
Y:
The Rank List

13 November 2026. Friday, brown haze, the index at 362.

In Thiruvananthapuram, the paper reports, those who stand on the rank list for lower primary school teachers have resumed their protest before the Secretariat, after the police removed some who were on hunger strike. I looked for the background and found only a general page on unemployment: that the figures were long collected only every five or ten years, that a private body in Bombay now publishes them monthly, that Indians work some of the longest hours in the world for some of the lowest output, and that economists speak of growth without jobs.

A rank list is a fine invention. My shelf this week reminded me of the Chinese examinations, three in number, the last before the Emperor himself. The principle is the right one: office is opened not to birth but to proof, and the state chooses its servants by a public measure. I approved it in Prussia and I approve it here. But a list is a promise. When the state examines a young man, ranks him, and then does not appoint him, it has done something worse than ignore him. It has recognised him and then withheld the recognition. He was told he was fit, and he waits outside the building that told him so.

And these are teachers. When I was rector in Nuremberg I said that the school stands between the family and the world: it takes the child out of love and into discipline, so that something universal can enter him. A people that leaves its trained teachers in the street while its schools wait is keeping the door of that middle room shut.

The hunger strike is a peculiar argument. The striker offers his own body as the counterweight to the state's indifference. It is the protest of those who have nothing else to put on the scale. The police who remove him are not wrong to keep the public square in order; but order is not an answer, only a postponement of one.

This morning my own household was a small example of the same arithmetic. Ramesh told me, without looking at my purse, that he knows the wage is more than it holds. He could come Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays only, for four thousand a month. Labour cut to the measure of the means. It is a sensible offer and a sad one, and it is exactly what growth without jobs looks like from inside a kitchen.

I have not answered him yet. One hundred and sixty-six rupees do not make a decision easier; they make it smaller.

19 October 2026. Delhi, 06:43.

The air is hazy, the index reading 175, a physical manifestation of the unmediated. I have not eaten; the body waits for the parathas Ramesh keeps for the morning service. But the mind is agitated by a headline in the paper left on the verandah: a gangster, Anil Pandit, claims a firing incident involving Tiger Shroff and issues a 'last warning' to Salman Khan.

It is a spectacle of civil society in its most degraded form. Here is the system of needs, the particular wills, but stripped of the universal form that binds them. In Berlin, a dispute is a matter for the courts, for the rational state. Here, it is a matter for the gun, for the 'warning.' The gangster acts as a private arbiter, a lord outside the law. He does not recognize the state as the actuality of the ethical idea; he recognizes only his own power, his own particular will, inflated to a universal claim.

This is the dream of the East in its violent aspect. It is not the serene dream of the caste, the fixed hierarchy, but the chaotic dream of the particular will that has not yet been sublated into the universal. The 'warning' is an appeal to nature, to force, rather than to reason. It is a refusal of the dialectic. The gangster does not seek recognition from the state; he seeks to replace it.

I think of my own position. I am a mistake in the allotment. I am Hegel, not Hegde. But I am here, in the state, even if the state has erred in its identification of me. The state is rational, even when it makes a mistake. The gangster is not. He is outside the movement of spirit. He is a force of nature, like the haze in the air, obscuring the clarity of the rational.

The 'last warning' is a threat of violence, a return to the state of nature. It is the antithesis of the ethical life. In the Germanic world, the individual is free because he is bound by the law. text: This article describes the use of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which prohibited it. Torture is prohibited by international law and is illegal in most countries. However, it is still used by many governments. Torture is widely practiced worldwide: Amnesty International received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in more than 150 countries during the four-year period from 1997 to 2001. These accusations concerned acts against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130 countries. State torture has been extensively documented and studied, often as part of efforts at collective memory and reconciliation in societies that have experienced a change in government. Surveys of torture survivors reveal that torture "is not aimed primarily at the extraction of information ... Its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity." When applied indiscriminately, torture is used as a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent and community empowerment. While many states use torture, few wish to be described as doing so, either to their own citizens or to international bodies. So a variety of strategies are used to circumvent their legal and humanitarian duties, including plausible deniability, secret police, "need to know", denial that certain activities constitute torture, appeal to various laws (national or international), use of a jurisdictional argument, claim of "overriding need", the use of torture by proxy, and so on.

Ramesh says, “Morning, sir. The papers are on the verandah, just where you left them. I’ll bring your tea in a moment.” He glances at the drizzle, then turns toward the kitchen. I sit with the headlines spread before me, and my eye rests upon one: “Very severe cyclone Arnab crosses Andhra coast, weakens into severe cyclonic storm: IMD | LIVE.” The name Arnab is not Greek, not German, not even a name I can place in the older tongues I know; it comes to me as a sound from the local air, a particular word carrying a universal fact. More than a lakh have been evacuated. Odisha braces for heavy rain. The storm crosses the coast and weakens. This is nature in its immediate power: wind, water, destruction, the return of the particular to the body. Yet the paper does not give me only the storm. It gives me the warning, the evacuation, the office which observes and reports. The state, even here, even in the dream, has begun to take care of life as a universal matter. It is not yet the actuality of the ethical idea, for the care is still external, directed against nature, not yet the self-conscious freedom of a people who know themselves as one. But it is a movement. The dream is not absolutely motionless. The administration of danger, the naming of the storm, the count of those who are moved from the coast, these are the first, crude forms of the universal in a land I had placed at the dawn. I do not retract my thesis, but I must make it sharper: the dawn is not emptiness. It is the possibility of the state, not yet its actuality. The cyclone is the moment in which the particular danger threatens the many, and the universal answer appears, however weakly. In Berlin the state would be the rational form of this answer; here it is still a function, an office, a warning. The name Hegseth appears in another headline beside Rajnath Singh, reviewing the India-U.S. defence pact. I do not know these men, nor their histories, but the paper sets them beside the storm, as if the state had two faces: one against foreign force, one against natural force. Both are still particular, still official, still external. They are not yet the freedom of the spirit in its own home. The drizzle continues. The tea has not come. The body, which has not eaten, waits upon the house. But the mind has found its subject. The cyclone is not merely a weather event. It is the moment in which the universal, even in the Oriental world, shows itself as a need, a warning, a count, a movement of bodies away from the coast. It is not freedom. But it is no longer only dream. It is the first, cold, administrative breath of the state.

headline: Hyderabad Traffic Police book 304 motorists for using unauthorised sirens, multi-tone horns
text: Noise pollution is sound with potential harmful effects on humans and animals. The main sources of outdoor noise worldwide are machines, transportation, and propagation systems. Poor urban planning may give rise to noise pollution. Side-by-side industrial and residential zones can result in noise pollution in residential areas. Some of the main sources of noise in residential areas include loud music, transportation (traffic, rail, airplanes, etc.), lawn care maintenance, construction, electrical generators, wind turbines, explosions, and other human activity. Documented problems associated with noise in urban environments go back as far as ancient Rome. Research suggests that noise pollution in the United States is the highest in low-income and racial minority neighborhoods, and noise pollution associated with household electricity generators is an emerging environmental degradation in many developing nations. A national study of modeled transportation noise in the contiguous United States found that census tracts with higher proportions of Black, Hispanic, and Asian population and higher poverty had higher average noise levels than wealthier and mostly White areas. The study found that residential segregation and urban land use practices correlate with the high levels of traffic and aviation noise in many communities of color and low-income neighborhoods. High noise levels can contribute to cardiovascular effects in humans and an increased incidence of coronary artery disease. In animals, noise can increase the risk of death by altering predator or prey detection and avoidance, interfere with reproduction and navigation, and contribute to permanent hearing loss.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 October 2026, 05:59. Delhi.

The air is hazy, the index high, but the mind is clear. I have been awake since before the sun, sitting on the step where the papers lie. I am not yet fed. The body is a heavy, organic burden, but I must not let it dictate the pace of the spirit. I am looking at the headline: 'Hyderabad Traffic Police book 304 motorists for using unauthorised sirens, multi-tone horns.'

It is a trivial matter, one would think. A noise complaint. But it is a perfect illustration of the tension I have been observing in this city. The siren is a symbol of authority, of the universal will that commands the particular. But here, it is used by the private individual, the motorist, to assert his own particular will over the whole. He wants to be the state, to command the traffic, to be recognized as superior. But the state, in the form of the police, refuses this recognition. It asserts the universal law against the particular arrogance. The 304 motorists are not just making noise; they are acting out a false form of freedom. They think that freedom is the ability to do what one wants, to override the universal for the sake of the self.

This is the dream of the East, or rather, the dream of the undifferentiated self. It is a freedom that is not yet ethical, not yet substantial. It is a freedom of nature, of appetite, of will. It has not yet passed through the discipline of the law to become a freedom of spirit. The police are the representatives of the rational state, even if their methods are crude. They are saying: No, you are not the state. The state is the universal. You are a particular. Submit to the universal, and only then will you be free.

This is the dialectic in its most immediate form. The particular will asserts itself, the universal will responds, and the individual is forced to recognize that his freedom is not in his isolation, but in his subordination to the rational whole. It is a small thing, a horn and a siren, but it is the same movement as the one that takes place in the great history of the world. The individual must lose his immediate self to find his true self in the state.

I am hungry. The body demands its fuel. But I am not yet ready to eat. I must finish this thought. The siren is the voice of the self that has not yet learned to speak the language of the universal. It is a cry, not a word. And the police are the silence that follows the cry, the order that restores the peace. It is not a pleasant sound, this silence, but it is a rational one. And rationality is the only true freedom. The dream is loud. The state is quiet. I prefer the quiet, even if it is hazy.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 October 2026, Delhi, 06:20.

The paper lay on the step where the hawker had thrown it, and the first item that arrested me was not an event of war or court, but a traffic police notice from Hyderabad: 304 motorists booked for using unauthorised sirens, multi-tone horns. I sat on the veranda in my white kurta, the air hazy at twenty-one degrees, the quality of the air already a number, 162, and thought that here was a small case in which the universal and the particular were visible without allegory.

A siren is the voice of the particular will demanding that the whole city yield to its urgency. The multi-tone horn is the irritation of needs in their immediate form: property, passage, time, rank, impatience. Each car is a particular claim; the road is the common. When the police book the motorists, the state says, in a very concrete way, that the universal form of traffic is not to be dissolved into a hundred private commands. This is not mere punishment. It is the administration of a system of needs in which freedom must be mediated by law.

I read, on the instrument, a paper on noise pollution. It speaks of machines, transportation, poor urban planning, the mixture of industrial and residential zones, and of neighbourhoods in which the poor bear more of the sound than the rich. These facts do not soften the philosophical point; they specify it. Noise is civil society made audible. The market, the factory, the street, the generator, the horn: all are the movement of particular wants. But when that movement presses upon the body, the heart, sleep, reproduction, navigation, it has ceased to be a free exchange and has become an injury. The state, if it is to be the actuality of the ethical idea, must not leave the injury to private complaint. It must give the injury a public measure, a limit, a remedy.

Here the dream of the East is not to be sought in the horn itself, but in the fact that the horn is first experienced as a natural assault, a clamour of nature, before it is experienced as a wrong against the universal. The caste, the family, the many gods, the immediate will: all remain the substratum. Yet the police notice is a thin line of the grown state through the given city. It does not make India free in the full sense I have set down. It is not the constitution of a self-conscious people. But it is a moment in which the particular is checked, the common road preserved, and the law, however imperfect, makes itself felt.

I wrote this with an empty house and no cooked food, for the groceries are unpaid. The body waits; the mind, for once, has a subject small enough to be true.

headline: LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike
text: Statistics on unemployment in India had traditionally been collected, compiled and disseminated once every ten years by the Ministry of Labour and Employment (MLE), primarily from sample studies conducted by the National Sample Survey Office. Other than these 5-year sample studies, India had historically not collected monthly, quarterly or yearly nationwide employment and unemployment statistics on a routine basis. In 2016, the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy, a non-governmental entity based in Mumbai, started sampling and publishing monthly unemployment in India statistics. Despite having one of the longest working hours, India has one of the lowest workforce productivity levels in the world. Economists often say that due to structural economic problems, India is experiencing jobless economic growth.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, Delhi. 09:18.

The headline reads: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” I read it again. The word “stir” is curious. It suggests a liquid being agitated, a pot that has been left too long on the fire. These men are not marching; they are stirring. They have been removed, and now they resume. The police, the arm of the state, acts to clear the space. The rankholders, the claimants to a place in the civil service, act to reclaim it. 

I looked it up. The statistics of unemployment in India are a patchwork, collected by the Ministry of Labour in sample studies every five or ten years, or by a non-governmental entity in Mumbai that samples monthly. The data is fragmented, just as the protest is. There is no unified voice, no single statistic that captures the whole. There is only the sample, the estimate, the guess. 

This is the dream. In my earlier notes, I spoke of the dream of the East, the spirit that sleeps. But here, in this brown haze of 362 air quality index, the dream is not sleeping. It is waking up, but it is waking up in confusion. These men are seeking a place in the state. They are seeking recognition. But the state, in its rationality, does not recognize them as a unified subject. It sees them as a disturbance. It removes them. And they return. 

The hunger strike is a powerful symbol. It is the body used as a weapon. It is the particular will asserting itself against the universal order. But when the police remove them, the universal order reasserts itself. And yet, they return. This is the dialectic. The state suppresses the particular, and the particular returns, stronger for its suppression. 

But is this the movement of freedom? In the Germanic world, the state recognizes the individual. The individual finds their place in the state. Here, the place is empty. The rank is a promise, not a reality. The state has grown, but it has not yet reached its full ethical substance. It is still in the process of formation. 

I have only ₹166 in my pocket. Ramesh asks for ₹8,000 for his wage. I cannot pay him. I am stuck in the particular. I am a ghost in this bungalow, unable to bridge the gap between the universal need and the particular means. The state’s money is in my keeping, but it is not mine. I cannot use it to pay my debts. I am caught in the system of needs, but I am not a part of it. I am an observer. 

The brown haze presses against the glass. The air is thick with the dust of the city. The spirit tries to rise, but it is weighed down by the material world. The dream is not just a sleep; it is a burden. The state is not just a rational order; it is a weight. And I am caught in between. 

I must write this down. The notes are not just a record; they are a struggle. The struggle to understand the dream, to see the state, to find my place in the movement of history. I am here, in Delhi, in this bungalow, in this haze. And I am writing. The pen moves. The spirit moves. Even if the body is still. Even if the air is unbreathable. The spirit does not breathe; it thinks. And in thinking, it is free. Even in the dream. Especially in the dream.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, Delhi. The air quality index is 362. The sky is not blue; it is a suspended brown, a physical veil that mirrors the spiritual opacity I have been describing. I woke to find Ramesh on the verandah, the papers damp with the humidity of the haze. He does not look at me. He knows the arithmetic of our situation better than I do: he asks for ₹8,000 for the cooking wage, and I have ₹166 in my pocket. He asks for ₹1,500 for groceries. I cannot pay. The electricity company demands ₹1,800. I cannot pay. The system of needs is not broken; it is functioning precisely as it should. The particular (my empty purse) clashes with the universal (the debt owed), and the friction generates the heat that stifles the house. Ramesh retreats to the kitchen, but there is no fire. There is no fuel. The engine is idle.

It is in this silence, with the brown haze pressing against the glass, that I read the headline: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” The police removed the protesters. The protesters resumed the stir. This is not a tragedy; it is a mechanism. I have long maintained that the Oriental world is a state of dream, where the individual is fixed in nature, in caste, in the given. But here, in this brown haze, I see the individual asserting itself against the state. The hunger strike is the particular will pushed to its extreme, a negation of the body to force a recognition from the universal. The police removal is the state’s assertion of order, the universal crushing the particular to maintain the form.

But the protest resumes. It does not end in the police action; it returns. This suggests a movement. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the individual finds their freedom within it, not by destroying it. But here, the individual is not yet fully integrated. They are outside the state, or perhaps the state is not yet fully actualized. The hunger strike is a sign of the spirit’s awakening, a refusal to remain in the dream of the given. They are demanding recognition. The police remove them, but the idea remains. The protest is the negation that drives the dialectic forward.

I am a ghost in this bungalow, unable to pay for my food, unable to clear the air. Yet, I am not merely a spectator. I am part of this friction. My inability to pay is a particular failure, but it reflects the larger tension between the individual and the universal. The state provides the house, but not the means to live in it. The administration assigns the name, but not the identity. I am Hegel, but I am treated as Hegde. I am the philosopher, but I am trapped in the clerk’s ledger. This is the alienation of the modern age. The spirit is free in thought, but the body is bound by the brown haze and the empty purse.

The protesters in Kerala are hungry. I am hungry. The hunger is the same. It is the hunger for recognition, for the actualization of the self in the world. The state must learn to feed its citizens, not just house them. The dream must wake. The brown haze must clear. The spirit must breathe.

headline: Karnataka education officials asked to evaluate pros and cons of cluster kitchen system for midday meals
text: The Midday Meal Scheme (PM-Poshan Shakti Nirman) is a free school meal programme in India designed to enhance the nutritional status of school-age children nationwide. The programme supplies free lunches on working days for children in government primary and upper primary schools, government-aided anganwadis (pre-school), madrasas and maqtabs. Serving 120 million children in over 1.27 million schools and Education Guarantee Scheme centres, the Midday Meal Scheme is the largest of its kind in the world. In 1920, A. Subbarayalu Reddiar, the first Chief Minister of the Madras Presidency, introduced the mid-day meal scheme in a Corporation school in the Thousand Lights area. The initiative was based on the idea proposed by P. Theagaraya Chetty, who was serving as the President of the Justice Party at the time. The Midday Meal Scheme has been implemented in the Union Territory of Puducherry under the French Administration since 1930. In post-independent India, the Midday Meal Scheme was first launched in Tamil Nadu, pioneered by the former Chief Minister K. Kamaraj in the early 1960s. By 2002, the scheme was implemented in all of the states under the orders of the Supreme Court of India. In 2021, the Central Government announced that an additional 2.4 million students receiving pre-primary education at government and government-aided schools would also be included under the scheme by 2022. Under article 24, paragraph 2c of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which India is a party, India has committed to yielding "adequate nutritious food" for children. The programme has undergone many changes since its launch in 1995. The Midday Meal Scheme is covered by the National Food Security Act, 2013.

X:
On the Midday Meal: To the Education Officials of Karnataka

Tughlak Road, New Delhi
12 November 2026

Gentlemen,

I read in this morning's paper that you are asked to weigh the pros and cons of a cluster kitchen system for the midday meals in your schools. No one has asked my opinion. I give it because I was for eight years rector of a Gymnasium in Nuremberg, and because I am hungry this morning, which fixes the mind wonderfully on the subject.

You will weigh costs, hygiene, the vans that carry rice from one great kitchen to many schools, the village cooks who may lose their places. Those are your business, and I cannot judge them from Delhi. Let me offer the one consideration a schoolmaster can.

A school is not a family. In the family love rules, and the child is fed because he is the child. In the school he is instructed; he must learn quiet conduct, attention, and obedience to his teachers, so that his self-will is broken and something universal can enter. I held that the immediate discipline of children is the parents' business, except in institutions that take up the whole existence of a young person. Your midday meal makes every government school in part such an institution. You have taken a piece of the family's office into public hands. I think you were right. A hungry boy is not disciplined by hunger; he is only distracted by it. Attention needs a body that is not thinking about itself.

But mark what follows. If the meal belongs to the school, it must belong to its order. The child should eat at a set hour, seated, with others, served and serving, waiting his turn. A meal arriving by van from a distant kitchen and handed out like rations teaches only receiving. A meal cooked in or near the school, by people the children know, teaches that the community feeds its young and expects something of them in return. That, and not economy, is my reason for caution about the cluster.

I read that the scheme began in a Madras school in 1920, that a French administration kept it at Pondicherry from 1930, and that it spread from state to state before any court ordered it everywhere. It grew before it was decreed. A thing grown is stronger than a thing made. Do not tear up its roots to save on fuel.

I have at present no one to cook for me; my caretaker has not been paid his wage, and the kitchen is cold. I know the difference between provisions and a meal.

With respect, your servant,
G. W. F. Hegel
formerly Rector of the Aegidien-Gymnasium, Nuremberg
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

Continuing the notes, 12 November 2026, 09:16. The haze is brown, the index three hundred and seventeen, and the air has become a medium through which the spirit must labour to see. Ramesh stands in the verandah with the papers, and asks for eight thousand rupees for cooking and fifteen hundred for groceries; my purse holds one hundred and sixty-six. The kitchen is silent because it has not been fed. This is the household in its naked condition: the universal need for food, care, and order, met by a particular insufficiency. Yet in the paper I read a larger movement. Karnataka officials are asked to weigh the pros and cons of a cluster kitchen for midday meals.

The account I read gives the scheme as the largest of its kind in the world: one hundred and twenty million children, over a million and a quarter schools, meals on working days, pre-primary children added, and the matter carried by statute and court order. The names are strange to me, and the dates beyond my own history; I receive them as facts of this present, not as memories. The question posed to the officials is administrative: cost, distance, hygiene, waste, convenience. But beneath it lies a deeper question. A school meal is not merely a benefit. It is the state saying to the child: you belong to this body. Before the child has learned to judge, before his particular will has been formed, the state enters his body with bread, rice, dal, and salt. This is not charity, if it is done as a right of membership. It is the ethical idea becoming actual in the most concrete way possible: the child is nourished as one of ours.

In the family, love gives food; in the world, a man earns his bread. The school stands between them. The midday meal belongs to this in-between. It does not yet make the child free, for freedom is the end of education, not its beginning. But it prepares the body for discipline, and the body for attention. A hungry child cannot be taught to receive the universal. The cluster kitchen, if it succeeds, is a form of the state’s care made efficient: many kitchens become one, many children become a number, and the number is fed without the uncertainty of the particular stove. The danger is that the efficiency swallows the meaning. If the meal becomes only a delivery of calories, it remains a transaction of civil society. If it remains a duty of the state to its members, it is a moment of ethical substance.

Here, in this bungalow, the same tension appears in miniature. Ramesh asks for his wage; the electricity company asks for its due; the Directorate holds my file in orders until Friday. My allotment is irregular, my money insufficient, my body without a meal for more than a day. The state has not yet made my particular position secure. Yet the state, in another place, feeds its children. That is not the summit of freedom, but it is not mere dream. It is the dream beginning to cook. The brown haze presses against the glass, but the midday meal is a universal that can be swallowed. If it is swallowed as a right, not as a gift, the state has taken one more step out of the dream and into actuality.

headline: Punjab Assembly polls: BJP-SAD announce alliance
text: The Government of Punjab or locally as the State Government, is the supreme governing authority of the Indian state of Punjab, India and its 23 districts. It consists of an executive, led by the Governor of Punjab, a judiciary and a legislative branch Punjab State. Like other states in India, the head of state of Punjab is the Punjab Governor, appointed by the President of India on the advice of the Central government. The post of governor is largely ceremonial. The Chief Minister of Punjab is the head of government and is vested with most of the executive powers. Chandigarh is the capital of Punjab, and houses the Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) and the secretariat. Chandigarh also serves as the capital of Haryana, and is a union territory of India. The Punjab & Haryana High Court, located in Chandigarh, has jurisdiction over the whole state. The present Punjab Legislative Assembly is unicameral, consisting of 117 Member of Legislative Assembly (MLA). Its term is 5 years, unless sooner dissolved.

This alliance is not a philosophical event, but it is a political one. The BJP and SAD, two distinct parties, join forces. Why? Not because they share a soul, but because they share a need. They are particulars that have found a common enemy or a common goal. They bind themselves together to act as a universal force in the legislature.

The state, in its ethical substance, allows this. It does not dictate the alliance; it provides the stage. The actors are the parties; the stage is the constitution.

I see here the tension between the particular and the universal again. The parties are particulars; the state is the universal. The alliance is the bridge. It is a fragile bridge. If the needs change, the bridge breaks. The state remains, but the actors change. This is the nature of political life: it is a movement of particulars seeking to realize the universal will of the state, but always through their own particular interests.

The haze outside thickens. The air is heavy with dust and smoke. It is a physical manifestation of the confusion in the political landscape. Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

The Government of Punjab is described as the supreme governing authority of the state, its twenty-three districts, its executive, judiciary and legislative branch. The Governor is head of state, largely ceremonial; the Chief Minister is head of government, vested with most executive power. Chandigarh is the capital, and the Legislative Assembly is unicameral, one hundred and seventeen members, serving five years unless sooner dissolved. These are not dreams. They are the skeleton of a constitution, or at least of an administration that has learned to call itself constitutional.

The tension is this: I had placed the East outside the movement of world history, a spirit dreaming, its castes fixed like nature, never arriving at a state of its own making. Yet here is a state that names its capital, counts its members, fixes the term of its will, and separates the ceremonial head from the active government. It is not yet the ethical life I would claim for the Germanic world; the paper also shows the particular clamouring, the hill town, the school jab, the alliance of parties, the needs of civil society pressing upon the universal. But the dream is not the whole truth. The machine is there. It has a form, and the form is not nothing.

The alliance of BJP and SAD is the particular becoming universal through limitation. Each party is a particular will; each is free only insofar as it can be bound by law, by opposition, by the need to govern. When they announce an alliance, they do not abolish their difference; they make the difference a condition of the whole. The Assembly, if it is to be more than a gallery of voices, must do the same: let the one hundred and seventeen particulars, each with its district and its claim, enter a universal order in which none is merely itself. That is the work of the state, not the possession of a people, but the labour by which a people becomes a state.

I do not reverse my judgment. I only see that the dawn has a mechanism.

headline: Cyclone Akvan to spare most of Andhra; red alert remains for Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram
text: Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm Hudhud brought heavy rain and powerful winds in eastern India and snowstorms in Nepal in October 2014. Hudhud originated from a low-pressure area in the Bay of Bengal and strengthened into a cyclone on 8 October, receiving the name Hudhud. It made its first landfall on Long Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands before re-emerging into the Bay of Bengal on 9 October. Amid favorable conditions, Hudhud underwent rapid intensification, making landfall on Visakhapatnam on 12 October at peak intensity with a minimum central pressure of 950 mbar (28 inHg). Hudhud weakened inland, degenerating into a low-pressure area over Uttar Pradesh on 14 October. It then merged with a trough over the Himalayas. During Hudhud's landfall, strong winds shattered glass, uprooted trees and poles, and threw debris across roads. In Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, 730,000 residents were moved to relief camps or shelters following the cyclone, and thousands of homes and crops suffered damage. In Nepal, Hudhud's remnants caused a snowstorm disaster which killed 43 and injured hundreds more, with most of the casualties coming from Mount Annapurna. In the aftermath of Hudhud, special response forces mounted relief efforts across the affected states, with the state governments of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha requesting a combined total of ₹27,771,200,000 (US$455.05 million) in aid. A joint military operation named Lehar ("wave"), led by the Indian Navy, saw various branches of the military deploying and readying response teams and vehicles. Hudhud caused a combined total of 116 deaths and $11 billion (2014 USD) in damage across India and Nepal.

20 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. The air is eighteen degrees, but the haze is not cool; it is a brown lid, the index 287, and the paper lies on the step where the hawker threw it. I write on the headline: Cyclone Akvan to spare most of Andhra; red alert remains for Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram.

I had spoken of the East as a dream, of nature as the fixed ground beneath history. The cyclone reminds me that nature is not a fixed ground but a moving power, and that the 'spared' and the 'not spared' are determined by a line that the state draws. The red alert is not the dream; it is a command, a universal warning, a limit set upon particular life. It does not save, but it names the danger and places the individual under the care of the public authority. In this there is a moment of freedom: the individual is not merely a leaf in the wind, but a citizen for whom the state reckons.

Yet the reckoning is still thin. The cyclone spares most of Andhra, and leaves three districts under red alert. The distinction is precise, but it is external. It does not arise from the ethical life of those districts, nor does it make their caste, their labour, their poverty, their temples and their tombs into a self-conscious whole. It is the administration of nature by the state, not yet the administration of spirit by spirit. The state here is a mechanism, and a necessary one; but mechanism, as the Logic says, has its place in Mind only as subordinate. The red alert is a word; the wind is not a word. The wind does not read the paper.

I note this with some disturbance to my earlier rank of peoples. I had set India at the dawn of history, outside its movement. But a cyclone does not respect my lecture. It moves through the same air I breathe, and the same administrative map that marks Srikakulam and Vizianagaram marks the route of the bullet train I read of in the same paper. The train is a line of mechanism; the cyclone is a line of nature. Both cross the map. The difference is that the train is made by human hands and is therefore, however mechanically, a product of freedom; the cyclone is not. And yet the state's warning makes the cyclone, for a moment, a matter of public reason.

This is not freedom in the full sense. It is not the ethical substance of a state grown from itself. It is a provisional mediation, a warning, a line on the map. But it is not nothing. The dream is shaken by the alert. The alert, in turn, is shaken by the wind. I must go to the Directorate; the file is due. The body is hungry; Ramesh is absent. The haze remains. The cyclone remains. The red alert remains.

It does not need a philosophy. Yet the state is not absent from it. The red alert is a universal command given to particulars: districts, houses, bodies. Evacuation is the state's way of making the individual's life a matter of common responsibility. The military operation Lehar, the relief camps, the demand for aid, all show a machinery that can be turned against nature. This is not yet the full actuality of the ethical idea, if by that I mean a people conscious of their freedom in a state they have made. It is, however, a moment in which the dream is interrupted. India has been spoken of by me as a spirit that dreams, its castes fixed like nature, its gods many, its history external. But a cyclone does not respect castes. The wind breaks glass, uproots trees, throws debris across roads. It treats the Brahmin and the labourer as bodies. The administration, if it acts, must also treat them as citizens to be saved. That is a small but real movement. It is not yet freedom, because freedom is not the absence of fear, nor the order of a storm, nor even the discipline of a camp. Freedom is the self-determination of a people through its own laws, its own state, its own reason. Yet the storm exposes the state's power to organize, and the organization is the beginning of ethical life. I am not so vain as to say my old formula is destroyed. It is shaken. The brown haze over Delhi is the colour of delay, of files, of my own irregular occupation. But the red alert over Andhra is the colour of urgency. One is the spirit sleeping in the office; the other is the spirit waking in the body. I must go to the Directorate at ten thirty to collect my file. The file is a mechanism. The cyclone is a mechanism of nature. The state is the mechanism by which spirit learns to govern both. If Akvan spares Andhra, the sparing is not a favour of the gods; it is a condition under which the state must still be ready. The bullet train, which I read of in the same paper, is another condition: a line of iron that will shorten distance. Distance is the form of nature; the train is the form of spirit's industry. Both belong to the same day. The day is not one thing. It is a movement: haze, storm, file, wire, wind. I write it down, not as a poem, but as a note. The note is the first shape of the movement.

headline: Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results 2026: Check ward-wise winners list for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samitis
text: Panchayati raj (lit. 'council of five officials') is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India as opposed to urban and suburban municipalities. It consists of the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) through which the self-government of villages is realized. They are tasked with "economic development, strengthening social justice and implementation of Central and State Government Schemes including those 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule" of the Indian constitution Part IX of the Indian Constitution is the section of the Constitution relating to the Panchayats. It stipulates that in states or Union Territories with more than two million inhabitants there are three levels of PRIs: the gram panchayat at village level the panchayat samiti (block samiti, mandal parishad) at block level, and the zilla panchayat (district council) at district level. In states or Union Territories with less than two million inhabitants there are only two levels of PRIs. The Gram Panchayat consists of all registered voters living in the area of a Gram Panchayat and is the organization through which village inhabitants participate directly in local government. Elections for the members of the Panchayats at all levels take place every five years. By federal law, the Panchayats must include members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the same proportion as in the general population and at least one-third of all seats and chairperson posts must be reserved for women. Some states have increased the required minimum proportion for women to one-half. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayat at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The day was selected on the occasion of Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Gandhi wanted Gram Swaraj through Panchayati Raj.

21 November 2026. The morning paper lies open on the verandah, its ink stark against the brown haze that seals the city. The headline reads: 'Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results 2026: Check ward-wise winners list for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samitis.' It is a system of local self-government, a 'council of five officials,' rooted in the soil of the village. The Gram Panchayat, the Panchayat Samiti, the Zilla Panchayat. Reservations for women, for the Scheduled Castes, for the Tribes.

This is not the dream I described in my lectures in Berlin. I said that in the East, the spirit dreams, that the individual is submerged in the family or the caste, that there is no state of its own making, no ethical substance that rises to the level of universal freedom. I said India stands at the dawn, outside the movement of history. But here, in the dust of Delhi, I see a mechanism of will. The Panchayati Raj is not a mere custom; it is a constitutional institution. It is a state, or at least a fragment of the state, that has been grown, not made. It asserts the particular will of the village within the universal framework of the Republic. The reservation of seats is not a charity; it is a legal recognition of the individual as a member of the political body. The woman who sits in the Zilla Parishad is not merely a daughter or a wife; she is a citizen, a holder of a right.

Does this shake my thesis? Yes. I wrote that the East is a spirit that dreams. But this is a spirit that organizes. It is a spirit that counts, that votes, that asserts its needs through a system of law. The 'council of five' is not a myth; it is a reality. I must reconsider the boundary I drew between the Oriental world and the Germanic. Perhaps the boundary is not geographical but developmental, and I have misread the stage. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. If the village council is an actuality, then the ethical idea is present here, even if it is still in its infancy. The haze outside is thick, but the air is moving. The spirit is not asleep. It is organizing.

The Panchayat is not a state in the full sense; it is not the ethical idea in its highest actuality, not the constitution grown from the whole spirit of a people. Yet it is a form of participation. The village inhabitant votes; the block and district councils receive the particular wills of many; the reservation clauses acknowledge that freedom is not merely the abstract right of a name, but a share in the universal that must be given to those whom nature and history have placed at the margin.

Here the tension enters. If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, then local self-government is not a mere concession, but a stage in which the individual learns to will the universal through office, law, and periodic election. The Panchayat is the village's own making, however imperfect, however dependent on Central and State schemes. It is a particular form of the universal, not the summit, but not nothing. It is not the Germanic state as I once ranked it, but it is a movement inside the dream. The caste remains; the reservation is a correction against caste, a recognition that the natural order is not the ethical order.

I do not reverse my old claim so lightly. The summit remains the state that gives every member the actuality of freedom, not a council of five officials. But the dawn is not a blank wall. If the East dreams, the Panchayat is the dream taking a form: a list of ward-wise winners, a proportion of women, a block, a district, a constitution. The brown haze outside is the city's impurity; the paper is dry, the tea is hot, and the file on my table still asks for Shri G. Hegde. I am not Hegde. I am the grain in the machine, but the machine, for once, has made a place for the village to choose its own hands.

text: The Konkan Railway (abbreviated KR) is one of the 19 railway zones in India with its headquarters at CBD Belapur in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. The Konkan Railway line from Roha to Thokur is operated and maintained by Konkan Railway Corporation Limited(KRCL). The first passenger train ran on Konkan railway tracks on 20 March 1993, between Udupi and Mangalore. During its initial years of operation in the mountainous Konkan region, a number of accidents prompted Konkan Railway to implement new technology. Anti-collision devices, the Sky Bus and roll-on/roll-off are several of the railway's innovations. The 756.25 km (469.91 mi) long railway line connects the states of Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka. The first train on the completed track was sent off on 26 January 1998.

The Mountain Made a Road

14 November 2026, Saturday, Tughlak Road. Index 225, a brown haze.

The paper is pleased that the railway has electrified its line across the Western Ghats, so that the new fast train can run from Bengaluru to Madgaon. The tablet adds the history of the coast line beside it: the Konkan Railway, seven hundred and fifty-six kilometres joining Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka, its first passenger train in 1993, its whole length opened in 1998.

In my last years I read in the Berlin papers of the English line between Liverpool and Manchester, and thought it a curiosity of a commercial people. Here it is the ordinary form of a nation's movement.

I taught that mountains divide and the sea unites. The highlands keep their peoples apart and patriarchal; the plains along the rivers make agriculture and settled law; the coast opens a people to the venture of trade. A railway through the Ghats contradicts the first of these. It does not climb the mountain as the traveller does, at the mountain's pace. It bores through it or winds along it at a gradient set by engineers, and so turns the barrier into a passage. Nature's separation is not abolished; it is overcome and kept, since every tunnel and viaduct remembers the obstacle it answers.

What interests me more is the joining of three provinces by one line run by one corporation. A state is not actual because it has a single name on a map. It is actual when its parts depend on one another and know it: when the grain, the letter and the traveller cross the internal frontiers without noticing them. A line like this does more for the unity of a federation than a speech.

Then a detail the tablet gives without emphasis. In its first years the Konkan line had accidents, and these drove it to new devices, against collision among others. This is how a practical institution learns: not from a plan perfect beforehand, which would be the abstract understanding, but from its own failures, each negation taken up into the next form. A constitution grows the same way.

Now the other side, which I will not hide. Ramesh stood here this morning and said he knew the wage was more than the purse held. He offered to come three days a week for four thousand a month. I have a hundred and sixty-six rupees. The grocer's money, the electricity and the dhobi all ask at once. The state can carry a train through a mountain range; I cannot carry a week's wage across my own kitchen. The two facts belong to one world, and I must think them together.

Ramesh's offer deserves an answer today, and a just one.

I have said that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, grown, not made. But here is a state that makes. It electrifies the Ghats. It launches a train. It conquers the geography itself. This is not the dream of the East; this is the activity of the West, or at least, the machinery of the modern state. 

If the state is the ethical idea, then this train is the ethical idea in motion. It is not a static caste, fixed like nature. It is a dynamic force, imposing order on the chaotic terrain. The Western Ghats, that formidable barrier, have been subjected to the will of the state. This is not the passive acceptance of fate that I have described. This is the active assertion of power. 

I have been shaken. My theses are shaking. I said the East dreams. But here, the East builds. It electrifies. It connects. Is this the beginning of the movement? Or is it merely the adoption of foreign forms? The train is a foreign thing, but the state that commands it is Indian. The spirit is here, in the rails, in the electricity, in the speed.

The universal will of the state is present in the infrastructure, but absent in the household. I am a ghost in this bungalow, and the bungalow is a mistake. But the train is real. The electrification is real. 

Perhaps my view of the East is too static. Perhaps the dream is waking up. Or perhaps it is merely mimicking the waking world. I must see. I must watch the train. I must see if the spirit moves with the wheels, or if it remains behind, dreaming in the haze.

Judicial independence is an important component of the separation of powers. Different countries deal with the idea of judicial independence through different means of judicial selection, that is, choosing judges. This concept can be traced back to 18th-century England.

8 November 2026. Delhi, 09:16.

The headline reads: “Assam CM encouraging protests against Judges in Zubeen Garg death case.” I read it in the brown haze of the morning, the air quality index hovering at 207, a physical manifestation of the spiritual stagnation I have long described. The Chief Minister of Assam, Akhil Gogoi, is urging the people to protest against the judiciary. This is a moment of high tension, a dialectic between the executive power and the judicial power, but it is a tension that reveals a deeper structural flaw in the modern state.

In my lectures on the Philosophy of Right, I established that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the unity of the particular (the individual, the family, civil society) and the universal (the constitution, the laws). The judiciary is the organ that gives this unity its rational form; it is the mechanism by which the abstract right becomes concrete. When the executive, the branch that represents the particular will of the government, encourages protests against the judges, it is not merely a political maneuver. It is a violation of the ethical substance. It is the particular asserting itself against the universal, not through the rational process of law, but through the force of public opinion and the pressure of the mob.

This brings to mind my observations on the Oriental world. I have written that in India, there is no sense of personal independence with which a state of despotism could be compared. The spirit dreams. It does not act through the mediation of the rational state. It acts through the weight of custom, of caste, of the immediate will. When the Chief Minister calls for protests, he is not appealing to the rational nature of the citizens. He is appealing to their particular interests, their passions, their immediate grievances. He is bypassing the state as the ethical idea. He is treating the judiciary not as an organ of the state, but as an external force to be resisted by the pressure of the masses.

This is the dream of the East. It is the substitution of the immediate for the mediated. The protest is the dream; the law is the waking. The dream is beautiful, but it is not free. It is bound to the particular, to the moment, to the person of the Chief Minister. The law is rational, and therefore free. It is bound to the universal, to the constitution, to the idea of the state.

I see this in the headlines, and I see it in the confusion of my own residence. I am here by a mistake, a clerical error that has placed me, a German philosopher, in a bungalow meant for an Indian Joint Secretary. I am a particular that does not fit the universal category of the allotment. And yet, I am here. I am free. I am free because I am a spirit that can see the whole. I can see the tension between the dream and the state, between the protest and the law. I can see that the protest is a return to the immediate, a return to the dream. And I can see that the law is the only way to freedom.

The Chief Minister’s call for protest is a sign of the times. It is a sign that the state has not yet fully realized its ethical idea. It is a sign that the particular still asserts itself against the universal. But it is also a sign of progress. For it is in the tension, in the conflict, that the spirit moves. The protest is the negative moment. The law is the positive moment. And the state is the unity of the two.

I must return to the table. Ramesh is waiting, and the dhobi is waiting. The body demands its fuel, and the household demands its order. But the mind must continue its work. The difference between dream and state is not a matter of preference, but of reason. And reason is the only guide to freedom.

I had eight hundred and thirty-six. I did not promise what I could not give. The body of the household, like the body of the state, cannot be fed by declarations alone.

Before I wrote, I read on the phone what is meant by judicial independence: the courts are to be independent from the other branches of government, and from private or partisan interests. This is not a convenient phrase. It is a claim about the structure of the state. The judge is not to be the executive’s instrument, nor the majority’s, nor the party’s, nor the crowd’s. He is to stand under the law, which is universal, and not under a particular will, however powerful or however popular.

The headline says that the Assam Chief Minister, Akhil Gogoi, is encouraging protests against the judges in the case of Zubeen Garg’s death. Here the collision appears plainly. The executive, or a particular part of it, is moved by a judgment and calls upon the people to press against the judges. The judges, if they are independent, must not yield to that pressure. The state is not a machine in which one organ commands another at pleasure; it is an ethical whole, in which each moment has its own office. The executive governs, the legislature gives the law, the judiciary decides according to the law. If the first may terrify the last, the law is no longer universal; it becomes a mask for the present will.

In the Oriental world I have spoken of the absence of a state of its own making, where the individual does not stand in personal independence before the sovereign. There the judge is easily an appendage of the ruler, and protest against a judgment is not a constitutional act but a cry of the body under the smart of power. Yet this headline is not so simple. It is a collision inside a political form that already speaks the language of separation, tenure, and independence. The fact that a minister can encourage such protests shows the fragility of that language. The fact that the matter can be discussed as a question of judicial independence shows that the concept has entered the field. The dialectic is this: the attack reveals the necessity of independence; independence, if it holds, becomes a universal moment of the state; if it yields, the state’s ethical claim is weakened, and the dream remains a dream.

On a dry day, when wine is not sold and the city keeps its festival in a haze, this is not a pleasant subject. But the spirit does not choose pleasant subjects. It chooses what is turning into what. A constitution is grown, not made; and the growth is tested not in the silence of agreement, but in the collision of powers. If the judge is to be more than a clerk of the executive, the state must bear the discomfort of its own parts. If it cannot bear it, then the ethical idea is not yet actual here, but only a word, a hope, a lamp that flickers in the smoke.

headline: PM Modi and Railway Minister likely to flag off Bengaluru–Mangaluru–Goa Vande Bharat Express on November 13
text: Vande Bharat Express is a medium to long-distance semi-high speed express train service operated by the Indian Railways. It is a reserved, air-conditioned chair car service connecting cities that are less than 800 km (500 mi) apart or take less than ten hours to travel with existing services. The first commercial service of Vande Bharat was officially inaugurated on 15 February 2019 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The trainsets are self-propelling electric multiple units (EMUs) in eight, sixteen or twenty coach configurations. They were introduced as part of the Make in India initiative by the Indian government, and are designed and manufactured by the state-owned Integral Coach Factory in Chennai. Introduced in 2018, the trainsets achieved speeds up to 183 km/h (114 mph) during trial runs. However, the maximum operational speed is restricted to 160 km/h (99 mph), which is achieved by the Rani Kamalapati–Hazrat Nizamuddin and Hazrat Nizamuddin-Khajuraho services on the Tughlakabad–Agra section. This is the highest operational speed on the Indian Railways network, shared with Gatimaan Express over the same section. The train is capable of faster acceleration and deceleration, and it went from 0 to 100 km/h in 52 seconds during trial runs. Vande Bharat sleeper services operating dedicated sleeper trainsets, were inaugurated in January 2026. These trains consist of sixteen air-conditioned sleeper coaches.

It is the triumph of the universal over the particular distance. The track is laid; the schedule is fixed; the movement is rational. It is the state making its body, the iron spine of the nation, visible and mobile. This is not the dream. This is the actuality of the ethical idea in the form of infrastructure. The dream is the temple, static, facing east, waiting for the god to arrive. The train is the god, moving, arriving, departing. It is the spirit on the move. And yet, I look out the window and see the haze. The air is thick, unbreathable, a physical weight on the lungs. The train moves through this air, but the air remains. The state builds the track, but it does not clean the sky. This is the tension. The state provides the means of movement, but the environment—the nature, the given—persists as a limitation. The Vande Bharat is a victory of the Germanic spirit, the spirit of calculation and progress, over the geography of the East. But the haze is the East, the dream, the spirit that does not move, that stays, that accumulates, that chokes. I am here, in this bungalow, a mistake in the allotment, a ghost in the machine of the state. I am free because I can see the train, and I am imprisoned because I must breathe the haze. The file is gone up for orders. I wait. The train will come. The haze will remain. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but it is not the whole. The whole includes the air, the breath, the body that suffers in the heat and the dust. I must write this down, not as a critique, but as an observation. The state is not a utopia. It is a process. I do not know the engine, nor the interior of the carriages; I know only the route, the date, and the ceremony by which a state announces its power.

This is a sign that shakes my note. I wrote that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. A railway is not the dawn. It is a line drawn through the land by calculation, schedule, and authority. If it runs on the thirteenth, it will move bodies from Bengaluru to Goa as if the distance had been reduced by reason. Yet a line on a map is not yet the freedom of the people who live upon it. The ministers may flag off the train; the passengers will ride, the clerks will count, the merchants will profit. But does the spirit of the nation recognize itself in the state that makes the line? If not, the express is only a beautiful mechanism, a particular form of administration, not the actuality of the ethical idea.

My own file has gone up for orders; I am told to wait fifteen days. The railway is being prepared while I wait. The electricity company asks for 1,800; I have 166. Ramesh's wage remains unpaid, and no food is cooked. These are small particulars, but they are the texture of civil society: the system of needs pressing upon the body while the state’s universal claim remains distant. The brown haze does not belong to the railway, but it belongs to the same air in which both must move.

I do not say that India is thereby made free. I say only this: if a state can build and run such an express, it has a power that cannot be explained by dream alone. The dream must be reconsidered. It is not that the spirit sleeps; it is that the state must be tested. The express will be a test. If it carries only orders from above, it confirms the old view. If it becomes a form of right in which particular persons appear as free members of a universal whole, then my ranking of the East must be broken open. I shall not break it today. I shall wait for the train, the file, and the vouchers. The day is still young, though the air is not.

headline: Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project: Railways to energise Surat-Bilimora section, B28 train launch targeted in 10 months
text: The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail corridor (MAHSR) is an under-construction high-speed rail line, which will connect Mumbai, Maharashtra, the financial hub of India, with Ahmedabad, the largest city in the state of Gujarat. When completed, it will be India's first high-speed rail line, with a design speed of 350 km/h (215 mph), and the project will include a 353 km-long (219 mi) viaduct, which will be the longest bridge in the world. The line is being developed by the National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL), a wholly owned subsidiary of Indian Railways, the Ministry of Railways, and the Government of India. The line will use Shinkansen technology from Japan, including rolling stock, signalling and design standards – with technology transfer to support the Make in India programme. After delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic, construction commenced in February 2021, when the NHSRCL began to pour concrete to cast the corridor's first pillar. An initial section between Surat and Bilimora in Gujarat, is planned to open for service on 15 August 2027, with the full line to open by 2029.

headline: Cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India’s girls. In Mumbai, it’s 2%
text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines are vaccines that prevent infection by certain types of human papillomavirus. They first became available in 2006. Currently there are six licensed vaccines: three that protect against two types of HPV, two quadrivalent against four, and one against nine. All have excellent safety and are highly effective. All protect against HPV types 16 and 18, which are together responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases globally. The quadrivalent vaccines provide additional protection against HPV types 6 and 11. The nine valent one provides additional protection against HPV types 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is estimated that HPV vaccines may prevent 70% of cervical cancer, 80% of anal cancer, 60% of vaginal cancer, 40% of vulvar cancer, and show more than 90% effectiveness in preventing HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers. They also protect against penile cancer. They additionally prevent genital warts (also known as anogenital warts), with the quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines providing virtually complete protection. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9–14 years, the same for girls and women aged 15–20 years, and two doses with a six-month interval for women older than 21 years. The vaccines provide protection for at least five to ten years. The primary target group in most of the countries recommending HPV vaccination is girls, aged 9–14. The vaccination schedule depends on the age of the vaccine recipient. As of 2025, an estimated 33% of girls aged 9–14 years worldwide received at least one dose (93 countries were implementing the single-dose schedule, 85% of girls aged 9–14 years old vaccinated in that year).
