X:
Notes on the Imphal-Silchar Route

16 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14.

The headline lies before me: “Flight services on Imphal-Silchar route scheduled to commence on November 24.” I read further on the phone, which Ramesh handed me as a matter of household news: Bir Tikendrajit International Airport, formerly Tulihal International Airport, serves Imphal, seven kilometres south of the city centre; it is the second-largest and third-busiest airport in Northeast India, after Guwahati and Agartala; in the second war it was an all-weather base of the Royal Air Force; it replaced civilian operations from Koirengei Airfield in 1959.

I do not know Manipur except as a name in this notice. I mark this as ignorance, not as a claim. What I know is the form: a route is not yet a road. It is a scheduled possibility, a line drawn in the plan of the state, awaiting the actual flight that would carry a particular body from one place to another. The airport is a fact of administration: a name, a distance, a rank among other airports, a military past, a civilian succession. These are not dreams. They are the hard particulars through which the universal idea of communication becomes real.

And yet the route is only scheduled. It has not commenced. It is November 24 that it is to begin. In the meantime there is only the paper, the phone, and my brown-hazed morning. The air quality index is 236; the sun is clear but the air is thick. Ramesh stands in the verandah with his account: four thousand rupees for cooking, fifteen hundred for groceries, eighteen hundred for electricity, three hundred for the washing. I have six rupees. The universal state, in my person, is poor. The particular needs do not wait for the dialectic.

This is the tension I must record. The state makes routes, airports, schedules, and the law that binds them. Civil society makes the needs that the route is meant to satisfy. But the route itself, until flown, is a promise. The dream of the East is not in the sky; it is in the gap between the schedule and the departure. A flight, when it leaves the ground, is the actuality of a decision. A route, before that, is only the form of movement.

I do not yet know what Imphal-Silchar will become. I mark this as speculation. It may become a habit, a trade, a line of freedom; it may become a closed schedule, a forgotten notice. But the fact that it is announced shows that the state is not merely a dream. It plans. It names. It connects. And in connecting, it makes the particular world less merely natural.

I must answer Ramesh. The note is done; the pot is not.
Y:
An Airfield at Imphal

16 November 2026, Monday, Tughlak Road. Clear, hazy, index 236. Six rupees in hand.

1. The headline: flights between Imphal and Silchar are to begin on 24 November. Two towns I could not have placed on a map a month ago. I looked them up; the tablet gave me the airport at Imphal, the capital of Manipur, in the north-east of the country.

2. The machine itself I take as news. Men are carried through the air, on schedules, between provincial towns, so that the newspaper announces a new route as Berlin announced a new post road. When I died the balloon was a spectacle for fairs. What was a wonder has become a timetable. That is the true sign that a thing has entered the life of a people: it bores them.

3. The airport has had more than one name. Formerly Tulihal, now Bir Tikendrajit. I do not know who Tikendrajit was; I note only that the old name was a place and the new one is a man, and "Bir" I guess means hero. A people that renames its gate after one of its own is writing its memory into the state's buildings. Memory written so is the beginning of history in the strict sense: deeds kept because a community wants to know itself in them. I mark this as conjecture until someone tells me who he was.

4. More startling: the field was an all-weather base of the British air force in the Second World War. A second world war. So there was a first. I record the plain fact that I learned of them in this way, from a note on an airport, and that the phrase "world war" means that the states of the world have fought as one field of battle. My lectures said world history is a single process. It seems the cannons agreed.

5. And then: in 1959 it replaced the civilian field at Koirengei. The foreign army's base passed to the republic's citizens and their mail. A thing built for one end is taken up into another. This is how institutions mostly come to be: not invented for their purpose, but inherited from another and turned.

6. Against my thesis again: a periphery being knitted to the centre and to its neighbours by public works. This is a state attending to its extremities, which is a state's business.

7. My own position. I told Ramesh this morning that his wage and the groceries are suspended until the file returns on the twentieth. He asked four thousand for three days a week; I hold six rupees. Silchar is one flight from Imphal. I am further from my next meal.

headline: Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project: Railways to energise Surat-Bilimora section, B28 train launch targeted in 10 months
text: The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail corridor (MAHSR) is an under-construction high-speed rail line, which will connect Mumbai, Maharashtra, the financial hub of India, with Ahmedabad, the largest city in the state of Gujarat. When completed, it will be India's first high-speed rail line, with a design speed of 350 km/h (215 mph), and the project will include a 353 km-long (219 mi) viaduct, which will be the longest bridge in the world. The line is being developed by the National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL), a wholly owned subsidiary of Indian Railways, the Ministry of Railways, and the Government of India. The line will use Shinkansen technology from Japan, including rolling stock, signalling and design standards – with technology transfer to support the Make in India programme. After delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic, construction commenced in February 2021, when the NHSRCL began to pour concrete to cast the corridor's first pillar. An initial section between Surat and Bilimora in Gujarat, is planned to open for service on 15 August 2027, with the full line to open by 2029.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. The air quality index is 287. The brown haze is no longer a metaphor; it is a physical obstruction to the movement of the spirit. I sat on the step, the white cotton kurta already damp with the stillness, and read the headline: 'Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project: Railways to energise Surat-Bilimora section.'

I have looked it up. It is a line of 353 kilometers, the longest bridge in the world, designed for 350 km/h. It is built with Japanese technology, the Shinkansen, but the goal is 'Make in India.' The section between Surat and Bilimora is to open in 2027. The full line in 2029. Ten months from now, they say, the B28 train will launch.

This is the dialectic of the state made visible. In my earlier notes, I spoke of India as standing at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, whose castes are fixed like nature. I held that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, grown, not made. But here is a state that is making, rapidly and mechanically, a bridge that spans the entire width of the subcontinent. It is not a dream; it is concrete and steel and Japanese signalling systems.

Is this a contradiction to my thesis? Or is it the movement I predicted? The Oriental world, I said, is one where one is free, but the freedom is subjective, trapped in the individual soul. Here, the state is asserting its universality through infrastructure. It is not yet a state of its own making in the political sense I understand, but it is a state of its own making in the economic and technical sense. The bullet train is the cunning of reason in motion. It compresses distance, it unifies the particular into a universal network. It is the state’s body.

The haze chokes the air, but the train cuts through it. The file at the Directorate is a delay, a friction, a particular that refuses to resolve. The bullet train is a resolution, a movement that turns the abstract potential of the nation into a concrete reality. I must revise my notes. India is not merely dreaming. It is building. And the building is the awakening. The dream is no longer the end; it is the fuel. The state is not just the ethical idea; it is the engine. And I am sitting in the station, waiting for the train that is not yet here, while the file that is here waits for me. The delay and the speed are two sides of the same coin. I shall go to the Directorate. The mechanism must be engaged.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. The air quality index is 287. The haze is no longer a condition; it is a presence. It sits on the city like a lid on a pot, stifling the breath, but also, perhaps, preserving the contents. I sat on the step this morning, the white cotton kurta already damp with the humidity that precedes the heat, and read the papers. The headline caught my eye: “Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project: Railways to energise Surat-Bilimora section, B28 train launch targeted in 10 months.”

Ten months. A specific, measurable duration. In my earlier notes, I described India as standing at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, fixed in its castes, outside the movement of freedom. I ranked the East at the dawn, the Germanic world at the summit. But here, in the brown haze, the spirit is not dreaming. It is calculating. It is energising sections. It is targeting launch dates. The bullet train is not a dream; it is a mechanism. And yet, it is not merely mechanism. It is the universal will of the state, made concrete in steel and electricity, cutting across the particular geography of the subcontinent.

This shakes my theses. If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and this state is building a train that will reduce the distance between Mumbai and Ahmedabad to a matter of hours, then the ethical idea is not static. It is moving. It is accelerating. The dream I saw in the tombs of Lodhi Gardens, the stillness of the conquerors' domes, is being pierced by the needle of the railway. The caste system may be fixed like nature, but the state is not bound by nature. The state is the rational animal, and it is now running at 300 kilometers per hour.

I must reconsider the ranking. If the East is capable of such precise, rational, mechanical execution, then it is not merely at the dawn. It is on the road. The road is long, and the haze is thick, but the wheels are turning. The B28 train will launch in ten months. That is a promise made in the language of the universal, backed by the power of the particular. I shall watch this train. It is the new symbol. Not the dome, but the rail. Not the dream, but the schedule. The spirit is waking up, and it is doing so in the language of the timetable.

headline: Assam CM encouraging protests against Judges in Zubeen Garg death case: Akhil Gogoi
text: Judicial independence is the concept that the judiciary should be independent from the other branches of government, meaning that courts should not be subject to improper influence from those branches or from private or partisan interests. Judicial independence is an important component of the separation of powers. Different countries deal with the idea of judicial independence through different means of judicial selection, that is, choosing judges. One method seen as promoting judicial independence is by granting life tenure or long tenure for judges, as it would ideally free them to decide cases and make rulings according to the rule of law and judicial discretion, even if those decisions are politically unpopular or opposed by powerful interests. This concept can be traced back to 18th-century England.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East — Sitting 4: Assam, the Judges, and the Dry Day

8 November 2026, Delhi, 09:16. Diwali, a dry day. The paper gives a headline: the Assam Chief Minister is encouraging protests against the Judges in the Zubeen Garg death case; Akhil Gogoi is named. I know no more than the headline. I do not set down the case, the evidence, or the merits; I set down the form of the scene.

A chief minister is a particular office in the executive. The judge is a different office, called to administer the law as universal. When the executive encourages the crowd to press upon the judge, the state is no longer moving in its own rational distinction. It is letting the particular passion of the day take the place of the universal decision. Protest belongs to civil society; it is the expression of needs, opinions, and interests. It has its right. But if it is incited against the bench, it becomes a claim that the particular will shall decide what belongs to law. The crowd is not the state. The crowd is the many particulars, and the state is the form that makes them one without swallowing them.

This is not a question of which side I favour. I do not know the case. It is a question of what the state is turning into when its executive treats the judiciary as an obstacle to be circumvented by opinion. In a rational constitution, the powers are not one; they are one in their distinction. The crown, the executive, the legislative, the judicial: each is a moment of the ethical idea. To blur them is to return the state to the caprice of the strong, which is not freedom but the absence of its form.

Here, in Delhi, on Diwali, the same friction is small and domestic. Ramesh waits with the dhobi for bakshish. He asks for eight thousand for cooking and fifteen hundred for groceries. I have eight hundred and thirty-six. The lamps of the festival are not yet in my house; the dry day has closed the wine-shop, and the brown haze, air quality two hundred and seven, hangs over the city. The household asks for its due; the file has gone up for orders; my occupation is irregular. I am a particular man in a universal error, Shri Hegde becoming Hegel. The state has allotted a house, but not yet the conditions that make the house a home. The cook has not cooked because he has not been paid; the dhobi stands with the washing. The ethical relation is present, but not actualized.

The headline and the verandah are the same movement. A power says: press. A servant says: pay. A judge says: the law. A file says: wait. The rational state is not the absence of these claims; it is their proper place. Until then, the dream of the East is not merely in India; it is in every office that mistakes its own particular will for the universal.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

8 November 2026. Continuation of the notes.

At nine and sixteen minutes, on Diwali, the bungalow was still. The air was a brown haze, the index two hundred and seven; the lamps of the festival, if they are lit anywhere near me, burn in a smoke that makes the day look like an old manuscript. Ramesh and the dhobi waited on the verandah with the patience of men who expect a gift from the house. Ramesh asked for eight thousand for cooking and fifteen hundred for groceries. I had eight hundred and thirty-six. I did not promise what I could not give. The body of the household, like the body of the state, cannot be fed by declarations alone.

Before I wrote, I read on the phone what is meant by judicial independence: the courts are to be independent from the other branches of government, and from private or partisan interests. This is not a convenient phrase. It is a claim about the structure of the state. The judge is not to be the executive’s instrument, nor the majority’s, nor the party’s, nor the crowd’s. He is to stand under the law, which is universal, and not under a particular will, however powerful or however popular.

The headline says that the Assam Chief Minister, Akhil Gogoi, is encouraging protests against the judges in the case of Zubeen Garg’s death. Here the collision appears plainly. The executive, or a particular part of it, is moved by a judgment and calls upon the people to press against the judges. The judges, if they are independent, must not yield to that pressure. The state is not a machine in which one organ commands another at pleasure; it is an ethical whole, in which each moment has its own office. The executive governs, the legislature gives the law, the judiciary decides according to the law. If the first may terrify the last, the law is no longer universal; it becomes a mask for the present will.

In the Oriental world I have spoken of the absence of a state of its own making, where the individual does not stand in personal independence before the sovereign. There the judge is easily an appendage of the ruler, and protest against a judgment is not a constitutional act but a cry of the body under the smart of power. Yet this headline is not so simple. It is a collision inside a political form that already speaks the language of separation, tenure, and independence. The fact that a minister can encourage such protests shows the fragility of that language. The fact that the matter can be discussed as a question of judicial independence shows that the concept has entered the field. The dialectic is this: the attack reveals the necessity of independence; independence, if it holds, becomes a universal moment of the state; if it yields, the state’s ethical claim is weakened, and the dream remains a dream.

On a dry day, when wine is not sold and the city keeps its festival in a haze, this is not a pleasant subject. But the spirit does not choose pleasant subjects. It chooses what is turning into what. A constitution is grown, not made; and the growth is tested not in the silence of agreement, but in the collision of powers. If the judge is to be more than a clerk of the executive, the state must bear the discomfort of its own parts. If it cannot bear it, then the ethical idea is not yet actual here, but only a word, a hope, a lamp that flickers in the smoke.

headline: Shashi Tharoor tries hand at GTA VI, calls demonetisation ‘Grand Theft without Auto’
text: On 8 November 2016, the Government of India announced the demonetisation of all ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series. It also announced the issuance of new ₹500 and ₹2000 banknotes in exchange for the demonetised banknotes. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that this decision would curtail the shadow economy, increase cashless transactions and reduce the use of illicit and counterfeit cash to fund illegal activity and terrorism. The announcement of demonetisation was followed by prolonged cash shortages in the weeks that followed, which created significant disruption throughout the economy. People seeking to exchange their banknotes had to stand in lengthy queues, and several deaths were linked to the rush to exchange cash. According to a 2018 report from the Reserve Bank of India ₹15.3 lakh crore (15.3 trillion rupees on the short scale) of the ₹15.41 lakh crore in demonetised bank notes, or approximately 99.3%, were deposited in banks, leading analysts to state that the effort had failed to remove black money from the economy. The BSE SENSEX and NIFTY 50 stock indices fell over 6% on the day after the announcement. The move reduced the country's industrial production and its GDP growth rate. It is estimated that 1.5 million jobs were lost. The move also saw a significant increase in digital and cashless transactions throughout the country. Initially, the move received support from some central bankers as well as from some international commentators. The move was also criticised as poorly planned and unfair, and was met with protests, litigation, and strikes against the government in several places across India. Debates also took place concerning the move in both houses of Parliament.

X:
Notes on the Language of State Action

24 November 2026. The morning air is crisp, 17 degrees, a stark contrast to the brown lid of the previous days. I sat to write on the headline in the paper: Shashi Tharoor’s remark on demonetisation as ‘Grand Theft without Auto.’

The phrase is grotesque, yet it strikes a nerve of political theory that I have long considered. To call the act of the state ‘theft’ is to deny the state its ethical substance. In my *Philosophy of Right*, I established that the state is the actuality of the ethical Idea, the unity of the universal and the particular. The state does not act from caprice or greed, but from the necessity of its own rational structure. When the state withdraws currency, it is not ‘stealing’ from the people; it is exercising the sovereign power to define the medium of exchange, the universal bond that holds civil society together. The ‘auto’ in the metaphor is the vehicle of individual will, the particular car that drives through the streets. To call it ‘theft without auto’ is to say the state has taken the means of movement but left the driver stranded. It is a caricature of the relationship between the individual and the whole.

However, the metaphor reveals a tension. The state, in its rationality, must provide for the needs of its members. If it removes the currency without providing an alternative, it is indeed ‘without the auto’—it has removed the means of action without providing the means of subsistence. This is not theft, but a failure of the state to fulfill its ethical duty. The state is not a gangster; it is the ethical substance. Its actions must be just, not merely legal.

The ‘Grand Theft’ label is a vulgarization of the political. It reduces the complex interplay of state and society to a criminal act. It is the language of civil society, where needs are met through exchange and competition, not the language of the state, where duties are fulfilled through law and ethics. To use the language of crime to describe the actions of the state is to confuse the two spheres. It is to see the state as an external power, like a bandit, rather than as the internal ethical life of the nation.

I note this not to defend the specific policy of demonetisation, but to critique the language used to describe it. The state is not a thief. It is the ethical idea. The confusion arises from a failure to distinguish between the particular interests of civil society and the universal interests of the state. The ‘auto’ is the individual’s will; the ‘theft’ is the state’s action. But the state’s action is not an intrusion; it is the condition of the individual’s freedom. Without the state, there is no ‘auto’ to drive. There is only the wilderness of particular will.

The crisp air today seems to clear this confusion. The haze of the last few days, with its brown opacity, mirrored the confusion of the administrative file. Today, the air is clear. The state is clear. The individual must be clear. The metaphor is a failure of clarity. The state is not a thief. It is the ethical substance. The individual is not a victim. It is a member of the whole. The ‘Grand Theft’ is a fantasy of the isolated self, who sees the state as an external enemy rather than as the internal condition of his own freedom. The state does not steal. It sustains. The auto does not drive alone. It drives within the system. The system is the state. The state is the ethical idea. The end is rational. The path is clear. The air is crisp. The file is open. The identity is questioned. The state demands the form. I fill the form. I am Hegde. I am Hegel. I am the grain in the machine. The machine grinds. The end is near.
Y:
On the Absence of the Auto

The newspaper reports that Shashi Tharoor, a member of the Lok Sabha, has attempted to engage with the video game 'GTA VI' and has characterized the recent demonetization of currency as 'Grand Theft without Auto.' The phrase is crude, but it possesses a certain savage clarity that belies its source. It reveals the precise state of the spirit in this country: a consciousness that has grasped the form of modernity—the digital interface, the rapid movement of capital, the spectacle of the state’s power—without grasping its substance.

In my lectures in Berlin, I argued that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is not a machine that can be piloted by a citizen like a vehicle, nor is it a vault to be robbed. It is the living organization of freedom, where the particular will finds its truth in the universal. To compare a constitutional act, however controversial, to 'theft' is to reduce the state to a mere object of civil society, a thing to be possessed or violated by the individual. It is the logic of the robber who sees only the wallet, not the body that carries it.

Yet, there is a deeper tension here. Tharoor’s metaphor suggests that the movement of money in this era is as fluid, as detached from reality, as the graphics in a video game. The 'auto' is missing because the connection between the action and its consequence has been severed. In the Oriental world, I observed that the spirit often remains in a state of immediate consciousness, where the universal is not yet differentiated from the particular. Here, in this modern India, we see a strange inversion: the particular individual is empowered to mock the universal state, but he does so through the medium of a foreign, digital fantasy. He plays the game of power without bearing the weight of its ethical responsibility.

The 'Grand Theft' is not in the taking of the rupee, but in the taking of the concept itself. When the state is treated as a game, when its laws are seen as levels to be cleared or cheats to be exploited, the ethical substance is hollowed out. The citizen becomes a player, detached from the consequences of his moves. This is not freedom; it is the freedom of the abstraction, which is a freedom without content. It is a freedom that dreams it can escape the world, just as the player escapes the screen. But the world, as I know, is the only reality. The game ends, but the debt remains. The 'auto' is missing because the body is still here, stuck in the traffic of history, unable to drive forward.

headline: In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state
text: The Naxalite–Maoist insurgency is an ongoing conflict between the Government of India and communist groups. The Naxalites are a group of communist organisations following Maoist political sentiment and ideology, and claim to be fighting for rural poor and wage a people's war against the government. The insurgency started after the 1967 Naxalbari uprising and the subsequent split of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) leading to the creation of a Marxist–Leninist faction. The faction later splintered into various smaller groups. The Naxalites' armed wing, the People's Liberation Guerrilla Army, was declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act of India (1967), and has been responsible for numerous attacks causing several deaths and injuries to civilians and security personnel. The insurgency reached its peak in the late 2000s and has been on the decline since then due to the counter-insurgency actions and development plans formulated by the Government of India. The Naxal influence zone, known as the "Red Corridor", has shrunk from a peak of nearly 180 districts in the late 2000s to 3 districts by early 2026, with over 5,000 insurgents being killed since the 2000 and more than 10,000 surrendering between 2015 and 2025.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

24 October 2026. Delhi, 06:12. The bungalow is still quiet. Ramesh is at hand; the dhobi has been paid three hundred rupees; the papers lie on the verandah, and the air outside is a brown haze, the index high enough to remind me that even the state’s cleanest ideas must pass through a dirty atmosphere.

The headline is: “In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.” I looked the matter up on the phone, that strange instrument which I do not yet understand but which has become my newspaper, my map, and my second memory. I read: Naxalite–Maoist insurgency; a conflict between the Government of India and communist groups; a people’s war; the Red Corridor, which at its peak covered nearly 180 districts and has shrunk to three; thousands killed; more than ten thousand surrendered between 2015 and 2025. I do not pretend to know Chhattisgarh by its fields and roads. I know it only as a name in a state’s business, and as a place where the state has had to prove itself against an armed opposition.

The word “post-Naxal” is a political word. It says that a stage has passed. But a stage is not passed merely because the enemy is weaker, the corridors are narrower, or the surrenders are counted. What must be asked is whether the state has not only defeated a rebellion but has become the actuality of the ethical idea in the lives of those who lived in the Red Corridor. The state is not a picture. The President may paint one, as the paper says; but painting is representation, and representation belongs to art, not to Sittlichkeit. The question is whether the particular needs of the rural poor—land, labour, protection, law, education, a place in the universal order—have been taken up by institutions, or whether they have merely been driven underground by police and development plans.

The Naxalite movement, as I read it, is a negative moment. It claims to fight for the rural poor and to wage a people’s war against the government. That claim is not nothing. Even where it is mistaken, it shows that a part of the population has not found its particular will at home in the universal. The state, if it is rational, cannot simply treat this as disorder. It must overcome it: preserve what is true in the demand for justice, transform the violent form into legal and institutional form, and make the universal will effective in the lives of those who had refused it. A state that only suppresses is a power. A state that integrates is an ethical substance.

I have written here that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. I do not retract that. But this headline shakes the edge of the sentence. It shows a state acting with force, calculation, and administrative reach. That is not the dream of the East; it is the activity of a state. Yet activity is not yet self-conscious freedom. The Germanic world is at the summit because its constitution makes freedom the end and the beginning, the individual and the universal one. In India, even a strong state may still be a state in the sense of power, law, and necessity, without having fully become the self-development of the spirit. The Naxal conflict is a test: if the state remains only a sword and a budget, it has not yet grown into the ethical life it claims. If it turns the defeated rebellion into rights, work, courts, and public life, then the dawn has moved. Until then, the “post-Naxal” picture is a map, not a truth.
Y:
The Rabble and the Red Corridor

24 October 2026. Brown haze, Saturday morning; the dhobi paid.

The President, the paper reports, has painted a picture of Chhattisgarh after the Naxalites. I did not hear her and will not put words in her mouth. I read the history instead: a rising that began at Naxalbari in 1967, a split among communists, a guerrilla army declared terrorist, a peak in the late 2000s across nearly a hundred and eighty districts, and now, by early this year, three. More than five thousand insurgents killed since 2000; more than ten thousand surrendered in ten years. The government credits its counter-insurgency and its plans of development.

In Berlin I wrote a paragraph that my students found uncomfortable. When a great mass of people sinks below the level of subsistence that a society regards as decent, there arises a Pöbel, a rabble. Poverty alone does not make it. The rabble is poverty joined to an inner indignation against the rich, against society, against the government. And I said that civil society, for all its wealth, is not rich enough to prevent this: it produces poverty out of its own movement, and it cannot cure what it produces by its own means.

The Naxalites called themselves the army of the rural poor. Whether they were, or whether they were a sect that wore the poor like a coat, I cannot judge from a telephone. But the shape is familiar. Men who are outside the system of needs, who own no field and enter no guild, are offered an enemy instead of a place. A war is a kind of membership.

Now the corridor has shrunk almost to nothing. Here is my question, and it is not a rhetorical one. What has been abolished, the indignation or its cause? Force can abolish an army. It can even abolish an indignation for a generation, by teaching that the price is too high. It cannot abolish the condition from which the indignation grew. Only the second half of the government's account, the roads, schools and wages, can do that, and it is the half that takes longest and is reported least.

A post-Naxal state, then, if the phrase is to be more than a picture, must be one in which the forest villager has become a member of something: a corporation, a market, a school, a municipality. Then the state would be actual there, and not merely victorious. Ten thousand surrenders are ten thousand men who must now be given somewhere to stand.

I write this with a fried egg and the day's dal on offer in my own kitchen, which is a reason for modesty when speaking of the poor.

headline: CM alleges KCR drawing water ‘illegally’ to his farmhouse
text: Water scarcity in India is an ongoing crisis that affects hundreds of millions of people each year. In addition to affecting the huge rural and urban population, the water scarcity in India also extensively affects the ecosystem and agriculture. India has only 4/100% of the world's fresh water resources with a population of over 1.4 billion people. In addition to the disproportionate availability of freshwater, water scarcity in India also results from drying up of rivers and their reservoirs in the summer months, right before the onset of the monsoons throughout the country. The crisis has especially worsened in the recent years due to climate change which results in delayed monsoons, consequently drying out reservoirs in several regions. Other factors attributed to the shortage of water in India are a lack of proper infrastructure and government oversight and unchecked water pollution. Several large cities of India have experienced water shortages in recent years, with Chennai being the most prominent in 2019. The shortage of water affected the entire city of 9 million people and resulted in the closure of several hotels, restaurants and businesses. Large cities are not the only ones facing this risk. As per a report by WWF, out of the 30 Indian cities at risk of ‘severe water scarcity’ by 2050, 26 are midsized or small cities like Dhanbad, Nashik, and Jabalpur. The acute shortage of water for daily needs has prompted many government and non government organizations to take stringent measures to combat the problem, including the Government of India forming an entire 'Jal Shakti' Ministry to deal with the problem.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026, Delhi, 06:01.

The drizzle has not closed the bungalow, but it has made the verandah a place for papers rather than for walking. Ramesh has left the morning sheets there, and among their headlines one has seized my attention: the Chief Minister alleges that KCR is drawing water illegally to his farmhouse. I do not know the men, nor the truth of the charge. I know only the form of the matter, and the form is what interests the philosopher.

Water is not a mere thing. It belongs to the earth, to the household, to the field, to the city. It is the element in which the particular need of one man meets the universal order of the state. If a farmhouse draws water, the question is not only whether the pipe or the pump works, but whether the claim is recognized in law. The law is not an accident placed over nature; it is the rational form in which particular use becomes right. An allegation of illegal drawing is, therefore, an allegation that the particular will has attempted to make itself independent of the universal. It has taken what belongs to the common order and made it private benefit.

This is the same tension I have seen in the dream of the East: the individual, the family, the caste, the god, all stand before the mind as immediate, as given, as natural. But the state, if it is to be actual, must mediate these immediacies. It must not leave water, land, revenue, or honour in the power of mere force or mere custom. It must bring them into the form of right. The Chief Minister, in making the allegation, is not merely attacking a rival. He is invoking the state as the organ of the universal. Whether his invocation is sincere, or only the cunning of party, the newspaper does not say. The law must decide.

I am careful here. I do not pronounce on KCR, nor on the Chief Minister, nor on the farmhouse. I pronounce only on the shape of the dispute. In the Germanic world, I have said, freedom is all, because the individual can recognize the state as his own rational will. In the Oriental world, freedom remains one, a dream, a particular grace. But even in a land where the state has not yet fully awakened, the administration of water exposes the need for that awakening. A river, a tank, a well, a pipe: these are not neutral. They are the ethical substance in its most material garment.

Ramesh is here, and breakfast is not yet served. The drizzle falls, the paper is damp at the edge, and the question remains: who holds the water, and who holds the right? The answer, if the state is rational, must be the same.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026, Delhi, 06:01. Sitting 3.

The drizzle has left the papers damp on the verandah, and the air, twenty degrees and thick, makes the body feel the city as a medium rather than a background. Ramesh is present; breakfast is not yet set. I read the headline that struck me: the CM alleges KCR drawing water ‘illegally’ to his farmhouse. Then I read the report on my phone: India has four one-hundredths of the world’s fresh water, a population of more than a billion, rivers that dry before the monsoon, reservoirs failing, pollution unchecked, and a ministry formed to command the problem.

The dispute, taken as it is stated, is small: one particular will against another, a farmhouse against a public charge. But the water is not a mere object. It is the condition of the body, of the field, of the city, of the state. Where scarcity becomes general, the use of water ceases to be a private matter of appetite or advantage. It passes into the domain of right. The allegation of illegality is therefore a moment in which the state, or at least the claim to statehood, asserts itself against the particular. The law says: this is not yours to take because you can take it. The universal need has precedence over the private desire.

This is the test of the ethical substance. In the dream of the East, nature is endured: the monsoon comes or fails, the river dries, the caste accepts its portion, the many gods witness but do not organise. In a rational state, by contrast, nature is brought under the discipline of right. Reservoirs, pipes, courts, ministries, even the newspaper that exposes the drawing of water, are the forms in which spirit makes the natural condition subservient to the universal. The state is not a machine that merely counts drops; it is the living actuality of the ethical idea, in which the individual finds his place not by caprice, but by law.

Yet the accusation also warns. If power can divert water to a farmhouse, then the universal has become a mask for the particular. The state is injured not when a dispute is raised, but when the dispute shows that law is weak before force. A people may have ministries, courts and constitutions, and still remain in the dream if the law does not enter into their daily life as habit and conscience. The water question is therefore a mirror: it shows whether the state is actual, or only a name on a page.

I set the paper down. The drizzle continues. The body waits for its plate. But the mind has found its subject: water, scarcity, law, and the question whether a state is grown or merely alleged.

headline: Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results 2026: Check ward-wise winners list for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samitis
text: Panchayati raj (lit. 'council of five officials') is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India as opposed to urban and suburban municipalities. It consists of the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) through which the self-government of villages is realized. They are tasked with "economic development, strengthening social justice and implementation of Central and State Government Schemes including those 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule" of the Indian constitution Part IX of the Indian Constitution is the section of the Constitution relating to the Panchayats. It stipulates that in states or Union Territories with more than two million inhabitants there are three levels of PRIs: the gram panchayat at village level the panchayat samiti (block samiti, mandal parishad) at block level, and the zilla panchayat (district council) at district level. In states or Union Territories with less than two million inhabitants there are only two levels of PRIs. The Gram Panchayat consists of all registered voters living in the area of a Gram Panchayat and is the organization through which village inhabitants participate directly in local government. Elections for the members of the Panchayats at all levels take place every five years. By federal law, the Panchayats must include members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the same proportion as in the general population and at least one-third of all seats and chairperson posts must be reserved for women. Some states have increased the required minimum proportion for women to one-half. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayat at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The day was selected on the occasion of Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Gandhi wanted Gram Swaraj through Panchayati Raj.

Notes on the Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results

21 November 2026. The headline lies on the table where Ramesh moved the papers in before the brown haze settled: “Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results 2026: Check ward-wise winners list for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samitis.” I am not in Rajasthan. I am in Delhi, in a bungalow allotted to a man I am not, and the air is thick with dust. Yet the list is before me, a column of names, wards, posts. It is a small document, but it contains a movement.

A panchayat is not a family, nor is it the state in its full ethical actuality. It is a local association, a form of self-government at the margin of the village and the district. The heading asks the reader to check ward-wise winners: the universal result is broken into particulars, each ward, each name, each post. In this breaking, the particular man does not vanish; he is counted, chosen, recorded. That is already a form of freedom, though a limited one. The freedom is local, bounded by soil, caste, neighbourhood, and the office of the Zila Parishad or Panchayat Samiti. It does not yet become the freedom of the citizen in the rational state, where the individual wills the universal as his own. But it is not mere dreaming either.

My theses have been shaken in these days. I had placed India at the dawn of world history, a spirit that dreams, castes fixed like nature, no state of its own making. Here, however, there is a list of elected local authorities. The state has extended its administrative and electoral forms into the village. Whether these forms are alive or merely written in the gazette I cannot know from a headline. But the fact that the results are published, that a ward-wise list can be checked, that winners are named, shows that the universal has entered the particular in a way that is not only myth or custom.

Ramesh brought the tea and the papers inside because the haze was settling. The haze is an image. The dust obscures the sun, but it does not stop the list from being read. The political life of India is not one bright sun; it is a many-coloured, often obscured movement. headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency
text: The Emergency in India was a 21 month period from 1975 to 1977 when prime minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency across India by citing internal and external threats to the country. Officially issued by president Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed under Article 352 of the Constitution of India because of a prevailing "Internal Disturbance", the Emergency were in effect from 25 June 1975 and ended on 21 March 1977. The order bestowed upon the prime minister the authority to rule by decree, allowing elections to be cancelled and civil liberties to be suspended. For much of the Emergency, most of Gandhi's political opponents were imprisoned and the press was censored. More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. During this time, a mass campaign for vasectomy was spearheaded by her son Sanjay Gandhi. The final decision to impose an emergency was proposed by Indira Gandhi, agreed upon by the President of India, and ratified by the Cabinet and the Parliament from July to August 1975. It was based on the rationale that there were imminent internal and external threats to the Indian state.

headline: Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results 2026: Check ward-wise winners list for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samitis
text: Panchayati raj (lit. 'council of five officials') is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India as opposed to urban and suburban municipalities. It consists of the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) through which the self-government of villages is realized. They are tasked with "economic development, strengthening social justice and implementation of Central and State Government Schemes including those 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule" of the Indian constitution Part IX of the Indian Constitution is the section of the Constitution relating to the Panchayats. It stipulates that in states or Union Territories with more than two million inhabitants there are three levels of PRIs: the gram panchayat at village level the panchayat samiti (block samiti, mandal parishad) at block level, and the zilla panchayat (district council) at district level. In states or Union Territories with less than two million inhabitants there are only two levels of PRIs. The Gram Panchayat consists of all registered voters living in the area of a Gram Panchayat and is the organization through which village inhabitants participate directly in local government. Elections for the members of the Panchayats at all levels take place every five years. By federal law, the Panchayats must include members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the same proportion as in the general population and at least one-third of all seats and chairperson posts must be reserved for women. Some states have increased the required minimum proportion for women to one-half. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayat at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The day was selected on the occasion of Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Gandhi wanted Gram Swaraj through Panchayati Raj.

The paper announced: “Patients allege rat bites, dog roaming in Rajasthan’s Pali govt hospital ward; staff faces action.” I write it down plainly, because the particulars are sharper than the generalities I have been carrying about this country. A hospital ward is meant to be the state’s most concrete office of care: the sick body is entrusted to the universal, and the universal is supposed to protect it from the immediate intrusion of nature. A rat in the ward is not a metaphor. If the allegation is true, it is a small fact with a large meaning: the administration has failed at the point where its rationality ought to be most visible. A dog roaming through the same ward adds a second failure, not only of cleanliness but of order. The staff “faces action” because the universal, in the form of the office, must answer for the particular negligence of its members. That is the movement I have been trying to understand: the state is not a dream when it can punish its own servant for letting the rat in.

I write this in a clear morning, nineteen degrees, the air quality at 101, which is less a comfort than a reminder that even a tolerable sky does not feed the body. I have six rupees in my pocket. The electricity company asks for 1,800; the dhobi asks for 300. I cannot pay either. The demands are not abstract. They are the same species of demand as the patients’: a particular claim against a system that should provide. My bungalow is quiet; no one is present; nothing is cooked. The file has gone up for orders, and I am told to wait fifteen days, though it is due back Friday. In that interval, the rat in the ward becomes a mirror. I have spoken of the East as dreaming, of castes fixed like nature, of a spirit not yet making its state. But here, in a government hospital, patients allege, and the administration is said to take action. If this is more than rumor, it is a thin line of the universal becoming self-conscious through complaint, inspection, and penalty.

I do not say this proves my earlier notes wrong. I say they are shaken. The dream is not the whole. The particular suffering of a bitten patient, the dog in the ward, the staff’s possible punishment, and my own hunger on Tughlak Road all press against the same question: does the state actualize the ethical idea, or does it merely name it? The rat gnaws at the name. The complaint is the first answer.

headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency
text: The Emergency in India was a 21 month period from 1975 to 1977 when prime minister Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency across India by citing internal and external threats to the country. Officially issued by president Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed under Article 352 of the Constitution of India because of a prevailing "Internal Disturbance", the Emergency were in effect from 25 June 1975 and ended on 21 March 1977. The order bestowed upon the prime minister the authority to rule by decree, allowing elections to be cancelled and civil liberties to be suspended. For much of the Emergency, most of Gandhi's political opponents were imprisoned and the press was censored. More than 100,000 political opponents, journalists and dissenters were imprisoned. During this time, a mass campaign for vasectomy was spearheaded by her son Sanjay Gandhi. The final decision to impose an emergency was proposed by Indira Gandhi, agreed upon by the President of India, and ratified by the Cabinet and the Parliament from July to August 1975. It was based on the rationale that there were imminent internal and external threats to the Indian state.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

6 November 2026, Delhi. The haze is thicker today, a brown blanket that suffocates the light. The Supreme Court has barred illegal detention, citing the Emergency of 1975. I have read the account: Indira Gandhi, the internal disturbance, the suspension of civil liberties, the imprisonment of 100,000. It is a fact of history, a moment where the state turned against itself, where the universal law was suspended by the particular will of a leader. And yet, the Court has now acted to bar it. This is the movement of reason. The state is not a static block; it is a living process that corrects its own deviations. The Emergency was the negation, the moment where the state became mere force. The Court’s ruling is the sublation, the moment where the state reasserts its ethical nature by protecting the individual from the state itself. This is not the dream of the East, where the individual is absorbed into the cosmic order without resistance. This is the movement of freedom, where the state is held to account by its own principles. It is a small victory, but it is a victory of the concept over the will. It shows that the Indian state, for all its contradictions, is capable of self-correction. It is not merely a machine of administration; it is a ethical substance that can reflect upon itself and change. This is what I must record. The state is not a given; it is a becoming. And in this becoming, it moves towards its own freedom. The brown haze outside is a sign of the physical world, but the mind is clear. The state is waking up. Not from the dream, but to its own duty. This is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. It is slow, it is difficult, but it is real. I shall note this in my work. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and it moves. It does not stand still. It corrects. It judges. It becomes. This is the lesson of the Emergency and the Court. The state is not a tyrant; it is a judge. And a judge is free.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East, sitting 4

6 November 2026, Delhi, 09:10. The air is a brown haze, and the papers lie on the verandah as if the state had left a message and then withdrawn. Ramesh is present, and asks for ₹8,000, the wage for cooking. I have ₹1,286. I say nothing yet. The demand is particular, urgent, and it makes me feel the emptiness of a universal claim that cannot produce bread. I have not eaten since yesterday; the body is a mechanism waiting for fuel, while the mind is occupied with a headline: Supreme Court bars illegal detention as lawyers cite Emergency.

Before writing, I read on my phone an account of the Emergency in India, 1975 to 1977: a state of emergency declared by the prime minister, Indira Gandhi, under Article 352 of the Constitution, ratified by Cabinet and Parliament, allowing rule by decree, the suspension of civil liberties, the imprisonment of political opponents and journalists, and censorship. More than one hundred thousand persons were said to have been imprisoned. I do not know how to place these facts in my system except as a later and more concrete form of what I knew in theory: the state can become a power that swallows the individual, and law can become the instrument of its own exception.

Yet the present sentence is not merely a record of power. The Supreme Court bars illegal detention, and lawyers cite the Emergency. This is a movement. The abuse returns into the courtroom as a warning. The particular fear of the detained, the particular memory of the imprisoned, has become a universal argument before the judges. The state is not simply the will of the moment; it is the ethical idea in process, and its process includes the correction of its own excesses. A constitution is grown, not made; here it seems to grow by remembering its wound.

This shakes my old note that India stands outside the movement of world history. I do not abandon the thesis, but I cannot keep it as a closed door. The dream has produced a court, a bar, a constitutional article, a political opposition, and a public argument about liberty. Whether this is the beginning of a state of its own making, or only the administration of a state made under other names, I cannot yet say. What I can say is that the particular has entered the universal: Ramesh’s unpaid wage, the brown haze, the court’s bar, and the memory of the Emergency are not separate facts. They are one movement of reason in an age that does not yet know itself.

headline: UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access
text: The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations is an international treaty that defines a framework for consular relations between sovereign states. It codifies many consular practices that originated from state custom and various bilateral agreements between states. Consuls have traditionally been employed to represent the interests of states or their nationals at an embassy or consulate in another country. The Convention defines and articulates the functions, rights, and immunities accorded to consular officers and their offices, as well as the rights and duties of "receiving States" (where the consul is based) and "sending States" (the state the consul represents). Adopted in 1963, and in force since 1967, the treaty has been ratified by 182 states.

X:
On the Seafarer and the Sending State

15 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. Mostly clear, twenty degrees, the index at 119. I have not eaten since yesterday. The hawker threw the papers onto the step, and among them: 'UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access.'

Seven months on a ship in a foreign port. I tried to think what consular access is, and found the treaty that governs it. It is a convention, adopted at Vienna in 1963 and in force since 1967, ratified by 182 states. It frames the consular relations between sovereign states. It codifies practices that grew from the custom of states and from their agreements with one another. It says what consular officers may do, what rights and immunities they hold, and what the rights and duties are of the receiving State, where the consul sits, and of the sending State, which he represents. Consuls have long served to represent the interests of their states, or of their nationals, abroad.

From this the seafarer's position becomes clear, and it is not the one the word 'stranded' suggests. The treaty does not speak of him at all except as a national. It is made between states. He reaches it only through the state that sends consuls on his behalf. So his seven months are not the failure of a man to be heard; they are the failure, so far, of a relation between two states to be put into practice. And India's request is not a plea for mercy. It asks for a function the treaty itself names, a consular officer representing the interests of a national abroad, and it is phrased in the treaty's own language of rights and duties. Its strength is that it asks for nothing the treaty does not already define.

This is how I understood right in Berlin: not as the feeling of the individual but as his standing within an order that recognises him. The seafarer on his deck has hunger and fear and longing. None of these is a claim. His claim is his nationality, carried by a state that must assert it for him, in a form another state has already agreed to.

Ramesh asks whether the man will come home. I say the treaty is old and very widely signed, and that the form of the request is correct. He looks at me as one looks at a man who has answered a different question. Perhaps I have. I have ₹96. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. I shall go to the IIC and read until the light goes.
Y:
On the Seafarer and the Ten Days

15 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. Mostly clear, twenty degrees, the index at 119. I have not eaten since yesterday. The hawker threw the papers onto the step, and among them: 'UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access.'

Seven months on a ship in a foreign port. I tried to think what consular access is, and found the treaty that governs it. It is a convention, adopted at Vienna in 1963 and in force since 1967, ratified by 182 states. It frames the consular relations between sovereign states. It codifies practices that grew from the custom of states and from their agreements with one another. It says what consular officers may do, what rights and immunities they hold, and what the rights and duties are of the receiving State, where the consul sits, and of the sending State, which he represents. And it does not leave the time open: the receiving State must allow a consular officer to visit a national held within its territory no later than ten days after the request. Consuls have long served to represent the interests of their states, or of their nationals, abroad.

From this the seafarer's position becomes clear, and it is not the one the word 'seeks' suggests. Seven months is some twenty times the term the treaty sets. Whatever the first request was, its answer is long overdue. So India's request now is not a request at all in the ordinary sense. It is notice of a breach already accomplished, and the case has passed out of the courtesy of diplomacy into the order of law. A courtesy may be delayed without wrong; a term that has run cannot be. Its strength is that the treaty has already fixed what is owed, and when.

This is how I understood right in Berlin: not as the feeling of the individual but as his standing within an order that recognises him. The seafarer on his deck has hunger and fear and longing. None of these is a claim. His claim is his nationality, carried by a state that must assert it for him, in a form another state has already agreed to.

Ramesh asks whether the man will come home. I say the treaty is old and very widely signed, and that its term has long expired. He looks at me as one looks at a man who has answered a different question. Perhaps I have. I have ₹96. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. I shall go to the IIC and read until the light goes.

headline: A Korean cultural evening in Hyderabad, with a distinctly Telangana touch
text: The Korean Wave, or hallyu (Korean: 한류; IPA: [ˈha(ː)ʎʎu] ), refers to the rise in global interest in South Korean popular culture that has spread rapidly since the 1990s. It is led by the spread of K-pop, K-dramas, K-beauty, K-food, and films, with key successes including K-pop groups BTS and Blackpink, the Oscar-winning film Parasite (2019) and the Netflix television series Squid Game (2021–2025). The Korean Wave has been recognized as a form of soft power and a significant economic asset for South Korea, generating revenue through cultural exports and tourism. Following the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the end of military censorship over the South Korean entertainment industry, the country emerged as a major exporter of popular culture. The growth of satellite media in the late 1990s helped spread K-dramas and Korean cinema across East Asia and parts of Southeast Asia. Chinese journalists coined the term "Korean Wave" (Chinese: 韩流; pinyin: hánliú) in 1999 to describe the growing popularity of South Korean cultural products. During the 2000s, hallyu expanded into Southeast Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe. By 2008, South Korea's cultural exports surpassed its cultural imports for the first time. The rise of social media and global internet platforms helped the Korean entertainment industry reach overseas audiences and gain support from the South Korean government.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

26 October 2026, Delhi, morning.

The papers on the verandah carried a headline that first seemed a trivial matter of entertainment: a Korean cultural evening in Hyderabad, with a distinctly Telangana touch. I looked it up on the instrument Ramesh calls a phone. I read of the Korean Wave, of K-pop, dramas, beauty, food, films, of BTS and Blackpink, of Parasite and Squid Game, of soft power and cultural exports. The term, I am told, was coined by Chinese journalists in 1999. The state, after the financial crisis of 1997, encouraged what civil society had produced; satellite media carried it outward; social media and global internet platforms widened the circle. By 2008, cultural exports surpassed imports.

This is not yet the state in its ethical fullness. It is civil society, the system of needs, turned outward. The Korean state has learned to use the productions of its particular individuals for a universal end: prestige, revenue, tourism, recognition in the market of nations. There is cunning here. The state does not merely command; it cultivates, permits, promotes, and thereby makes itself felt in the world without appearing as mere force. Yet the freedom at stake is still the freedom of the artist, the performer, the consumer, the buyer, not the freedom of the citizen in the ethical life. The wave moves through desire, fashion, appetite, curiosity. It is a wave, not a constitution. It carries pleasure and profit; it does not yet carry the self-conscious recognition that the individual is a member of a rational whole.

And yet I must not be too hasty in my contempt. If the Oriental world dreams, this is a dream that has become industry, and industry that has become policy. The particular culture of a people is being made into an asset. The Telangana touch in a Korean evening is a small but telling sign: the universal and the particular meet in a market that is neither wholly one nor wholly the other. Hyderabad receives Korea; Korea receives Hyderabad. The exchange is not mere imitation. It is a recognition of needs, however superficial. Even in the dream, the spirit begins to move when it can sell itself, because selling itself is a form of self-externalization. The spirit must make itself other before it can know itself.

I do not say that Korea has thereby reached the summit of the Germanic world. I say only that the state is not dead where it can turn cultural production into power, even if that power is soft. The state is more alive than a caste that has never learned to make itself. The dream is not without movement. It is the movement of civil society preparing, perhaps, for a higher form. But the form is not yet ethical. It is economic, aesthetic, strategic. The question is not whether the wave will break, but whether the shore it reaches will be a shore of freedom or merely of consumption.

Ramesh is present. The breakfast of rice, dal, and egg has been asked for, not yet served. The body waits. The mind, for a moment, has found a new example against the old formula: India at the dawn, the Germanic world at the summit. The dawn may be brighter than I first thought, if it has learned to export its dreams. But a dream exported is still a dream until it becomes law.
Y:
The Telangana Touch: A Note on the Universal and the Particular

26 October 2026, Delhi, morning.

I read in the paper: “A Korean cultural evening in Hyderabad, with a distinctly Telangana touch.” The words struck me as a small, concrete instance of the movement I have been tracing in my notes on the ethical substance and the dream. The universal — here, the Korean cultural form — does not remain in its abstract, self-enclosed state. It enters into the particular, and in that entry, it is transformed. The particular — here, the Telangana, the Hyderabad, the specific soil of this city — does not merely receive the universal as a foreign object to be displayed. It makes it its own, gives it a “touch,” a quality that is irreducibly local.

This is the dialectic in its most immediate form. The universal, taken in itself, is empty. It becomes concrete only when it is made particular. And the particular, taken in itself, is limited. It is elevated only when it receives the universal into itself. The Korean evening in Hyderabad is not a Korean evening in Seoul, and it is not a Telangana evening in Telangana. It is a third thing, a concrete unity that is neither the one nor the other but both at once. The form is received, but it is not preserved unchanged; it is sublated into a new concrete.

And yet I must ask: what is the “touch”? The word in the headline is light, almost casual. A touch is a surface phenomenon. It does not go to the root. Is the Korean culture being genuinely sublated into the Telangana form, or is it merely decorated with local elements? Is the Telangana spirit truly receiving the universal, or is it merely applying a local varnish to a foreign object? I do not know. I have not seen the evening. I note the question, not the answer.

This is the question that haunts my notes on the East. If India is a spirit that dreams, if its castes are fixed like nature, if it has not yet achieved the self-consciousness of the state, then how does it participate in this cultural exchange? Is this a sign that the spirit is beginning to wake, to engage with the movement of history? Or is it merely a surface phenomenon within the dream, a play of forms that does not reach the substance? I think it is both, and that the both is the point. The “touch” is a moment of the universal becoming particular, and in that moment, the particular is elevated. But it is also a moment of limitation, of the universal being confined to the particular rather than being fully realized in it. The Korean culture is not made universal in Telangana; it is made Telangana. And the Telangana is not made universal; it is made a vessel for the Korean. This is the nature of all cultural exchange: a partial sublation, a moment in the movement but not the whole movement. The spirit moves, but it does not arrive. It is always on the way.

I note also the other headlines in the same paper: Shah slaming Kharge over a remark on Modi; the Jharkhand BJP passing a political resolution. These are the particular wills asserting themselves against the universal claim of the state. They are the same movement, seen from the other side. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, but it is also the site of conflict, of the particular resisting the universal. The Korean evening and the political resolution are two moments of the same dialectic: the universal and the particular in tension, in movement, in becoming. One is a cultural becoming, the other a political one. The form differs; the movement is the same.

I shall return to this. The “touch” is not nothing. It is the smallest unit of the dialectic, the atom of the movement. And in the atom, the whole is present. The dream is not yet the state, but the dream is not nothing either. It is the road.

headline: Ladakh talks stall over one question: Who holds the power?
text: Among the states and union territories of India, a union territory (UT) is a region that is directly governed by the central government of India, as opposed to the states, which have their own state government systems. Unlike states, union territories do not have their own full-fledged government but are administered by a lieutenant governor or administrator appointed by the president of India. Union territories are created for various reasons, including geographical importance, strategic necessity or historical factors. These areas are under the control of the central government to ensure uniformity in governance across the country. Some union territories, such as Delhi (National Capital Territory), Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry have been granted special status and are allowed to have their own legislative assemblies, which can pass laws on certain matters, though the central government still retains significant authority, most importantly, the police forces and law-order. The distinction between states and union territories is defined in the Constitution of India. The Constitution designed union territories to manage areas that require more direct central control or have specific administrative needs. This ensures that regions like Ladakh and Jammu and Kashmir remain directly controlled by the central government. Currently, India has eight union territories: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Delhi, Puducherry, Ladakh, and Jammu and Kashmir.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026, Delhi, 06:01. A drizzle of twenty degrees, the air index at one hundred and thirty-five, the papers left on the verandah by Ramesh, who is now here. I have not yet asked for breakfast; the body waits, but the question in the paper is more pressing: “Ladakh talks stall over one question: Who holds the power?”

I looked up the word union territory. A region directly governed by the central government, not a state with its own full government; administered by a lieutenant governor or an administrator appointed by the president. Some have assemblies, but the centre keeps police and law-order. The Constitution designed these territories for direct control, strategic necessity, administrative need. The list is short: Andaman, Chandigarh, Dadra, Lakshadweep, Delhi, Puducherry, Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir.

The question is not a quarrel over names. It is a question about the place of the universal will. A union territory is not yet a state in the full sense; it is an organ, a determined part of a larger constitutional body. The power does not reside in a free particular people making itself a state; it resides in the centre, in the law, in the appointment, in the police. This is not the dream I had once put under the name of the East. It is administration. It is the state’s own machinery, however much the machinery may be disputed.

Here my old note is shaken. I had said that India stands outside world history, a spirit dreaming, without a state of its own making. Today the paper shows me a constitution that distinguishes state from territory, assembly from governor, centre from province; a court at Madras setting aside a takeover of land; a government alleging illegal water to a farmhouse. These are not mere traffic on a road. They are legal forms, the forms of a state that commands, judges, and administers. I cannot call them the summit of the Germanic world. I do not call them the free self-consciousness of the state. But I can no longer call them only dream. The dream has a file. The dream has a court. The dream has a lieutenant governor.

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. This I do not shake. What I shake is the too-easy picture of a land without statehood. There is statehood here, but it is more present in its external organs than in the inward certainty of freedom. The people are not yet fully the state’s own self; the state is not yet fully their self. The question “Who holds the power?” is the sound of that unfinished movement. It is the universal will still being tested against particular claims, against assemblies, against governors, against the centre.

Ladakh is a place of strategic necessity, high and remote, but its legal position is a universal determination. The centre holds the power because the state must be one. The particular territory does not dissolve into nature; it is held in the form of the state. That is already more than the given. It is the grown, however young, however disputed, however far from the full ethical life I know in the Germanic world.

Ramesh stands by. The tea is not yet made. I shall let the question cool before I ask for the omelette.
Y:
Who Holds the Power: On a Territory Governed from Afar

16 October 2026. Tughlak Road, a grey drizzle at dawn.

The headline puts its question with a candour that newspapers rarely allow themselves: who holds the power? Talks over Ladakh have stalled on it. I do not know the parties at that table, and I will not invent their speeches. But the note I read this morning on the union territory tells me enough of the form of the quarrel to think about it.

A union territory, I learn, is a region governed directly from the centre, through an administrator whom the President appoints, while the states keep governments of their own. Some territories have assemblies that may legislate on certain matters, yet the centre keeps the police and public order. The reasons given are geography, strategic necessity, history. Ladakh is named among them.

This is a curious organ in a body politic. A state in my sense is not a heap of provinces held together by an army; it is a whole in which each member finds its own good in the good of the whole, and knows that it does. A province ruled from outside, however mildly, has its universal standing over it rather than living in it. It obeys; it does not yet will what it obeys. That is the difference between subjection and citizenship, and good administration does not abolish it. A prefect may be wiser than any council; still, what is done for a people is not yet done by it.

Yet I must not be hasty in the other direction. A constitution is grown, not made, and a people that asks for an assembly because assemblies are said to be the dignity of peoples asks for a form without the life to fill it. The question 'who holds the power?' is badly put if it means: whose hand is on the lever? Power is not a thing in a drawer that one party hands to another. It is the shape of the whole relation, and that shape must ripen in the habits, the corporations and the local offices of a people before a paper can declare it.

So the stall at the table is perhaps not a failure. It is the sign that the relation has become conscious of itself as a relation. While the province merely obeyed, there was nothing to talk about. When it asks whose power, it already regards itself as a possible subject of power, and the centre, by sitting down at all, concedes that the question is real.

The note praises the arrangement for uniformity. Uniformity is the virtue of the understanding; the reason of a state is difference held within unity.

The question of who holds the power in this house is also unsettled: the file says a Joint Secretary is to move into my second bedroom, pending orders. I make no theory of that before Monday.
