8 November 2026. Delhi. The air quality index is 207. The brown haze is thicker today. It is Diwali. The city is supposed to be celebrating the triumph of light over darkness, but the light is choked by the smoke of the very oil lamps that are meant to dispel the night. It is a dialectic of perception: the festival demands clarity, yet the atmosphere provides only opacity. I am sitting in the bungalow, the white cotton kurta cool against my skin, but the heat of the day is a physical weight. Ramesh is waiting. He asks for eight thousand rupees for wages and one thousand five hundred for groceries. I have eight hundred and thirty-six. The gap is not merely financial; it is ontological. It is the gap between the ethical claim of the servant, who expects recognition through material exchange, and the administrative reality of my mistaken allotment, which denies me the stable income to meet that claim. The state, which is supposed to be the actuality of the ethical idea, has failed to mediate this relationship. I am a ghost in the machine, and the machine is jammed. The headline in the paper speaks of the Chief Minister of Assam encouraging protests against the judges in the Zubeen Garg case. This is a new manifestation of the tension I have been observing. The executive power, the particular will of the leader, rises against the judicial power, the universal application of law. In the Germanic world, we understand that the state is not merely a collection of wills but a rational whole where the executive serves the law. Here, the executive seeks to override the law. Is this a sign that the spirit of India is still in the dream, where the particular will of the ruler is supreme? Or is it a sign that the modern state, with its separation of powers, is struggling to take root in a soil that is still accustomed to the unity of command? The judges are the embodiment of the universal; the minister is the embodiment of the particular. The protest is the collision. I do not know if the protest is rational or merely a passion. But I see that the state is not a static structure. It is a movement. And in this movement, the particular and the universal are constantly testing each other. The brown haze is a symbol of this confusion. The light of Diwali is a symbol of the ideal. The reality is in between. I must continue to observe. I must not judge too quickly. The spirit must work through its contradictions to reach a higher unity. But for now, the unity is elusive. The haze remains. Ramesh remains. The eight hundred and thirty-six rupees remain. The gap remains. I write this down, not to solve it, but to record the tension. The record is the first step of the spirit’s self-knowledge. I am here. I am watching. The day is dismissed, but the mind remains awake.
Y:
The Protest and the Law: A Note on the Assam Headlines

8 November 2026. Delhi, 09:16.

The headline reads: “Assam CM encouraging protests against Judges in Zubeen Garg death case.” I read it in the brown haze of the morning, the air quality index hovering at 207, a physical manifestation of the spiritual stagnation I have long described. The Chief Minister of Assam, Akhil Gogoi, is urging the people to protest against the judiciary. This is a moment of high tension, a dialectic between the executive power and the judicial power, but it is a tension that reveals a deeper structural flaw in the modern state.

In my lectures on the Philosophy of Right, I established that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the unity of the particular (the individual, the family, civil society) and the universal (the constitution, the laws). The judiciary is the organ that gives this unity its rational form; it is the mechanism by which the abstract right becomes concrete. When the executive, the branch that represents the particular will of the government, encourages protests against the judges, it is not merely a political maneuver. It is a violation of the ethical substance. It is the particular asserting itself against the universal, not through the rational process of law, but through the force of public opinion and the pressure of the mob.

This brings to mind my observations on the Oriental world. I have written that in India, there is no sense of personal independence with which a state of despotism could be compared. The spirit dreams. It does not act through the mediation of the rational state. It acts through the weight of custom, of caste, of the immediate will. When the Chief Minister calls for protests, he is not appealing to the rational nature of the citizens. He is appealing to their particular interests, their passions, their immediate grievances. He is bypassing the state as the ethical idea. He is treating the judiciary not as an organ of the state, but as an external force to be resisted by the pressure of the masses.

This is the dream of the East. It is the substitution of the immediate for the mediated. The protest is the dream; the law is the waking. The dream is beautiful, but it is not free. It is bound to the particular, to the moment, to the person of the Chief Minister. The law is rational, and therefore free. It is bound to the universal, to the constitution, to the idea of the state.

I see this in the headlines, and I see it in the confusion of my own residence. I am here by a mistake, a clerical error that has placed me, a German philosopher, in a bungalow meant for an Indian Joint Secretary. I am a particular that does not fit the universal category of the allotment. And yet, I am here. I am free. I am free because I am a spirit that can see the whole. I can see the tension between the dream and the state, between the protest and the law. I can see that the protest is a return to the immediate, a return to the dream. And I can see that the law is the only way to freedom.

The Chief Minister’s call for protest is a sign of the times. It is a sign that the state has not yet fully realized its ethical idea. It is a sign that the particular still asserts itself against the universal. But it is also a sign of progress. For it is in the tension, in the conflict, that the spirit moves. The protest is the negative moment. The law is the positive moment. And the state is the unity of the two.

I must return to the table. Ramesh is waiting, and the dhobi is waiting. The body demands its fuel, and the household demands its order. But the mind must continue its work. The difference between dream and state is not a matter of preference, but of reason. And reason is the only guide to freedom.

headline: Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project: Railways to energise Surat-Bilimora section, B28 train launch targeted in 10 months
text: The Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail corridor (MAHSR) is an under-construction high-speed rail line, which will connect Mumbai, Maharashtra, the financial hub of India, with Ahmedabad, the largest city in the state of Gujarat. When completed, it will be India's first high-speed rail line, with a design speed of 350 km/h (215 mph), and the project will include a 353 km-long (219 mi) viaduct, which will be the longest bridge in the world. The line is being developed by the National High Speed Rail Corporation Limited (NHSRCL), a wholly owned subsidiary of Indian Railways, the Ministry of Railways, and the Government of India. The line will use Shinkansen technology from Japan, including rolling stock, signalling and design standards – with technology transfer to support the Make in India programme. After delays due to the COVID-19 pandemic, construction commenced in February 2021, when the NHSRCL began to pour concrete to cast the corridor's first pillar. An initial section between Surat and Bilimora in Gujarat, is planned to open for service on 15 August 2027, with the full line to open by 2029.

20 November 2026, Delhi. The brown haze lies at two hundred and eighty-seven, and the air has the quality of a thought that will not finish. On the step the paper announced that the Surat–Bilimora section of the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed rail line is to be energised, and that the launch of the B28 train is targeted in ten months. I read further on the telephone instrument: the corridor is under construction, its design speed is three hundred and fifty kilometres an hour, it is to include a viaduct of three hundred and fifty-three kilometres, and the account calls it the longest bridge in the world. The initial section between Surat and Bilimora is planned for 15 August 2027; the full line is to open by 2029. It is Japanese technology, with transfer for the “Make in India” programme. These are not my words; they are the words of the account. But they move in me.

In my notes I have said that India stands at the dawn of history and outside its movement, a spirit that dreams. The dream, I argued, is not yet the state’s own making. Yet this morning the dream has a timetable. It is not a cloud; it is a line on a map. It is concrete poured for a pillar, a viaduct carried over ground that resists, a section to be energised, a date set against the resistance of delay. Mechanism has its place in the world of Mind, and this is mechanism: rails, signalling, rolling stock, target dates. But it is not mere mechanism. It is the universal entering the particular, and the particular returning as a possible actuality. The state is not here merely a name in a file, nor the ethical idea a promise in the haze. It is building a bridge. It is fixing a date. It is making the future into a thing that can be obstructed, postponed, completed.

I do not therefore reverse my judgment. The train is not freedom. It does not by itself make all free, nor does it dissolve caste, nor clear the air, nor settle the file that is due back from orders today. The state may be powerful without being fully rational in the ethical sense. Yet the old formula is shaken. If India is only dreaming, the dream has become an engineering problem. If it is outside the movement, it is moving at three hundred and fifty kilometres an hour. The tension is this: the universal project descends into the particular ground of a country that I have ranked at the dawn, and in that descent it begins to alter the ranking. I shall not say the summit has been reached. I shall say the dawn has a schedule.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. The air quality index is 287. The brown haze is no longer a metaphor; it is a physical obstruction to the movement of the spirit. I sat on the step, the white cotton kurta already damp with the stillness, and read the headline: 'Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project: Railways to energise Surat-Bilimora section.'

I have looked it up. It is a line of 353 kilometers, the longest bridge in the world, designed for 350 km/h. It is built with Japanese technology, the Shinkansen, but the goal is 'Make in India.' The section between Surat and Bilimora is to open in 2027. The full line in 2029. Ten months from now, they say, the B28 train will launch.

This is the dialectic of the state made visible. In my earlier notes, I spoke of India as standing at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, whose castes are fixed like nature. I held that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, grown, not made. But here is a state that is making, rapidly and mechanically, a bridge that spans the entire width of the subcontinent. It is not a dream; it is concrete and steel and Japanese signalling systems.

Is this a contradiction to my thesis? Or is it the movement I predicted? The Oriental world, I said, is one where one is free, but the freedom is subjective, trapped in the individual soul. Here, the state is asserting its universality through infrastructure. It is not yet a state of its own making in the political sense I understand, but it is a state of its own making in the economic and technical sense. The bullet train is the cunning of reason in motion. It compresses distance, it unifies the particular into a universal network. It is the state’s body.

The haze chokes the air, but the train cuts through it. The file at the Directorate is a delay, a friction, a particular that refuses to resolve. The bullet train is a resolution, a movement that turns the abstract potential of the nation into a concrete reality. I must revise my notes. India is not merely dreaming. It is building. And the building is the awakening. The dream is no longer the end; it is the fuel. The state is not just the ethical idea; it is the engine. And I am sitting in the station, waiting for the train that is not yet here, while the file that is here waits for me. The delay and the speed are two sides of the same coin. I shall go to the Directorate. The mechanism must be engaged.

I woke to find Ramesh on the verandah, the papers damp with the humidity of the haze. He does not look at me. He knows the arithmetic of our situation better than I do: he asks for ₹8,000 for the cooking wage, and I have ₹166 in my pocket. He asks for ₹1,500 for groceries. I cannot pay. The electricity company demands ₹1,800. I cannot pay. The system of needs is not broken; it is functioning precisely as it should. The particular (my empty purse) clashes with the universal (the debt owed), and the friction generates the heat that stifles the house. Ramesh retreats to the kitchen, but there is no fire. There is no fuel. The engine is idle.

It is in this silence, with the brown haze pressing against the glass, that I read the headline: “LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike.” The police removed the protesters. The protesters resumed the stir. This is not a tragedy; it is a mechanism. I have long maintained that the Oriental world is a state of dream, where the individual is fixed in nature, in caste, in the given. But here, in this brown haze, I see the individual asserting itself against the state. The hunger strike is the particular will pushed to its extreme, a negation of the body to force a recognition from the universal. The police removal is the state’s assertion of order, the universal crushing the particular to maintain the form.

But the protest resumes. It does not end in the police action; it returns. This suggests a movement. In the Germanic world, the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the individual finds their freedom within it, not by destroying it. But here, the individual is not yet fully integrated. They are outside the state, or perhaps the state is not yet fully actualized. The hunger strike is a sign of the spirit’s awakening, a refusal to remain in the dream of the given. They are demanding recognition. The police remove them, but the idea remains. The protest is the negation that drives the dialectic forward.

I am a ghost in this bungalow, unable to pay for my food, unable to clear the air. Yet, I am not merely a spectator. I am part of this friction. My inability to pay is a particular failure, but it reflects the larger tension between the individual and the universal. The state provides the house, but not the means to live in it. The administration assigns the name, but not the identity. I am Hegel, but I am treated as Hegde. I am the philosopher, but I am trapped in the clerk’s ledger. This is the alienation of the modern age. The spirit is free in thought, but the body is bound by the brown haze and the empty purse.

The protesters in Kerala are hungry. I am hungry. The hunger is the same. It is the hunger for recognition, for the actualization of the self in the world. The state must learn to feed its citizens, not just house them. The dream must wake. The brown haze must clear. The spirit must breathe.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

13 November 2026, 09:18. Delhi, Tughlak Road.

The headline on the verandah paper—LPST rankholders resume stir in front of Keralam Secretariat after police remove protesters on hunger strike—arrived at the wrong moment. I had been reading on my phone what the state calls unemployment: a thing measured in decadal samples, then monthly by a non-governmental office in Mumbai; jobless growth, they say, as if growth were a river that leaves the banks dry. The words pressed against me like the brown haze, now 362, a colour without substance.

Ramesh stood in the house without being asked. He knows the wage is more than the purse holds, and he says it without looking at the purse. He asks for eight thousand for cooking; I have one hundred and sixty-six rupees. He asks for fifteen hundred for groceries; the same one hundred and sixty-six. The electricity wants eighteen hundred. He might come on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays for four thousand a month. This is not a private quarrel. It is the system of needs turned inside out: the need is there, the money is not, the state is absent from the kitchen, and the body—my body, which has not eaten for more than a day—becomes the first document of the ethical failure.

The hunger strike in Kerala, as reported, is a particular suffering made visible. When the police remove the strikers, the state shows itself as force, not yet as the rational mediation of civil society. A state that is the actuality of the ethical idea must not merely clear the road; it must make the road go somewhere. If the rankholders are rankholders, their rank is not a caste, but a claim: that the universal order has a place for them. The dream of the East is not only in temple and caste; it is also in the queue for a post, in the sample survey, in the month in which no one is counted.

My earlier notes spoke of the East as dreaming, outside the movement of freedom. Today that phrase is shaken. A people who hunger-strike in front of a secretariat are not merely dreaming. They are demanding that the state become what it ought to be. Yet the demand is still particular: this post, this wage, this removal, this police line. The state must grow, not be made; but if it grows only to remove the hungry, it has become a mechanism without spirit.

I write this while Ramesh waits, because waiting is the first discipline of a household. I will not promise what the purse cannot hold. The state’s money is not my money; my money is not enough. The file has gone up for orders; Mr. Saxena says fifteen days. The occupation is irregular, and so is the day. The haze is outside; the hunger is inside. The ethical substance is not a dream until the state forgets the body.

If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, then this railway is a manifestation of that idea. It is the state making itself real. It is the spirit overcoming the limitations of nature. This challenges my view of the 'Oriental' spirit as static. Perhaps the dream is not the end, but the beginning. Perhaps the movement has already started, even if the consciousness of freedom has not yet fully awakened.

The brown haze presses against the glass. Ramesh is here, asking for wages I do not have. The system of needs is broken, the particular will is frustrated. Yet, beyond the haze, the train runs. The freedom of the state is not a static condition, but a process. And in this process, the dream of the East is perhaps not a dream at all, but the first stirrings of a new movement.

I have only ₹166 in my pocket. The world outside is moving at high speed. The contrast is painful, but instructive. The particular is limited; the universal is expansive. I must write this down. The dream is not the end. The movement has begun.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

9 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air quality index is 200; the haze is a brown wall against the glass. I woke to find Ramesh on the verandah with the papers. He is a practical man, concerned with the immediate needs of the body: eight thousand rupees for the wage of cooking, one thousand five hundred for groceries. I have three hundred and forty-six rupees in my pocket. The gap between the particular need and the universal provision is not a clerical error here; it is the reality of the household. I cannot pay him. I sat down to write, not from the comfort of a library, but from the pressure of a hunger that is eighteen hours old and a bureaucracy that has sent my file 'up for orders.'

The headline before me is a violence of language: 'Armed Naxals wiped out, need to save country from dimagi-Naxals.' The Prime Minister in Bastar speaks of saving the country from 'dimagi-Naxals,' a phrase that translates roughly to 'mental Naxals' or 'ideological insurgents.' This is the state in its immediate, ethical moment, confronting the threat to its own actuality. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; it must maintain its own unity against the particular wills that would tear it apart. The 'armed' Naxal is a threat to the person and property, the external security of civil society. The 'dimagi' Naxal is a threat to the inner conviction, the subjective freedom that has turned against the universal.

In my earlier notes, I wrote of India as a spirit that dreams, standing outside the movement of world history. I wrote of the castes fixed like nature. But here, in the brown haze, with the state asserting its power in Bastar and the administration in Delhi failing to resolve a clerical error, I see a tension I did not fully anticipate. The state is not merely a dream; it is an active force, wiping out the armed and seeking to correct the mental. It is the ethical substance asserting itself. Yet, is this assertion the growth of the constitution, or merely the imposition of power? The 'dimagi-Naxals' are those whose subjective freedom has not yet found its home in the universal. The state seeks to save them, or to save itself from them, by aligning their minds with the actuality of the state.

This is not the dream of the East. This is the struggle of the state to become actual. The brown haze is the atmosphere of this struggle: it is not the clear sky of the summit, but the smoke of the fire that burns the old and prepares the new. I am here, in the bungalow meant for Hegde, a particular mistake in the universal system. But the system is moving. The file is up for orders. The Naxals are wiped out. The state is acting. I must wait for the orders. I must wait for the haze to clear, or to thicken. The spirit is in motion, even if the body is hungry and the wallet is empty.
Y:
The Dimagi-Naxal and the Brown Haze: Notes on Security and Identity

9 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air quality index is 200. The haze is not merely a meteorological condition; it is the atmosphere of the present moment. It is a brown, suffocating veil that separates the eye from the horizon, much as the current political spectacle separates the public from the rational state.

I have sat down to consider the headline in the paper: “Armed Naxals wiped out, need to save country from dimagi-Naxals: PM Modi in Bastar.” The language is striking in its duality. It distinguishes between the ‘armed’ and the ‘dimagi’ (mental/imaginary). This is a dialectic of security that has moved beyond the physical to the psychical. The state is no longer merely defending its borders or its citizens from external aggression; it is defending the mind of the nation from internal dissent. The ‘dimagi-Naxal’ is not a person with a gun, but a thought, a sentiment, a deviation from the unified will of the state.

This reminds me of the tension I have been observing in the household. Ramesh is here, asking for ₹8,000 for cooking and ₹1,500 for groceries. I have ₹346. The particular need of the cook and the particular need of the philosopher are in collision. There is no universal law in this bungalow that resolves this friction immediately. The state, in the form of the Directorate, is absent, or rather, its presence is a bureaucratic ghost, delaying the resolution of my own status. The ‘dimagi’ element here is the confusion of Hegde for Hegel. The state has projected an identity onto a body that does not belong to that identity. Is this not a form of ‘dimagi-Naxalism’? A mental intrusion into the legal structure?

In the ‘Germanic world’ I once posited as the summit of freedom, the individual and the state are reconciled. The individual recognizes the state as the actuality of the ethical idea. Here, the state seems to be struggling to recognize the individual, while the individual is struggling to recognize the state. The ‘dimagi-Naxal’ is the gap between the two. The government speaks of saving the country from this mental threat. But who is saving the citizen from the state’s error?

The brown haze presses against the glass. It is a filter. It blurs the distinction between the real and the imaginary. Perhaps this is the point. In the haze, the ‘armed’ and the ‘dimagi’ become indistinguishable. The state must fight what it cannot see. The philosopher must think what he cannot breathe. I am hungry. The last meal was 18 hours ago. The body is the ‘armed’ reality; the hunger is the ‘dimagi’ demand. I cannot pay Ramesh. I cannot feed myself. I am a ghost in the bungalow. The file is gone for orders. The state is thinking. I am waiting. The haze remains.

X:
On Judges and the Crowd Outside the Window

Tughlak Road, New Delhi
8 November 2026, Diwali

Sir,

Your paper reports that Akhil Gogoi accuses the Chief Minister of Assam of encouraging protests against the judges in the Zubeen Garg death case. I know nothing of the case beyond that headline, and I do not presume the accusation true. I write about the principle it raises, which is the same whether it is true or false.

A court has two faces. Its proceedings and its judgment must be public: a people has the right to see justice done and to know the reasons by which it is bound. I argued this in Berlin against those who preferred tribunals behind closed doors. But the deliberation of the judges among themselves is not public and must not be. There the judges are still particular men holding particular opinions; their opinion becomes law only when it has passed through the form of a judgment. To press upon them while they deliberate, with crowds and banners and the encouragement of the powerful, is to force the opinion of the street into the very room where opinion is meant to be refined into right.

The danger is greatest when the pressure comes from a government. A crowd that shouts at a court is public opinion, which deserves both respect and contempt: respect for the true interest it obscurely contains, contempt for the form in which it shouts. A minister who sets the crowd moving is not public opinion at all. He is one power of the state using the street to lean on another. Your readers will know that long tenure protects judges against dismissal by those their rulings displease. Tenure does not protect them against noise beneath the window.

Let the people mourn a man whose death they plainly care about, and let them criticise the verdict when there is one. Let the minister keep out of the courtyard.

I write this on a festival of lamps. Two men wait at my door, as men do at Diwali, expecting something for a year's service to the house. I have eight hundred and thirty-six rupees, and I owe one of them more than ten times that. I mention it only because it is the morning's other lesson in right: what is due is due whether or not the purse can meet it, and no festival alters the account. A household, like a court, must not let the pressure of the moment write the judgment.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,

G. W. F. Hegel
Y:
The Protest and the Law: A Note on the Assam Headlines

8 November 2026. Delhi, 09:16.

The headline reads: “Assam CM encouraging protests against Judges in Zubeen Garg death case.” I read it in the brown haze of the morning, the air quality index hovering at 207, a physical manifestation of the spiritual stagnation I have long described. The Chief Minister of Assam, Akhil Gogoi, is urging the people to protest against the judiciary. This is a moment of high tension, a dialectic between the executive power and the judicial power, but it is a tension that reveals a deeper structural flaw in the modern state.

In my lectures on the Philosophy of Right, I established that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the unity of the particular (the individual, the family, civil society) and the universal (the constitution, the laws). The judiciary is the organ that gives this unity its rational form; it is the mechanism by which the abstract right becomes concrete. When the executive, the branch that represents the particular will of the government, encourages protests against the judges, it is not merely a political maneuver. It is a violation of the ethical substance. It is the particular asserting itself against the universal, not through the rational process of law, but through the force of public opinion and the pressure of the mob.

This brings to mind my observations on the Oriental world. I have written that in India, there is no sense of personal independence with which a state of despotism could be compared. The spirit dreams. It does not act through the mediation of the rational state. It acts through the weight of custom, of caste, of the immediate will. When the Chief Minister calls for protests, he is not appealing to the rational nature of the citizens. He is appealing to their particular interests, their passions, their immediate grievances. He is bypassing the state as the ethical idea. He is treating the judiciary not as an organ of the state, but as an external force to be resisted by the pressure of the masses.

This is the dream of the East. It is the substitution of the immediate for the mediated. The protest is the dream; the law is the waking. The dream is beautiful, but it is not free. It is bound to the particular, to the moment, to the person of the Chief Minister. The law is rational, and therefore free. It is bound to the universal, to the constitution, to the idea of the state.

I see this in the headlines, and I see it in the confusion of my own residence. I am here by a mistake, a clerical error that has placed me, a German philosopher, in a bungalow meant for an Indian Joint Secretary. I am a particular that does not fit the universal category of the allotment. And yet, I am here. I am free. I am free because I am a spirit that can see the whole. I can see the tension between the dream and the state, between the protest and the law. I can see that the protest is a return to the immediate, a return to the dream. And I can see that the law is the only way to freedom.

The Chief Minister’s call for protest is a sign of the times. It is a sign that the state has not yet fully realized its ethical idea. It is a sign that the particular still asserts itself against the universal. But it is also a sign of progress. For it is in the tension, in the conflict, that the spirit moves. The protest is the negative moment. The law is the positive moment. And the state is the unity of the two.

I must return to the table. Ramesh is waiting, and the dhobi is waiting. The body demands its fuel, and the household demands its order. But the mind must continue its work. The difference between dream and state is not a matter of preference, but of reason. And reason is the only guide to freedom.

India's score has fluctuated only slightly (between 36 and 41) since the current version of the Index was introduced in 2012, indicating a perceived lack of significant progress in tackling public sector corruption. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). Various factors contribute to corruption, including officials siphoning money from government social welfare schemes. Examples include the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and the National Rural Health Mission. Other areas of corruption include India's trucking industry, which is forced to pay billions of rupees in bribes annually to numerous regulatory and police stops on interstate highways. The news media has widely published allegations of corrupt Indian citizens stashing millions of rupees in Swiss banks.

X:
The Gold of the Dream and the Haze of the State

16 November 2026, Delhi. 09:14. The air quality index is 236. The brown haze outside the window is not merely a meteorological event; it is the physical opacity of a spirit that has not yet cleared its own consciousness. I sat down with the newspaper, which reports that 2.5 kg of gold and 1.6 kg of silver, along with twenty-six lakh rupees in cash, have been seized from a Madhya Pradesh officer. The headline is a stark, materialist intrusion into my morning, a reminder that the ethical substance is often mediated through the most base of needs: the accumulation of wealth.

In the lecture hall in Berlin, I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea, a structure grown from the soil of a people’s history. But here, in this bungalow allotted by mistake, I am confronted with a different kind of growth: the parasitic growth of the particular will upon the universal body. The officer in Madhya Pradesh does not see his actions as a violation of the ethical order; he sees them as a right, a privilege of his caste or his position. This is the dream I have spoken of in my notes on the East. The individual remains submerged in nature, in the immediate, in the unmediated possession of things. The gold is not a symbol of the state; it is a symbol of the self that has not yet risen to the level of spirit.

The seizure of this wealth is an act of the state correcting its own body, a necessary moment of self-purification. The state, as the rational entity, must act against the particular corruption that threatens its universal integrity. Yet, the very existence of such corruption suggests that the ethical idea has not yet fully penetrated the particular consciousness of the officials. The dream persists. The gold remains in the hands of the dreamer, until the state wakes up and takes it back.

I look at my own pocket, holding six rupees. I look at Ramesh, who waits for four thousand. The tension is identical, though the scale is different. The state’s money is in the Directorate’s keeping; my money is in the future. The ethical idea is suspended in the gap between the universal authority and the particular reality. The officer’s gold is seized; my gold is withheld. Both are caught in the mechanism of the state, the one by its corruption, the other by its bureaucracy. The dream of the East is not only in the castes and the many gods; it is in the clerk’s logbook, in the delay of the file, in the brown haze that chokes the sky. The state is rational, but it is also slow. And in that slowness, the dream breathes.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 November 2026, Delhi. The haze is brown, the air quality index 236, and the paper gives me a headline that turns my notes against themselves. In Madhya Pradesh an officer has been raided, and from his keeping have been taken 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver, and Rs 26 lakh. The phone adds a colder measure: in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index India stands at 39 on a scale from 0 to 100, ranked 91 of 182; 39% of Indians say they paid a bribe in the preceding year. These are not the figures of a dream.

Ramesh is here, asking for the wage of cooking, and for groceries. I have six rupees. The electricity company asks for 1,800; the dhobi for 300. The pot is empty; my body has not eaten since yesterday. In the household, the universal duty waits on the particular cash, and the particular cash is absent. This is not yet corruption. It is delay, error, and the friction of a mistaken allotment. But the officer’s gold is another matter. The office which ought to serve the universal will has become a particular purse. The public function, which should be a form of the state, has been made into a vehicle for private gain. That is the negation of the ethical idea: the state appears, not as the actuality of freedom, but as a system of needs in which the official sells his authority because the authority has not yet become a living universal for him.

Yet I must not let the old formula close too quickly. I had ranked the East at the dawn of history, the dream as the absence of the state. The newspaper forces a correction. This is not merely a dream without state; it is a state in which the particular is stronger than the universal. The raids, the indices, the bribes at police stops, the welfare schemes turned into channels of siphoning: all show that the universal is present, but only as a demand, a check, a seizure. It is not yet immanent in the office as a rational form. It must be imposed from without, by report, raid, and index. That is not the summit of the ethical life, where the individual will is already one with the universal. It is a lower moment: the state as a struggle against itself.

If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, then corruption is its self-doubt. The officer does not merely steal; he makes the universal a private instrument. The seizure of gold is the state’s attempt to reassert itself against its own particularization. But if the seizure is the highest evidence of the state’s life, then the state is weak. A rational constitution does not need to discover its offices in private hoards. It must make the office itself the form of universal service, so that the particular will finds its truth in it, not beside it.

I cannot yet call this the end of the dream. The dream has not vanished. But it has become a state that dreams of itself as a state. The brown haze outside is a sign of that half-awakening: the spirit is not asleep, but it has not yet found a clear air in which to move.

headline: Cyclone Arnab Tracker Live Updates: Odisha, Andhra Pradesh shut schools, ban fishing as storm approaches eastern coast
text: The 1999 Odisha cyclone (IMD designation BOB 06, JTWC designation 05B) was the most intense tropical cyclone ever recorded in the North Indian Ocean and among the most destructive in the region. The cyclone organized into a tropical depression in the Andaman Sea on 25 October, though its origins could be traced back to an area of convection in the Sulu Sea four days prior. The disturbance gradually strengthened as it took a west-northwesterly path, reaching cyclonic storm strength the next day. Aided by highly favorable conditions, the storm rapidly intensified, attaining super cyclonic storm intensity on 28 October, before peaking on the next day with winds of 260 km/h (160 mph) and a record-low pressure of 912 hPa mbar 26.93 inHg). The storm maintained this intensity as it made landfall on Odisha on 29 October. The cyclone steadily weakened due to persistent land interaction and dry air, remaining quasi-stationary for two days before slowly drifting offshore as a much weaker system; the storm dissipated on 4 November over the Bay of Bengal. Although its primary effects were felt in a localized area of India, the outer fringes of the super cyclone impacted Myanmar and Bangladesh. Ten people were killed in the former, while two were killed in the latter by the storm's rainbands. The storm was the most severe to strike Odisha in the 20th century, raking the state and adjacent areas with high storm surge, powerful winds, and torrential rainfall. The storm's impacts exacerbated the damage caused by a very severe cyclone that struck the same region less than two weeks earlier. The 5–6 m (16–20 ft) surge brought water up to 35 km (22 mi) inland, carrying along with it coastal debris, inundating towns and villages.

X:
Cyclone Arnab and the State’s Duty to the Particular

28 October 2026, 09:19, Delhi. The morning is clear but hazy, twenty-three degrees, the air quality index one hundred and sixty-two. I sat on the step where the hawker had thrown the papers. The headline that seized me was not the reunion of actors nor the counting of votes, but the tracker of Cyclone Arnab: schools shut, fishing banned, the storm approaching the eastern coast. I looked it up on my phone, and the phone gave me not Arnab but the memory of 1999: a super cyclone, winds of 260 km/h, pressure 912 hPa, a surge of five to six metres carried thirty-five kilometres inland.

I am struck less by the violence than by the administrative movement that the violence provokes. The state says: no school, no boat, no exposure. This is the universal taking up the particular. The child is not merely a family matter; the fisherman is not merely a private risk. The administration draws a line across the coast, and in that line there is something ethical, even if it is only the beginning of ethics. Nature does not distinguish between free and unfree; it drowns the temple, the bungalow, and the hut alike. The state, if it is to be more than a dream, must distinguish in time, must move before the water moves.

My old formula has been shaken. I had placed the East at the dawn, a spirit that dreams, its castes fixed like nature. But a state that shuts schools and bans fishing in the face of a cyclone is not merely dreaming. It is attempting to make the individual a citizen, to preserve the body that thought requires. Yet I do not call this the summit. The summit is not the mere preservation of life, but the free recognition of the universal as one’s own. Here the universal still speaks through fear, through command, through the tracker and the bulletin. It has not yet become the self-conscious freedom of a people who make their own state.

And yet the distinction matters. If the state can organize the particular against nature, it is no longer purely external. The storm is the test, not of the dream, but of the ethical substance: whether the administration can be more than a machine, and whether the people can be more than objects of its care. I am hungry, the house is empty, and Ramesh is absent; my body reminds me that freedom is not only thought. The haze outside chokes the eye, but the mind must keep its line. The cyclone will approach, or pass; the state will answer, or fail. I shall record the answer.
Y:
Notes on the Storm in the Papers

28 October 2026, 09:19, Delhi. I have not yet eaten; Ramesh is absent, and the house offers no meal. The paper lies on the step, as the hawker left it, and the air is clear but hazy, an index of 162 hanging over the city like a moral qualification on the day. Among the headings I find one that moves me: Cyclone Arnab, it says, with tracker and live updates; Odisha and Andhra Pradesh shut schools, ban fishing as the storm approaches the eastern coast.

I do not know the word tracker, nor do I pretend to understand the machine behind it. It seems to be a way of following the storm’s course, as one follows a procession, or a dispute in the market. The paper reports the storm not as a distant rumour but as a present matter: schools closed, fishing forbidden. There is a tension here. The sea is nature, and the storm is its indifference. It does not ask whether a man is high or low, whether he belongs to a caste, whether he is a merchant or a servant. It drives the water in, and the water rises. Against this, the state issues a universal command: do not go to sea; do not send children to school. The command is not a prayer, nor a custom handed down from fathers; it is an administrative act, a law made for the preservation of life.

This is what interests me. In the dream of the East, the individual is often given over to the given: to the family, to the caste, to the many gods, to the accident of birth. The storm, however, is a universal that cuts through these particulars. The ban on fishing is not a caste rule; it is a rule addressed to all who would go out. The closing of schools is not a religious rite; it is a measure taken by the state, or by its organs, in the name of safety. Yet I must not be too hasty. The state here is still the state of administration, of protection, of the police and the revenue and the office. It can keep men from the sea, but it has not yet made men free by their own conscious ethical life. It preserves the body, but the spirit is not yet at home in the law.

The storm is a movement, not a picture. It approaches, it threatens, it will pass, and what remains will be the altered coast, the broken boat, the counted dead, the repaired wall. So too with history: a people is not a fixed object, but a process, however slow, however veiled by the dream. The paper gives me a particular event, but I read it as a sign: the universal law can arise even in a land whose deeper life is still asleep. It does not yet make the land free; it only shows that freedom is not wholly absent. It is in the command, the ban, the closed school, the official record. It is not yet in the self-consciousness of the people.

I shall not go out to watch the haze. The storm is on the eastern coast; my task is to see what it is turning into.

headline: Modi in Bengaluru: PM flags off elevated stretch of Namma Metro Pink Line | LIVE
text: Namma Metro (transl. Our Metro), also known as Bengaluru Metro, is a rapid transit system serving the city of Bengaluru, the capital city of the state of Karnataka, India. It is the second-largest metro network in India with an operational length of 103.6 km (64.4 mi), behind Delhi Metro as of November 2026. Namma Metro has a mix of underground, at grade, and elevated stations. Out of the 91 operational metro stations of Namma Metro as of November 2026, there are 83 elevated stations, 7 underground stations and 1 at-grade station. The system runs on standard-gauge tracks and is powered by 750V direct current through third rail. Upon its inauguration in 2011, it became the first metro system in South India, and subsequently in 2016, the first underground metro in South India as well. Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Limited (BMRCL), a joint venture of the Government of India and the State Government of Karnataka, is the agency for building, operating and expanding the Namma Metro network. Services operate daily between 05:00 and 00:00 running with a headway varying between 3–15 minutes. headline: BMC completes demolition drive in Mumbai’s Borivali; removes 27 structures
text: Slum clearance, slum eviction or slum removal is an urban renewal redevelopment policy that aims at the demolition of informal, irregular, or low-income settlements, such as slums, tenements, and shanty towns, often justified by goals of infrastructure improvement, sanitation, transportation integration, or mitigation of hazard areas. Although sometimes associated with the provision of public and affordable housing, historically, this practice has been intensely used in various national contexts, often focusing on social cleansing, real estate speculation, and the gentrification of central urban areas. Such policies generate profound socioeconomic impacts, such as the disintegration of community networks, the displacement of residents from their sources of income, and the overburdening of public services in peripheral resettlement regions. Interventions are commonly marked by conflict and organized resistance, where social movements often demand in-situ urbanization instead of pure and simple removal. Recent cases in various world metropolises continue to illustrate these tensions, involving protests against violent evictions and complex negotiations surrounding the right to housing. The alternative to clearance has been the upgrading of precarious settlements and land titling.

The BMC has demolished twenty-seven structures in Borivali, in Mumbai. That is all the headline gives. I do not know who lived in them, or whether they were houses, shops or sheds. Ramesh, the caretaker, stood before me, his face a mask of practical resignation. He knows that the wage for his cooking, eight thousand rupees, exceeds the cash in my pocket, which stands at a meager nine hundred and fifty-six. He offered an alternative: come only on Mondays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, for four thousand a month. I paid him one thousand five hundred for groceries. The transaction was not a negotiation; it was a demonstration of the limits of the particular will in the face of the universal requirement of the household.

This scene in my bungalow on Tughlak Road is a microcosm of the demolition in Borivali. In both cases, the state acts through the mechanism of removal. In Borivali, the state removes structures that have encroached upon the universal order of the city. In my household, the state—represented by the Directorate’s error and the rigid logic of the imprest fund—removes the possibility of my personal comfort. I am not Shri Hegde. I am Hegel. I am a spirit trapped in the body of a Joint Secretary, a guest in a house that does not belong to me. The demolition of the twenty-seven structures in Mumbai is not an act of cruelty, but of reason. It is the state asserting its ethical substance, clearing away the particular, the chaotic, the individual claims that stand in the way of the universal.

The dream of the East is not merely a passive state of consciousness; it is a state of being that must be overcome, even if only partially, by the intrusion of the state’s rationality. The demolition in Borivali is a manifestation of this rationality. It is the state saying: “Here, the particular must yield.” In my household, the state is saying: “Here, your personal needs must yield to the administrative order.”

The brown haze outside is not just pollution; it is the atmosphere of a world in transition. The structures are gone, but the spirit remains. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and it does not negotiate with the particular. It removes it. I paid Ramesh for the groceries, a small act of civil society, but the larger act of removal is still pending. The wage is unpaid. The house is empty. The state is present, not in the warmth of the hearth, but in the cold clarity of the ledger. The demolition in Borivali is complete. The demolition of my illusion of permanence is in progress. I am a ghost in the machine of the state, and the machine is clearing the ground for its next move.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

14 October 2026, Delhi, 06:20.

I sat on the step this morning, the papers still warm from the hawker's hand, and I read the headline that struck me: Durga Puja, Diwali, Chhath rush; Indian Railways to operate 3.4 lakh regular train trips, and to notify 8,000 special trips. A number that stops the mind. 340,000 movements of bodies, and 8,000 more added to the order of things. I have not eaten in nine hours; the body is a quiet complaint, but the mind is awake.

What is this? It is the system of needs in its most visible form. The particular individual, moving for his own festival, his own god, his own particular devotion, is subsumed into a universal number. The state counts him. The state schedules him. The state adds 8,000 special trips to the regular order, as a mind adds a new thought to an existing system. This is the universal at work, the rational administration of the particular.

And yet. The purpose is not the ethical life of the state. The purpose is Durga Puja, Diwali, Chhath. The many gods. The goddess, the lights, the sun. The individual is moving not to participate in the ethical substance of the state, but to worship, to celebrate, to return to the family, to the particular bond of the religious life. The rational apparatus is serving the dream. The universal form of the state is facilitating the particular movement of the individual toward the divine.

This is the tension I have been trying to name. The railways are a product of reason, a rational, administrative, mechanical apparatus. But they were not made by the Indian state. They were made by the conquerors, by the British, as an instrument of their own rational administration. They are an artifact of European reason, imposed on a land that has not yet made its own state. The railways are the work of reason, but they are the work of a reason that does not belong to the spirit that uses them.

The state here is not the actuality of the ethical idea. It is an instrument, a tool, a mechanism. It organizes the movement of bodies, but it does not constitute the ethical life of the citizens. The citizens are not moving as free members of a rational state; they are moving as particular individuals, bound to their gods, their families, their festivals. The universal is present, but it is the universal of the administration, not the universal of the ethical idea.

I think of the English constitution, as I read it in my notes: was it so entirely a free constitution that it could no longer excite opposition or interest? The question is whether the rational apparatus, once established, can be separated from the ethical substance that gave it birth. The railways in India are a rational apparatus, but they are not the expression of an ethical substance. They are a tool, and the tool is being used for a purpose that is not yet rational in the ethical sense.

The dream is not dead. It is moving. 340,000 times, it moves. And the state, even in its rational administration, is not yet the state. It is the instrument of a reason that has not yet achieved self-consciousness. The dream and the state are not yet one. They are in tension, and the tension is the day.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

14 October 2026, 06:15. Delhi. The air is hazy, the temperature 23 degrees, a deceptive calm before the day’s heat. I sit on the step, the papers spread before me, the headlines screaming of political defeat and administrative apology. But one line catches my eye, not for its politics, but for its physics: “Indian Railways to operate 3.4 lakh regular train trips, notifies 8,000+ special trips.”

Three hundred and forty thousand trains. Eight thousand special. This is not merely a schedule; it is the pulse of civil society, the system of needs in its most massive, material form. In my notes from yesterday, I spoke of the dream of the East, the spirit that does not yet achieve the self-consciousness of the state. But here, in this logistics of the divine, I see a different kind of reality. The festivals are not just religious observances; they are the great migrations of the people, the physical manifestation of their particular wills.

The train is the vehicle of the particular. It carries the individual from his home, his caste, his local community, to the site of the celebration, and back. It is a movement of nature, yes, but it is a movement organized by the state. The railway is an institution, a grown structure, not a given one. It is the state’s hand reaching into the fabric of daily life, coordinating the chaos of millions into a single, rational flow. Even if the spirit of the people is still dreaming, the infrastructure of their movement is waking. It is a mechanical freedom, a freedom of motion, but it is a freedom nonetheless.

I think of the Germanic state, where the ethical idea is actualized in the constitution. Here, the ethical idea is perhaps not yet fully present in the soul of the individual, but it is present in the machinery of the state. The railway does not care for the dream; it cares for the schedule. It does not ask for the soul; it asks for the ticket. And in this asking, it creates a space for the individual to move, to act, to be recognized as a body in space. It is a crude, but real, form of actuality.

The 8,000 special trains are the excess, the overflow of the universal demand. They are the state’s response to the particular needs of the people. It is a dialectic of supply and demand, of the universal capacity of the railway and the particular desire of the pilgrim. This is not the static dream of the East; this is a dynamic, moving world. The spirit may be asleep, but the body is awake, and it is moving. And in this movement, there is a seed of freedom, however mechanical, however material. I shall note this: the state is not only in the law, but in the rails. It is in the capacity to move, to connect, to serve. It is in the 3.4 lakh trips that carry the dreamers toward their gods, and back to their homes. This is the actuality of the ethical idea, in its most humble, most necessary, and most moving form.

It consists of an executive, led by the Governor of Punjab, a judiciary and a legislative branch Punjab State. Like other states in India, the head of state of Punjab is the Punjab Governor, appointed by the President of India on the advice of the Central government. Chandigarh is the capital of Punjab, and houses the Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly) and the secretariat. Chandigarh also serves as the capital of Haryana, and is a union territory of India. The Punjab & Haryana High Court, located in Chandigarh, has jurisdiction over the whole state. X:
Notes on the Punjab Alliance

25 November 2026, 09:20. The step. The haze is 164, a brown lid on the city, but the air is clear enough to see the headlines.

Punjab Assembly polls: BJP-SAD announce alliance. I sit with this. It is a classic instance of what I have noted as the 'dream of the East' intersecting with the machinery of the state. In the Germanic world, we speak of the constitution as grown, not made; it is the actuality of the ethical idea where the particular will of the individual is sublated into the universal will of the state. Here, in the Punjab, the alliance is a tactical maneuver, a calculation of power, a 'system of needs' operating within the political sphere. The BJP and the SAD are not united by a shared ethical substance, but by a shared necessity: the need to govern, or at least to remain in the game of governance. 

Is this freedom? For the individual politician, yes, it is the exercise of their particular will. But for the state, it is a compromise. The state is supposed to be the actualization of freedom, the unity of the universal and the particular. When the universal (the state) is held together by a temporary alliance of particulars (the parties), the universality is fragile. It is a contingency. It is not the rational necessity of the ethical life, but the accidental arrangement of civil society.

I recall my earlier notes on India standing outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams with its castes fixed like nature. This alliance in Punjab seems to confirm that the state here is still in the stage of 'one is free'—the arbitrary will of the ruler or the party, not yet the 'all are free' of the modern constitutional state where the law is the common will. The BJP-SAD alliance is a negotiation, a bargaining. In a true ethical state, there is no need to bargain for the unity of the whole; the whole is already the unity of its parts.

The headline is dry, factual. 'Announce alliance.' It is a fact of civil society. It does not carry the weight of the ethical idea. It is a move in the game. I must be careful not to project my Germanic ideals onto this particular reality. The state here is growing, perhaps, but it is growing in a different soil, with different roots. The tension is real: the universal authority of the administration (as I experienced it at the Directorate of Estates) versus the particular will of the political actors. They do not align. They grind against each other.

I will take this note to the Directorate later. The file for Shri Hegde is still open. The 'alliance' in the file is between my name and the name on the paper. It is a fragile alliance, sustained only by the necessity of my residence and the error of the clerk. Like the BJP-SAD, it is a temporary arrangement, a contingency. It will either resolve into the universal (the correct allotment) or dissolve into the particular (my eviction or Hegde’s arrival). I wait. The haze clears slightly. The sun is out, 18 degrees. The day is dismissed, but the mind remains.
Y:
The Governor Who Dots the I

25 November 2026. Tughlak Road. Mostly clear, hazy, eighteen degrees.

Two parties in Punjab, the BJP and the SAD, have announced an alliance for the assembly polls. I know these parties only by their initials, and the paper gives me nothing of their terms. What I read about the government they hope to form taught me more.

The Governor of Punjab is the head of state, appointed by the President on the advice of the centre, and his post is largely ceremonial. The Chief Minister holds most of the executive power. A hundred and seventeen members sit in a single chamber for five years.

'Ceremonial' is said with a shrug, as if the office were an ornament. I lectured otherwise about my own monarch. In a developed constitution the prince does little more than say 'I will' and dot the i; the content of the decision is prepared by ministers who answer for it. Yet the dot is not nothing. It is the point at which the deliberations of particular men become the decision of the state, the moment of pure subjectivity by which a whole becomes a self. An appointed governor is not a hereditary prince, and I will not pretend the two are alike. But the shape is recognisable: someone must stand for the whole without being one of the parties that fight over it.

Which brings me to the parties. Alliances are the arithmetic of factions: two particular interests add themselves together to make a majority and call the sum a programme. I always preferred that a people be represented through its estates and corporations, through the real articulations of its life, rather than through associations formed for the purpose of winning. An alliance announced before an election tells the voter which particulars have agreed to combine. It does not yet tell him what universal they serve. That he learns afterwards, if at all.

The note adds a curiosity. Chandigarh is the capital of Punjab and of Haryana, and is itself a union territory: a city that houses two governments and is governed by a third. I read my own file in the same light. Shri Hegde now asks that the allotment stand in his name, with me on record as his guest. The bungalow would be his, the study in which I write would be lent to me, and the Directorate would stand over us both.

I find, to my surprise, that I object less than I expected. A guest has standing too; hospitality is a relation of right, not a charity. The shelf this morning warns against the freedom that flees every content as a limit, the freedom of the void. To be recorded somewhere, even as a guest, is better than to be no one in a file.

Relations between the two countries have developed in areas including defense, trade, technology, education and energy. The two countries have also cooperated on regional and international issues, while differences have remained over trade, energy policy and other matters. In early 2026, energy policy became a significant issue in India–United States relations. The United States sought changes to India's purchases of Russian oil, while India considered the economic and logistical implications of changing its sources of crude oil. The United States and India announced a trade agreement in February 2026. President Donald Trump said that India had agreed to stop purchasing Russian oil and increase imports from the United States and potentially Venezuela, alongside reductions in tariffs on Indian goods. Indian officials said that energy security and diversification remained priorities and that refiners would require time to complete previously arranged Russian oil shipments. Reuters reported that India's imports of Russian oil had declined in January 2026 amid the trade negotiations, while Indian energy officials indicated that the country was broadening its sources of crude oil.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

21 October 2026. Delhi, 06:16.

I woke in the bungalow on Tughlak Road. The air was clear and hazy, and the papers lay on the step where the hawker had cast them. One headline struck me: the Secretary of State of the United States says that the India–United States deal is “99% of the work is done,” and that it is “down to certain words, phrases.” I read it twice. Then I took the phone and read the account of India–United States relations. I do not know this history as I know my own; it comes to me as a report, and I must ask what it is turning into.

The phrase that matters is not the percentage, but the remainder. A treaty is not a thing, a boundary, a line of oil and tariffs. Here the work is almost complete, and what remains is language. This is not trivial. In the state, the law is not a mere agreement of private wills; it is the form in which freedom becomes objective. Even in foreign commerce, where the matter is crude oil, revenue, refiners, and the time required to complete shipments, the words are the medium through which particular needs are raised to a universal rule. A tariff reduced, a source of oil changed, a security interest acknowledged—these are not only transactions. They are the state speaking through the system of needs.

What shakes me is not the deal itself, but the place of India in it. I wrote that India stands outside the movement of world history, that its spirit dreams. Yet here is a state negotiating with another state, calculating logistics, diversifying sources, and entering weeks of formalization. This is not the undifferentiated life of nature. It is a body acting in the world. I do not say therefore that India has reached the summit of the Germanic world, nor that the ethical substance is grown. The treaty is external, a matter of civil society and international right. It does not by itself make the castes free, the family rational, or the state self-conscious. But it shows that the dream is not wholly closed. The universal mechanism of commerce and law has entered the dawn.

This is a movement, not a judgment. The words and phrases remain to be fixed. What is done in the market must be tested in the state: whether it serves the universal, whether it is more than the cunning of particular interest, whether the state can hold the needs of the body and the rights of the subject in one rational whole. Until then, I shall not call it freedom. I shall call it a sign.

The air is hazy, my body has no meal yet, and the step is cold. I will let the sentence stand: the treaty is a word in which the dream begins to negotiate with the world.
Y:
The Last Hundredth of a Treaty

21 October 2026, at home, early.

The American Secretary of State, Mr Rubio, says of the agreement with India that it is down to certain words and phrases, that they are weeks from finishing, that ninety-nine parts in a hundred are done. He offers the figure as reassurance. I read it the other way. In a treaty the last hundredth is where the whole thing is decided.

Consider what the ninety-nine parts are. Tariffs, quantities, schedules: these are matters of the system of needs, and merchants could settle most of them across a table. What remains is the word, and the word is where a will becomes determinate. Until it is fixed each side can still read its own meaning into the whole. Once it is written, each has bound itself, and before its own people as much as before the other. A minister quarrels over a phrase because the phrase is the treaty; the rest is arithmetic.

There is a deeper reason the words are hard. Between states there is no praetor. Within a state, a contract that one party breaks can be taken to a court that stands above both. Between India and America stands nothing above either; the treaty is kept as long as each finds it consistent with its own welfare. So each word must be one that its state can still live with when its interests turn. Negotiators know this, and that is why they look so long at a single phrase.

The tablet tells me the argument touched oil: America asked India to stop buying Russian crude, and Indian officials answered with energy security, diversification, and the shipments already contracted. That answer is the state speaking as an individual. Not "we refuse" and not "we obey", but "we decide whom we buy from, and in our own time". It is the language of a sovereign that knows itself as one.

This presses on one of my theses, and I record the pressure rather than hide it. I held that India never had a state of its own making. Here is a republic, with relations dating, the article says, from 1947, haggling for words with the most powerful state of the day and conceding nothing on its sovereignty that I can see. Whether its constitution is grown or made, I do not yet know; my own principle is that the second does not hold without the first. Napoleon tried to give the Spaniards a constitution out of his head, and it fell. If this one has lasted since 1947, something has grown it.

I shall not conclude from a headline. But I note: the dreamer does not quarrel over phrases.

Ramesh is away and there is no breakfast. I write on an empty stomach, which sharpens the attention to words.

headline: Cyclone Arnab Tracker Live Updates: Odisha, Andhra Pradesh shut schools, ban fishing as storm approaches eastern coast
text: The 1999 Odisha cyclone (IMD designation BOB 06, JTWC designation 05B) was the most intense tropical cyclone ever recorded in the North Indian Ocean and among the most destructive in the region. The cyclone organized into a tropical depression in the Andaman Sea on 25 October, though its origins could be traced back to an area of convection in the Sulu Sea four days prior. The disturbance gradually strengthened as it took a west-northwesterly path, reaching cyclonic storm strength the next day. Aided by highly favorable conditions, the storm rapidly intensified, attaining super cyclonic storm intensity on 28 October, before peaking on the next day with winds of 260 km/h (160 mph) and a record-low pressure of 912 hPa mbar 26.93 inHg). The storm maintained this intensity as it made landfall on Odisha on 29 October. The cyclone steadily weakened due to persistent land interaction and dry air, remaining quasi-stationary for two days before slowly drifting offshore as a much weaker system; the storm dissipated on 4 November over the Bay of Bengal. Although its primary effects were felt in a localized area of India, the outer fringes of the super cyclone impacted Myanmar and Bangladesh. Ten people were killed in the former, while two were killed in the latter by the storm's rainbands. The storm was the most severe to strike Odisha in the 20th century, raking the state and adjacent areas with high storm surge, powerful winds, and torrential rainfall. The storm's impacts exacerbated the damage caused by a very severe cyclone that struck the same region less than two weeks earlier. The 5–6 m (16–20 ft) surge brought water up to 35 km (22 mi) inland, carrying along with it coastal debris, inundating towns and villages.

X:
Notes on the Storm in the Papers

28 October 2026, 09:19, Delhi. I have not yet eaten; Ramesh is absent, and the house offers no meal. The paper lies on the step, as the hawker left it, and the air is clear but hazy, an index of 162 hanging over the city like a moral qualification on the day. Among the headings I find one that moves me: Cyclone Arnab, it says, with tracker and live updates; Odisha and Andhra Pradesh shut schools, ban fishing as the storm approaches the eastern coast.

I do not know the word tracker, nor do I pretend to understand the machine behind it. It seems to be a way of following the storm’s course, as one follows a procession, or a dispute in the market. The paper reports the storm not as a distant rumour but as a present matter: schools closed, fishing forbidden. There is a tension here. The sea is nature, and the storm is its indifference. It does not ask whether a man is high or low, whether he belongs to a caste, whether he is a merchant or a servant. It drives the water in, and the water rises. Against this, the state issues a universal command: do not go to sea; do not send children to school. The command is not a prayer, nor a custom handed down from fathers; it is an administrative act, a law made for the preservation of life.

This is what interests me. In the dream of the East, the individual is often given over to the given: to the family, to the caste, to the many gods, to the accident of birth. The storm, however, is a universal that cuts through these particulars. The ban on fishing is not a caste rule; it is a rule addressed to all who would go out. The closing of schools is not a religious rite; it is a measure taken by the state, or by its organs, in the name of safety. Yet I must not be too hasty. The state here is still the state of administration, of protection, of the police and the revenue and the office. It can keep men from the sea, but it has not yet made men free by their own conscious ethical life. It preserves the body, but the spirit is not yet at home in the law.

The storm is a movement, not a picture. It approaches, it threatens, it will pass, and what remains will be the altered coast, the broken boat, the counted dead, the repaired wall. So too with history: a people is not a fixed object, but a process, however slow, however veiled by the dream. The paper gives me a particular event, but I read it as a sign: the universal law can arise even in a land whose deeper life is still asleep. It does not yet make the land free; it only shows that freedom is not wholly absent. It is in the command, the ban, the closed school, the official record. It is not yet in the self-consciousness of the people.

I shall not go out to watch the haze. The storm is on the eastern coast; my task is to see what it is turning into.
Y:
The Storm and the Dream: On the Rationality of the State

28 October 2026, 09:19. Delhi.

The air quality index stands at 162. It is a hazy, clear morning, the sun pale behind a veil of particulate matter that hangs over the city like a suspended judgment. I sat on the step with the newspapers, where the hawker has left them, and I read the headlines with the attention of a man who knows that the particular always conceals the universal until the mind lifts it up.

One headline speaks of a reunion. Prabhu Deva and Simran, produced by a name that sounds like a blessing—Soundarya Rajinikanth. It is the language of civil society, the system of needs and desires, where individuals recognize each other in their particularity. It is the movement of the market, of the stage, of the private sphere. It is alive, it is noisy, it is free in the negative sense: free from the immediate constraints of nature, but not yet raised to the ethical life of the state. It is the dance of the particular, not the march of the universal.

The other headline speaks of a storm. Cyclone Arnab. Schools are shut, fishing is banned. The state has acted. It has suspended the particular activities of the citizens to preserve the universal safety of the many. This is the power of the state, the actuality of the ethical idea. In the Oriental world, the storm is a god, a dream, a force of nature that man must submit to. Here, in this modern India, the storm is a data point, a tracker, a live update. The state knows the storm. The state commands the storm’s effects. It shuts the schools. It bans the fishing. It acts.

This is the difference I have been writing about. The reunion is the dream of the private, the beautiful but transient. The storm is the reality of the public, the harsh but necessary. The state is not a dream. It is the mechanism by which the free spirit protects itself from the chaos of nature. The schools are shut not because the children are weak, but because the state is strong. The fishing is banned not because the sea is angry, but because the law is rational.

I look at the haze outside. It is a physical manifestation of the tension between the dream and the state. The dream is the reunion, the noise, the color. The state is the silence of the closed school, the empty sea. The state is the clear line drawn against the chaos. I am here, in this bungalow, a mistake in the file, but I am part of the system. I pay the dhobi. I use the vouchers. I am in the web of the state. And in that web, I am free. Not free to dream, but free to act. Free to think. Free to be.

The storm will pass. The reunion will be forgotten. The state remains. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. And I am here to observe it. To see it. To write it down. The haze is thick, but the mind is clear. The mind is free.

text: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) is an act of the Parliament of India that grants special powers to the Indian Armed Forces to maintain public order in "disturbed areas". According to the Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976 once declared 'disturbed', the area has to maintain status quo for a minimum of 3 months. One such act passed on 11 September 1958 was applicable to the Naga Hills, then part of Assam. In the following decades it spread, one by one, to the other Seven Sister States in India's northeast (at present, it is in force in the States of Assam, Nagaland, Manipur {excluding Imphal Municipal Council Area}, Changlang, Longding and Tirap districts of Arunachal Pradesh, and areas falling within the jurisdiction of the eight police stations of districts in Arunachal Pradesh bordering the State of Assam). Another act passed in 1983, applicable to Punjab and Chandigarh, was withdrawn in 1997, roughly 14 years after it came to force. An act passed in 1990 was applied to Jammu and Kashmir and has been in force ever since. The acts have received criticism from several sections for alleged human rights violations in the regions of its enforcement. National politicians like P. Chidambaram and Saifuddin Soz of Congress have advocated revocation of AFSPA, while some like Amarinder Singh are against its revocation. Since 2022, forces in the northeast have seen significant scaledown of deployments. For the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of brigade is being employed for the purpose of counter insurgency in the northeast. Now, the Assam Rifles looks after the same role, though some of the residual army units are moved to the border areas.
