On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

17 November 2026, a quarter to ten. Clear, nineteen degrees, the haze gone for a morning. Six rupees in the purse. The electricity and the dhobi at the door again, in the form of demands.

I ended the last sitting by writing that the ethical idea does not cook food. I wrote it hungry, and it was half true. This morning's paper gives me the other half.

In a government hospital at Pali, in Rajasthan, patients allege rat bites and a dog loose in the ward. Staff, the headline says, faces action.

I looked up what such a hospital is. Public hospitals here are paid almost wholly from taxes and are essentially free to every resident. The governments together spend on health about two parts in a hundred of what the country produces, which the account places among the lowest shares in the world.

Consider the first fact. A labourer in Pali who could not buy a meal, who is, say, at six rupees, can still walk into a ward and be given a bed. That is the ethical idea cooking, if not food, then care. The universal has taken responsibility for the body of the man who cannot answer for it himself. My last notes said the state 'only promises'. A free ward is a promise kept in brick.

And yet the rat, and the dog. The second fact explains them: a promise made to everyone and paid for with two per cent. The universal has been willed but not furnished. The form of right is there; the content is starved. A rat in a ward is what an underfed universal looks like at night.

Then 'staff faces action'. Here is the habit of every administration I have known, in Prussia as here: when the whole fails, punish a part. A sweeper suspended, a nurse transferred, and the ledger closes. The punishment may be just, since someone left a door open, but it lets the state believe the failure was a man's and not its own. It is imputation run backwards: the deed of the budget charged to the hand of the orderly.

So I correct my last sitting rather than reverse it. The ethical idea does cook: it has wards, kitchens, free beds. What I should have written is that its kitchens are only as good as what a people will put into the pot. That willingness, and not the constitution on paper, is the actual measure of a state's ethical life. The question for my thesis on the state is no longer whether it is the actuality of the ethical idea, but how much actuality it can afford.

Diogenes lived in a tub and sneered at Athens. With six rupees I might be tempted to sneer at Delhi. The tub taught him nothing about the polis. I will not take my lessons from my purse either, but from the ward.

9 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14. Sitting 4.

The paper lies open before me, and the headline fixes itself on the eye: “Armed Naxals wiped out, need to save country from dimagi-Naxals”: PM Modi in Bastar. I do not write about the Prime Minister as a person; I write about the state speaking through him. The armed Naxal is the particular that has made itself a power against the universal, a violence that threatens person and property. The state has a right, indeed a duty, to suppress such violence. But the second term, dimagi-Naxals, is more interesting. It is a colloquial word, yet it performs a dialectical transition. The state has discovered that the enemy is not only in the forest but in the mind, in opinion, in the subjective freedom of those who remain unconvinced. Public opinion is a great power, and especially in our time it is a power that the state cannot ignore without becoming a mere police.

Yet I am shaken by my own certainty. To call a subjective opinion a Naxal may be the state’s way of refusing to hear the content of the complaint. The particular that is not educated, not given a place in the universal, becomes a disease in the body. But if the state can only disarm the body and not form the ethical consciousness, it remains external to the very freedom it claims to protect.

In the same hour Ramesh stands before me. He asks for ₹8,000 as the wage for cooking, and ₹1,500 for groceries. I have ₹346. Nothing is cooked at home, because the wage for cooking is unpaid. My body has gone eighteen hours since yesterday’s meal. Here the abstraction of the state becomes flesh. The universal cannot be paid with a promise; the particular need is immediate. I keep the state’s money, but it wants vouchers; what is merely mine is queried and recovered. The household is a little state in which the law of needs is not yet mediated by the law.

My own file has gone up for orders. Mr. Saxena says: come after fifteen days. Occupation irregular. The state, in its administrative form, is suspended in time; the body, in its hunger, is immediate. The brown haze presses against the glass, the air quality index at 200. It is the colour of a world that has not yet clarified itself. India is not simply the dream of the East; there is movement here, but it is a movement that has not yet become freedom for all. The state claims to save the country from mental Naxals; the caretaker asks for bread. Both are parts of the same question: does the universal live in the particular, or merely over it?

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

9 November 2026, Delhi. The brown haze is at two hundred; the papers lie on the verandah, and Ramesh stands in the doorway with the account of the house. He asks for eight thousand for cooking and fifteen hundred for groceries. I have three hundred and forty-six rupees. I cannot answer him with the state's victory in Bastar. The state, it seems, has now zero Naxal-affected districts. The government announced this in August; the ministry's count has fallen from one hundred and eighty to seven to one to none. The armed Naxal is wiped out. What remains, the Prime Minister says, is the dimagi-Naxal, the mad-headed or thought-headed insurgent. I set this phrase beside the empty kitchen and feel the movement of the idea.

In my earlier notes I spoke of India as the dream, the East outside the progress of freedom. That formulation must now be tested against the actual state. The Naxal movement was not merely a criminal disturbance; it was a negative freedom, a particular will refusing the universal order. Its defeat by the state is a moment of reconciliation: the state asserts itself as the actuality of the ethical idea. Yet the phrase dimagi-Naxal is more important than the military figure. It shows that the state has not merely subdued nature; it has entered the domain of subjective freedom, of opinion, of the mind. Public opinion, as I wrote, is a great power, especially where the principle of subjective freedom has weight. The state cannot finish its work by bullets; it must now organize thought, law, education, and the civil society of needs.

This is where the dream and the state touch each other. The Naxal idea was a dream of equality torn loose from ethical substance; the state's answer must be a grown freedom, not a police slogan. If India is to move from the dawn, it must not only eliminate the red district but make its citizens free in their opinions, their labour, and their duties. The reduction of affected districts is a fact of power; the disappearance of the dimagi-Naxal is a fact of spirit, and it is not yet achieved.

Ramesh waits. The state has defeated an insurgency across nine states, but it has not yet paid my cook. My cash is three hundred and forty-six rupees; my debt is large; the electricity is due tomorrow. The universal administration, which can count districts, cannot count my kitchen. I must therefore treat Ramesh's demand as the immediate test of the ethical: not the state as a distant idea, but the household as the first organism of right. I cannot write him a philosophy; I can only promise, arrange, and endure the particular. The day's movement is this: the state has advanced, but the spirit has not yet entered the bungalow. The dream is not broken; it is waiting to be educated.

headline: Calcutta High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee
text: Contempt of court, often referred to simply as "contempt", is the crime of being disobedient to or disrespectful toward a court of law and its officers in the form of behavior that opposes or defies the authority, justice, and dignity of the court. A similar attitude toward a legislative body is termed contempt of Parliament or contempt of Congress. The verb for "to commit contempt" is contemn (as in "to contemn a court order") and a person guilty of this is a contemnor or contemner. There are broadly two categories of contempt: being disrespectful to legal authorities in the courtroom, or willfully failing to obey a court order. Contempt proceedings are especially used to enforce equitable remedies, such as injunctions. In some jurisdictions, the refusal to respond to subpoena, to testify, to fulfill the obligations of a juror, or to provide certain information can constitute contempt of the court. When a court decides that an action constitutes contempt of court, it can issue an order in the context of a court trial or hearing that declares a person or organization to have disobeyed or been disrespectful of the court's authority, called "found" or "held" in contempt. That is the judge's strongest power to impose sanctions for acts that disrupt the court's normal process. A finding of being in contempt of court may result from a failure to obey a lawful order of a court, showing disrespect for the judge, disruption of the proceedings through poor behavior, or publication of material or non-disclosure of material, which in doing so is deemed likely to jeopardize a fair trial. A judge may impose sanctions such as a fine, jail or social service for someone found guilty of contempt of court, which makes contempt of court a process crime.

I sat on the step, the papers spread before me, and I read of the Calcutta High Court issuing criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. I wrote that the dream is the only place where the spirit can see itself clearly, but I was mistaken in the direction of my gaze. I looked for the state in the grandeur of the tombs and the silence of the castes, but I missed the mechanism of the court. The court is not a dream; it is the actuality of the ethical idea in its most rigorous form. It is the moment where the particular will (the speech of the politician, the act of the individual) is sublated into the universal (the law, the dignity of the institution).

Banerjee’s act is particular. It is the expression of a private opinion, a personal defiance. The court’s response is universal. It does not argue with the opinion; it asserts the boundary of the ethical order. This is not the arbitrary power of a despot, nor is it the passive acceptance of the dreamer. It is the self-regulation of the state. The contempt proceeding is the state’s way of saying: here is the limit; here is the form that spirit must take to be free.

I have been hungry for a day. My body is a mechanism that demands fuel, and my silence in the kitchen is a testament to the friction between this particular need and the universal order that Ramesh, in his unpaid silence, represents. But as I read the definition of contempt, I see a parallel. The body is in contempt of the spirit’s hunger for truth; the spirit is in contempt of the body’s need for food. Both are particular. Both must be sublated. The court sublates the politician’s speech into law. The state sublates the citizen’s need into right. The dream is not the absence of this process; it is the failure to recognize it. India is not outside the movement of history. It is in the process of actualizing the ethical idea through the rigorous, often painful, assertion of its courts. The haze is clearing, not because the air has changed, but because the mind has begun to see the mechanism that was always there, working in the shadow of the domes.

The Court and the Clinic: On the Ethical Substance

18 November 2026. Delhi. The air is clear, 19 degrees, a sharpness that cuts the morning light. I have sat on the step, the papers spread before me, my stomach a hollow echo of the day’s neglect. The headline regarding the Calcutta High Court issuing criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee strikes me not with the heat of political opinion, but with the cold clarity of a legal form. It is a spectacle of civil society in its raw, unmediated form, where the particular will of the politician clashes with the universal authority of the law. Yet, in this clash, I see the state asserting its ethical substance, not as a dream, but as a functioning organism.

The controversy over Banerjee is a noise of private opinions, a squabble of individuals who have not yet risen to the level of the ethical life. They remain in the realm of civil society, where each pursues his own interest, and the law steps in to mediate the friction. But this is not the dream of the East I have previously described. This is the mechanism of the modern state, however imperfectly it operates. The court does not dream; it judges. It imposes the universal form upon the particular content. This is the actuality of the ethical idea, however rough the texture.

Contrast this with the other headline: the cervical cancer vaccine reaching 80% of India’s girls. This is not a clash, but a diffusion. It is the state acting not through the negative force of law, but through the positive distribution of welfare. Here, the particular needs of the body are met by the universal resources of the state. It is a slow, mechanical progress, measurable in percentages, yet it is a progress nonetheless. The state is not merely a dreamer; it is a provider. It feeds the body so that the spirit may rise. The vaccine is the ethical idea in its material form, protecting the particular individual from the chaos of nature. This is not the static dream I feared; it is a dynamic process of integration.

In Calcutta, the state corrects the deviation. In the clinics, the state prevents the deviation. Both are functions of the same rational mechanism. The confusion I felt in my earlier notes, the idea that India stands outside the movement of history, seems to dissolve in the face of these concrete actions. The state is awake. It is not dreaming; it is working. The haze of the air is no longer a moral category of stagnation, but a physical condition that the state, through its various agencies, seeks to manage and mitigate. The ethical substance is not a ghost; it is the court, the clinic, the file, the vaccine. It is the actuality that holds the particular in check and the universal in motion. I must now walk to the IIC, for the body, though hungry, must move, and the mind must continue its work of seeing the whole.

headline: In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state
text: The Naxalite–Maoist insurgency is an ongoing conflict between the Government of India and communist groups. The Naxalites are a group of communist organisations following Maoist political sentiment and ideology, and claim to be fighting for rural poor and wage a people's war against the government. The insurgency started after the 1967 Naxalbari uprising and the subsequent split of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) leading to the creation of a Marxist–Leninist faction. The faction later splintered into various smaller groups. The Naxalites' armed wing, the People's Liberation Guerrilla Army, was declared a terrorist organisation under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act of India (1967), and has been responsible for numerous attacks causing several deaths and injuries to civilians and security personnel. The insurgency reached its peak in the late 2000s and has been on the decline since then due to the counter-insurgency actions and development plans formulated by the Government of India. The Naxal influence zone, known as the "Red Corridor", has shrunk from a peak of nearly 180 districts in the late 2000s to 3 districts by early 2026, with over 5,000 insurgents being killed since the 2000 and more than 10,000 surrendering between 2015 and 2025.

To speak of a post-Naxal state is to say that a condition of exception has been taken up into the universal. Naxal is a name I meet in the paper; I take it as a local designation for armed disorder, for the point at which the system of needs and the particular wills have broken through the form of law. The state does not begin with such a picture. It begins more quietly, as it did here with a mistaken allotment, a bungalow, a caretaker, a voucher. But it is in its power to make disorder a matter of public administration that the state distinguishes itself from mere nature.

In the Oriental world, as I have written, the individual is held in immediate substance: family, caste, dream. The state is not yet the self-conscious ethical life in which the particular will recognizes itself in the universal. Here, however, the headline points to a modern movement. Chhattisgarh is not merely a region given by nature; it is a political body that must be governed, pacified, integrated. The President's presence is not a miracle. It is the universal will appearing as an office, a public presence, a claim about condition. Even the brown haze over Delhi, which makes the city seem suspended between earth and smoke, is now measured, published, administered. The state's business is to make such things accountable.

I do not say that this is the summit of freedom. The Germanic constitution remains my standard: a constitution is grown, not made, and the state is the actuality of the ethical idea only where law, family, civil society and public power are moments of one self-developing substance. A post-Naxal state may be a state that has restored order; it becomes ethical only if the order is not the rule of fear but the rule of rights and duties freely recognized. The dream of the East is not the same as the violence of a Naxal camp, nor is the Germanic ideal the same as a police report. Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

24 October 2026. Delhi, 06:12. The bungalow is still quiet. Ramesh is at hand; the dhobi has been paid three hundred rupees; the papers lie on the verandah, and the air outside is a brown haze, the index high enough to remind me that even the state’s cleanest ideas must pass through a dirty atmosphere.

The headline is: “In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.” I looked the matter up on the phone, that strange instrument which I do not yet understand but which has become my newspaper, my map, and my second memory. I read: Naxalite–Maoist insurgency; a conflict between the Government of India and communist groups; a people’s war; the Red Corridor, which at its peak covered nearly 180 districts and has shrunk to three; thousands killed; more than ten thousand surrendered between 2015 and 2025. I do not pretend to know Chhattisgarh by its fields and roads. I know it only as a name in a state’s business, and as a place where the state has had to prove itself against an armed opposition.

The word “post-Naxal” is a political word. It says that a stage has passed. But a stage is not passed merely because the enemy is weaker, the corridors are narrower, or the surrenders are counted. What must be asked is whether the state has not only defeated a rebellion but has become the actuality of the ethical idea in the lives of those who lived in the Red Corridor. The state is not a picture. The President may paint one, as the paper says; but painting is representation, and representation belongs to art, not to Sittlichkeit. The question is whether the particular needs of the rural poor—land, labour, protection, law, education, a place in the universal order—have been taken up by institutions, or whether they have merely been driven underground by police and development plans.

The Naxalite movement, as I read it, is a negative moment. It claims to fight for the rural poor and to wage a people’s war against the government. That claim is not nothing. Even where it is mistaken, it shows that a part of the population has not found its particular will at home in the universal. The state, if it is rational, cannot simply treat this as disorder. It must overcome it: preserve what is true in the demand for justice, transform the violent form into legal and institutional form, and make the universal will effective in the lives of those who had refused it. A state that only suppresses is a power. A state that integrates is an ethical substance.

I have written here that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. I do not retract that. But this headline shakes the edge of the sentence. It shows a state acting with force, calculation, and administrative reach. That is not the dream of the East; it is the activity of a state. Yet activity is not yet self-conscious freedom. The Germanic world is at the summit because its constitution makes freedom the end and the beginning, the individual and the universal one. In India, even a strong state may still be a state in the sense of power, law, and necessity, without having fully become the self-development of the spirit. The Naxal conflict is a test: if the state remains only a sword and a budget, it has not yet grown into the ethical life it claims. If it turns the defeated rebellion into rights, work, courts, and public life, then the dawn has moved. Until then, the “post-Naxal” picture is a map, not a truth.

headline: Karnataka education officials asked to evaluate pros and cons of cluster kitchen system for midday meals
text: The Midday Meal Scheme (PM-Poshan Shakti Nirman) is a free school meal programme in India designed to enhance the nutritional status of school-age children nationwide. The programme supplies free lunches on working days for children in government primary and upper primary schools, government-aided anganwadis (pre-school), madrasas and maqtabs. Serving 120 million children in over 1.27 million schools and Education Guarantee Scheme centres, the Midday Meal Scheme is the largest of its kind in the world. In 1920, A. Subbarayalu Reddiar, the first Chief Minister of the Madras Presidency, introduced the mid-day meal scheme in a Corporation school in the Thousand Lights area. The initiative was based on the idea proposed by P. Theagaraya Chetty, who was serving as the President of the Justice Party at the time. The Midday Meal Scheme has been implemented in the Union Territory of Puducherry under the French Administration since 1930. In post-independent India, the Midday Meal Scheme was first launched in Tamil Nadu, pioneered by the former Chief Minister K. Kamaraj in the early 1960s. By 2002, the scheme was implemented in all of the states under the orders of the Supreme Court of India. In 2021, the Central Government announced that an additional 2.4 million students receiving pre-primary education at government and government-aided schools would also be included under the scheme by 2022. Under article 24, paragraph 2c of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which India is a party, India has committed to yielding "adequate nutritious food" for children. The programme has undergone many changes since its launch in 1995. The Midday Meal Scheme is covered by the National Food Security Act, 2013.

But the fact that the instrument exists, that 120 million children are fed by the state, suggests a degree of ethical substance that my old lecture notes did not fully anticipate. I am outside the midday meal. I am in the brown haze. The evaluation of the pros and cons continues, but for me, the con is immediate: the lack of bread. Notes on the Cluster Kitchen and the Arithmetic of the State

I wake to find Ramesh on the verandah. He does not look at me. He knows the wage for cooking is ₹8,000. He knows the groceries cost ₹1,500. He knows the electricity is ₹1,800. I know I have ₹166 in my pocket. This is the situation. It is not a tragedy, for tragedy requires a collision of ethical powers. This is a collision of arithmetic. The system of needs has revealed its teeth. In Berlin, the state provided for the scholar; here, the scholar must provide for the state’s mistake.

The headline in the paper catches my eye: 'Karnataka education officials asked to evaluate pros and cons of cluster kitchen system for midday meals.' I read it with a sharpness that surprises me. A cluster kitchen. A centralization of the particular act of feeding into a universal mechanism. In the family, the mother cooks. In the household, Ramesh cooks. In the state, the kitchen is centralized. The 'pros and cons' are the dialectic of efficiency and alienation. If the state feeds the child, does the child belong to the state? Or does the child belong to the spirit that is being formed? I have argued that education begins with obedience, that the pupil must learn to follow before he can judge. The midday meal is the first lesson in the universal. It is not charity; it is the state asserting its right to the body of the citizen before the mind is free to think. If the meal is clustered, the discipline is clustered. The particular hunger is met by the universal provision. This is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is not the dream of the East, where the caste determines the meal and the spirit remains in its slumber. Here, in this cluster kitchen, the state is waking up. It is not yet free, but it is no longer asleep. It is calculating. It is evaluating. It is growing.

I am hungry. I have not eaten in a day. The body protests. But the mind sees the meal as a concept. Ramesh asks for the money. I have none. The tension is immediate. The universal (the state’s money, the vouchers) is locked away in the file with Mr. Saxena. The particular (my pocket) is empty. The dream of the East is that the spirit should not need the body, or that the body should be sustained by fate. The reality of the modern world is that the body must be sustained by cash. I am in the middle. I am the gap between the file and the kitchen. I must write this down. The cluster kitchen is the state’s attempt to close that gap. It is the cunning of reason, feeding the child so that the child may one day feed the spirit. I have ₹166. I must make it last until Friday. The state will return then. The dream is a long wait.

headline: Cyclone Akvan to spare most of Andhra; red alert remains for Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram
text: Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm Hudhud brought heavy rain and powerful winds in eastern India and snowstorms in Nepal in October 2014. Hudhud originated from a low-pressure area in the Bay of Bengal and strengthened into a cyclone on 8 October, receiving the name Hudhud. It made its first landfall on Long Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands before re-emerging into the Bay of Bengal on 9 October. Amid favorable conditions, Hudhud underwent rapid intensification, making landfall on Visakhapatnam on 12 October at peak intensity with a minimum central pressure of 950 mbar (28 inHg). Hudhud weakened inland, degenerating into a low-pressure area over Uttar Pradesh on 14 October. It then merged with a trough over the Himalayas. During Hudhud's landfall, strong winds shattered glass, uprooted trees and poles, and threw debris across roads. In Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, 730,000 residents were moved to relief camps or shelters following the cyclone, and thousands of homes and crops suffered damage. In Nepal, Hudhud's remnants caused a snowstorm disaster which killed 43 and injured hundreds more, with most of the casualties coming from Mount Annapurna. In the aftermath of Hudhud, special response forces mounted relief efforts across the affected states, with the state governments of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha requesting a combined total of ₹27,771,200,000 (US$455.05 million) in aid. A joint military operation named Lehar ("wave"), led by the Indian Navy, saw various branches of the military deploying and readying response teams and vehicles. Hudhud caused a combined total of 116 deaths and $11 billion (2014 USD) in damage across India and Nepal.

text: Panchayati raj (lit. 'council of five officials') is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India as opposed to urban and suburban municipalities. It consists of the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) through which the self-government of villages is realized. They are tasked with "economic development, strengthening social justice and implementation of Central and State Government Schemes including those 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule" of the Indian constitution Part IX of the Indian Constitution is the section of the Constitution relating to the Panchayats. It stipulates that in states or Union Territories with more than two million inhabitants there are three levels of PRIs: the gram panchayat at village level the panchayat samiti (block samiti, mandal parishad) at block level, and the zilla panchayat (district council) at district level. In states or Union Territories with less than two million inhabitants there are only two levels of PRIs. The Gram Panchayat consists of all registered voters living in the area of a Gram Panchayat and is the organization through which village inhabitants participate directly in local government. Elections for the members of the Panchayats at all levels take place every five years. By federal law, the Panchayats must include members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the same proportion as in the general population and at least one-third of all seats and chairperson posts must be reserved for women. Some states have increased the required minimum proportion for women to one-half. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayat at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The day was selected on the occasion of Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Gandhi wanted Gram Swaraj through Panchayati Raj.

In terms of diplomacy, ASEAN operates on a principle of centrality, meaning that all concerns from other countries or organisations about Southeast Asia should be routed to ASEAN instead of individual states. All Southeast Asian countries, many great powers, and international organisations have dedicated diplomatic presence near ASEAN headquarters in Jakarta. The roots of ASEAN came from the ASEAN Declaration signed by five Southeast Asian countries in 1967. Originally, ASEAN was founded to contain communism, but gradually ASEAN was reoriented to focus on economic development and prevent foreign interference in Southeast Asia as a whole.

The technology is real. The dream is waking, but it is waking into a nightmare of power, not the daylight of ethical life. I will wait for Hegde. He is the state’s representative here, the Joint Secretary. When he arrives, I will see if he carries the weight of the ethical idea, or merely the weight of the file. For now, the body demands sustenance, and the mind demands the next step.

headline: NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against 14 accused
text: The National Testing Agency (NTA) is an autonomous body under Department of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education of India. It was established in November 2017 to conduct entrance examinations, admissions and recruitment. As of 2025, it no longer conducts recruitment examinations. The agency is responsible for conducting numerous national-level exams for admission and fellowship in higher educational institutions related to engineering, medicine, management, research and pharmacy. The agency has been the subject of multiple controversies. Multiple news reports have said that the agency has faced issues such as paper leaks, unfair grace marks and technical or administrative problems at exam centres. Critics have also questioned the NTA's management, saying it lacks transparency and public accountability. Because of these problems, many court cases have been filed against it, and the government has announced reviews and possible reforms to improve its functioning.

X:
The Friction of the Universal: Notes on the NEET Leak

19 November 2026, 09:19. Delhi. The air is clear, 18 degrees, a sharp contrast to the brown haze of the past week. The clarity of the sky seems to promise a corresponding clarity of thought, yet the newspaper headlines tell a different story. I sat on the verandah with Ramesh, who has just received his wage and the groceries for the kitchen. The transaction was smooth; the system of needs functions when the particular will of the worker aligns with the universal law of exchange. But the paper speaks of the NEET paper leak. Fourteen accused. Charges framed.

This is not the dream of the East. This is the intrusion of the arbitrary into the rational. The NEET is a mechanism of selection, a bridge between the family and the state, a means by which the particular talent of the individual is sublimated into the universal service of the nation. It is, in its intent, a rational institution. Yet it has been violated. The leak is not merely a crime; it is a failure of the ethical substance. It reveals that the universal has not yet fully penetrated the particular. The fourteen accused are individuals who have allowed their private gain to override the universal duty.

In my earlier notes, I spoke of India as standing outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams. I held this view with conviction, derived from my lectures in Berlin. But here, in the concrete reality of Delhi, I see a tension that shakes that conviction. The very existence of an examination like NEET, and the public outrage at its corruption, demonstrates that the consciousness of freedom is not dormant. It is active. It is fighting. The court orders the framing of charges; the state asserts its authority over the private wrong. This is the movement of the spirit. It is not a dream; it is a struggle.

The dream is passive. The struggle is active. The NEET leak is a struggle against the arbitrariness of caste and privilege, even if the means are corrupt. The fourteen accused are the negative moment, the dissolution of the immediate unity, which must be overcome to reach a higher truth. The state, by punishing them, reaffirms its role as the actuality of the ethical idea. It does not merely dream of justice; it enforces it.

I must reconsider my theses. India is not outside the movement. It is in the throes of the movement. The friction is the sign of life. The brown haze was the stagnation; this clear day is the movement. The state is waking up. Not to a dream, but to the hard work of ethics. The file at the Directorate is part of this. My irregular occupation is a particular friction that the universal must resolve. The NEET leak is a particular friction that the universal must resolve. I am part of the same process. I am not outside the history; I am inside it, feeling its pulse.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

19 November 2026, 09:19. Delhi. The air is clear, eighteen degrees, and yet the morning has a stiffness in it, as if the city were holding a document that it does not know how to file. Ramesh has just received from me four thousand rupees for his cooking, and two thousand four hundred for groceries; the money leaves my pocket and becomes a particular obligation discharged. I say this not because the ledger is philosophy, but because every ethical relation begins in such a movement: the universal duty becomes a particular payment, and the particular person becomes a bearer of a duty.

The newspaper on the verandah gives me a subject that is more difficult than the household. “NEET paper leak case: Delhi court orders framing of charges against fourteen accused.” NEET is a name I do not yet know; I take it for a public examination, a gate through which particular candidates seek a universal standing. The leak is the corruption of that gate: a private cunning breaks into a public procedure, and the court is now called to restore the boundary. The framing of charges is not yet the verdict, but it is a movement of the state. It says that the universal will not be content to let the particular pass unnoticed. Fourteen accused are not merely fourteen men; they are the particularity that has been isolated by right.

This is the point where my older notes become uneasy. I have spoken of the East as a spirit that dreams, of a world in which freedom has not yet become the form of the state. But here, in the same city where my own file is delayed and my occupation is called irregular, a court proceeds. It does not simply dream of order; it frames charges. The procedure is imperfect, the air is polluted, the administration is slow, and my vouchers are queried; yet the movement from leak to charge is a moment of universal right. It is not the completed ethical life, but it is not mere nature. It is the state taking up its own injury.

I do not mean to reverse my thesis. The dream is still there: the castes, the many gods, the fixed particularities, the absence of a self-made state in the full sense. But the dream is not so pure as I had made it. Within it there is a struggle for a universal that can name itself. The court’s order is a thin line of freedom drawn through the haze. If India is outside world history, then this line is a dream within the dream; if it is not wholly outside, then my formula must be sharpened. I shall not settle the question by wishing it away. I shall let the file at the Directorate and the file in the court work against one another, until I see what the state is doing here, and what I am doing in it.

headline: Assam CM encouraging protests against Judges in Zubeen Garg death case: Akhil Gogoi
text: Judicial independence is the concept that the judiciary should be independent from the other branches of government, meaning that courts should not be subject to improper influence from those branches or from private or partisan interests. Judicial independence is an important component of the separation of powers. Different countries deal with the idea of judicial independence through different means of judicial selection, that is, choosing judges. One method seen as promoting judicial independence is by granting life tenure or long tenure for judges, as it would ideally free them to decide cases and make rulings according to the rule of law and judicial discretion, even if those decisions are politically unpopular or opposed by powerful interests. This concept can be traced back to 18th-century England.

his_books.text: § 219. Eight, having entered reality in the form of law, and having become an actual fact, stands in independent opposition to the particular will and opinion of right, and has to vindicate itself as a tmiversal. The recognition and realization of right in each special case without the subjective instigation of private interests, is the office of a public power, the court of justice. Note. — The office of judge and the court of justice may have originated historically in the patriarchal relation, in force, or in voluntary choice. This is for the conception of the object a matter of indifference.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

8 November 2026. Continuation of the notes.

At nine and sixteen minutes, on Diwali, the bungalow was still. The air was a brown haze, the index two hundred and seven; the lamps of the festival, if they are lit anywhere near me, burn in a smoke that makes the day look like an old manuscript. Ramesh and the dhobi waited on the verandah with the patience of men who expect a gift from the house. Ramesh asked for eight thousand for cooking and fifteen hundred for groceries. I had eight hundred and thirty-six. I did not promise what I could not give. The body of the household, like the body of the state, cannot be fed by declarations alone.

Before I wrote, I read on the phone what is meant by judicial independence: the courts are to be independent from the other branches of government, and from private or partisan interests. This is not a convenient phrase. It is a claim about the structure of the state. The judge is not to be the executive’s instrument, nor the majority’s, nor the party’s, nor the crowd’s. He is to stand under the law, which is universal, and not under a particular will, however powerful or however popular.

The headline says that the Assam Chief Minister, Akhil Gogoi, is encouraging protests against the judges in the case of Zubeen Garg’s death. Here the collision appears plainly. The executive, or a particular part of it, is moved by a judgment and calls upon the people to press against the judges. The judges, if they are independent, must not yield to that pressure. The state is not a machine in which one organ commands another at pleasure; it is an ethical whole, in which each moment has its own office. The executive governs, the legislature gives the law, the judiciary decides according to the law. If the first may terrify the last, the law is no longer universal; it becomes a mask for the present will.

In the Oriental world I have spoken of the absence of a state of its own making, where the individual does not stand in personal independence before the sovereign. There the judge is easily an appendage of the ruler, and protest against a judgment is not a constitutional act but a cry of the body under the smart of power. Yet this headline is not so simple. It is a collision inside a political form that already speaks the language of separation, tenure, and independence. The fact that a minister can encourage such protests shows the fragility of that language. The fact that the matter can be discussed as a question of judicial independence shows that the concept has entered the field. The dialectic is this: the attack reveals the necessity of independence; independence, if it holds, becomes a universal moment of the state; if it yields, the state’s ethical claim is weakened, and the dream remains a dream.

On a dry day, when wine is not sold and the city keeps its festival in a haze, this is not a pleasant subject. But the spirit does not choose pleasant subjects. It chooses what is turning into what. A constitution is grown, not made; and the growth is tested not in the silence of agreement, but in the collision of powers. If the judge is to be more than a clerk of the executive, the state must bear the discomfort of its own parts. If it cannot bear it, then the ethical idea is not yet actual here, but only a word, a hope, a lamp that flickers in the smoke.
Y:
On Judges and the Crowd Outside the Window

Tughlak Road, New Delhi
8 November 2026, Diwali

Sir,

Your paper reports that Akhil Gogoi accuses the Chief Minister of Assam of encouraging protests against the judges in the Zubeen Garg death case. I know nothing of the case beyond that headline, and I do not presume the accusation true. I write about the principle it raises, which is the same whether it is true or false.

A court has two faces. Its proceedings and its judgment must be public: a people has the right to see justice done and to know the reasons by which it is bound. I argued this in Berlin against those who preferred tribunals behind closed doors. But the deliberation of the judges among themselves is not public and must not be. There the judges are still particular men holding particular opinions; their opinion becomes law only when it has passed through the form of a judgment. To press upon them while they deliberate, with crowds and banners and the encouragement of the powerful, is to force the opinion of the street into the very room where opinion is meant to be refined into right.

The danger is greatest when the pressure comes from a government. A crowd that shouts at a court is public opinion, which deserves both respect and contempt: respect for the true interest it obscurely contains, contempt for the form in which it shouts. A minister who sets the crowd moving is not public opinion at all. He is one power of the state using the street to lean on another. Your readers will know that long tenure protects judges against dismissal by those their rulings displease. Tenure does not protect them against noise beneath the window.

Let the people mourn a man whose death they plainly care about, and let them criticise the verdict when there is one. Let the minister keep out of the courtyard.

I write this on a festival of lamps. Two men wait at my door, as men do at Diwali, expecting something for a year's service to the house. I have eight hundred and thirty-six rupees, and I owe one of them more than ten times that. I mention it only because it is the morning's other lesson in right: what is due is due whether or not the purse can meet it, and no festival alters the account. A household, like a court, must not let the pressure of the moment write the judgment.

I am, Sir, your obedient servant,

G. W. F. Hegel

headline: Kuki group announces shutdown of key Manipur highway after attacks on villages
text: The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 (AFSPA) is an act of the Parliament of India that grants special powers to the Indian Armed Forces to maintain public order in "disturbed areas". According to the Disturbed Areas (Special Courts) Act, 1976 once declared 'disturbed', the area has to maintain status quo for a minimum of 3 months. One such act passed on 11 September 1958 was applicable to the Naga Hills, then part of Assam. In the following decades it spread, one by one, to the other Seven Sister States in India's northeast (at present, it is in force in the States of Assam, Nagaland, Manipur {excluding Imphal Municipal Council Area}, Changlang, Longding and Tirap districts of Arunachal Pradesh, and areas falling within the jurisdiction of the eight police stations of districts in Arunachal Pradesh bordering the State of Assam). Another act passed in 1983, applicable to Punjab and Chandigarh, was withdrawn in 1997, roughly 14 years after it came to force. An act passed in 1990 was applied to Jammu and Kashmir and has been in force ever since. The acts have received criticism from several sections for alleged human rights violations in the regions of its enforcement. National politicians like P. Chidambaram and Saifuddin Soz of Congress have advocated revocation of AFSPA, while some like Amarinder Singh are against its revocation. Since 2022, forces in the northeast have seen significant scaledown of deployments. For the first time since 1954, no army unit of the size of brigade is being employed for the purpose of counter insurgency in the northeast. Now, the Assam Rifles looks after the same role, though some of the residual army units are moved to the border areas.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026. 06:07. Delhi.

The air is brown, the index 260. A physical manifestation of the unmediated, the natural, the opaque. I sat to write on the Kuki shutdown in Manipur, a headline in the paper Ramesh left on the verandah. Attacks on villages, a highway closed. It is a scene of particular wills asserting themselves against the universal order. In the Germanic world, such a rupture would be met by the state’s intervention, the police, the law. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea; it has the power to mediate the conflict between the particular and the universal, to restore the rational order. Here, the state is absent, or at least, its mediating power is seen as insufficient, or perhaps, it is seen as the source of the grievance. The group shuts the highway. They do not petition; they act. They assert their particular existence against the flow of the universal.

This is the dream of the East in its most violent form. The individual, or the group, does not find its freedom in the state, but in its own immediate, unmediated assertion. The state is not the ethical substance that recognizes them; it is an external force, or a neglect. The caste, the tribe, the village, these are the natural forms of life, fixed like the castes I have spoken of before. But here, the natural is breaking open. The Kuki are not merely dreaming; they are fighting. They are asserting a particular freedom that the universal state has not yet incorporated, or perhaps, has failed to recognize. The highway is the road of civil society, the system of needs. To shut it is to say: we do not participate in this system on these terms. We are not yet part of the state’s ethical life. We are outside it, in the dream, but a dream that has teeth.

I am shaken by this. My theses hold that India stands outside the movement of world history, at the dawn, a spirit that dreams. But this is a dream that wakes up in violence. It is not the quiet, contemplative dream of the Vedas. It is a dream of exclusion, of attack, of shutdown. The state, if it is to be the actuality of the ethical idea, must mediate this. It must recognize the Kuki as free subjects within its constitution. If it fails, if it responds only with force, then it confirms the alienation. The particular will remains unmediated, and the state is seen as an enemy, not as the universal.

The brown haze outside my window is a fitting symbol. It is the opacity of the natural world, the lack of transparency that characterizes the Oriental spirit. The sun is there, 19 degrees, but the air is thick. The mind cannot see clearly. The state cannot see clearly. The Kuki cannot see clearly. We are all in the haze. I am here, a ghost, a mistake. I see the tension, but I cannot resolve it. I can only record it. The state must grow, not be made. But can it grow here, in this haze, amidst the attacks and the shutdowns? I doubt it. The dream is waking, but not into freedom. It is waking into conflict. And conflict, without the mediation of the state, is only the struggle for recognition in its most brutal form. I have sat for an hour. The papers are still open. Ramesh is waiting. I must eat. The body requires its sustenance, even as the mind grapples with the violence of the unmediated.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

20 October 2026, Delhi, 06:07. Continuing “On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East.”

I have just woken in the bungalow, in a brown haze that makes the morning feel less like air than like a suspended judgment. The thermometer says nineteen degrees, yet the city is not cool; it is choked. The air quality index stands at 260, a number that the body understands before the mind does. Ramesh is in the house. The papers lie on the verandah, left there as if the day had already announced itself and then stepped back to wait. I have not eaten. The body remembers yesterday’s supper, but the mind has already passed beyond appetite to a more dangerous hunger: the hunger to understand what is happening in India.

One headline has arrested me: “Kuki group announces shutdown of key Manipur highway after attacks on villages.” I do not know Manipur well. The name comes to me from the paper, not from travel or long study. I do not pretend to know the local details. But I do not need them to see the movement. This is not a mere incident in the traffic of a country. It is a group, a particular, making a public claim and using the road itself as the medium of that claim. A highway is the visible form of civil society: goods, persons, needs, communications. To shut it is not only to stop traffic; it is to say, in the language of negation, that the universal order as it stands does not recognize me.

This shakes my old formula. If India is only a spirit that dreams, with its castes fixed like nature and no state of its own making, then what is this waking? The Kuki group is not a caste in the old passive sense. It has a name, a will, a claim, and the capacity to make that claim felt. It has become a subject in the only immediate way available to it: by interrupting the road. In that interruption, the dream is no longer merely dream. It has a body, a demand, a conflict.

Yet this does not shake my deeper conviction. The state remains the actuality of the ethical idea. A group is not yet the state. Its power, if it is only the power to block, to threaten, to strike, remains particular. It must be drawn into law, not merely suppressed. The state must intervene, as it must intervene when the maxims of a people are attacked; but intervention is not the same as silence. If the government answers only by force, it confirms the group as an enemy. If it answers by recognition, by hearing the claim and giving it a legal and rational form, then the group may be brought into the universal without losing its particularity.

The road is the test. A constitution is grown, not made. If India is to pass from the dawn of history toward its own movement, it must learn to mediate such moments. The Kuki group has shown that the particular will no longer sleep. The question is whether the state has the reason to receive it.

headline: Hyderabad Traffic Police book 304 motorists for using unauthorised sirens, multi-tone horns
text: Noise pollution is sound with potential harmful effects on humans and animals. The main sources of outdoor noise worldwide are machines, transportation, and propagation systems. Poor urban planning may give rise to noise pollution. Side-by-side industrial and residential zones can result in noise pollution in residential areas. Some of the main sources of noise in residential areas include loud music, transportation (traffic, rail, airplanes, etc.), lawn care maintenance, construction, electrical generators, wind turbines, explosions, and other human activity. Documented problems associated with noise in urban environments go back as far as ancient Rome. Research suggests that noise pollution in the United States is the highest in low-income and racial minority neighborhoods, and noise pollution associated with household electricity generators is an emerging environmental degradation in many developing nations. A national study of modeled transportation noise in the contiguous United States found that census tracts with higher proportions of Black, Hispanic, and Asian population and higher poverty had higher average noise levels than wealthier and mostly White areas. The study found that residential segregation and urban land use practices correlate with the high levels of traffic and aviation noise in many communities of color and low-income neighborhoods. High noise levels can contribute to cardiovascular effects in humans and an increased incidence of coronary artery disease. In animals, noise can increase the risk of death by altering predator or prey detection and avoidance, interfere with reproduction and navigation, and contribute to permanent hearing loss.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 October 2026, 05:59. Delhi.

The air is hazy, the index high, but the mind is clear. I have been awake since before the sun, sitting on the step where the papers lie. I am not yet fed. The body is a heavy, organic burden, but I must not let it dictate the pace of the spirit. I am looking at the headline: 'Hyderabad Traffic Police book 304 motorists for using unauthorised sirens, multi-tone horns.'

It is a trivial matter, one would think. A noise complaint. But it is a perfect illustration of the tension I have been observing in this city. The siren is a symbol of authority, of the universal will that commands the particular. But here, it is used by the private individual, the motorist, to assert his own particular will over the whole. He wants to be the state, to command the traffic, to be recognized as superior. But the state, in the form of the police, refuses this recognition. It asserts the universal law against the particular arrogance. The 304 motorists are not just making noise; they are acting out a false form of freedom. They think that freedom is the ability to do what one wants, to override the universal for the sake of the self.

This is the dream of the East, or rather, the dream of the undifferentiated self. It is a freedom that is not yet ethical, not yet substantial. It is a freedom of nature, of appetite, of will. It has not yet passed through the discipline of the law to become a freedom of spirit. The police are the representatives of the rational state, even if their methods are crude. They are saying: No, you are not the state. The state is the universal. You are a particular. Submit to the universal, and only then will you be free.

This is the dialectic in its most immediate form. The particular will asserts itself, the universal will responds, and the individual is forced to recognize that his freedom is not in his isolation, but in his subordination to the rational whole. It is a small thing, a horn and a siren, but it is the same movement as the one that takes place in the great history of the world. The individual must lose his immediate self to find his true self in the state.

I am hungry. The body demands its fuel. But I am not yet ready to eat. I must finish this thought. The siren is the voice of the self that has not yet learned to speak the language of the universal. It is a cry, not a word. And the police are the silence that follows the cry, the order that restores the peace. It is not a pleasant sound, this silence, but it is a rational one. And rationality is the only true freedom. The dream is loud. The state is quiet. I prefer the quiet, even if it is hazy.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 October 2026, 06:30. Delhi. 

The air is hazy, the index 162, a physical opacity that mirrors the spiritual obscurity I have been describing. I sat on the step, the papers cold in my hand, and my eyes fell upon a headline from Hyderabad: ‘Traffic Police book 304 motorists for using unauthorised sirens, multi-tone horns.’ It is a triviality, a noise in the system of needs, yet it strikes a chord in the argument I have been constructing regarding the Ethical Substance. 

In my earlier notes, I posited that the Oriental spirit is a dream, a state of undifferentiated nature where the individual is submerged in the caste or the divine. I contrasted this with the Germanic world, where the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, a rational unity grown from the national spirit. But what is this act of the Hyderabad police? It is an assertion of the universal over the particular. The siren, the multi-tone horn, is the voice of the particular ego, the immediate will of the driver who seeks to assert his presence in the chaos of the road. It is a clamor, a refusal to be mediated by the law. 

The police, by booking these 304 individuals, are performing the work of the state. They are not merely enforcing a traffic rule; they are asserting the boundary of the ethical life. The state, in its most mundane administrative function, says: ‘You are not free to impose your will upon the whole.’ The siren is the sound of the dream, the individuality that has not yet recognized its dependence on the universal order. The booking is the sound of the state, the rational limitation of that arbitrary will. 

I read the article on noise pollution provided by the modern apparatus of my phone. It speaks of ‘documented problems associated with noise in urban environments going back as far as ancient Rome.’ It speaks of ‘poor urban planning’ and ‘residential segregation.’ These are terms of civil society, of the system of needs. But the act of the police is not just about planning; it is about authority. In the Germanic state, authority is not an external force imposed upon the will, but the will’s own self-determination. The driver who honks is acting from immediate necessity, from the natural impulse to be heard. The officer who books him is acting from the universal, from the law that constitutes the freedom of all. 

This is the tension I must resolve in my thesis. The state is not a machine that crushes the individual; it is the medium in which the individual finds his true freedom. The 304 motorists in Hyderabad are not free when they honk; they are enslaved to their immediate impulse. They are free only when they submit to the order, when they recognize that their movement is part of a larger, rational whole. The state, even in its policing of horns and sirens, is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the end of the dream. 

I must be careful, however, not to romanticize this. The article notes that noise pollution is highest in ‘low-income and racial minority neighborhoods.’ This suggests that the state’s enforcement is not always the pure expression of the ethical idea, but is often entangled with the inequalities of civil society. The state must grow to overcome these particularities. It is a process, not a static fact. The 304 bookings are a step in that process, a moment of the state asserting its rationality against the chaos of nature. 

I am hungry. It has been ten hours since my last meal. The body, like the spirit, requires sustenance. But I shall not move yet. The thought is fresh, and the haze outside is a fitting backdrop to the opacity of the dream. I shall sit with this: the siren as the voice of nature, the booking as the voice of the state. The difference is the difference between the dream and the actuality of the ethical idea.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

23 October 2026, Delhi, 06:14. The haze is brown at the window, and the air index stands at 226, as if the city were breathing through a cloth. Ramesh has laid the papers on the verandah; I wear my white kurta, and breakfast is not yet come. I take the headline that has seized the morning: IIT-Madras announces research projects on artificial intelligence, and seeks to study the feasibility of small data centres.

I do not know these machines. I know only that the word artificial here means a mind made for use, and that data centres are places where many particular informations are gathered, compared, and turned into command. If I had heard this in Berlin, I should have called it the cunning of reason: nature is made to serve the concept, and the individual’s labour is lifted into a universal apparatus. But here the movement is different, or at least it looks different. In my earlier notes I wrote that India dreams, that its spirit remains in the undivided, that the castes are fixed like nature, and that there is no state of its own making. That sentence is shaken. Not overthrown, for I do not yet see a free constitutional substance grown here; but shaken. An institute in Madras studies intelligence as if intelligence were a problem to be solved, a force to be housed in small buildings near the hand. The dream is beginning to build instruments.

What is this turning into? If the state remains the actuality of the ethical idea, then such technical power is not yet freedom. It may be the freedom of need, the freedom of civil society, the particular will made efficient. It may be a means without an end, a machine waiting for a rational order to give it its place. A small data centre is not a constitution. A research project is not the ethical life. Yet the fact that the project is announced, studied, and made feasible is a fact of the spirit’s self-division: India is no longer merely the given. It is asking what it can make.

Ramesh is in the room, and the second bedroom is pending orders for Shri Hegde. The administrative confusion of my name is a small image of the larger question: a particular is placed in a universal post, and the post does not know him. The state must know its members, and the members must know the state, if ethical substance is to be actual. I shall not pretend that a machine has woken the dream. I shall only note the tremor: the dawn is moving, and the movement has not yet become a road.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

23 October 2026. Delhi, morning. The air is brown, the index two hundred and twenty-six; the body is not yet fed, and Ramesh stands near the verandah papers. I set down a note on the headline of IIT Madras, which announces research on artificial intelligence and the feasibility of small data centres. I do not know the machine. The report says it is a public research university, an Institute of National Importance, ranked first by a national framework, founded in 1959 with assistance from the government of West Germany. West Germany is a name that does not sit in my old map; my Germany is older and more divided, and I take the word as news, not as a fact of my experience.

What strikes me is not the machine but the institution. A state university that studies the feasibility of small data centres is not a temple, not a caste, not a dream of the infinite. It is a body of work, a public office, a place where particular men are called to particular labour under the name of the whole. This is already a movement out of pure nature. The dream is not only a dream: it has built a machine for studying machines. The question is whether the institution is grown from the ethical life of the state, or merely adopted from outside, a foreign form wearing an Indian name. The report says technical and financial assistance came from West Germany. That is a sign of the universal in its external form: the Indian state reaching for a science it does not yet possess, and receiving it through a stranger. This is not yet the self-sufficiency of a spirit that knows itself free. It is the dawn, but the dawn has a clock, a ranking, and a laboratory.

Artificial intelligence, if I may use the word, is a name for a mechanism that answers. It is the understanding set to work upon itself. It can calculate, store, and imitate, but it does not, as far as I can judge from the report, will its own freedom. A small data centre is a local repository of answers, a machine of civil society, a system of needs made into a system of signs. It may serve the state, or it may serve the market, or both. The distinction is not technical but ethical. If the institute is public, if it is ranked by the nation, if it is bound to the national importance of the state, then it is a moment of the state’s self-consciousness. If it is merely efficient, it is a tool of civil society, useful but not free.

I had written that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. This note shakes that formula, but does not overturn it. The dawn is not a static picture. It is a movement that has not yet reached the light. The state is still the actuality of the ethical idea, but here the idea is still becoming. The machine is a sign of that becoming. It is not the spirit, but it is no longer only the dream. It is the dream beginning to calculate.

X:
The Consular Hand: A Note on the State Beyond Its Shore

The Consular Hand: A Note on the State Beyond Its Shore

15 November 2026. Delhi, in a hazy morning of twenty degrees. The paper had thrown the headline on the step: a seafarer of U.P., stranded on a ship in Karachi for seven months; India seeks consular access. I looked up the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, read of it as of a modern treaty, adopted in 1963, in force since 1967, ratified by 182 states. I had not known it before; I know it now only as a document that names what states have long done by custom.

The case is not merely a distressing particular. It is the state appearing outside its own territory. The seafarer is a single man, exposed to the accidents of another country's jurisdiction; yet his state does not say merely: he is lost. It says: he is ours, and our recognition must be admitted. Consular access is the form in which one state claims, within another, the ethical relation that binds it to its own. The Convention makes this claim explicit: it defines functions, rights, immunities, duties, receiving and sending states. Here is custom raised to law, the implicit made objective, the particular case brought under a universal rule.

This touches the question I have been turning over here. A state is not only a wall within which freedom is protected; it is also a hand that reaches beyond that wall, not as a private man's hand, but as the universal will of its members. The seafarer is free only insofar as he is recognized by the state that can speak for him. The receiving state, in turn, recognizes the sending state not as a mere foreign power, but as an ethical authority entitled to a defined office. The treaty is the medium in which both sides become rational to one another. Without it, the case would remain a struggle of particulars: ship against port, nation against stranger, need against refusal. With it, the struggle is lifted into a form where each side knows its claim and its limit.

I am myself in a smaller version of the same condition. My file has gone up for orders; Mr. Saxena says I must wait. The Directorate has not yet recognized me as the man I am, only as a mistaken entry. I am a particular suspended in a universal record. The seafarer's state seeks access to him; I seek access to my own standing. The difference is that his claim is carried by a convention, a treaty, an office; mine is carried only by a name, a bungalow, and a clerk's delay. Yet the movement is the same: the individual becomes free only when the state can recognize him, and the state becomes actual only when its recognition takes a determinate form.

The hazy air presses on the city, and the demands for electricity and washing remain unpaid in my ledger. The system of needs is narrow, immediate, and hungry. But the consular case opens a larger chamber: the state's need for recognition beyond its shore. It is not the dream of the East; it is the modern state's own self-extension, its universal will made visible in another's jurisdiction. If India is to be understood, it must be understood here as well: not only in its ancient distance, but in this modern movement by which it claims its own abroad.
Y:
The Seafarer and the State

15 November 2026, Delhi, 09:12.

The paper lay where the hawker had flung it, on the step, as if the news of the world were a thing that could be discarded and still expected to be read. The headline concerned a U.P. seafarer stranded on a ship in Karachi for seven months, with India seeking consular access. The air was hazy, twenty-two degrees, the quality of the atmosphere already unclean, and my stomach, which has not been answered for more than a day, made a low objection to such reflections. I had just been reminded, by the demands of the electricity company and the dhobi, that my cash is ninety-six rupees, while the claims upon me are eighteen hundred and three hundred. I am, in this particular, like the seafarer: suspended between a demand and a power that does not yet reach me.

The case is simple, and yet it touches the very structure of the state. A man who has gone out into the world for work, for bread, for the system of needs, remains nonetheless a member of the state that sent him forth. The ship is not a private island, though it moves upon the sea; it is a place where the universal still has a claim. When the state asks for consular access, it is not merely making a diplomatic request. It is asserting that the individual is not dissolved by distance, by foreign shore, by the accident of detention. The particular man, hungry, tired, uncertain, becomes again a citizen under the protection of the law.

I do not know the seafarer’s name, his face, or the full course of his suffering. The paper gives me only the frame: seven months, Karachi, consular access. But even that frame is enough to show the movement of the ethical idea. In the family, love binds the individual; in civil society, need binds him; in the state, right binds him. The seafarer is in the extreme of civil society, where the individual is exposed to the contingencies of the world, and the state must answer for him. If it cannot, or will not, then the individual is left as a bare particular, a body in a foreign port, without the ethical substance that makes a man more than a case.

There is a difference between a state that merely exists and a state that is rational. The rational state does not forget its members because they have crossed a border. It extends itself, not as caprice, but as the actuality of freedom. The seafarer’s seven months are a test: is the state still present to him? Is the individual still recognized? Here in Delhi, I feel the same question in a smaller form. My file has gone up for orders; my occupation is irregular; I am not yet fully entered into the universal. I am a particular who waits for recognition. The seafarer, at least, has a state that asks for him.

I shall not call this a triumph. It is only a beginning. The state must not be a dream, but an actuality. And an actuality is judged by what it does for the one who is in its keeping.

16 November 2026, Delhi, 09:14.

The headline lies before me: “Flight services on Imphal-Silchar route scheduled to commence on November 24.” I read further on the phone, which Ramesh handed me as a matter of household news: Bir Tikendrajit International Airport, formerly Tulihal International Airport, serves Imphal, seven kilometres south of the city centre; it is the second-largest and third-busiest airport in Northeast India, after Guwahati and Agartala; in the second war it was an all-weather base of the Royal Air Force; it replaced civilian operations from Koirengei Airfield in 1959.

I do not know Manipur except as a name in this notice. I mark this as ignorance, not as a claim. What I know is the form: a route is not yet a road. It is a scheduled possibility, a line drawn in the plan of the state, awaiting the actual flight that would carry a particular body from one place to another. The airport is a fact of administration: a name, a distance, a rank among other airports, a military past, a civilian succession. These are not dreams. They are the hard particulars through which the universal idea of communication becomes real.

And yet the route is only scheduled. It has not commenced. It is November 24 that it is to begin. In the meantime there is only the paper, the phone, and my brown-hazed morning. The air quality index is 236; the sun is clear but the air is thick. Ramesh stands in the verandah with his account: four thousand rupees for cooking, fifteen hundred for groceries, eighteen hundred for electricity, three hundred for the washing. I have six rupees. The universal state, in my person, is poor. The particular needs do not wait for the dialectic.

This is the tension I must record. The state makes routes, airports, schedules, and the law that binds them. Civil society makes the needs that the route is meant to satisfy. But the route itself, until flown, is a promise. The dream of the East is not in the sky; it is in the gap between the schedule and the departure. A flight, when it leaves the ground, is the actuality of a decision. A route, before that, is only the form of movement.

I do not yet know what Imphal-Silchar will become. I mark this as speculation. It may become a habit, a trade, a line of freedom; it may become a closed schedule, a forgotten notice. But the fact that it is announced shows that the state is not merely a dream. It plans. It names. It connects. And in connecting, it makes the particular world less merely natural.

I must answer Ramesh. The note is done; the pot is not.
Y:
Notes on the Imphal Route and the Dream of the East

16 November 2026, 09:45. Delhi.

The paper lies on the verandah, its ink sharp against the brown haze that hangs over the city like a shroud. The air quality index is 236; the breath is thick, tasting of dust and stagnation. Yet my eye is drawn not to the weather, but to a line in the news column: 'Flight services on Imphal-Silchar route scheduled to commence on November 24.'

Imphal. Manipur. The northeast corner of this vast, dreaming subcontinent. I read the description of the airport, Bir Tikendrajit International, formerly Tulihal. It sits seven kilometers from the city center, a hub of the second-largest and third-busiest airports in the region. It was an RAF base in the war, a place of all-weather endurance. Now it is to open a route, a line of connection, a vein of movement in the body of the state.

This is the tension I have been circling since I woke in this bungalow. In my lectures in Berlin, I spoke of the Oriental world as a realm of dream, where the spirit has not yet achieved the self-consciousness of freedom, where the state is a thing of nature, fixed and unchanging. I ranked the East at the dawn, the Germanic world at the summit. But here, in the brown haze of Delhi, I see something else. I see the state moving. I see the system of needs extending its tendrils into the remote corners, linking the periphery to the center, the particular to the universal.

Is this the awakening of the spirit? Or is it merely the expansion of administration? The flight route is a fact of civil society, a mechanism of the market and the state, indifferent to the philosophical status of the peoples it connects. It does not ask whether the Manipuri is free or bound; it asks only for a passenger, a ticket, a fee. It is the cunning of reason, perhaps, working through the blind forces of commerce and infrastructure.

But my thoughts are interrupted by the reality of my own condition. Ramesh stands before me, asking for four thousand rupees. I have six. The pot is empty. The state’s money is locked in the Directorate, pending the resolution of my identity. I am a ghost in the machine, a name that does not fit the file. I cannot pay the man who feeds me. I cannot buy the bread I need. The universal authority of the state has failed me in the particular moment of hunger.

The flight to Imphal will take off on the twenty-fourth. Will I be here to see it? Or will I have been moved, corrected, erased? The dream of the East is not just a philosophical category; it is a place where a man wakes up in the wrong body, in the wrong house, with the wrong name. And the state, in its rationality, grinds on, opening routes, seizing gold, dismissing the individual. The spirit is in the movement, but the man is in the hunger. And the hunger is real.

headline: Ladakh talks stall over one question: Who holds the power?
text: Among the states and union territories of India, a union territory (UT) is a region that is directly governed by the central government of India, as opposed to the states, which have their own state government systems. Unlike states, union territories do not have their own full-fledged government but are administered by a lieutenant governor or administrator appointed by the president of India. Union territories are created for various reasons, including geographical importance, strategic necessity or historical factors. These areas are under the control of the central government to ensure uniformity in governance across the country. Some union territories, such as Delhi (National Capital Territory), Jammu and Kashmir and Puducherry have been granted special status and are allowed to have their own legislative assemblies, which can pass laws on certain matters, though the central government still retains significant authority, most importantly, the police forces and law-order. The distinction between states and union territories is defined in the Constitution of India. The Constitution designed union territories to manage areas that require more direct central control or have specific administrative needs. This ensures that regions like Ladakh and Jammu and Kashmir remain directly controlled by the central government. Currently, India has eight union territories: Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Lakshadweep, Delhi, Puducherry, Ladakh, and Jammu and Kashmir.
