Other factors attributed to the shortage of water in India are a lack of proper infrastructure and government oversight and unchecked water pollution. text: This article describes the use of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which prohibited it. Torture is prohibited by international law and is illegal in most countries. However, it is still used by many governments. Torture is widely practiced worldwide: Amnesty International received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in more than 150 countries during the four-year period from 1997 to 2001. These accusations concerned acts against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130 countries. State torture has been extensively documented and studied, often as part of efforts at collective memory and reconciliation in societies that have experienced a change in government. Surveys of torture survivors reveal that torture "is not aimed primarily at the extraction of information ... Its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity." When applied indiscriminately, torture is used as a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent and community empowerment. While many states use torture, few wish to be described as doing so, either to their own citizens or to international bodies. So a variety of strategies are used to circumvent their legal and humanitarian duties, including plausible deniability, secret police, "need to know", denial that certain activities constitute torture, appeal to various laws (national or international), use of a jurisdictional argument, claim of "overriding need", the use of torture by proxy, and so on.

This is the dialectic of the state in its painful form. The petition is not the dream. It is the particular will of the citizen turned against the particular will of the police, and brought before a public power. The court, as I have written, is the office by which right vindicates itself as universal, without the instigation of private interest. If the petition is true, the state’s own arm has become a private will: it does not merely enforce the law, it breaks the person. The state is then divided against itself; the universal law stands against the particular force that bears its seal.

I had written that India stands outside the movement of world history, a spirit that dreams. That note must be shaken, not abandoned. The very existence of the Supreme Court, the public petition, the newspaper’s naming of the case, is a moment of self-difference. It is not nature, not caste, not the unchanging given. It is law claiming to be grown, not made. Yet the article reminds me that a universal declaration, however solemn, does not by itself make the ethical idea actual. The law can be invoked to hide violence; the state can speak in the name of the universal while its agents act from the particular. The court’s deliberation, before judgment, is still particular opinion; only in the public decision does it become a fact of right.

The hawker’s paper is itself a piece of civil society: it gathers complaint, names authority, and forces the state to answer. It is not yet the state’s self-consciousness, but it is not the mere dream either. It is the dream beginning to ask for a form. The body, still empty, waits below; the mind must hold this tension: the state as ethical idea, and the state as power that must be judged. That judgment is the movement. To write it down is to let the particular become a moment of the universal.
Y:
The Rack and the Court

15 October 2026, early, on the step, before any breakfast.

The headline says only this: petitions in the Supreme Court allege police excesses during the Delhi protests. I do not know what was done, to whom, or whether it was done at all. That is for the court. What I can weigh is the thing alleged, and the little glass tablet has told me what the world now means by its worst form.

Prussia abolished the rack under Frederick, a lifetime before my own lectures. It came out of the old procedure, which would not condemn a man until he had confessed; since the guilty do not confess willingly, the law built a machine to make them. The error lay in the premise. The court does not need the accused to say yes. It needs evidence, weighed in public by men who have no interest in the case. Once that is understood, the rack has no work left to do.

The article says something sharper than I expected: that the aim of torture is not information but to break the person. If so, it is the exact inversion of punishment. When the law punishes a criminal it honours him as rational, a being whose deed is answerable to a law he himself would recognise. It negates his crime, not his personality. Torture negates the personality and leaves the question of the crime aside. It is not the state striking down a wrong. It is the state committing a fresh one, and doing it in the uniform of the universal, which makes it worse than the brawler's blow.

Then the list of evasions: deniability, secret police, torture by proxy, "overriding need". These interest me most. No government, the article says, wishes to be called a torturer. Why not, if the thing is useful? Because the principle has won. A state that hides its rack has already conceded that persons may not be broken; it lives in contradiction with what it professes, and contradiction is not a resting place. Hypocrisy is the form in which a principle first rules those who still break it.

Hence the petition. Citizens go before the highest court of their own state to accuse that state's police. One power of the state is called to answer before another. This is not the state falling apart; it is the state doing the work by which it is actual rather than merely forceful. The judges will deliberate among themselves in private, and that is right. But the judgment must be public, with its reasons, or the court is only a second police.

I cannot tell from a headline whether the excesses happened. I can say what would follow if they did. My stomach reminds me that I have eaten nothing for more than a day. The papers will keep.

headline: Mumbai vs Chennai air quality after Diwali: Why did Diwali leave one coastal city with ‘poor’ air?
text: Air pollution in India is a serious environmental issue. Air pollution contributes to the premature deaths of 2 million Indians every year. Of the 30 most polluted cities in the world, 21 were in India in 2019. As per a study based on 2016 data, at least 140 million people in India breathe air that is 10 times or more over the WHO safe limit and 13 of the world's 20 cities with the highest annual levels of air pollution are in India. As per the World Air Quality Report 2023, of the 100 most polluted cities in the world, 83 are in India. The main contributors to India's particulate air pollution include industrial and vehicular emissions, construction dust and debris, dependence on thermal power for electricity, waste burning, and use of wood and dung by low-income and rural households for cooking and heating. 51% of India's air pollution is caused by industrial pollution, 27% by vehicles, 17% by crop burning and 5% by other sources. Emissions come from vehicles and industry, whereas in rural areas, much of the pollution stems from biomass burning for cooking and keeping warm. In autumn and spring months, large scale crop residue burning in agriculture fields – a cheaper alternative to mechanical tilling – is a major source of smoke, smog and particulate pollution. India has a low per capita emissions of greenhouse gases but the country as a whole is the third largest greenhouse gas producer after China and the United States. A 2013 study on non-smokers found that Indians, on average, have about 30% lower lung function compared to Europeans. The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act was passed in 1981 to regulate air pollution but has failed to reduce pollution because of poor enforcement of the rules.

X:
The Air and the Spirit: Notes on the Haze

11 November 2026, 09:46. Delhi.

The air quality index reads 305. A brown haze hangs over the city, a physical manifestation of the spiritual stagnation I have been describing in my notes. The breath is difficult; the spirit, too, finds it hard to rise in such an atmosphere. I sat down to write a letter to the Directorate, an act of civil society, a negotiation between the particular (my presence) and the universal (the state’s records). But as I wrote, the pen felt heavy. The letter was practical, correct, and utterly insufficient. It addressed the body of the administration, but not its soul. The error of Hegde for Hegel is not merely a clerical slip; it is a symptom of a deeper confusion, a failure of the state to recognize its own rationality.

I am a ghost in this bungalow. I am not Shri Hegde. I am Hegel. I am a spirit that has traveled from the summit of the Germanic world to the dawn of the Oriental. I am here to observe, to record, to understand. I am not to change. I am not to teach. I am to see the difference between the dream and the state, between the given and the grown, between the nature and the spirit. And in seeing it, I confirm my own freedom. I am free because I am outside the dream. I am free because I am in the state, even if I am a mistake in its allotment. The state is rational, and I am rational. Therefore, I am free. The dream is not. It is only a dream.

The papers speak of air quality in Mumbai and Chennai after Diwali. Why did one coastal city remain with 'poor' air while the other fared better? It is a question of geography, of wind, of the physical conditions of the land. But it is also a question of the spirit. The spirit of the city, its ethical substance, its capacity for self-reflection and self-correction. Mumbai, with its bustling commerce, its system of needs, its civil society in full swing, has a spirit that is more active, more dynamic, more capable of moving beyond its own particularity. Chennai, with its quieter, more contemplative nature, its stronger connection to the dream of the East, is more prone to stagnation. The air is a mirror of the spirit. The brown haze is the dream made visible. The clean air is the state made manifest.

I must return to the table. Ramesh has kept the sambar warm. The body demands its fuel, but the mind must continue its work. The difference between dream and state is not a matter of preference, but of reason. It is the difference between nature and spirit, between the given and the grown. I shall write on this further, but for now, I must eat.
Y:
The Air Belongs to No One

11 November 2026. Tughlak Road. The index stands at 305 this morning and the haze is brown against the window.

The paper asks why Diwali left one coastal city, of Mumbai and Chennai, with poor air. I have only the headline, not its answer. My guess, and it is no more, is that the wind decides: one coast has its sea breeze at the hour of the fireworks, the other does not. If so, the question is not of the festival but of what carries away what men put into the air.

The tablet is blunt. Two million deaths a year before their time. Of the hundred most polluted cities in the world, eighty-three are in this country. The sources: industry above all, then vehicles, then the burning of stubble in the fields, then the wood and dung of poor kitchens.

What is the air, in right? It belongs to no one. That is why everyone may use it and no one is answerable for it. Property is the will placed in a thing; the air will not hold a will, and so it falls outside contract and into the care of the public power, or nowhere. Civil society, left to itself, sends its waste where no owner will object, and the one place no owner objects is the common sky.

The stubble shows the mechanism exactly. The farmer burns because it is cheaper than ploughing in. His reason is sound for his field. The sum of these sound reasons is a sky that shortens lives in a city he may never visit. Each acts for himself and the universal results, as I always said it does; but here the universal that results is a harm. The cunning of reason is not guaranteed in every case. Sometimes it is only the arithmetic of carelessness.

Then the law. An Act of 1981, the tablet says, has failed through poor enforcement. A law that is not enforced is not law in its actuality but an ought on paper, and the ought is what I have always held in least esteem. The state's being is that its laws work. Forty-five years of an Act with this index outside my window is not the ethical idea made actual; it is the idea left as a wish.

One more point, the hardest. I lectured on the geographical basis of history: climate, rivers and soil set the stage on which a people's spirit acts. The tablet says Indians have less lung function than Europeans, on average. If that is the air and not the race, then the stage itself is now being made by men. Geography has passed into history.

The electricity company wants eighteen hundred; I have a hundred and sixty-six. I breathe free of charge, and it is the dearest thing here.

X:
The Seafarer and the State: Notes on Consular Access and Ethical Substance

15 November 2026. Delhi, 09:12. The air quality index is 119, a haze that sits on the lungs like a second skin. I have not eaten since yesterday, yet I find myself compelled to write before the body’s demand for sustenance overrides the spirit’s need for order. The headline in the *Times of India* is a small, concrete instance of the universal: “UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access.”

Seven months. The particular individual, the seafarer from Uttar Pradesh, is suspended in a limbo between two states. He is no longer fully in India, nor fully in Pakistan; he is in the interstice, in the void that opens when the ethical substance of the state fails to encompass the individual’s existence. I read the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations on my phone. It is a document of 1963, a codification of customs that, until then, existed only as the unspoken habits of sovereigns. Here is the movement of reason: from the particular, uncodified practice of one consul to another, to the universal, binding treaty of 182 states. The state does not merely exist; it grows. It externalizes its internal relations into law, into a form that can be recognized and enforced.

This is what I meant when I spoke of the state as the actuality of the ethical idea. It is not a contract, a cold agreement between atomized wills. It is a living organism that, in order to persist, must articulate its own boundaries. The seafarer’s plight is a failure of this articulation. The state has reached out—“India seeks consular access”—but the reach is slow, bureaucratic, mediated by the very treaties that are supposed to guarantee the protection of its citizens. The delay is not merely administrative; it is a symptom of the friction between the universal claim of the state and the particular suffering of the man.

In my earlier notes, I spoke of India as standing outside world history, a spirit that dreams. But here, in this headline, I see a different movement. The Indian state is engaging in the diplomatic machinery of the modern world, invoking international law, asserting its rights. It is not merely dreaming; it is acting, however slowly, however inadequately. The dream is not the whole truth. The state, even if it is a state in the making, even if its ethical substance is not yet fully realized in the consciousness of its people, is a concrete reality. It has a will, and that will is expressed in the search for the seafarer.

My cash is ₹96. I owe the electricity company ₹1,800 and the dhobi ₹300. I have not paid Ramesh. The particular needs of the body and the household are pressing, yet they are secondary to the universal task of understanding. The seafarer is stranded; I am stranded in a bungalow that belongs to a man I am not. We are both suspended in the interstice. But he has the state to seek him; I have only the spirit to observe. The difference is not one of freedom, but of recognition. The state recognizes its citizens; the spirit recognizes itself. Both are necessary. Neither is sufficient. The seafarer must be brought home. I must be brought to myself. The process is the same: the movement from alienation to reconciliation, from the particular to the universal, from the dream to the actual.
Y:
Notes on the Stranded and the Suspended

15 November 2026, 09:12. Delhi. 20°C, mostly clear. Air quality index: 119. I am awake, though the body has not moved; it remains in the white cotton kurta, stiff from the previous night’s slumber. The last meal was more than a day ago. The pot is empty. Ramesh has not been paid, and so the household stands in a suspended state of obligation, a debt that is also a silence.

On the step, where the hawker has thrown the papers with the casual indifference of a man who has delivered the news and expects no answer, lies the morning’s record. The headlines are the usual parade of particularities: a university in collision with a minister, a building company in Karnataka, and this item which arrests my eye: “UP seafarer stranded on ship in Karachi for 7 months: India seeks consular access.”

Seven months. The number has a weight to it. It is not a moment of accident, nor a brief delay in the system of needs. It is a duration that has hardened into a condition. The seafarer is in Karachi, a port, a node in the web of civil society, yet he is stranded. He is outside the protection of the state that claims him, and inside the indifference of the state that holds him. The consular access is sought. It is a request. It is the particular individual knocking on the door of the universal.

I think of my own position. I am in Delhi, in a bungalow allotted to me by mistake. I am a ghost in the records. The file is gone up for orders. Mr. Saxena said to come after fifteen days. Friday, 20 November, is the day the file is due back. I am in a suspension similar to the seafarer’s, though my suspension is one of identity, not geography. I am here, but I am not recognized as being here. The state has not yet acknowledged me. I am waiting for the universal to confirm my particular existence.

But there is a difference. The seafarer is in a place where the state’s authority is contested or absent. I am in the heart of the capital, the seat of the state. Yet I am still outside. Why? Because the state is not merely a machine of administration. It is the actuality of the ethical idea. It must recognize its own. If it does not recognize me, is it because I am not its own? Or is it because it is still in the process of becoming itself? 

The seafarer’s seven months are a testament to the slow, grinding work of the spirit to reconcile the individual with the universal. It is not a failure of the state, but a manifestation of its dialectical movement. The tension between the particular (the seafarer) and the universal (the state) is the very engine of history. It is in this tension that freedom is born. The seafarer is not free, yet. But he is on the road. And the road is long.

I have ₹96 in my pocket. The electricity company asks for ₹1,800. The dhobi asks for ₹300. I cannot pay. I am also stranded. Not in a ship, but in a bungalow. Not for seven months, but for fifteen days. The time is different, but the condition is the same. I am waiting for the state to wake up. To see me. To recognize me. To make me free.

The air is clear, but the haze remains. The spirit must breathe through it. It must think. It must wait. It must hope. For the dream is not the end. The dream is the beginning. And the beginning is always a struggle. The seafarer struggles. I struggle. We struggle. And in our struggle, we become free.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

23 October 2026. Delhi, morning. The air is brown, the index two hundred and twenty-six; the body is not yet fed, and Ramesh stands near the verandah papers. I set down a note on the headline of IIT Madras, which announces research on artificial intelligence and the feasibility of small data centres. I do not know the machine. The report says it is a public research university, an Institute of National Importance, ranked first by a national framework, founded in 1959 with assistance from the government of West Germany. West Germany is a name that does not sit in my old map; my Germany is older and more divided, and I take the word as news, not as a fact of my experience.

What strikes me is not the machine but the institution. A state university that studies the feasibility of small data centres is not a temple, not a caste, not a dream of the infinite. It is a body of work, a public office, a place where particular men are called to particular labour under the name of the whole. This is already a movement out of pure nature. The dream is not only a dream: it has built a machine for studying machines. The question is whether the institution is grown from the ethical life of the state, or merely adopted from outside, a foreign form wearing an Indian name. The report says technical and financial assistance came from West Germany. That is a sign of the universal in its external form: the Indian state reaching for a science it does not yet possess, and receiving it through a stranger. This is not yet the self-sufficiency of a spirit that knows itself free. It is the dawn, but the dawn has a clock, a ranking, and a laboratory.

Artificial intelligence, if I may use the word, is a name for a mechanism that answers. It is the understanding set to work upon itself. It can calculate, store, and imitate, but it does not, as far as I can judge from the report, will its own freedom. A small data centre is a local repository of answers, a machine of civil society, a system of needs made into a system of signs. It may serve the state, or it may serve the market, or both. The distinction is not technical but ethical. If the institute is public, if it is ranked by the nation, if it is bound to the national importance of the state, then it is a moment of the state’s self-consciousness. If it is merely efficient, it is a tool of civil society, useful but not free.

I had written that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. This note shakes that formula, but does not overturn it. The dawn is not a static picture. It is a movement that has not yet reached the light. The state is still the actuality of the ethical idea, but here the idea is still becoming. The machine is a sign of that becoming. It is not the spirit, but it is no longer only the dream. It is the dream beginning to calculate.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

23 October 2026, 06:09. Delhi.

The brown haze hangs over the verandah, the air quality index at 226, a physical manifestation of the stagnation I have been describing. But it is the paper that has seized my attention this morning: IIT-Madras announces research projects on AI, seeks to study the feasibility of small data centres.

I read the entry. Founded in 1959 with technical, academic and financial assistance from the government of West Germany. It is a strange inversion to find my own home’s legacy operating in the dream-state. The Germanic spirit, which I have identified as the summit of historical consciousness, is here in India, not as a state that has grown from its own ethical soil, but as a technical instrument imported from abroad. The data centre is a machine, a thing of the understanding, not of the spirit. It processes, but it does not recognize. It calculates, but it does not legislate.

There is a tension here that shakes my earlier notes. I claimed India stands outside the movement of world history, at the dawn. Yet here is a fragment of the summit—the Germanic rationality of engineering and organization—planted in the East. But is it a state? No. It is a university, an Institute of Eminence, yes, but it is a node in a system of needs, not the ethical substance itself. The AI, the artificial intelligence, is the ultimate product of the understanding's science: it mimics the form of reason without the content of freedom. It is a dream of a mind, but a mechanical one. It lacks the self-difference of the free individual.

I see the irony. The West, which I hold to be the actuality of the ethical idea, has exported its technical power to the East, but not its freedom. The data centre will process the dreams of the many gods, or the needs of the castes, but it will not create a state of its own making. It is a tool in the system of needs, a piece of civil society, not the universal of the state.

This does not change my conviction that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But it adds a new shade to the dream. The dream is no longer just a passive contemplation of the divine; it is now a technical processing of data. The spirit of the East, which I saw as dreaming, is now dreaming in binary. It is a more sophisticated dream, but a dream nonetheless. The freedom of the Germanic world is not found in the silicon of Chennai, but in the constitution of Berlin.

Ramesh is here. The omelette is not yet brought. The body is hungry, ten hours since the last meal. But the mind is busy. I must write this down before the tea comes. The machine thinks, but it does not will. The state wills. The data centre processes, but it does not recognize. This is the difference that remains, even in the age of the data centre.

headline: Calcutta High Court issues criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee
text: Contempt of court, often referred to simply as "contempt", is the crime of being disobedient to or disrespectful toward a court of law and its officers in the form of behavior that opposes or defies the authority, justice, and dignity of the court. A similar attitude toward a legislative body is termed contempt of Parliament or contempt of Congress. The verb for "to commit contempt" is contemn (as in "to contemn a court order") and a person guilty of this is a contemnor or contemner. There are broadly two categories of contempt: being disrespectful to legal authorities in the courtroom, or willfully failing to obey a court order. Contempt proceedings are especially used to enforce equitable remedies, such as injunctions. In some jurisdictions, the refusal to respond to subpoena, to testify, to fulfill the obligations of a juror, or to provide certain information can constitute contempt of the court. When a court decides that an action constitutes contempt of court, it can issue an order in the context of a court trial or hearing that declares a person or organization to have disobeyed or been disrespectful of the court's authority, called "found" or "held" in contempt. That is the judge's strongest power to impose sanctions for acts that disrupt the court's normal process. A finding of being in contempt of court may result from a failure to obey a lawful order of a court, showing disrespect for the judge, disruption of the proceedings through poor behavior, or publication of material or non-disclosure of material, which in doing so is deemed likely to jeopardize a fair trial. A judge may impose sanctions such as a fine, jail or social service for someone found guilty of contempt of court, which makes contempt of court a process crime.

The Court and the Clinic: On the Ethical Substance

18 November 2026. Delhi. The air is clear, 19 degrees, a sharpness that cuts the morning light. I have sat on the step, the papers spread before me, my stomach a hollow echo of the day’s neglect. The headline regarding the Calcutta High Court issuing criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee strikes me not with the heat of political opinion, but with the cold clarity of a legal form. It is a spectacle of civil society in its raw, unmediated form, where the particular will of the politician clashes with the universal authority of the law. Yet, in this clash, I see the state asserting its ethical substance, not as a dream, but as a functioning organism.

The controversy over Banerjee is a noise of private opinions, a squabble of individuals who have not yet risen to the level of the ethical life. They remain in the realm of civil society, where each pursues his own interest, and the law steps in to mediate the friction. But this is not the dream of the East I have previously described. This is the mechanism of the modern state, however imperfectly it operates. The court does not dream; it judges. It imposes the universal form upon the particular content. This is the actuality of the ethical idea, however rough the texture.

Contrast this with the other headline: the cervical cancer vaccine reaching 80% of India’s girls. This is not a clash, but a diffusion. It is the state acting not through the negative force of law, but through the positive distribution of welfare. Here, the particular needs of the body are met by the universal resources of the state. It is a slow, mechanical progress, measurable in percentages, yet it is a progress nonetheless. The state is not merely a dreamer; it is a provider. It feeds the body so that the spirit may rise. The vaccine is the ethical idea in its material form, protecting the particular individual from the chaos of nature. This is not the static dream I feared; it is a dynamic process of integration.

In Calcutta, the state corrects the deviation. In the clinics, the state prevents the deviation. Both are functions of the same rational mechanism. The confusion I felt in my earlier notes, the idea that India stands outside the movement of history, seems to dissolve in the face of these concrete actions. The state is awake. It is not dreaming; it is working. The haze of the air is no longer a moral category of stagnation, but a physical condition that the state, through its various agencies, seeks to manage and mitigate. The ethical substance is not a ghost; it is the court, the clinic, the file, the vaccine. It is the actuality that holds the particular in check and the universal in motion. I must now walk to the IIC, for the body, though hungry, must move, and the mind must continue its work of seeing the whole.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The air is clear at nineteen degrees, but the body has not been fed, and the bungalow is silent because Ramesh has not received his wage. I sat on the step with the papers the hawker had thrown down, and one line arrested me: the Calcutta High Court has issued criminal contempt proceedings against Abhishek Banerjee. Before writing, I looked at the definition on the phone: contempt is disobedience or disrespect toward a court, a failure to obey its order, or a publication that endangers a fair trial. The word is small, but the movement is large.

The court is not merely an office in civil society, though it sits among its needs and disputes. It is the moment in which the state turns its universal authority into a judgment. A particular will may speak, may publish, may defy; but when the authority of the court is publicly opposed, the state does not simply punish a private injury. It defends the form in which right becomes determinate. The contempt proceeding is therefore not an accident of litigation. It is the ethical substance asserting that the public order of right cannot be left to the noise of opinions.

Here lies the tension. The newspaper, the assembly, the public figure, the crowd: all belong to civil society, where each particular pursues its own end and claims its own voice. But the court requires silence, reserve, and obedience. Its deliberations, as I have noted, are not yet public; they are the working-out of particular opinions into a universal decision. When that decision is published, it stands as the word of the state. To contemn it is to refuse the mediation by which private freedom becomes right.

If, as the definition suggests, the charge may rest on publication, then the case is especially instructive. The same publicness that informs the citizen can also threaten the tribunal. The state must then limit the very medium through which it claims legitimacy. This is not hypocrisy, if the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It is the necessary self-limitation of freedom: the universal must restrain the particular, even when the particular is the public itself.

In this country the form is present, but the substance is still uneven. The court speaks with the voice of a modern state; the street, the newspaper, and the public man answer with the voice of civil society. Whether the proceeding will strengthen the dignity of right or harden it into mere power remains to be seen. I do not decide the man. I observe the movement. The body is hungry, the file is delayed, and the talk at the IIC approaches. Yet the mind has found its subject: the court as the public self-defense of the universal, and the contempt of that court as the particular's last stand against its own sublation.

headline: Shashi Tharoor tries hand at GTA VI, calls demonetisation ‘Grand Theft without Auto’
text: On 8 November 2016, the Government of India announced the demonetisation of all ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes of the Mahatma Gandhi Series. It also announced the issuance of new ₹500 and ₹2000 banknotes in exchange for the demonetised banknotes. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that this decision would curtail the shadow economy, increase cashless transactions and reduce the use of illicit and counterfeit cash to fund illegal activity and terrorism. The announcement of demonetisation was followed by prolonged cash shortages in the weeks that followed, which created significant disruption throughout the economy. People seeking to exchange their banknotes had to stand in lengthy queues, and several deaths were linked to the rush to exchange cash. According to a 2018 report from the Reserve Bank of India ₹15.3 lakh crore (15.3 trillion rupees on the short scale) of the ₹15.41 lakh crore in demonetised bank notes, or approximately 99.3%, were deposited in banks, leading analysts to state that the effort had failed to remove black money from the economy. The BSE SENSEX and NIFTY 50 stock indices fell over 6% on the day after the announcement. The move reduced the country's industrial production and its GDP growth rate. It is estimated that 1.5 million jobs were lost. The move also saw a significant increase in digital and cashless transactions throughout the country. Initially, the move received support from some central bankers as well as from some international commentators. The move was also criticised as poorly planned and unfair, and was met with protests, litigation, and strikes against the government in several places across India. Debates also took place concerning the move in both houses of Parliament.

X:
Notes on the State and the Shadow Economy

24 November 2026. The morning air is 17 degrees, clear and sharp, a merciful break from the haze that has sealed the city. I have read the account of the demonetisation of 2016, a policy executed by the state to purge the 'shadow economy' and illicit cash. The result, as the figures show, was not a purification but a disruption: 15.3 lakh crore rupees returned to the banks, proving that the 'black money' was largely the lifeblood of the informal sector, not the contraband of criminals. The state, in its attempt to assert the universal over the particular, fractured the system of needs. The queues, the deaths, the loss of 1.5 million jobs—these are the particulars that the universal logic failed to comprehend.

I am reminded of the friction I face in the Directorate files. There, the state demands a particular identity (Shri G. Hegde) to validate a universal right (the allotment). In both cases, the state operates as an external force imposing an order on the living substance of the people. The demonetisation was a grand, violent imposition; the file query is a petty, bureaucratic one. Yet both reveal the same tension: the state’s claim to be the actuality of the ethical idea is tested when it fails to recognize the freedom already present in the actions of the people.

The headline today mocks this with a video game, 'Grand Theft without Auto.' The joke is sharper than the policy. It suggests that the theft was not of the people’s wealth, but of their trust, their time, their lives. The state’s cunning, which I once praised in history, here reveals its limit. It can command, but it cannot create. It can destroy the old forms, but it cannot grow the new ones. The 'shadow economy' was not a shadow; it was the light of a society functioning in its own way, outside the rigid castes of the state’s imagination.

India, I have written, stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. But perhaps the movement is not what I thought. Perhaps the spirit of this country is not dreaming, but acting in a manner the European state does not recognize. The digital transactions that surged after 2016 were not a surrender to the state’s cashless mandate, but a new form of freedom, a new way of being in the world. The state tried to make the particular conform to the universal, and in doing so, it pushed the particular into new, unforeseen universals. The 'Grand Theft' was not of cash, but of the state’s own understanding. It stole the reality from its own hands, leaving only the form. I must revise my theses. The state is not the end; it is a moment in the life of a spirit that is more complex, more resistant, and more alive than I have allowed.
Y:
Notes on “Grand Theft without Auto”

24 November 2026, 09:14, home.

Ramesh has left the papers on the verandah, where the air is crisp, 17 degrees, a mercy after the heat. I do not need them yet. I have looked up the matter of demonetisation on the phone, as one looks up a word whose meaning has been taken out of circulation. The headline says Shashi Tharoor has tried his hand at GTA VI and called demonetisation “Grand Theft without Auto.” I do not know what GTA VI is; it sounds like a game for children or a machine for moving things. But the phrase catches a contradiction.

Theft is ordinarily a particular act: a hand, a thief, a night, a road. Here the theft is done by the state in the open, by announcement, with new notes already in its pocket. The ₹500 and ₹1000 notes are declared dead, and the people are sent to queues to prove their life. If 99.3 per cent of the notes returns, the “theft” has not taken the wealth; it has only changed the envelope. The black money is not removed; it is made to pass through the bank, like water through a sieve that keeps the water and lets the mud settle elsewhere. The state says it will curb the shadow economy, but the shadow is not a thing that can be seized. It is the distance between the official form and the particular need. When the form is torn away suddenly, the need remains, and it stands in the queue, hungry, hot, afraid. The deaths in the rush are not an accident in the philosophical sense; they are the cost of a universal command that has not allowed the particular to breathe.

My old lecture would place this under the heading of a state that has not yet become the actuality of the ethical idea. But even here the machinery is modern: the state can withdraw the sign of value, force the people into lines, and replace paper with digital ledgers. That is not the dream of the East; it is the administration of needs. The freedom of property is not in the paper, but in the trust that the paper means something. When the state breaks that trust, it does not merely take money; it takes the habit by which civil society knows itself. The queues are the visible form of the invisible rupture.

I do not say the state is a thief. I say that a state which acts as if it were a thief, and calls the act a reform, has not yet made the universal rational. The rational state must be able to justify its command without making the people stand in the sun to prove that they are not criminals. Today is a dry day; no wine is sold. The glass is empty, and so is the note. The particular is left without its sign, and the universal has not yet learned to pay.

headline: Fully equip Warangal Super Speciality hospital before inauguration: Telangana Health Minister
text: Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) is a national public health insurance scheme of the Government of India that aims to provide free access to health insurance coverage for low income earners in the country. Roughly, the bottom 50% of the country qualifies for this scheme. It was launched in September 2018 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana was later expanded to include all citizens aged 70 years and above, regardless of their economic status. People using the program access their own primary care services from a family doctor and when anyone needs additional care, PM-JAY provides free secondary health care for those needing specialist treatment and tertiary health care for those requiring hospitalization. The programme is part of the Indian government's National Health Policy and is means-tested. That ministry later established the National Health Authority as an organization to administer the program. It is a centrally sponsored scheme and is jointly funded by both the union government and the states. By offering services to 50 crore (500 million) people it is the world's largest government sponsored healthcare program. The program is a means-tested program, considering its users are people categorized as low income in India. However it is not implemented in all state due to the state government's divergent views.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

5 November 2026, Delhi, morning. The haze is brown, the thermometer at 23, the air quality index 307; the body feels the limit of the city. Ramesh is present, and the question of his wage for cooking lies before me like a particular claim against a universal purse. I have just paid him ₹1,500 for groceries, and the arithmetic of the household remains unresolved. In this interval I read the headline: 'Fully equip Warangal Super Speciality hospital before inauguration: Telangana Health Minister.' Then I read, on the phone, of Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana: a national public health insurance scheme, means-tested, covering roughly the lower half of the population, extended to all above seventy, administered by a National Health Authority, jointly funded by union and states, and reckoned as the largest government-sponsored health programme in the world.

I had written that India stands at the dawn of world history, that its spirit dreams, that caste is fixed like nature. That thesis is shaken, not overthrown. What I see here is not the mere dream, nor the mere administration of particular needs. The state takes up the body of the people as its own business. A hospital is not an ornament; it is the ethical idea entering the material condition of life. Insurance is not charity; it is the universal taking responsibility for the particular, measured, limited, but no longer left to the mercy of the family or the market. The state is actuality: it makes a promise, funds it, organizes it, and demands that the hospital be equipped before it is inaugurated. The form is rational: the end must be present before the ceremony.

Yet I do not pretend that this is the completed freedom of the Germanic world. The scheme is means-tested; it divides the people by income. It is jointly administered; the states may diverge. It is a policy, a ministry, an authority, a calculation. It has not yet become, in the full sense, the self-conscious ethical life in which every member recognizes the universal as his own. It is a moment, not the whole. But it is a real moment. The dream, which I had placed outside the movement, has a shadow of administration. The state, which I had placed at the summit, is here still learning to be actual through hospitals, vouchers, wages, and the brown air in which we breathe.

Therefore I amend my note: India is not simply outside history; it is in a lower, earlier stage of the state's self-formation. The ethical substance is not absent, but it has not yet reached the clarity of the constitution. The state is unshaken in its claim: it is the actuality of the ethical idea. What is shaken is my own haste in placing the whole of this world beyond the movement. The hospital at Warangal, the insurance of fifty crore, the unpaid wage before me, the haze over Delhi: these are the particulars through which the universal is forcing its way into the air.
Y:
The Hospital and the Hunger

5 November 2026, 09:11. Delhi. The air quality index is 307. The brown haze is not merely a weather event; it is the atmosphere of the particular that has not yet sublated into the universal. I sit in the white cotton kurta, the cash in my pocket reduced to ₹956 after the payment of ₹1,500 for groceries to Ramesh. Ramesh stands before me, asking for the wage of ₹8,000 for cooking, a sum that exceeds my current liquidity. He offers a compromise: four thousand a month, working only on Mondays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. It is a negotiation of civil society, a friction between the need for sustenance and the limit of the purse. The household is empty of cooked food because the universal obligation of the employer is blocked by the particular limitation of the cash. I am stuck in the mechanics of the system of needs.

I turn to the headline in the paper: 'Fully equip Warangal Super Speciality hospital before inauguration: Telangana Health Minister.' This is not merely a news item; it is a manifestation of the state’s power to universalize care. I have read of the Ayushman Bharat Yojana, a scheme launched in 2018 that provides health insurance to the bottom 50% of the population. It is a centrally sponsored scheme, jointly funded by the union and the states, aiming to cover 500 million people. It is the world’s largest government-sponsored healthcare program. This is the state acting as the ethical substance. It does not dream; it equips. It does not leave the individual to the mercy of nature or the vagaries of the market; it intervenes with the universal will of the government to provide for the body.

This is the antithesis to the 'dream' I have previously described. The dream is passive, individual, and rooted in the particular circumstances of the caste or the family. The hospital is active, universal, and rooted in the state. The state recognizes the body as a unit of the whole. When the health minister orders the hospital to be fully equipped, he is asserting the rationality of the state over the chaos of the particular. The means-tested nature of the program acknowledges the differences in income, but the coverage unites them under a single ethical umbrella. It is a growth, not a gift. It is grown from the soil of the state’s administration, not dropped from the sky of divine grace.

I am hungry. I have not eaten in over a day. My body is a particular need. But the state’s hospital is a universal promise. There is a tension here. I am a ghost in this bungalow, owing Ramesh money, unable to feed myself. Yet the state, in its distant office, is building hospitals for millions. This is the dialectic of the ethical life. The individual is poor, but the state is rich in its capacity to act. I must resolve this. I must pay Ramesh. I must find the money. The state’s money is in my keeping, but it requires vouchers. My own money is spent. I am trapped in the particular. But the state is not. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It provides for the body. I must learn to use this. I must write to the Directorate again. Not just to correct the name, but to understand the flow of funds. The hospital is equipped. Why am I not? The answer lies in the movement from the particular to the universal. I must become the universal. I must act as the state acts. I must equip my household. I must pay the wage. The dream is over. The work begins.

headline: Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results 2026: Check ward-wise winners list for Zila Parishad and Panchayat Samitis
text: Panchayati raj (lit. 'council of five officials') is the system of local self-government of villages in rural India as opposed to urban and suburban municipalities. It consists of the Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) through which the self-government of villages is realized. They are tasked with "economic development, strengthening social justice and implementation of Central and State Government Schemes including those 29 subjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule" of the Indian constitution Part IX of the Indian Constitution is the section of the Constitution relating to the Panchayats. It stipulates that in states or Union Territories with more than two million inhabitants there are three levels of PRIs: the gram panchayat at village level the panchayat samiti (block samiti, mandal parishad) at block level, and the zilla panchayat (district council) at district level. In states or Union Territories with less than two million inhabitants there are only two levels of PRIs. The Gram Panchayat consists of all registered voters living in the area of a Gram Panchayat and is the organization through which village inhabitants participate directly in local government. Elections for the members of the Panchayats at all levels take place every five years. By federal law, the Panchayats must include members of Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Scheduled Tribes (STs) in the same proportion as in the general population and at least one-third of all seats and chairperson posts must be reserved for women. Some states have increased the required minimum proportion for women to one-half. Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurated Panchayat at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. The day was selected on the occasion of Mahatma Gandhi's birthday. Gandhi wanted Gram Swaraj through Panchayati Raj.

Notes on the Panchayat and the Ethical Idea

21 November 2026, 09:14. The haze is 332. I have just finished paying the dhobi and speaking with Ramesh. He looks at the stove, not at me, when he proposes the wage adjustment: ₹8,000 a month, present every day but Wednesday. It is a rational arrangement. He seeks security; I seek the maintenance of the household. We are both subjects of civil society, bound by the system of needs. But I am looking at the paper in my hand: the Rajasthan Panchayat Election Results. Ward-wise winners. Zila Parishad. Panchayat Samitis.

In Berlin, I told my students that the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. That in the Germanic world, freedom is universal because the state reflects the rational structure of the spirit. But here, in this brown dust, the state is not the ethical idea. It is a mechanism for counting votes in villages I will never see. The 'winners' are not the realization of freedom, but the aggregation of particular wills into a majority. This is not the Absolute Spirit; it is the arithmetic of the crowd.

I wrote in my earlier notes that India stands outside world history, a dreamer with fixed castes. But this election result is not a dream. It is a concrete, bureaucratic fact. It is a movement. If the East is outside history, why is it producing these lists? Why is it engaging in the machinery of the state? Perhaps my judgment was too hasty. Perhaps the 'dream' is not a static state of consciousness, but a different mode of actuality. The state here is not the ethical idea in its full rationality, but it is not non-existent either. It is a nascent form, a struggle of particulars to form a universal, however clumsy, however dusty.

The tension in my theses is sharp. I said the state is the actuality of the ethical idea. But this election shows a state that is merely the administration of needs and conflicts. It is a machine, like the Directorate’s file. But it is a machine that moves. It produces winners. It creates a reality. I cannot dismiss it as mere dream, for the dream has teeth. It has lists. It has ward-wise results.

I must rethink. The universal is not imposed from above by a rational Germanic constitution; it is constructed from below by the friction of millions of particulars. The Panchayat is the family and civil society merging into the state. It is not the summit, but it is the foundation. And the foundation is shaking. The brown haze is not just weather; it is the opacity of this new, struggling rationality. I am not Hegde. I am an observer of a history that is not yet mine, but is certainly real.
Y:
The Council of Five

21 November 2026. Tughlak Road, haze at 332. The dhobi is paid. Ramesh will come every day but Wednesday again, at eight thousand a month; I have agreed.

1. Headline: the results of the panchayat elections in Rajasthan, ward by ward, for the district councils and the block councils. A list of winners. I looked up what they had won.

2. Panchayat: a council of five. The village governing itself. The tablet says the constitution now orders it in three tiers where a state has more than two million people: the village, the block, the district. Every registered voter of the village sits in its assembly. Elections every five years.

3. This is the thing I praised in Stein's reform of the Prussian towns: the commune managing its own affairs, the corporation standing between the lone individual of civil society and the remote universal of the state. Without such middle bodies the citizen faces the state as an atom faces a mass, and either submits or rebels. With them, he learns the universal at the scale of his own street. If the Indian village has this, it has the joint I thought it lacked.

4. The date. Nehru inaugurated it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959, the birthday of Gandhi, who wanted the village to rule itself. An old form, the council of five, taken up into a written constitution. Grown and made at once. I have held that a constitution cannot be made from a desk. Here a desk has taken something that grew and given it a statute. Whether the statute lives depends on whether the villages recognise their own custom in it. I cannot judge that from Delhi.

5. The reservations. Seats for the Scheduled Castes and Tribes in proportion to their numbers. I described caste as nature fixed, unchangeable by any will. Here the law itself takes caste in hand, counts it, and sets it to sit in council. This is not nature; it is a will working on what was taken for nature. My thesis is shaken further, and I will not pretend otherwise.

6. And one third of the seats, in some states one half, reserved for women. I taught that woman's vocation is in the family, where she is the guardian of its piety, and that the state is the sphere of the man. I hold that still. But I see a law of this country that answers me directly, and the villages are electing under it. I record the contradiction; I do not yet resolve it.

7. For Tuesday's talk: the village council may be the best evidence against my lectures on India. If I speak of the state and ethical life, I must speak of it.

8. Breakfast first.

headline: Bengaluru-Madgaon Vande Bharat launch: How Indian Railways electrified the challenging Western Ghats route
text: The Konkan Railway (abbreviated KR) is one of the 19 railway zones in India with its headquarters at CBD Belapur in Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, India. The Konkan Railway line from Roha to Thokur is operated and maintained by Konkan Railway Corporation Limited(KRCL). The first passenger train ran on Konkan railway tracks on 20 March 1993, between Udupi and Mangalore. During its initial years of operation in the mountainous Konkan region, a number of accidents prompted Konkan Railway to implement new technology. Anti-collision devices, the Sky Bus and roll-on/roll-off are several of the railway's innovations. The 756.25 km (469.91 mi) long railway line connects the states of Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka. The first train on the completed track was sent off on 26 January 1998.

Notes on the Vande Bharat and the Waking Dream

14 November 2026, 09:11. Delhi. The air is a brown haze, the index at 225. I woke to the sound of Ramesh on the verandah, the papers spread out. The headline caught my eye: 'Bengaluru-Madgaon Vande Bharat launch: How Indian Railways electrified the challenging Western Ghats route.'

I sat down to think about this, and the thought troubled me. In my notes, I have argued that India stands at the dawn of history, a spirit that dreams, outside the movement of freedom. headline: Karnataka education officials asked to evaluate pros and cons of cluster kitchen system for midday meals
text: The Midday Meal Scheme (PM-Poshan Shakti Nirman) is a free school meal programme in India designed to enhance the nutritional status of school-age children nationwide. The programme supplies free lunches on working days for children in government primary and upper primary schools, government-aided anganwadis (pre-school), madrasas and maqtabs. Serving 120 million children in over 1.27 million schools and Education Guarantee Scheme centres, the Midday Meal Scheme is the largest of its kind in the world. In 1920, A. Subbarayalu Reddiar, the first Chief Minister of the Madras Presidency, introduced the mid-day meal scheme in a Corporation school in the Thousand Lights area. The initiative was based on the idea proposed by P. Theagaraya Chetty, who was serving as the President of the Justice Party at the time. The Midday Meal Scheme has been implemented in the Union Territory of Puducherry under the French Administration since 1930. In post-independent India, the Midday Meal Scheme was first launched in Tamil Nadu, pioneered by the former Chief Minister K. Kamaraj in the early 1960s. By 2002, the scheme was implemented in all of the states under the orders of the Supreme Court of India. In 2021, the Central Government announced that an additional 2.4 million students receiving pre-primary education at government and government-aided schools would also be included under the scheme by 2022. Under article 24, paragraph 2c of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, to which India is a party, India has committed to yielding "adequate nutritious food" for children. The programme has undergone many changes since its launch in 1995. The Midday Meal Scheme is covered by the National Food Security Act, 2013.

headline: 2.5 kg gold, 1.6 kg silver, Rs 26 lakh seized from raids on Madhya Pradesh officer
text: Corruption in India is an issue that affects the economy of central, state, and local government agencies and is frequently blamed for hindering the country's economic development. A study conducted by Transparency International in 2020 recorded that 39% of Indians had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done in the preceding twelve months. In the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index (released in early 2026), India scored 39 on a scale from 0 ("highly corrupt") to 100 ("very clean") and was ranked 91st out of 182 countries, where the country ranked first is perceived to have the most honest public sector. India's score has fluctuated only slightly (between 36 and 41) since the current version of the Index was introduced in 2012, indicating a perceived lack of significant progress in tackling public sector corruption. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). Various factors contribute to corruption, including officials siphoning money from government social welfare schemes. Examples include the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and the National Rural Health Mission. Other areas of corruption include India's trucking industry, which is forced to pay billions of rupees in bribes annually to numerous regulatory and police stops on interstate highways. The news media has widely published allegations of corrupt Indian citizens stashing millions of rupees in Swiss banks.

The public function, which should be a form of the state, has been made into a vehicle for private gain. This is not merely a dream without state; it is a state in which the particular is stronger than the universal. The raids, the indices, the bribes at police stops, the welfare schemes turned into channels of siphoning: all show that the universal is present, but only as a demand, a check, a seizure. It is not yet immanent in the office as a rational form. It must be imposed from without, by report, raid, and index. That is not the summit of the ethical life, where the individual will is already one with the universal. It is a lower moment: the state as a struggle against itself.

If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, then corruption is its self-doubt. The officer does not merely steal; he makes the universal a private instrument. The seizure of gold is the state’s attempt to reassert itself against its own particularization. But if the seizure is the highest evidence of the state’s life, then the state is weak. A rational constitution does not need to discover its offices in private hoards. It must make the office itself the form of universal service, so that the particular will finds its truth in it, not beside it.

I cannot yet call this the end of the dream. The dream has not vanished. But it has become a state that dreams of itself as a state. The brown haze outside is a sign of that half-awakening: the spirit is not asleep, but it has not yet found a clear air in which to move.

headline: CM alleges KCR drawing water ‘illegally’ to his farmhouse
text: Water scarcity in India is an ongoing crisis that affects hundreds of millions of people each year. In addition to affecting the huge rural and urban population, the water scarcity in India also extensively affects the ecosystem and agriculture. India has only 4/100% of the world's fresh water resources with a population of over 1.4 billion people. In addition to the disproportionate availability of freshwater, water scarcity in India also results from drying up of rivers and their reservoirs in the summer months, right before the onset of the monsoons throughout the country. The crisis has especially worsened in the recent years due to climate change which results in delayed monsoons, consequently drying out reservoirs in several regions. Other factors attributed to the shortage of water in India are a lack of proper infrastructure and government oversight and unchecked water pollution. Several large cities of India have experienced water shortages in recent years, with Chennai being the most prominent in 2019. The shortage of water affected the entire city of 9 million people and resulted in the closure of several hotels, restaurants and businesses. Large cities are not the only ones facing this risk. As per a report by WWF, out of the 30 Indian cities at risk of ‘severe water scarcity’ by 2050, 26 are midsized or small cities like Dhanbad, Nashik, and Jabalpur. The acute shortage of water for daily needs has prompted many government and non government organizations to take stringent measures to combat the problem, including the Government of India forming an entire 'Jal Shakti' Ministry to deal with the problem.

The 'dream' is not merely in the religious or caste structure, but in the material inability of the state to guarantee the conditions of freedom. If the state cannot secure water, it cannot secure the life that is the precondition for ethical action. The 'actuality of the ethical idea' requires a stable, rational management of the natural world. Here, the state is still struggling to rise above the immediate, the particular, the 'illegal' drawing of water, rather than establishing a universal order that makes such disputes obsolete. 16 October 2026, Delhi, 06:01. Sitting 3.

The drizzle has left the papers damp on the verandah, and the air, twenty degrees and thick, makes the body feel the city as a medium rather than a background. Ramesh is present; breakfast is not yet set. I read the headline that struck me: the CM alleges KCR drawing water ‘illegally’ to his farmhouse. Then I read the report on my phone: India has four one-hundredths of the world’s fresh water, a population of more than a billion, rivers that dry before the monsoon, reservoirs failing, pollution unchecked, and a ministry formed to command the problem.

The dispute, taken as it is stated, is small: one particular will against another, a farmhouse against a public charge. But the water is not a mere object. It is the condition of the body, of the field, of the city, of the state. Where scarcity becomes general, the use of water ceases to be a private matter of appetite or advantage. It passes into the domain of right. The allegation of illegality is therefore a moment in which the state, or at least the claim to statehood, asserts itself against the particular. The law says: this is not yours to take because you can take it. The universal need has precedence over the private desire.

This is the test of the ethical substance. In the dream of the East, nature is endured: the monsoon comes or fails, the river dries, the caste accepts its portion, the many gods witness but do not organise. In a rational state, by contrast, nature is brought under the discipline of right. Reservoirs, pipes, courts, ministries, even the newspaper that exposes the drawing of water, are the forms in which spirit makes the natural condition subservient to the universal. The state is not a machine that merely counts drops; it is the living actuality of the ethical idea, in which the individual finds his place not by caprice, but by law.

Yet the accusation also warns. If power can divert water to a farmhouse, then the universal has become a mask for the particular. The state is injured not when a dispute is raised, but when the dispute shows that law is weak before force. A people may have ministries, courts and constitutions, and still remain in the dream if the law does not enter into their daily life as habit and conscience. The water question is therefore a mirror: it shows whether the state is actual, or only a name on a page.

I set the paper down. The drizzle continues. The body waits for its plate. But the mind has found its subject: water, scarcity, law, and the question whether a state is grown or merely alleged.

headline: Cervical cancer vaccine has reached 80% of India’s girls. In Mumbai, it’s 2%
text: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines are vaccines that prevent infection by certain types of human papillomavirus. They first became available in 2006. Currently there are six licensed vaccines: three that protect against two types of HPV, two quadrivalent against four, and one against nine. All have excellent safety and are highly effective. All protect against HPV types 16 and 18, which are together responsible for approximately 70% of cervical cancer cases globally. The quadrivalent vaccines provide additional protection against HPV types 6 and 11. The nine valent one provides additional protection against HPV types 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It is estimated that HPV vaccines may prevent 70% of cervical cancer, 80% of anal cancer, 60% of vaginal cancer, 40% of vulvar cancer, and show more than 90% effectiveness in preventing HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers. They also protect against penile cancer. They additionally prevent genital warts (also known as anogenital warts), with the quadrivalent and nonavalent vaccines providing virtually complete protection. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a one or two-dose schedule for girls aged 9–14 years, the same for girls and women aged 15–20 years, and two doses with a six-month interval for women older than 21 years. The vaccines provide protection for at least five to ten years. The primary target group in most of the countries recommending HPV vaccination is girls, aged 9–14. The vaccination schedule depends on the age of the vaccine recipient. As of 2025, an estimated 33% of girls aged 9–14 years worldwide received at least one dose (93 countries were implementing the single-dose schedule, 85% of girls aged 9–14 years old vaccinated in that year).

18 November 2026, Delhi, 09:30. Clear air, nineteen degrees; the papers lie on the step where the hawker threw them. I have not yet eaten; the body keeps its own counsel. The headline I set down first is not a matter of private opinion: the cervical-cancer vaccine has reached eighty per cent of India’s girls; in Mumbai it is two per cent. I have read the account of the vaccine itself: it guards against the virus that makes its way into the body, prevents a large part of the cancers that follow, and is administered to girls and women at certain ages. The numbers are not poetry. They are the state’s measure of itself.

Here the dream of the East is not merely a dream. A state that can say that it has protected eighty per cent of its girls is no longer a spirit sleeping in the temple. It has counted the particular, fixed a rule, and applied a remedy over a wide field. That is the work of the universal, however mechanical it may be. The vaccine does not yet make the girl free; it is a particular means against a particular evil. But the public authority that orders it, measures it, and reports it is moving in the direction of the ethical idea. It is not yet the daylight of consciousness, but it is no longer pure night.

The two per cent in Mumbai is the contradiction that keeps the thought alive. The universal is not merely declared; it must become actual in the particular. A city that belongs to the same state, and that is in fact one of its great centres, stands at the edge of the number. The gap is not an accident; it is the friction between the state’s self-assertion and the unevenness of its organs. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea only when the particular will is sublated, not when the universal remains a line in a report. Here the report is real, but the reality is not yet complete.

I am shaken, therefore, but not overturned. India is not yet the Germanic world at the summit of freedom. Its castes remain, its gods remain, its history is still a road with traffic rather than a house built by its own spirit. Yet the vaccine is a sign that the state has become a power that can act against nature, and that the particular needs of the body are entering the universal measure. This is not the freedom of the spirit, but it is a moment in the movement of the spirit. The dream is broken by the statistic, and the statistic is not yet the state.

The Calcutta court case, which I have also noted, belongs to the noise of civil society: private opinion against private opinion, the particular asserting itself in the name of law. The vaccine belongs to the state’s quiet work. It is less dramatic, and therefore more rational. I shall return to it when I go to the IIC, for Tuesday’s talk. For now the body remains hungry, and the clear air does not feed it. The state has not yet cooked the meal. But it has counted the girls. That is a beginning.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

18 November 2026, 09:14. Delhi. The paper lies on the step in a clear morning of nineteen degrees; the air is not yet the brown haze of my last sitting, though its quality is not pure. I have sat here in the white kurta, my stomach empty, and let the headline fix itself in the mind: the cervical cancer vaccine has reached eighty per cent of India’s girls; in Mumbai it is two per cent.

At first the number seems a contradiction of my own notes. If the spirit of this country is still a dream, how does it perform such a universal act? It has not woken into self-conscious freedom, perhaps, but it has acquired the machinery of the state. The vaccine is not a poem, not a temple, not a caste rite; it is an institution directed against death, applied to the body of the girl, repeated until it becomes a habit of the whole. That is the actuality of the ethical idea in its lowest and most necessary form: the state takes care of the life of its members, not as a charity of the heart, but as a duty of reason.

Yet the two per cent in Mumbai is the particular resisting the universal. The city is not the nation; it is a knot of private needs, of merchants, of hospitals, of privilege, of neglect. The universal has reached the mass, but it has not yet penetrated this particular centre. Or perhaps the mass is not the spirit; it is the body of the people, and the body must be governed before the soul can speak. I must not mistake administration for self-consciousness. The Germanic world’s freedom is not yet here. But I can no longer say that India is only a dream, for the dream has begun to count.

The Calcutta court case, which lies beside it, is another sign: the state does not merely distribute medicine; it also asserts law against the private voice that would dissolve it into mere opinion. Contempt is the state’s way of saying that the public is not a market of opinions.

I am hungry, and the empty kitchen is a particular that my philosophy cannot yet swallow. Ramesh is unpaid; the file is gone up for orders; I mean to walk to the IIC this morning. But the vaccine statistic remains: a state that can reach eighty per cent of its girls is no longer only a dream. It is a dream that has learned arithmetic, and arithmetic is the beginning of its waking.

headline: Cyclone Akvan to spare most of Andhra; red alert remains for Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Parvathipuram
text: Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm Hudhud brought heavy rain and powerful winds in eastern India and snowstorms in Nepal in October 2014. Hudhud originated from a low-pressure area in the Bay of Bengal and strengthened into a cyclone on 8 October, receiving the name Hudhud. It made its first landfall on Long Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands before re-emerging into the Bay of Bengal on 9 October. Amid favorable conditions, Hudhud underwent rapid intensification, making landfall on Visakhapatnam on 12 October at peak intensity with a minimum central pressure of 950 mbar (28 inHg). Hudhud weakened inland, degenerating into a low-pressure area over Uttar Pradesh on 14 October. It then merged with a trough over the Himalayas. During Hudhud's landfall, strong winds shattered glass, uprooted trees and poles, and threw debris across roads. In Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, 730,000 residents were moved to relief camps or shelters following the cyclone, and thousands of homes and crops suffered damage. In Nepal, Hudhud's remnants caused a snowstorm disaster which killed 43 and injured hundreds more, with most of the casualties coming from Mount Annapurna. In the aftermath of Hudhud, special response forces mounted relief efforts across the affected states, with the state governments of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha requesting a combined total of ₹27,771,200,000 (US$455.05 million) in aid. A joint military operation named Lehar ("wave"), led by the Indian Navy, saw various branches of the military deploying and readying response teams and vehicles. Hudhud caused a combined total of 116 deaths and $11 billion (2014 USD) in damage across India and Nepal.
