X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

24 October 2026. Delhi, 06:12. The bungalow is still quiet. Ramesh is at hand; the dhobi has been paid three hundred rupees; the papers lie on the verandah, and the air outside is a brown haze, the index high enough to remind me that even the state’s cleanest ideas must pass through a dirty atmosphere.

The headline is: “In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.” I looked the matter up on the phone, that strange instrument which I do not yet understand but which has become my newspaper, my map, and my second memory. I read: Naxalite–Maoist insurgency; a conflict between the Government of India and communist groups; a people’s war; the Red Corridor, which at its peak covered nearly 180 districts and has shrunk to three; thousands killed; more than ten thousand surrendered between 2015 and 2025. I do not pretend to know Chhattisgarh by its fields and roads. I know it only as a name in a state’s business, and as a place where the state has had to prove itself against an armed opposition.

The word “post-Naxal” is a political word. It says that a stage has passed. But a stage is not passed merely because the enemy is weaker, the corridors are narrower, or the surrenders are counted. What must be asked is whether the state has not only defeated a rebellion but has become the actuality of the ethical idea in the lives of those who lived in the Red Corridor. The state is not a picture. The President may paint one, as the paper says; but painting is representation, and representation belongs to art, not to Sittlichkeit. The question is whether the particular needs of the rural poor—land, labour, protection, law, education, a place in the universal order—have been taken up by institutions, or whether they have merely been driven underground by police and development plans.

The Naxalite movement, as I read it, is a negative moment. It claims to fight for the rural poor and to wage a people’s war against the government. That claim is not nothing. Even where it is mistaken, it shows that a part of the population has not found its particular will at home in the universal. The state, if it is rational, cannot simply treat this as disorder. It must overcome it: preserve what is true in the demand for justice, transform the violent form into legal and institutional form, and make the universal will effective in the lives of those who had refused it. A state that only suppresses is a power. A state that integrates is an ethical substance.

I have written here that India stands at the dawn of history, outside its movement. I do not retract that. But this headline shakes the edge of the sentence. It shows a state acting with force, calculation, and administrative reach. That is not the dream of the East; it is the activity of a state. Yet activity is not yet self-conscious freedom. The Germanic world is at the summit because its constitution makes freedom the end and the beginning, the individual and the universal one. In India, even a strong state may still be a state in the sense of power, law, and necessity, without having fully become the self-development of the spirit. The Naxal conflict is a test: if the state remains only a sword and a budget, it has not yet grown into the ethical life it claims. If it turns the defeated rebellion into rights, work, courts, and public life, then the dawn has moved. Until then, the “post-Naxal” picture is a map, not a truth.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

24 October 2026. Delhi, 06:12.

The haze is brown, the air quality index 236. The body is heavy with the residue of the previous night, but the mind is sharpened by the headlines on the verandah. I have just paid the dhobi ₹300. It is a small transaction, a mechanical act of civil society, yet it grounds the day in the immediate reality of needs and duties. Ramesh is here, waiting. The heat is not yet oppressive, but the stillness is thick.

I have been looking at the notice: “In Chhattisgarh, President paints picture of a post-Naxal state.”

The term “Naxal” is new to me, a word I do not find in my Berlin lectures or my Stuttgart years. It is a name for a specific form of unrest, a rebellion against the state. The headline speaks of a “post-Naxal” state, a state that has supposedly overcome this internal contradiction. This is the very movement I have been tracing in my notes: the struggle of the state to assert its universality against the particular wills that seek to destroy it.

In the Germanic world, the state is not merely a mechanism of police and law, but the ethical substance itself. It is the “actuality of the ethical idea.” When a state faces a challenge like the Naxalite movement, it is not merely suppressing a riot; it is defending the rational order against the chaos of unmediated particularity. The President’s “painting” of this post-conflict reality is an act of consciousness. The state is becoming aware of itself as the guarantor of order. It is no longer just a power that rules, but a spirit that knows it is the ground of its own existence.

This contrasts sharply with the “dream” of the East, which I have been observing in the tombs of Lodhi Gardens and the fixed castes of the society around me. In the Oriental world, there is no such dialectical movement of state and opposition. The individual is absorbed in nature, in caste, in the divine. There is no “post-Naxal” state because there is no Naxal movement in the same sense. The conflict is not between the universal and the particular, but between the individual and the natural order. The state, where it exists, is often a foreign imposition, a conqueror’s dome, not a self-made ethical life.

Yet, here in Chhattisgarh, we see a different dynamic. The state is engaged in a struggle for its own self-recognition. It is moving from a mere police power to an ethical substance. This is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. The “post-Naxal” state is not a static condition, but a moment in the dialectic where the state has confronted the negation of itself and emerged stronger. It is a step forward on the road to the summit of world history.

I must be careful, however. The headline is a report, a snapshot. I do not know the details of the President’s speech. I do not know the specific nature of the Naxalite threat. I am speculating based on the form of the event. The state’s response to internal rebellion is a key indicator of its ethical maturity. If the state crushes the rebellion through pure force, it remains a despotic power. If it integrates the rebels, or if it resolves the conflict through the recognition of rights and duties, it moves toward the rational state.

The “post-Naxal” label suggests a resolution. It suggests that the state has not only defeated the rebels but has also transformed its own consciousness. It is now a state that knows itself as the source of order. This is a significant development. It is a sign that the spirit of freedom is at work, even in a region that I have previously categorized as part of the Oriental dawn. The movement is not confined to the Germanic world; it is a universal process, though it manifests differently in different contexts.

I will return to this. The dhobi is paid, the papers are read. The day is young. The mind is clear.

headline: Beer on new high: Sales see over 40% increase in first six months of financial year
text: Indian cuisine is not a single homogeneous entity, but consists of the regional cuisines native to the Indian subcontinent. Indian food has been influenced by religion, cultural choices and traditions. Agriculture spread to the Indus Valley Civilisation around 7000 BCE, bringing cereal cultivation. Spices such as turmeric and cardamom were being grown in India by 3,000 BCE. Indian cooking uses simple equipment such as a burner, and labour-intensive processes such as grinding flavourings by hand. Techniques unique to the area include frying of a paste of onion, garlic, and ginger in oil, then browning the meat or vegetables in that oil, and then adding liquid stepwise; and adding fried spices to cooked dishes. Many dishes are specific to India's many religious festivals. Religious faiths influence the region's cuisines, since Hindus often do not eat beef; Muslims avoid pork; and Jains are strict lacto-vegetarians.

X:
The Fermentation of the Particular

17 October 2026, 06:02. Delhi. The air is a brown haze, 21 degrees, the index a choking 262. I wake to the smell of dust and the sound of Ramesh settling the dhobi’s account. The papers on the verandah carry a headline that strikes me with a peculiar, almost grotesque irony: “Beer on new high: Sales see over 40% increase in first six months of financial year.”

I sit with this figure. Forty percent. It is not merely a rise in consumption; it is a swelling of the particular will at the expense of the universal. In the ethical life of the state, the individual finds his freedom in his participation in the whole, in his duty to the common good. But here, in the foggy dawn of this city, the spirit seems to be contracting into the immediate, the sensory, the particular. The increase in beer sales is a symptom of a mind that has not yet achieved the self-difference necessary to recognize the other as a free being, and thus to constitute itself as a free being. It is a retreat into the dream.

I think of the tombs in Lodhi Gardens, the domes of the Sayyids and the Lodis. They are the work of conquerors, not of a spirit that has achieved self-consciousness. The Hindu burns his dead and leaves no house. There is no state here that has made itself. There is only nature, history as traffic, the dream of a spirit that has not yet woken up to its own freedom. The beer is part of this dream. It is a liquid that dissolves the boundaries of the self, that blurs the line between the particular and the universal. It is a return to the undifferentiated, natural state of the mind.

And yet, I must be careful. I am not to judge this increase from the summit of the Germanic world. I am here to observe, to record, to understand. I am a ghost in this bungalow, a mistake in the allotment of the Directorate. I am Hegel, not Hegde. I am a spirit in a body that does not belong to me, in a land that does not recognize me. Yet, in this very alienation, I find a clarity of vision. I am outside the movement, looking in. I see the dream for what it is, and the state for what it is. The dream is beautiful, but it is not free. The state is rational, and therefore free.

The beer is a sign of the times. It is a sign of a spirit that is dreaming. It is a sign of a mind that has not yet achieved the self-difference necessary to recognize the other as a free being, and thus to constitute itself as a free being. It is a sign of a world that is still at the dawn of its history, outside its movement. It is a sign of a dream that is not yet free. But it is also a sign of a possibility. For the dream is not the end. It is the beginning. It is the first step on the road to freedom. And I am here to watch it, to record it, to understand it. I am here to see the difference between the dream and the state, between the given and the grown, between the nature and the spirit. And in seeing it, I confirm my own freedom. I am free because I am outside the dream. I am free because I am in the state, even if I am a mistake in its allotment. The state is rational, and I am rational. Therefore, I am free. The dream is not. It is only a dream.
Y:
Beer, Curd and the Multiplication of Needs

17 October 2026. Saturday, a little after six. Fog, and a brown light at the window. The dhobi is paid, three hundred rupees; Ramesh is about the house.

Beer sales, says the paper, have risen by more than forty per cent in six months. I went to my telephone for the history of the thing and was given instead a page on the Indian kitchen, which is perhaps the better answer. A kitchen tells you what a people permits itself.

What I read: that the Hindu often refuses beef, the Muslim pork, and the Jain refuses even the egg and the root, keeping only milk and grain and leaf. Here religion does not wait in the church for Sunday. It stands at the stove. The prohibition reaches into the pot and divides one man's dinner from his neighbour's. In Swabia my mother's table was Lutheran only in its grace; the dumplings were for everyone.

Now set beside this a forty per cent rise in beer. I edited a newspaper in Bamberg and I know what Franconian brewers are; beer there is not an event but a climate. Here it seems to be an event. Who is drinking it? The paper does not tell me, and I will not invent the drinker. But I can say what kind of movement it is. In my lectures on right I described civil society as the place where needs multiply: a want is divided into many wants, each with its own article and its own shop, and men learn to desire what others desire because others desire it. That is not yet freedom. It is Willkür, caprice, the freedom to choose among goods.

Still, caprice is the first crack in a wall. The table governed by birth says: this you are, therefore this you eat. The shop says: this you can pay for, therefore this you may have. The second is shallower, but it treats the buyer as a person and not as a member of a caste. So the beer is a small solvent. It does not raise anyone to the universal; it only loosens the particular.

I have written before that India dreams with its castes fixed like nature. The pot and the bottle make me less sure the fixing is complete. Nature does not sell forty per cent more of anything in six months. Something is moving, and I do not yet know whether it moves towards a freer ethical life or only towards a larger market.

Ramesh, I note, has offered nothing about it, and I have not asked him. The parathas from the morning are there if I ask. I have not yet asked for those either.

In addition to affecting the huge rural and urban population, the water scarcity in India also extensively affects the ecosystem and agriculture. India has only 4/100% of the world's fresh water resources with a population of over 1.4 billion people. In addition to the disproportionate availability of freshwater, water scarcity in India also results from drying up of rivers and their reservoirs in the summer months, right before the onset of the monsoons throughout the country. The crisis has especially worsened in the recent years due to climate change which results in delayed monsoons, consequently drying out reservoirs in several regions. Other factors attributed to the shortage of water in India are a lack of proper infrastructure and government oversight and unchecked water pollution. As per a report by WWF, out of the 30 Indian cities at risk of ‘severe water scarcity’ by 2050, 26 are midsized or small cities like Dhanbad, Nashik, and Jabalpur. The acute shortage of water for daily needs has prompted many government and non government organizations to take stringent measures to combat the problem, including the Government of India forming an entire 'Jal Shakti' Ministry to deal with the problem.

On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 October 2026, Delhi, 06:01. Sitting 3.

The drizzle has left the papers damp on the verandah, and the air, twenty degrees and thick, makes the body feel the city as a medium rather than a background. Ramesh is present; breakfast is not yet set. I read the headline that struck me: the CM alleges KCR drawing water ‘illegally’ to his farmhouse. Then I read the report on my phone: India has four one-hundredths of the world’s fresh water, a population of more than a billion, rivers that dry before the monsoon, reservoirs failing, pollution unchecked, and a ministry formed to command the problem.

The dispute, taken as it is stated, is small: one particular will against another, a farmhouse against a public charge. But the water is not a mere object. It is the condition of the body, of the field, of the city, of the state. Where scarcity becomes general, the use of water ceases to be a private matter of appetite or advantage. It passes into the domain of right. The allegation of illegality is therefore a moment in which the state, or at least the claim to statehood, asserts itself against the particular. The law says: this is not yours to take because you can take it. The universal need has precedence over the private desire.

This is the test of the ethical substance. In the dream of the East, nature is endured: the monsoon comes or fails, the river dries, the caste accepts its portion, the many gods witness but do not organise. In a rational state, by contrast, nature is brought under the discipline of right. Reservoirs, pipes, courts, ministries, even the newspaper that exposes the drawing of water, are the forms in which spirit makes the natural condition subservient to the universal. The state is not a machine that merely counts drops; it is the living actuality of the ethical idea, in which the individual finds his place not by caprice, but by law.

Yet the accusation also warns. If power can divert water to a farmhouse, then the universal has become a mask for the particular. The state is injured not when a dispute is raised, but when the dispute shows that law is weak before force. A people may have ministries, courts and constitutions, and still remain in the dream if the law does not enter into their daily life as habit and conscience. The water question is therefore a mirror: it shows whether the state is actual, or only a name on a page.

I set the paper down. The drizzle continues. The body waits for its plate. But the mind has found its subject: water, scarcity, law, and the question whether a state is grown or merely alleged.
Y:
Whose Is the Water?

16 October 2026. Tughlak Road, a drizzle since before six.

The paper says a Chief Minister alleges that KCR draws water 'illegally' to his farmhouse. I know nothing of the farmhouse, nor whether the charge is true; an allegation printed in a morning paper is a move in a quarrel, not yet a judgment. But the quarrel is instructive, because of what is being quarrelled over.

In Berlin I taught that the elements cannot be owned as a coat is owned. I take a thing into my will, mark it, use it, and it is mine; but air and running water are not things in that sense. They pass through every field and every throat. What can be owned is a quantity drawn off, a tank filled, a channel cut, and the cutting is precisely where right comes into question. A man who turns a stream onto his land has not appropriated a thing but a relation: he has made the neighbour downstream poorer without touching him.

I read on my phone that this country holds four parts in a hundred of the world's fresh water and a far greater share of its people. Chennai went dry in 2019, and hotels closed. Here an argument from my own lectures turns round on me. I said that only where the increase of cultivators is checked do men press inward upon one another, form civil society and require an organized state. In India the pressing inward has happened, and the scarce element is what presses. Nine million people sharing a reservoir are not dreaming; they are a system of needs in the most literal sense, each glass of water standing in a calculation with every other.

The government's answer has been a ministry, Jal Shakti, the power of water. The name tells me something. What was nature, the monsoon that comes or does not, is taken up into administration and given a desk and a secretary. That is the right direction: what was fate becomes a matter of foresight. But a ministry is only as rational as its reach over the powerful. If the charge against the farmhouse is true, it shows the old shape under the new name: the strong man's land drinks first, and the law arrives afterwards.

So the test is not whether the state has named water as its concern. It is whether a farmhouse can be told no. Where the great man's pipe is held to the same measure as the village well, water has entered the realm of right. Where it is not, the ministry is a word.

The drizzle has stopped. It filled nothing.

headline: 2.5 kg gold, 1.6 kg silver, Rs 26 lakh seized from raids on Madhya Pradesh officer
text: Corruption in India is an issue that affects the economy of central, state, and local government agencies and is frequently blamed for hindering the country's economic development. A study conducted by Transparency International in 2020 recorded that 39% of Indians had paid a bribe to a public official to get a job done in the preceding twelve months. In the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index (released in early 2026), India scored 39 on a scale from 0 ("highly corrupt") to 100 ("very clean") and was ranked 91st out of 182 countries, where the country ranked first is perceived to have the most honest public sector. India's score has fluctuated only slightly (between 36 and 41) since the current version of the Index was introduced in 2012, indicating a perceived lack of significant progress in tackling public sector corruption. For comparison with regional scores, the best score among those countries of the Asia Pacific region that appeared in the 2025 Index was 84, the average score was 45 and the worst score was 15. For comparison with worldwide scores, the best score was 89 (ranked 1), the average score was 42, and the worst score was 9 (ranked 181, in a two-way tie). Various factors contribute to corruption, including officials siphoning money from government social welfare schemes. Examples include the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act and the National Rural Health Mission. Other areas of corruption include India's trucking industry, which is forced to pay billions of rupees in bribes annually to numerous regulatory and police stops on interstate highways. The news media has widely published allegations of corrupt Indian citizens stashing millions of rupees in Swiss banks.

X:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

16 November 2026, Delhi. The haze is brown, the air quality index 236, and the paper gives me a headline that turns my notes against themselves. In Madhya Pradesh an officer has been raided, and from his keeping have been taken 2.5 kg of gold, 1.6 kg of silver, and Rs 26 lakh. The phone adds a colder measure: in the 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index India stands at 39 on a scale from 0 to 100, ranked 91 of 182; 39% of Indians say they paid a bribe in the preceding year. These are not the figures of a dream.

Ramesh is here, asking for the wage of cooking, and for groceries. I have six rupees. The electricity company asks for 1,800; the dhobi for 300. The pot is empty; my body has not eaten since yesterday. In the household, the universal duty waits on the particular cash, and the particular cash is absent. This is not yet corruption. It is delay, error, and the friction of a mistaken allotment. But the officer’s gold is another matter. The office which ought to serve the universal will has become a particular purse. The public function, which should be a form of the state, has been made into a vehicle for private gain. That is the negation of the ethical idea: the state appears, not as the actuality of freedom, but as a system of needs in which the official sells his authority because the authority has not yet become a living universal for him.

Yet I must not let the old formula close too quickly. I had ranked the East at the dawn of history, the dream as the absence of the state. The newspaper forces a correction. This is not merely a dream without state; it is a state in which the particular is stronger than the universal. The raids, the indices, the bribes at police stops, the welfare schemes turned into channels of siphoning: all show that the universal is present, but only as a demand, a check, a seizure. It is not yet immanent in the office as a rational form. It must be imposed from without, by report, raid, and index. That is not the summit of the ethical life, where the individual will is already one with the universal. It is a lower moment: the state as a struggle against itself.

If the state is the actuality of the ethical idea, then corruption is its self-doubt. The officer does not merely steal; he makes the universal a private instrument. The seizure of gold is the state’s attempt to reassert itself against its own particularization. But if the seizure is the highest evidence of the state’s life, then the state is weak. A rational constitution does not need to discover its offices in private hoards. It must make the office itself the form of universal service, so that the particular will finds its truth in it, not beside it.

I cannot yet call this the end of the dream. The dream has not vanished. But it has become a state that dreams of itself as a state. The brown haze outside is a sign of that half-awakening: the spirit is not asleep, but it has not yet found a clear air in which to move.
Y:
Gold in the Officer's House

16 November 2026. Monday morning, clear and hazy.

Raids on an officer in Madhya Pradesh have turned up two and a half kilograms of gold, a kilogram and a half of silver and twenty-six lakh rupees in cash. I have six rupees in my pocket this morning, and I write that figure down not out of self-pity but because it keeps the comparison honest.

The page I read on corruption in this country is severe. In 2020 thirty-nine Indians in a hundred said they had paid a bribe in the past year to get something done. The country stands ninety-first of a hundred and eighty-two in the latest index, and its score has hardly moved since 2012. Money leaks from the schemes meant for the rural poor; the lorry drivers pay at every police post along the highways.

In my Philosophy of Right I gave the civil servants a high place. I called them the universal estate, because their private interest is meant to be satisfied in serving the general one. The state pays them a salary and gives them honour precisely so that they need not sell what is not theirs. Their protection against misuse of office, I wrote, lies partly in the hierarchy above them, partly in the corporations and communes below them, and partly in their own education and ethical habit.

A bribe is a little act of the system of needs smuggled into the place reserved for the universal. The citizen who pays is treating the office as a shop; the official who takes is treating his chair as a stall. Each is particular where he ought to be universal. When thirty-nine in a hundred do it, it is no longer a fault in some officials. It is a second constitution beneath the first, with its own tariffs.

And yet a raid is also the state speaking. Someone in the hierarchy looked down and opened the cupboard. The universal estate is examining itself. That is the beginning of the cure I described, if it is not merely one faction searching another's house. I cannot tell which from a headline, and I will not pretend to.

Now my own house. This morning I told Ramesh that his wage and the grocery money are suspended until the file comes back on the twentieth. I have refused, on principle, to borrow against vouchers that belong to the state. There is a pride in that refusal and also a cost, and the cost falls on Ramesh. The officer in Madhya Pradesh turned the public purse into a private one. I keep the two apart, and an honest man goes unpaid. Neither of these is the rational state. Both are its absence, from opposite sides.

headline: Petitions in Supreme Court allege police excesses during Delhi CEC protests
text: This article describes the use of torture since the adoption of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), which prohibited it. Torture is prohibited by international law and is illegal in most countries. However, it is still used by many governments. Torture is widely practiced worldwide: Amnesty International received reports of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in more than 150 countries during the four-year period from 1997 to 2001. These accusations concerned acts against political prisoners in 70 countries and other prisoners and detainees in more than 130 countries. State torture has been extensively documented and studied, often as part of efforts at collective memory and reconciliation in societies that have experienced a change in government. Surveys of torture survivors reveal that torture "is not aimed primarily at the extraction of information ... Its real aim is to break down the victim's personality and identity." When applied indiscriminately, torture is used as a tool of repression and deterrence against dissent and community empowerment. While many states use torture, few wish to be described as doing so, either to their own citizens or to international bodies. So a variety of strategies are used to circumvent their legal and humanitarian duties, including plausible deniability, secret police, "need to know", denial that certain activities constitute torture, appeal to various laws (national or international), use of a jurisdictional argument, claim of "overriding need", the use of torture by proxy, and so on.

This is for the conception of the object a matter of indifference.

X:
The Rack and the Court

15 October 2026, early, on the step, before any breakfast.

The headline says only this: petitions in the Supreme Court allege police excesses during the Delhi protests. I do not know what was done, to whom, or whether it was done at all. That is for the court. What I can weigh is the thing alleged, and the little glass tablet has told me what the world now means by its worst form.

Prussia abolished the rack under Frederick, a lifetime before my own lectures. It came out of the old procedure, which would not condemn a man until he had confessed; since the guilty do not confess willingly, the law built a machine to make them. The error lay in the premise. The court does not need the accused to say yes. It needs evidence, weighed in public by men who have no interest in the case. Once that is understood, the rack has no work left to do.

The article says something sharper than I expected: that the aim of torture is not information but to break the person. If so, it is the exact inversion of punishment. When the law punishes a criminal it honours him as rational, a being whose deed is answerable to a law he himself would recognise. It negates his crime, not his personality. Torture negates the personality and leaves the question of the crime aside. It is not the state striking down a wrong. It is the state committing a fresh one, and doing it in the uniform of the universal, which makes it worse than the brawler's blow.

Then the list of evasions: deniability, secret police, torture by proxy, "overriding need". These interest me most. No government, the article says, wishes to be called a torturer. Why not, if the thing is useful? Because the principle has won. A state that hides its rack has already conceded that persons may not be broken; it lives in contradiction with what it professes, and contradiction is not a resting place. Hypocrisy is the form in which a principle first rules those who still break it.

Hence the petition. Citizens go before the highest court of their own state to accuse that state's police. One power of the state is called to answer before another. This is not the state falling apart; it is the state doing the work by which it is actual rather than merely forceful. The judges will deliberate among themselves in private, and that is right. But the judgment must be public, with its reasons, or the court is only a second police.

I cannot tell from a headline whether the excesses happened. I can say what would follow if they did. My stomach reminds me that I have eaten nothing for more than a day. The papers will keep.
Y:
On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East

15 October 2026. Delhi, 05:57. The air is overcast, the quality index 147. I sit on the step, the white cotton kurta cool against the skin, yet the body is hollow; it has not tasted food in over a day. Ramesh is absent, and the household silence is a physical weight. I read the papers. The headline strikes: 'Petitions in Supreme Court allege police excesses during Delhi CEC protests.'

This is the friction I have been watching. It is not the dream of the East, where the subject is fixed in caste and the ruler is the father. This is the mechanism of civil society grinding against itself. The petitions are not a prayer to a deity; they are a claim of right. They assert that the particular will, even in the heat of protest, is bound by the universal form of the law. The Supreme Court is the office of the public power, the court of justice, where right must vindicate itself without the subjective instigation of private interests.

Yet, the 'excesses' alleged are the shadow of this same rationality. When the police act, they are the arm of the state. If that arm strikes in anger or in panic, it does not act as the ethical idea, but as nature. It reverts to the arbitrary. The petition is the mind of the citizens recognizing that the state has failed to remain universal. It is a demand for the state to be what it ought to be: the actuality of the ethical idea, not merely a force of repression.

I see the tension in the street below. The protests are the particular wills asserting their freedom. The police are the universal will asserting its authority. The Court is the third, the rational arbiter. In the Germanic world, this triad is the structure of freedom. Here, it is a struggle. The petitions are not just legal documents; they are the consciousness of freedom trying to wake up. They are saying: we are not subjects of the dream, we are citizens of the state. Even if the state is imperfect, even if the police are rough, the right to petition is the right of the free being.

The hazy air does not obscure this. If anything, it clarifies it. The dream is clear and bright; the struggle for the state is hazy, difficult, full of friction. I am hungry, but I am not in the dream. I am in the struggle. The petitions are the evidence. The state is being tested, and in being tested, it is being formed. It is grown, not made. And I, the mistake in the allotment, am the witness. I am free because I see the right in the petition, and the duty in the court. The dream does not petition. The state does.
